name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Milwaukee man wrongly accused of threatening the president still facing deportation
description: Months after Ramón Morales Reyes was falsely accused by the Department of Homeland Security of penning letters threatening to assassinate President Donald Trump, his children Ana and Antonio say that their family continues to live in fear while awaiting the outcome of their father’s deportation case.  “My dad was framed for something that he did […]
text:
Antonio Morales (center left) and his sister Ana (center right) share their experiences since their father was wrongly accused of threatening President Donald Trump. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)Months after Ramón Morales Reyes was falsely accused by the Department of Homeland Security of penning letters threatening to assassinate President Donald Trump, his children Ana and Antonio say that their family continues to live in fear while awaiting the outcome of their father’s deportation case. 
The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
“My dad was framed for something that he did not do, and DHS knew exactly what they posted beforehand,” Ana Morales, 25, said at a press conference Friday at the Milwaukee office of Voces de la Frontera. “As a daughter, seeing my dad being framed for something he did not do was very heartbreaking,” she added.
Attorney Mark Thomsen said the family is seeking $5 million in damages caused by the federal government’s accusations against Morales Reyes, which the agency has yet to retract. Thomsen was joined by immigration attorney Cain Oulahan, Morales Reyes’ children, Voces de la Frontera Executive Director Christine Neumann-Oritz, and Milwaukee Turners Executive Director Emilio de Torre. 
Accused of something he didn’t do
In May 2025, Morales Reyes, then 54, was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, leaving his unoccupied vehicle on the roadside. Voces de la Frontera received a hotline call reporting the arrest. 
Born in Mexico, Morales Reyes has lived in the United States since 1986. His family described him as a hard worker and proud family man, who worked as a dishwasher.
His arrest came as the Trump administration ramped up arrests and deportations in 2025, the deadliest year in two decades for people being detained by ICE. Trump pledged to go after “the worst of the worst.” 
Morales Reyes had two encounters with law enforcement, both dating back to 1996, according to NPR. One was a hit-and-run incident in which he was arrested but not charged. The other was a disorderly conduct and property damage ticket relating to a dispute with his wife.
Attorney’s Mark Thomsen (far left) and Cain Oulahan (right) explain the case involving Ramon Morales-Reyes. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem posted a statement on her agency’s website calling Morales Reyes an “illegal alien who threatened to assassinate President Trump.” 
DHS also released images of a letter, handwritten in English, that said: “we are tired of this president messing with us Mexicans” and stating “I will self deport myself back to Mexico but not before I use my 30 yard 6 to shoot your precious president in is head — I will see him at one of his big ralleys .” The reference to “30 yard 6”appears to be an incorrectly written reference to the high caliber rifle round .30-06.
Morales Reyes couldn’t have written the letter, however, his family, attorneys, and advocates said, since he could not speak English and did not read or write proficiently even in Spanish. 
Morales Reyes had applied for a U-visa, granted to victims of crimes, after he was  assaulted during an armed robbery in September 2023. Detectives from the Milwaukee Police Department were actively investigating whether someone was trying to frame him when ICE agents arrested him and publicized the  accusation that he was a would-be assassin. It was later determined that a man who had been arrested for assaulting Morales Reyes had written the letter in an effort to get him deported before he could testify in court.
Lasting harm
In June 2025, Morales-Reyes was released from ICE custody on bond. Yet he continues to face deportation proceedings, with a hearing expected in December in which a judge may make a decision on whether Morales Reyes can remain in the country. The family has received online harassment and threats since Morales Reyes was accused of writing the letter, Ana Morales said.
“He’s been going through depression, anxiety,” she said during the Friday press conference. “He doesn’t like going out anymore because he feels like everyone knows him due to what he was framed as. And ever since, it has taken a lot from us.” 
Emilio de Torre, executive director of the Milwaukee Turners. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Ana’s brother Antonio Morales took over the mic when  his sister began to cry. “They really wanted to make this hurt us as much as possible, inflict as much pain, and they knew what they were doing intentionally,” he said of the Homeland Security arrest and accusations against his father.
“It was hard seeing your dad all over social media posted as some sort of, you know, some sort of assassin almost,” he added. “And that’s just not who my father is. Anyone who knows my father knows that isn’t him. It was just really scary seeing all those comments online, the fear that it caused my family seeing how everybody just…threatening us online over something that was just a false accusation. And I really think DHS knew that. I really think that they knew what they were doing. They wanted to do this to us. They want to do this to more immigrants, and they really want to keep terrorizing the community going forward.”
Thomsen asked members of the public to “imagine learning on social media that your father, or your grandfather, or your uncle, or your brother, or your sister was being accused of attempting to kill the president of the United States.” He added, “Imagine what that means, and then imagine that the person that is saying it is the strongest government in the world. … This was a lie, and they knew it was a lie. The lie is still up.”
Gesturing to Ana and Antonio Morales, he said, “Check it out folks, these are two young people with the courage to stand up to the biggest government on the planet, the most powerful government on the planet, and say, ‘Do the right thing America.’ If these two young folks can do it, everybody sitting at home safely can do it.”
Looking ahead
Although DHS has said in subsequent statements that Morales Reyes is no longer under investigation for threatening the president, the agency has continued to call for his deportation. Noem’s original press release accusing him of the assassination threat is still up on the government website. The Wisconsin Examiner reached out to DHS asking specifically whether the agency plans to remove the post and correct the record. The agency has not responded. 
Ana Morales (left) and Antonio Morales (right) (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Oulahan said that although Morales Reyes has a hearing in December, if a judge decides to deport him, he could remain in the country while his case is appealed. Thomsen said that the federal government has six months to respond to the family’s claim for compensation under the federal Tort Act, after which filing a civil lawsuit would be an option. Thomsen stressed, however, that avenues of recourse against the federal government are limited and that the second Trump administration has shown a willingness to violate or disregard court orders. 
De Torre said the federal government is “deceiving the public about everyday people.”
“They’re disrupting us emotionally, as you can see from Ana and Antonio. … It is disrupting our economy. It is disrupting our ability to attend houses of worship, go to school, and bring home food for our families. And on top of this, they then deny that they are doing this. Telling us that what we see is not real. How we feel and how we’re suffering is an illusion. And I’m sitting here today to say this is not so.”
Asked to describe some of her favorite memories of her father, Ana recalled how he would take her to the park and bike riding, one of his favorite activities. “I remember as a little kid on his days off I would always want corn, I’m obsessed with corn even to this day,” she said. Despite working second shift her father would always make time, she said. 
Antonio described his father as fond of video games. “He definitely made me a gamer,” he said. Occasionally Morales Reyes would let his son play. “I was just so amazed by these games,” he recalled, smiling. “It was really fun.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Klobuchar, Demuth pound pavement at the Minnesota State Fair in campaign for governor
description: After 20 consecutive years shaking sweaty hands and waving to babies at the Minnesota State Fair, Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar and her baby blue cottage-style booth is as much a fixture here as greasy cheese curds and costumed llamas. Arriving at the crowded Agriculture Horticulture building with a slew of staffers and a photographer on […]
text:
Sen. Amy Klobuchar talks to fairgoers and supporters Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, and Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth talks to fairgoers and supporters Friday, Aug. 28, 2026 at the Minnesota State Fair. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)After 20 consecutive years shaking sweaty hands and waving to babies at the Minnesota State Fair, Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar and her baby blue cottage-style booth is as much a fixture here as greasy cheese curds and costumed llamas.
Arriving at the crowded Agriculture Horticulture building with a slew of staffers and a photographer on Friday morning, Klobuchar began another day of greeting supporters fanning themselves and sucking on frozen apple cider pops.
One of them was Andy Stoltmann of Rosemount. She asked where he lived and then told him that Rosemount is a growing city, which will be good for the local economy.
“It’s nice to see political people walking around, see them for real instead of seeing them on TV,” Stoltmann said.
The Reformer caught back up with Klobuchar in the Horticulture building’s bee and honey section.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar talks to fairgoers and supporters in the bees and honey section of the horticulture building during the Minnesota State Fair Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
“You missed me. I found the queen bee,” Klobuchar informed the Reformer. She went back to the hive on display and found the queen bee again.
Klobuchar and her Republican opponent for governor, House Speaker Lisa Demuth, have both spent nearly every day at the fair to get in front of voters who aren’t at home to see their television ads.
Numerous polls show Klobuchar leading against Demuth for Minnesota governor. Klobuchar is serving her fourth term in the U.S. Senate and was first elected to her seat in 2006. Demuth has served as Minnesota House speaker for nearly two years and is serving her fourth term in the Minnesota House. She was first elected in 2018.
Demuth spent many hours at her booth listening to the concerns of Minnesotans, most notably the fraud in Minnesota’s social safety net programs that occurred under Gov. Tim Walz’s watch. The House speaker — and Minnesota Republicans in general — are hoping voters’ frustration with fraud will propel them to their first statewide win in 20 years.
Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth talks to fairgoers at her campaign booth for Minnesota governor during the Minnesota State Fair Friday, Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
The House speaker on Aug. 28 spoke in the fair’s Lee & Rose Warner Coliseum where students were presenting their beef heifers for awards. Klobuchar was also there and spoke first, receiving a loud cheer from the audience and name-dropping a few Minnesota beef cattle ranchers, including Haley Ammann, who wrote a children’s book about one of her calves.
“We need more domestic beef, right?” Klobuchar asked the cheering crowd. “We do not need foreign beef on an unfair playing field for our cattle ranchers. I will stand up for that.”
Klobuchar was referring to President Donald Trump’s signing of a proclamation last month that would allow 300,000 metric tons of beef to enter the U.S. at a reduced tariff rate. The move has angered many cattle ranchers who are concerned that the foreign beef would hinder domestic profits for U.S. producers.
Demuth didn’t mention Trump’s beef tariff exemption, though she has said it would not be good for Minnesota ranchers.
Demuth did offer one subtle jab at Klobuchar after she left the coliseum:
“I will agree with you all in this room that the Minnesota State Fair is the best state fair in the country.”
It’s a reference to Klobuchar’s 2020 bid for president when she refused to declare the Minnesota State Fair the best in the country while campaigning hard in Iowa. Klobuchar has since said that Minnesota has the best state fair.
Demuth grew up in central Minnesota and represents a rural, agriculture-heavy district. While students presented their heifers for awards, Demuth quipped to her staffers that she had never heard of that particular breed as the student and heifer galloped by and, in one black heifers’ case, said, “That one is particularly spicy” as it repeatedly shook its head and huffed.
Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth speaks while 4H members show their cows at the Minnesota State Fair Friday, Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
After congratulating the 4-H students, Demuth began to trek back to her booth. Outside the coliseum, a 6-year-old stopped her and asked her to sign his “I’m a Lisa fan” fan.
Demuth later said she wondered whether she should have signed her name in cursive, as the boy probably wouldn’t be able to read it.
On Aug. 28, Demuth told the Reformer she was waiting to get a funnel cake from her favorite booth, Auntie M’s, which happens to be based in Paynesville — her district. She finally indulged on Sept. 1. 
Demuth has spent hours in front of her campaign booth — across the street from the Ball Park Cafe’s garlic fries — assuring supporters waiting in line to see her that she will bring “common sense” back to Minnesota. Her running mate, Ryan Wilson, echoed her sentiments while several times offering to take photos of Demuth with the people lined up to meet her.
Demuth greeted and took selfies with people wearing “Trump 2028” hats and nodded as people told her they were tired of Minnesota being a nationwide news bite because of fraud.
A mannequin dressed like Donald Trump stands with a Trump 2028 hat, which the booth also sells, at the Minnesota GOP booth at the Minnesota State Fair Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
One was Mike Oliver of Mankato, who said he’s tired of the lack of oversight in government programs.
“It’s not just the fraud. The excess spending, no accountability. There’s so many people that moved to Minnesota because of handouts,” he said.
Demuth said the state fair is different this year for her because she now has her own booth, and people are recognizing her and sharing their thoughts with her about how Minnesota is being run.
“The fair puts policy and politics into perspective if people want to have that conversation, and I think that’s a really good thing where it’s not all consuming. You can have these conversations and … go out and grab food or a ride,” Demuth said.
Klobuchar said people want to talk about her run for governor and her plans, but they also thank her for her office’s help getting a passport for a wedding or with adoption paperwork, for example.
“There are plenty of people that will bring things up that they’re worried about, and you talk to them about that. Then other people just want you to see their kid or their new baby,” Klobuchar said. “People know me, and I think trust me around here.” 
Sen. Amy Klobuchar talks to fairgoers and supporters during the Minnesota State Fair Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska Lt. Gov. Dahlstrom reverses herself, puts Treg Taylor back in governor’s race
description: Late Friday night, Alaska Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom said she will reverse a decision she made Monday and will certify former attorney general Treg Taylor as a final-four candidate in Alaska’s race for governor. Taylor’s reinstatement means he replaces his lieutenant governor, Candi English, who had taken Taylor’s spot as the fourth candidate in the […]
text:
Alaska Attorney General Treg Taylor speaks at a news conference on Thursday, Dec. 15, 2022, at the Alaska State Capitol in Juneau. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)Late Friday night, Alaska Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom said she will reverse a decision she made Monday and will certify former attorney general Treg Taylor as a final-four candidate in Alaska’s race for governor.
Taylor’s reinstatement means he replaces his lieutenant governor, Candi English, who had taken Taylor’s spot as the fourth candidate in the race. Taylor’s wife, Jodi, had taken English’s spot as the lieutenant governor candidate.
Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins finished first in the August primary, followed by Republican candidates Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Taylor.
In Alaska, the top four candidates from the primary, regardless of political party, advance to the November general election.
Dahlstrom’s decision came five days after she disqualified Taylor and a state House candidate, Jose Tagle, for failing to provide personal financial information on time, as required by state law. 
Dahlstrom also restored Tagle, the sole opponent against Rep. Ted Eischeid, D-Anchorage, to the ballot.
The Alaska Public Offices Commission, which regulates political candidates and campaigns, had recommended that the two be disqualified.
That recommendation was still in place on Friday night, but Dahlstrom said the Department of Law — which Taylor led until last year — had conducted an independent review of candidates’ financial disclosure statements.
That review, which Dahlstrom did not release Friday night, showed ”numerous potential discrepancies between filed statements and public records,” Dahlstrom said in a written statement.
“On the basis of that additional information, the Lieutenant Governor will certify the two candidates,” Dahlstrom’s statement said.
Starting last year, the Alaska Public Offices Commission had raised concerns about Taylor’s financial disclosure form, which did not list hundreds of tenants who rent from Taylor. Taylor and his wife bought Anchorage’s Inlet View Tower in 2023. 
Taylor registered as a candidate for office on June 1, submitting a new public officer financial disclosure form. State law allows 30 days for amendments, but Taylor’s form wasn’t amended with the partial names of renters until late July.
Because of that missed deadline, the Public Offices Commission voted 4-1 in late August to recommend that Taylor be disqualified. The commission also recommended that Tagle, who had filed a blank disclosure form, be disqualified. Dahlstrom adopted both recommendations on Aug. 31. 
Since then, concerns had been raised about possible omissions by other candidates, including Wilson, whose personal financial disclosure form did not disclose her ownership of Denali Disposal, a garbage company. 
Unlike Taylor’s case, no formal complaint had been filed before the primary.
“The Department of Law’s informal review has raised questions about the recommendations made on August 31,” said Dahlstrom in her statement. “I will not withhold certification from two candidates on recommendations that, in light of this additional information, I cannot apply with confidence across the field of candidates. Certification decisions have to rest on a process that can be defended as to every candidate.”
Taylor, who previously called on Republican candidates to consolidate their campaigns, issued a statement celebrating the decision.
The former attorney general said his campaign has “been about standing up to political insiders and special interests.”
“Candi and I are running to end these types of political games and put power back where it belongs: with Alaskans. Alaskans should decide our elections. Not political insiders. Not special interests. Not the establishment,” Taylor said.
The first ballots for Alaska’s November general election are scheduled to be mailed to voters starting Sept. 18.

name: VTDigger
title: Hartford considers a stricter car camping ban
description:
Some selectboard members worried it would create more hardship for people experiencing homelessness and criminalize them for being unhoused.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Hartford considers a stricter car camping ban.
text:
Anthony Heath walks past the Upper Valley Haven’t Leahy Shelter and Resource Center on his way to charge his phone in White River Junction, Vt., on Thursday, June 18, 2026. The low-barrier shelter is on schedule to be completed in September, said Haven Executive Director Will Towne. “Hopefully I get a room in it if I’m still homeless,” said Heath who is living in a tent. Photo by James M. Patterson/Valley News

This story by Sofia Langlois was first published in the Valley News on Sept. 2, 2026.
HARTFORD — The town is grappling with a possible addition to its parking rules to clearly define “camping,” which is prohibited in municipal lots.
Some selectboard members worried it would create more hardship for people experiencing homelessness and criminalize them for being unhoused.
Town Manager Gail Ostrout said she receives “100 messages a week” regarding vehicles that remain parked for an extended period and create hazards. With the current ordinance, police are not able to take action, aside from writing a ticket.
Hartford Police proposed adding a definition of camping to the town’s parking ordinance, Chapter 220, which reads:
“A person shall be deemed to be camping if they occupy a tent or other temporary shelter, or if they use a motor vehicle, recreational vehicle, trailer, or other conveyance as a residence or place to keep the majority of their personal belongings or household possessions, regardless of whether the person sleeps in the vehicle overnight.”
Already, the ordinance states that camping or overnight sleeping is not permitted in municipal lots, and violators will be towed. However, without a definition of camping, there’s too much gray area to enforce, said Lt. William Furnari of the Hartford Police community outreach division.
“We are not going out of our way looking for cars to tow. We are trying to address those folks who, through a pattern of behavior like this, are living in the parking lot in a way that is unsafe to folks,” said Furnari.
Selectboard member Miranda Dupre worries the definition is too subjective and is hesitant about the idea of making it “basically illegal to be homeless and safe,” she said at the meeting.
She further expressed that those without residences may be safest sleeping in their car there and could just need somewhere to rest without bothering anyone.
“Where else do they go?” said Dupre.
Furnari argued that other community members aren’t feeling safe with the current situation of people essentially living in the public lots. Specifically, he pointed to those who disturb the peace and leave waste outside of the vehicle.
“We found some pretty bad stuff that we don’t want in our parking lot that could make people sick,” said Furnari.
Selectboard member Ashley Andreas said she worries this new definition will lead to police hassling more people and that the language could apply to people who aren’t causing problems, including those who simply keep most of their belongings in the car or are struggling to find housing.
Andreas added that if police could provide alternative suggestions to the people told to leave, such as a different piece of land where camping may be more appropriate, it could help “address this problem more structurally before bringing on more enforcement,” she said.
While there is a strong effort to coordinate resources, it’s not always successful, said Ostrout.
“Everyone in the police department has made an attempt to be sensitive to people’s struggles and tried to come up with creative solutions around that,” said Ostrout.
Dupre said she worries the stricter ordinance could drive more people onto private properties as a last resort.
With police now enforcing metered street parking and directing more people to the free South Main parking lot, Furnari said, the community has an incentive to make sure it’s safe and accessible for everyone.
Further, removal does not equate to an arrest.
“It’s a civil violation. It’s a traffic ticket or municipal ticket. I just want to clarify: It’s not an arrest,” said Chief Constance Kelley. “There’s no criminal affectation to it.”
Erik Krauss, the vice chair of the selectboard, said that although he appreciated the intent, the proposed definition, as it stands, is “not well crafted.” He suggested reaching out to the Vermont League of Cities and Towns for advice and referencing how other municipalities have defined camping before Hartford changes its ordinance.
The selectboard is passing along questions and requests regarding the new definition so Hartford Police can possibly return with a new version at the next regular meeting on Sept. 15 in Hartford Town Hall.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana’s forgotten millionaire and the danger of erasing history
description: I went for a stroll in Dublin, Ireland.  I stumbled upon a colorful statue of Oscar Wilde, reclining on a rock. You probably have heard of him. Irish poet, writer, playwright, and social critic. His titles include “The Importance of Being Earnest” and “The Picture of Dorian Gray.” He exposed hypocrisy and loved men. In the […]
text:
William Andrews Clark (right), his son, William Andrews Clark, Jr., (left) and Williams Andrews Clark III (center). (Courtesy of UCLA)I went for a stroll in Dublin, Ireland.  I stumbled upon a colorful statue of Oscar Wilde, reclining on a rock.
You probably have heard of him. Irish poet, writer, playwright, and social critic. His titles include “The Importance of Being Earnest” and “The Picture of Dorian Gray.”
He exposed hypocrisy and loved men.
In the 1800s.
He was jailed for “gross indecency.”
Turns out a man from Montana created one of the world’s greatest collections of Oscar Wilde works.
I could see a Montanan creating the world’s best collection of barbed wire. Or, bottles of beer.
But Oscar Wilde? Totally unexpected.
So, let me introduce you to a Montanan you should know: Born in Deer Lodge, a Butte lawyer and businessman. Had a mansion in Butte. He was one of the richest men in Montana.  Like a billionaire today.
Owned  Mowitza Lodge on Salmon Lake, a legendary lodge today.  He died there.
Any ideas?
He donated $200,000 to found the Los Angeles Philharmonic and covered its expenses for about 15 years. He helped create the Hollywood Bowl. He shaped the cultural life of Los Angeles. He created an amazing collection of rare books and manuscripts. More than 10,000. He donated his library and grounds to UCLA.  And a large endowment.
Among the gifted treasures,  his world-class collection of Oscar Wilde.
Any ideas who he is?
He holds an important place in queer history, American history, and Montana history
You know his name.  You probably just don’t know his story.
It’s called “queer erasure” — the removal, concealment, or reinterpretation of queer people.
His name: Will Clark; officially, William Andrews Clark, Jr., son of Sen. William Andrews Clark who was one of Montana’s U. S. Senators, 1899-1900 and 1902-1907.  You know, the Copper King; the founder of Las Vegas and the namesake of Clark County, Nevada.
You may have heard more of his half-sister, Huguette Clark.  She lived to be 104 and is immortalized through the book, “Empty Mansions.”  She owned a 15,000 square foot, 42-room mansion on Fifth Avenue in New York City. After she died in 2011, it sold for $54.8 million.
Will Clark has his own story.  It was hidden for generations.
Will’s partner was Harrison Post. In the day, they weren’t called “queer” or even “gay.” It was illegal. Criminal.
Post was his employee, secretary, confidant, protégé. Post was described by some as Clark’s “perverted disciple.”
They “lived” in mansions across the street in L.A. It provided deniability. They couldn’t marry.  They could not present themselves as a couple. Yet, together, they created a world-class library — something really special.
Painted on the ceiling of the library vestibule are 14 different men, all naked, bearing Harrison’s face.  And it is 100 years old, this year. Its centennial.
When Will died, personal correspondence was destroyed, especially between Will and his father. And, of course, his partner. It created an “archival silence.”
The absence of evidence can be evidence.
Erasure is a thing.
What we know: When the Copper King died, he left a substantial fortune to his son. He was not disinherited.
Will named his gift to UCLA after his father, the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library —a testament to their relationship.
Will was a philanthropist, a bibliophile, and a patron of the arts. He was creative force in one of America’s greatest cities.
And, he was a gay man from Montana.
His story teaches us about how our gay siblings lived 100 years ago. And, today.
Queer history is our history. Montana history.
We just don’t tell it very well.
Sadly, erasure isn’t an historical artifact.
It’s happening again.
There is a recent Executive Order: “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History.” Really. I won’t even mention who signed it. You know.
New erasures. Anything perceived as disparaging or ideologically “improper.” To whom?
Materials about slavery, Native Americans, LGBTQ history, and climate change.  Gone.
The National Park Service stripped references to transgender people from its website for Stonewall, a place synonymous with gay rights.
A judge ordered materials restored.
What uncomfortable part of our history will they try to erase next?
What has disappeared without notice?
This year, UCLA is hosting a celebration, “Private Passions, Public Legacies:  William Andrews Clark Jr. and the Making of Los Angeles.”
That’s right.  UCLA is celebrating the contributions of a gay Montana man to the City of Los Angeles.  Check it out.
Our history is about more than dinosaurs, mining, and the Unabomber. It includes gay people, Native Americans, women,  immigrants, a few criminals, and Will Clark and Harrison Post.
Our history is important, even the parts that may be uncomfortable to some.
People tried to sanitize and erase Will Clark’s history. It didn’t work.
Embrace our history, learn from it.
Our history is a public trust.
You can’t erase it.  Don’t even try.

title: BPG Sports Expands its Portfolio with Four New Youth Sports Additions
description: The sports management firm, BPG Sports, of Buccini Pollin Group announced the acquisition of the Coastal Lacrosse Academy in a press release, September 2. The group also entered into management agreements with three other youth sports programs.   Buccini Pollin Group’s sports management firm, BPG Sports, announced the firm is acquiring the Coastal Lacrosse A[...]
text:
A member of the Coastal Elite Lacrosse Club in action. Photo courtesy of BPG Sports Lacrosse Media Team.
The sports management firm, BPG Sports, of Buccini Pollin Group announced the acquisition of the Coastal Lacrosse Academy in a press release, September 2. The group also entered into management agreements with three other youth sports programs.
 
Buccini Pollin Group’s sports management firm, BPG Sports, announced the firm is acquiring the Coastal Lacrosse Academy and entering into “long-term management agreements” with three other youth sports programs in a press release on September 2. The three programs involved in the management agreements are the Bagel Bombers baseball program, Lady Bombers softball program and Delmarva Rush Soccer Club. 
Coastal Lacrosse Academy and Delmarva Rush Soccer Club will be rebranded into the Coastal Elite Lacrosse Club and Henlopen Recreational Soccer, according to the press release. 
BPG Sports’ acquisition of Coastal Elite Lacrosse Club adds to its youth lacrosse portfolio that includes the BPG Nationals, Brotherly Love Lacrosse Club, Duke’s Elite Lacrosse Club and the Phantom Girls Lacrosse program. BPG Sports will serve over 1,000 lacrosse players across the Mid-Atlantic region following the acquisition of Coastal Elite Lacrosse Club, according to the press release.    
“These transactions reflect exactly what BPG Sports was built to do – bring the top clubs, coaches, and venues under one roof and give young athletes a best-in-class experience,” senior vice president and general manager of BPG Sports, Steve Cavalier, said via the press release. “Each of these organizations has built a fantastic local reputation, and our goal is to strengthen what they’ve achieved, invest in their players and facilities, and enhance the experience for all.”
BPG Sports’ management of Henlopen Recreational Soccer adds to its club soccer portfolio that includes The Sporting Athletic Club and its New Jersey and Pennsylvania affiliates, Sporting Athletic Club PA and Sporting Athletic Club NJ. 
BPG Sports’ management of the Bagel Bombers and Lady Bombers are the firm’s first baseball and softball programs. BPG Sports will take over the day-to-day operations as well as the management of the two programs, according to the press release.
In total, BPG Sports has a portfolio of 11 different programs across four different sports that serve 4,500 athletes and their families, according to the press release. 
To learn more about BPG Sports, its club programs and its facilities click here to view the company’s website.

name: Maryland Matters
title: The ballot takes shape, as state officials certify a handful of third-party hopefuls for Nov. 3
description: While most attention was focused on the redistricting question and whether it would make the ballot, election officials this week were quietly certifying a handful of third-party candidates and putting their names on the ballot.
text:
The Maryland State Board of Elections office in Annapolis. (File photo by Danielle E. Gaines/Maryland Matters)Sam Husseini’s name will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot as a Green Party candidate for Maryland’s 4th District seat in Congress, after state election officials certified his candidacy this week.
It wasn’t easy.
Like the handful of other third-party candidates whose candidacies were accepted Monday, Husseini had to overcome a “huge hurdle” to get on the general election ballot, that candidates in the two major parties don’t have to deal with. And he will continue to deal with challenges that include limited campaign funds, lack of exposure and scant party support.
“We don’t have the right machinery that the establishment parties do,” Husseini said. “So it’s a matter of translating that discontent that I think exists in the public to organize itself so that it forces a change at the ballot box.”
The Maryland Board of Elections finalized ballots and certified all third-party candidates Monday for the Nov. 3 general election, more than two months after state-run primaries for the Democratic and Republican parties picked the candidates for those parties.
Of the 17 independents and third-party candidates who were listed at the time of the June 23 primary as having filed a notice of intent to run for office, just five were able to make the official ballot Monday, mostly Green Party candidates and a few Working Class Party candidates.
Write-in candidates have until Oct. 15 to file their candidacy paperwork, but their names will not appear on any ballots.
Third-party candidates know the odds, but they won’t give up the fight

Green Party and Working Class Party candidates had until early July to submit a Declaration of Intent and have an established campaign committee to be approved to run.
For Republicans and Democrats, they were able to advance to the Nov. 3 ballot after winning their primaries. Third-party candidates have to hold their own nominating processes — but first they have to be accepted as a party by the state.
Under Maryland law, third parties that did not receive 1% of the total votes cast for the highest office in the previous general election have to 10,000 valid voter signatures to be ballot certified for the next election.
The Green Party met this qualification during the 2024 presidential election, when candidate Jill Stein received 1% of the Maryland vote, and reserved its spot for a party nominee this year.
The Working Class Party was not so lucky. Cathy White and Cathy Permut, the party’s gubernatorial running mates, said they collected more than 12,000 signatures to secure their spot on the final ballot, according to the party’s campaign website.
Green Party gubernatorial candidate Andy Ellis said these disparities between rules for principal party candidates and third-party candidates leave a subsect of voters and candidates out of the competition.
Matthew Crenson, professor emeritus in political science at Johns Hopkins University, agreed.
“You’re simply not a part of the game,” said Crenson, who has an expertise in Maryland politics.
Maryland voters can only participate in primary elections if they are registered with either major political party. Voters who do not select a party when registering are marked as “unaffiliated.”
Getting on the ballot is just part of the battle: Third-party or unaffiliated candidates are often excluded from high-profile campaign debates. A debate between incumbent Gov. Wes Moore (D) and Republican challenger Dan Cox on Maryland Public Television is set for Oct. 6. Current MPT policy requires candidates to obtain 10% in a public poll in order to qualify for the debate, meaning third-party candidates are typically left out of the conversation.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Ellis and other third-party candidates are working to require that broadcasters allow all ballot-qualified parties to be included in the debate. A House bill in this year’s legislative session that would have required that all certified candidates be included in televised debates died in a House committee.
Ellis said the exclusion of third-party candidates contributes to their lack of exposure leading up to elections. But he said third-party votes are especially important for the upcoming election, which he deemed “the epitome of the failure of the two-party system.”
He noted that the governor’s campaign this fall is a rematch of the 2022 race between Cox and Moore. Dissatisfaction with both principal party candidates, Ellis said, will sway voters toward their other options this fall.
“That’s a really good opportunity for people to say ‘I’m frustrated with this system, I want something different and I’m going to make a vote that can be registered for that,’” he said.
Crenson said that when people decide to be affiliated with a third-party, it’s likely they do so because they believe major parties are corrupt and no longer align with the previously held values.
But he noted it’s also common for voters to feel a third-party vote is a symbolic gesture with no true influence. Voters take into account that their vote wouldn’t be enough to close the gap between the major party candidates’ victory and defeat.
Ultimately, they end up voting for a major-party candidate, at the risk of having a “throw-away vote.”
“Although, you may get a kind of moral righteousness … voting on the basis of pure principle, rather than political pragmatism,” Crenson said.
Maryland restrictions make it especially difficult for these candidates, and give the public an impression that the candidates aren’t true participants in the election, Crenson added.
Maryland Supreme Court says redistricting ballot question can go to voters

Democrats account for about half of the registered voters in Maryland, with Republicans making up about one-quarter and the other quarter made largely of unaffiliated voters and small numbers of third-party voters. In June, the most recent month for which numbers are available, the 4.3 million registered voters in the state included 6,169 Greens, 4,985 Working Class Party members, and 999,221 voters who were not affiliated with any party.
Husseini, a senior analyst for the nonprofit Institute for Public Accuracy, said he had to take a brief leave of absence from his day job in order to campaign for his position, but he’s enjoyed the process of campaigning and interacting with voters. He said he decided to run after Green Party activists pushed him to consider it. He’s campaigning against a two-party system because he feels Maryland residents are tired of not seeing change surrounding topics including state spending and “repressive” entities, like Immigrations and Customs Enforcement.
“There’s an incredible hunger out there,” Husseini said. “It’s just simply, you know, showing people the right levers to pull to affect that change.”
The third-party candidates certified this week include White and Permut, and Greens: Ellis and his running mate, Owen Silverman Andrews, Husseini, 6th District candidate Moshe Landman and 8th District Nancy Wallace.
It takes long canvassing hours and typically more than 10,000 signatures – to account for any signatures that may be deemed invalid – to get third parties on the ballot. Which is why, despite the long odds, Ellis sees certification as a victory in itself.
“Whenever we actually get to see our names on the ballot, we know that it’s the work of a grassroots group who put us there,” Ellis said. “We’re proud of that and excited about that.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: What to do if your vote is challenged: Practical advice as midterm elections approach
description: As the 2026 midterm elections enter the final stretch, it’s important to know your rights in case your vote is challenged. The best way to ensure that your vote is counted is to advocate for yourself. I’m a an attorney and lecturer for the University of Southern California’s undergraduate civil rights advocacy initiative, Agents of Change. Here are […]
text:
Elizabeth May marks her ballot while voting at Second Presbyterian Church in Little Rock’s Pleasant Valley neighborhood on Tuesday, March 3, 2026. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)As the 2026 midterm elections enter the final stretch, it’s important to know your rights in case your vote is challenged.
The best way to ensure that your vote is counted is to advocate for yourself. I’m a an attorney and lecturer for the University of Southern California’s undergraduate civil rights advocacy initiative, Agents of Change. Here are several straightforward ways to ensure your vote is counted and two practical remedies for you to consider if your vote remains challenged.
A major part of ensuring that you are able to vote is doing the necessary preparation before you even get to the polling place. Read on to find out how and where to register, where and when you can cast your ballot, and what numbers to call for any information you can’t find online.
 
Are you registered to vote? Check it out
Before you vote, you need to ensure that you’re registered to vote. You can verify your registration status using this tool. If you can’t use an online tool, then call your local election office or a voter help line like the ones listed in the hotline section below.
If you find you’re not registered, you can use this tool from the National Conference of State Legislatures to find your state’s online registration application. If you need to do this in person, then call your local election office for instructions.
At this point, you may have missed your state’s deadline for voter registration. But it may not be too late to register.
Many states allow same-day registration at the polling site. You can find your state’s same-day voter laws detailed here. Ask the poll worker, at the correct polling location, for a same-day registration form; complete the form and then ask for a “conditional ballot.” A conditional ballot allows election officials to count your vote after verifying your voter eligibility. If you can’t research online, you can call your local election office to find out if you can register on Election Day.
 
Gather documents to verify your identity
If you live in a state that requires identity verification to vote in person, gather the required documents — which may range from a driver’s license to bank statements with identifying information — before traveling to the correct polling place. You can find your county election office’s contact information here. This webpage includes a table listing each state’s acceptable ID documents and possible exceptions for some people. You may also call your local election office to find out what’s required.
Absentee voters: Locate your state’s identity verification rules here.
 
Find the correct polling location
You can ensure that you’re headed to the right polling place with this tool. Or call your county election office to find your polling place and its hours of operation; you can look up your county’s election office contact information here.
Once you know your polling place and its hours, you can go there and check in. In most cases, you’ll be handed a ballot, shown where to vote and asked to put your ballot in a machine or a box, and then you can go merrily along your way.
But the moment of check-in is where things might go wrong.
 
Problems at your polling place
Here are potential vote challenges and ways to overcome them.
Possibility No. 1: Out-of-order polling machines.
If you’re asked to leave because of malfunctioning machines, don’t. Instead, ask for a paper ballot.
Possibility No. 2: You’re in line and officials announce the polls have closed.
If you’re in line at the polling location before it closes, don’t let them turn you away at closing time if you haven’t voted. You have the legal right to vote under those circumstances, so stay in line and wait to cast your ballot.
Possibility No. 3: You’re not on the registered voters list.
If you’re told you can’t vote because your name is not on the voter roster, ask the poll site worker to check again and to check what’s called the list of supplemental voters. If they still can’t find your name, ask the poll worker to verify that you’re at the right location.
Possibility No. 4: Someone claims you shouldn’t be allowed to vote.
If your voting eligibility remains challenged after ensuring you’re at the right polling location, ask to cast a provisional ballot, which is available in every state except Idaho and Minnesota. You can find details about your particular state’s provisional ballot rules here.
Track your provisional ballot here.
 
Call a hotline
If you are not given a provisional ballot, call an election hotline for help. Here are four hotlines, run by members of the nonpartisan Election Protection coalition, that can help you:
English: 866-OUR-VOTE/866-687-8683, the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law
Spanish: 888-VE-Y-VOTA/888-839-8682, the National Association of Latino Elected and Appointed Officials Education Fund
Asian Languages: 888-API-VOTE/888-274-8683, Asian and Pacific Islander American Vote
Arabic: 844-YALLA-US/844-925-5287, Arab American Institute
 
Report voter intimidation
If someone tries to scare you into voting or not voting for a candidate, stand your ground and demand a ballot from the poll site, call one of the hotlines above to report the intimidation, and file a claim with the FBI later by phone at 800-CALL-FBI — 800-225-5324 — or online at tips.fbi.gov.
 
File a lawsuit
If you are still blocked from voting, consider legal action — but get advice on your exact situation from one of the hotlines, which have free lawyers on hand. It’s a good idea to write down the names of people who prevented you from voting and to ask people who witnessed the incident for their contact information.
This is an updated version of a story that was originally published on Oct. 28, 2024. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.
Karen Figueroa-Clewett is a lecturer for the Agents of Change program in the Department of Political Science and International Relations, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Former Bethel judge’s apparent resignation as top public defender remains unconfirmed
description: This story was originally published by KYUK.  Former Bethel judge Terrence Haas became the state’s top public defender in September 2023. Last week, he announced in a resignation letter sent to Gov. Mike Dunleavy that he was stepping down. That letter was shared with KYUK, in an email by the Anchorage Daily News, who first […]
text:
The Nora Guinn Justice Center in Bethel, Alaska on July 14, 2023. (Photo by Josiah Swope/KYUK)This story was originally published by KYUK. 
Former Bethel judge Terrence Haas became the state’s top public defender in September 2023. Last week, he announced in a resignation letter sent to Gov. Mike Dunleavy that he was stepping down. That letter was shared with KYUK, in an email by the Anchorage Daily News, who first reported on the story.     
Former Alaska Public Defender Terrence Haas announced his apparent resignation on Aug. 28, 2026, a little less than three years after being appointed to the position by Gov. Mike Dunleavy. (Photo courtesy of Terrence Haas/KYUK)

In the letter, Haas wrote that the governor’s office had made his job untenable because of the response of the governor’s office to a recent legal pleading which, among other allegations, claims that Haas was romantically involved with his now-wife when he was a Bethel Superior Court judge and she was his law clerk.
As of Sept. 4, the governor’s office still hadn’t confirmed Haas’s resignation or provided comment on the allegations against him.
The allegations stem from a new filing in a case first assigned to Haas in 2021. In August of 2022, a Bethel jury convicted Kasigluk resident Peter Albrite of five counts of first-degree sexual abuse of a minor. Four years later, the 65-year-old Albrite is still awaiting sentencing, and his case remains open amid questions about his competency.
This June, Albrite’s defense attorney filed a motion for a new trial. The motion claims Albrite was never evaluated for competency prior to standing trial. Since his conviction, the motion claims the court has found Albrite not competent at least five times.
The motion also claims the court denied Albrite a fair and impartial trial due to what it alleges were overlapping romantic relationships between judge Haas, his former law clerk, and the public defender assigned to the case at the time, Danail Mizinov. KYUK has withheld the name of the former law clerk, based on the fact that she did not have direct responsibility for legal decisions made in the Albrite case.
Mizinov said in a sworn deposition cited in the motion that he began a romantic relationship with the clerk in early 2022, while Albrite’s case was still pending. That relationship ended before the trial.
When Haas learned of the relationship, Mizinov alleged that his interactions with Haas deteriorated. He said the judge made unreasonable demands and criticized his defense strategy in front of the prosecutor.
In the months leading up to the trial, Mizinov said he believed Haas – who was married to a different woman at the time – was also romantically involved with the clerk. Mizinov produced text messages sent to him by the clerk in which she mentioned late-night drinking sessions with Haas in Bethel. The texts include details that Mizinov interpreted as indicating that there was “more going on.”
Haas has wholly denied the allegations. In an email to the state prosecutor for the case shared with KYUK, he wrote that both he and the former clerk — who he married in 2025 — testified unequivocally under oath that no romantic or intimate relationship occurred during her clerkship. The former clerk is currently an attorney with the Alaska Office of Public Advocacy.
Alleged performance concerns
Prior to his appointment as a Bethel Superior Court judge in 2018, Haas served as a public defender in Bethel for a decade. With his decision to step away from the judgeship in 2023 to head the Public Defender Agency, he became Mizinov’s boss.
A year and half later, Haas gave Mizinov the option of resigning or being fired for cause. In a May 2024 letter, he criticized Mizinov’s performance and what he said was a failure to adequately prepare for serious cases. Despite language in the letter that implied Mizinov had been dismissed, Haas testified in a recent deposition that he did not ultimately terminate him. Mizinov currently works as an attorney with the Office of Public Advocacy. In 2023, Mizinov also applied for the top public defender spot that Haas was ultimately appointed to.
The Alaska Office of Special Prosecutions has argued that Haas’s concerns about Mizinov’s performance were at the root of their poor interactions. Assistant Attorney General Bailey Woolfstead, the prosecutor in the Albrite case, claimed in a recent court filing that any hostility perceived by Mizinov was due to Haas’s frustration with Mizinov’s level of preparedness during trial. The filing claims that, rather than act impartially, Haas had taken steps to protect Albrite’s rights and raise issues on his behalf during trial based on his concerns about Mizinov’s performance.
Reactions and re-hiring
In his Aug. 28 resignation letter, Haas wrote that his wife had gone through enough and that he would not expose her to further public controversy. Haas said the job had been the greatest honor of his legal career, but he was also critical of Dunleavy.
“Your administration has concluded that the political consequences of an allegation matter more than determining whether it is true,” Haas wrote.
In an emailed statement shared with KYUK, Mizinov called Haas’s resignation a positive step forward for the agency. He wrote it was also a positive step for attorneys with “an extremely difficult, thankless job that should not be further denigrated by the personal, petty grievances of their superiors.”
A spokesperson for the Alaska Judicial Council – which under state statute screens and nominates at least two applicants for the top public defender position – said on Sept. 2 that the timeline for doing that was unclear. As of Friday, they said the governor’s office had still not sent written confirmation to the council confirming a vacancy at the agency.
The Alaska Public Defender Agency confirmed by email on Sept. 2 that Haas is no longer head of the agency, and that attorney Ariel Toft is currently serving as Acting Public Defender.
Oral arguments regarding the motion for a new trial in the Albrite case are scheduled for Sept. 21 in Fairbanks court.
This story was originally published by KYUK, public media for the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta.

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA looks to boost salvage logging as wildfires scorch record amount of state land
description: Summer wildfires burning through Washington just broke another record.  They’ve scorched more than 886,000 acres. Of those, 93,000 acres are on state trust land, marking the record for the largest amount of state-managed land burned by fires in a season since recordkeeping began in 2000.  Two-thirds of that state land was forests, meaning a hit […]
text:
The Board of Natural Resources passed a resolution that allows the Department of Natural Resources to auction salvage harvests worth $2 million or less without board approval. (Photo provided by the Department of Natural Resources)Summer wildfires burning through Washington just broke another record. 
They’ve scorched more than 886,000 acres. Of those, 93,000 acres are on state trust land, marking the record for the largest amount of state-managed land burned by fires in a season since recordkeeping began in 2000. 
Two-thirds of that state land was forests, meaning a hit to revenue from timber sales. Money from logging on Washington’s public land helps pay for schools and other parts of state and local government.
Officials are now racing to sell the charred timber before it molds or becomes even less valuable. The state’s Board of Natural Resources this week voted to allow the Department of Natural Resources to sell more burned forestland without board approval.
Public Lands Commissioner Dave Upthegrove touted it as a strategy to maximize value to the trust.”
“It cuts the timeline to bring (timber sales) to auction by about two months,” said Michael Kearney, the department’s product sales and leasing division manager.  
Before the resolution, the department could appraise and sell burnt timber, in what’s called salvage harvests, without board approval if it was worth less than $250,000. After this week’s board vote, that threshold is $2 million. 
The move better positions the department in the niche market of burned and rotting wood. It can be used as an industrial wood fuel, for landscaping, or to produce certain types of cabinets or house siding and roofing.
With so much land burning around the West this summer, burned timber is plentiful. 
“We weren’t the only impacted forest land out there. There’s tribal land, there’s private, there’s a lot of federal land,” said Alfred Watson, the department’s regional manager for northeast Washington. “There’s going to be a lot of competition in that market.”
The scale of a salvage timber harvest is limited. 
After a wildfire, some tree species quickly decline in value, and rough terrain makes many state forests inaccessible to logging. And, with the magnitude of this year’s wildfire season, the department doesn’t have the resources to harvest it all. 
Of the roughly 60,000 acres of fire-scarred state forest, “I doubt we would even be able to approach 10% of that,” said Kearney, noting that the department’s estimate is around 4,000 acres. “We very likely don’t have the capacity or time to try to do that much.”
Before auction, salvage harvests will still require several internal reviews and a State Environmental Policy Act review from the Department of Ecology.
Lost revenue in the Sinlahekin fire
Twelve miles west of Tonasket, the Sinlahekin fire, which started on July 26 and continues to burn over 166,000 acres, has cost the department hundreds of thousands of dollars in lost timber revenue. As of Sept. 4, the fire is 38% contained. 
During the fire, four state timber parcels planned for auction during the next fiscal year went up in flames. Two of those sales, named Ten Mile and Cold Park, would have brought in at least $800,000, based on their comparison with past sales of similar size, according to Kearney. 
Those sales, now salvage harvests, have combined appraised minimum bids totaling $218,000, Kearney said, costing the department around $600,000 in lost revenue. 
The Sinlahekin fire also tore through four timber sales that were already auctioned. Per the sale contract, purchasers are still responsible for paying the full amount.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Feds seek to ‘streamline’ Arctic oil permitting, ending environment studies of individual projects
description: The Trump administration on Friday moved to exempt oil projects in federal territory on the west side of the North Slope from environmental reviews that have been standard for decades. An industry-initiated proposed rule announced by the U.S. Bureau of Land Management would eliminate the need for review of individual development projects in the National […]
text:
The northeastern part of the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska is seen on June 26, 2014. The Trump administration is proposing a new rule to eliminate the need for environmental studies of individual oil projects in the reserve. (Photo by Bob Wick/U.S. Bureau of Land Management)The Trump administration on Friday moved to exempt oil projects in federal territory on the west side of the North Slope from environmental reviews that have been standard for decades.
An industry-initiated proposed rule announced by the U.S. Bureau of Land Management would eliminate the need for review of individual development projects in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska, or NPR-A.
Those projects would be excluded from requirements for individual reviews, as is prescribed by the National Environmental Policy Act, which was signed into law in 1970.
Instead of being subject to case-by-case studies, NPR-A projects would be covered by a single environmental study, under the rule. The BLM would also be required to issue permits to covered projects within 60 days of developers’ applications, under the proposed rule.
The quicker approvals are in the nation’s interest, Trump administration officials said.
“Responsible development shouldn’t be held back by redundant paperwork. By utilizing over 20 years of rigorous environmental data, we are replacing slow, case-by-case reviews with a standardized process that maintains our high environmental standards, while giving operators the predictability they need to build,” BLM Director Steve Pearce said in a statement. “This is about working smarter, honoring the Trump administration’s commitment to energy security, and ensuring Alaskans directly benefit from the resources in their backyard.” 
The statement describes the rule as one that will “streamline” permitting.
The proposal comes in response to a petition submitted in May by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association. The trade organization asked the Trump administration for a new system to fast-track development in the Arctic region that has become increasingly attractive to oil companies.
In its petition, the industry group said the BLM need not do case-by-case environmental analysis of new development projects in the reserve because past environmental impact studies for previously approved projects and management policies have already covered the questions sufficiently.
“Those collective (National Environmental Policy Act) reviews have spanned a period of almost three decades and have generated a substantial amount of information and analyses regarding the environmental impacts associated with production sites in the NPR-A and similar adjacent lands, and the mitigation of those impacts,” the petition said. “For sites meeting the common specifications of those that have already been exhaustively analyzed, the environmental impacts and the mitigation of those impacts are well-studied and well-known.”
The proposed rule is set to be published Sep. 8 in the Federal Register. That will launch a 60-day public comment period, to end Nov. 9.
Opposition expressed
Environmental groups have opposed the idea since May, when AOGA submitted its petition and the Trump administration launched the formal process that resulted in Friday’s proposed rule.
They reiterated their opposition Friday.
“This rule rigs our system for fossil fuel interests by requiring BLM to approve massive oil projects while eliminating the public’s freedom to say ‘No’ to unwanted developments on these shared lands. No company should get a blank check to develop the Western Arctic,” Matt Jackson, Alaska senior manager of The Wilderness Society, said in a statement.
“What we’re seeing here is a concerted attack by the Trump administration to greenlight oil and gas drilling in the Western Arctic while ignoring the harm it will cause to these irreplaceable public lands and also the government’s obligation to protect these lands for wildlife and future generations,” Erik Grafe, an attorney for the environmental law firm Earthjustice, said in a statement. The proposal “flaunts basic environmental laws meant to protect land, wildlife and people,” Grafe added.
 

Two caribou in the Teshekpuk herd are seen on June 27, 2014, in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska. The reserve holds rich oil formations, but it also has habitat important to caribou, migratory birds and other wildlife. (Photo by Bob Wick/U.S. Bureau of Land Management)
 

	Last week, in anticipation of the rule announcement, the leader of a North Slope Native organization issued a statement of opposition.
“Once again, the Trump administration is moving forward with a catastrophic proposal without consulting or considering the communities who will bear its consequences,” Rosemary Ahtuangaruak, executive director of Grandmothers Growing Goodness, said in an Aug. 27 statement. “In the past, we have worked directly with the government to prevent the worst impacts of oil and gas development in the Western Arctic. This new categorical exclusion shuts us out of the process, silencing the people who know the land best and puts our way of life – and future generations – at risk just to serve corporate greed.” 
Other organizations representing the North Slope’s Indigenous people have expressed a more mixed view of the idea.
That was reflected in comments submitted to the BLM in July, during the initial scoping process that led to Friday’s announcement, by the North Slope Borough, the for-profit Arctic Slope Regional Corporation and the Iñupiat Community of the Arctic Slope, a Tribal government,
The groups are “generally supportive of efforts to streamline permitting for production sites in the NPR-A,” the joint comment document said. However, they said they had concerns that the new rule might not allow for proper consultation with local communities and might not adequately protect subsistence resources.
Industry interest
The 23-million-acre petroleum reserve is currently seen as a highly prospective area for new oil development in the Arctic. The northeastern part of the reserve has drawn keen industry interest in recent years, largely because of related geological formations called Nanushuk and Torok that run through it.
ConocoPhillips, the dominant company operating in that part of the North Slope, has numerous fields already producing oil or in development that tap into Nanushuk and Torok oil.
One is the huge Willow project in the reserve, under construction and expected to start producing in late 2029. It is on track to be the westernmost producing oil field in Arctic Alaska, and the company has said peak production is expected to be 180,000 barrels a day from a resource that is estimated at about 600 million barrels.
A federal lease sale held in March, part of a series conducted by the government since 1999, drew a record $163 million in high bids.
Oil  is not the only resource of interest in the Indiana-sized reserve. The site is used by caribou herds, migratory birds and other wildlife, and the area is important for traditional subsistence food-gathering by residents of the region’s Native villages. 
The reserve is also famous for its paleontological resources; an area along the Colville River has yielded numerous significant discoveries of Arctic dinosaurs.
The reserve has had a history of management changes that resulted in a multiple-use approach balancing development with conservation.
It was established by President Warren Harding in1923 as a potential source of petroleum for the nation’s military forces. A federal law passed in 1976 gave the BLM authority over the reserve, and a 1980 amendment to that act established a series of environmental protections. Among those protections was the designation of a special area for Teshekpuk Lake, the largest Alaska lake above the Arctic Circle.
Trump administration policies have sought to strip protections from the Teshekpuk Lake area and the caribou herd that bears the lake’s name. Those policies have resulted in litigation.
The petroleum reserve went undeveloped for most of its history, with only sporadic exploration until the end of the 20th century.
Industry and government attention began to shift to the petroleum reserve after Arco Alaska in the 1990s discovered the large Alpine field on state land bordering the reserve, at the Colville River Delta. Arco’s assets, including Alpine, are now owned by ConocoPhillips. That company in 2015 became the first to produce oil from land within the reserve boundaries. Since then, other production in the reserve has followed.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Judge rules Green Party candidate accused of being GOP plant can be kicked off ballot in PA-07
description: The decision marks a turning point in a dispute between Tupone and the Pennsylvania Green Party itself, which challenged Tupone’s nomination papers and accused him of being a Republican plant.
text:
Andrew Tupone in front of the Pennsylvania Capitol in Harrisburg. (Photo courtesy of the Tupone campaign)This story was updated at 8:16 p.m. on September 4, 2026 to include a comment from Andrew Tupone.
A Commonwealth Court judge ruled Friday afternoon that Andrew Tupone, a hopeful Green Party candidate in the 7th Congressional District, can be removed from the ballot despite collecting sufficient signatures to appear on it.
Tupone, however, said he plans to appeal.
“The establishment parties are fighting to keep me off the ballot but I’m not backing down,” he said. “I will continue this fight and appeal this decision because the people of the 7th Congressional District deserve a real choice and a true progressive candidate who will stand up for them.”
He added that, if the appeal fails, he will mount a write-in campaign.
The move marks a turning point in a dispute between Tupone and the Pennsylvania Green Party itself, which challenged Tupone’s nomination papers and accused him of being a Republican plant.
“The Election Code vests with political parties and political bodies the right to ‘nominate’ — i.e., ‘select’ — the candidates they wish to place on the ballot in the General Election,” Judge Stella Tsai wrote in her order. 
Why is the Green Party trying to kick a Green Party candidate off the ballot in the Pa.?

Tupone, she noted, never got such a sign-off from the state Green Party, which actively opposed him appearing on the ballot under their banner.
The Green Party’s objection to his nomination papers noted Tupone was a registered Republican until earlier this year, and that they had never heard of him until he began collecting signatures. He was represented in court by Wally Zimolong, an attorney who has worked on high-profile election issues in Pennsylvania with Republicans, including U.S. Sen. Dave McCormick and President Donald Trump.
Tupone previously told the Capital-Star that he was “trying to buck the establishment of both parties … I’m running for universal healthcare, ending the genocide in Gaza and standing up to the establishment parties.”
He added, “My political beliefs always remained the same.”
The 7th Congressional District is among the most competitive in the country, and the outcome of November’s election there could prove pivotal in determining whether Democrats or Republicans control the U.S. Congress next year.
Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Ryan Mackenzie will face Democratic challenger Bob Brooks, who is backed by Gov. Josh Shapiro and a number of prominent figures in Democratic politics like Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. The race is rated a “toss up” by Cook Political Report.
Chris Robinson, a spokesperson for the state Green Party, said when reached that he was unaware of the order, but would “read it tomorrow.”
A separate objection to Tupone’s nomination papers, filed by Democratic voters in the 7th Congressional District, has not been ruled on. It challenged many of Tupone’s signatures on technical grounds.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho Supreme Court rules state officials must re-write abortion initiative ballot statements
description: The Idaho Supreme Court on Friday unanimously ruled that state officials must redraft explanations of the effect of voting for or against the proposed abortion rights initiative that will appear on voters’ Nov. 3 general election ballots. The court does not have the authority to write new language, but told the offices of the Idaho […]
text:
The exterior of the Idaho Supreme Court building in Boise as seen on Jan. 14, 2026. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)The Idaho Supreme Court on Friday unanimously ruled that state officials must redraft explanations of the effect of voting for or against the proposed abortion rights initiative that will appear on voters’ Nov. 3 general election ballots.
The court does not have the authority to write new language, but told the offices of the Idaho Attorney General and Secretary of State that they must submit revised ballot language to the court by 5 p.m. Saturday — around 24 hours after the decision was entered. 
Idaho Supreme Court Justice Gregory Moeller, right, asks a question during a hearing in this  April 25, 2025, file photo. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
The decision, written by Justice Gregory Moeller, found that neither the “yes” or “no” effect statements met the law’s requirements. 
“A statement is not ‘clear’ if it leaves voters uncertain about a principal legal consequence of their choice, and it does not describe ‘the effect’ of a vote if it materially misstates that consequence,” Moeller wrote. “Conciseness permits Respondents to omit unnecessary detail; it does not permit them to convey an inaccurate picture of the effect of a specific vote.” 
The ballot “effect statements,” required under state law to be a clear and concise explanation of the impacts of a yes or no vote, were written by Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and Secretary of State Phil McGrane. 
The state’s high court heard oral arguments Wednesday and issued a speedy ruling as election officials neared a Sept. 11 deadline to be able to send ballots to military and overseas voters. 
Supporters of the initiative, called Prop 1, filed a lawsuit on Aug. 27, arguing that the drafted effect statements of “yes” or “no” votes on the ballot measure were “misleading” and “confusing.” 
Attorneys representing Labrador and McGrane defended the statements in court, arguing they were the clearest and shortest way to inform voters. 
Joe Parris, a spokesperson for the secretary of state, said Friday the office is working to comply with the order.
“We appreciate the Idaho Supreme Court’s prompt review of Proposition One yes-and-no effect statements,” Parris said in an email. “As directed by the court, we are working closely with the Attorney General’s Office to prepare and submit revised statements. We remain focused on meeting all necessary deadlines to ensure ballots are printed and distributed on schedule.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Why did the Idaho Supreme Court find the ballot statements violated the law’s requirements? 

The proposed initiative, drafted by the group Idahoans United for Women and Families, would repeal Idaho’s strict abortion ban, allowing abortions up to fetal viability or beyond in cases of a medical emergency. It would also enumerate rights related to reproductive healthcare, such as access to contraception and IVF, and privacy in healthcare decisions. 
Under Idaho’s abortion laws, it is a felony to perform nearly any abortion, except to prevent the death of the mother, or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors may also be sued for a minimum of $20,000 for performing an abortion. 
The effect statements, as drafted by state officials, were: 
“A YES vote would create reproductive rights, including a right to abortion before a fetus’s ability to survive and after a fetus’s ability to survive in cases of a medical emergency, and provide liability protections for healthcare providers.”
“A NO vote would make no change to Idaho’s current law, which protects the life of the unborn while allowing abortion in reported cases of rape or incest, or when necessary to protect the life of the mother.”
The court found that the “yes” statement’s phrasing of “liability protections” did not accurately portray that the criminal and civil liability protection would only be for doctors providing the type or reproductive healthcare outlined in the initiative. 
It also said the “yes” statement’s use of the phrase “the fetus’s ability to survive” was “awkward,” and less clear when other descriptions on the ballot used the term “fetus viability.” The “yes” statement also did not mention that Prop 1 would offer rights to reproductive healthcare and privacy outside of abortion, the justice said. 
The officials’ “no” statements also did not accurately portray the law as it stands, Moeller wrote. The ballot language said the current law allows abortions to “protect the life,” of the mother. However, the law says abortions may be provided to “prevent the death” of the mother, which Moeller said is substantially different. 
“The choice of phraseology matters: ‘protect the life’ reasonably communicates a broader circumstance than ‘prevent the death,’” the decision said. 
The court also found that the “no” statements were unclear because they excluded describing the felony penalties and the time and reporting limitations on the rape and incest exemptions in the law. 
“By presenting these conditional carve-outs from a criminal prohibition as circumstances in which the law affirmatively ‘allow[s]’ abortion, the statement inaccurately enlarges the exceptions and understates the prohibition they qualify,” the justice wrote.
Idaho Supreme Court orders officials to revise abortion ballot initiative language, impact statement

The initiative’s proponents previously sued over the proposed ballot titles, which are the short and longer explanations of the initiative that appear on the ballot. The Idaho Supreme Court ruled in 2025 that Labrador’s office must revise the short ballot title. 
Melanie Folwell, lead organizer of Idahoans United, said that Friday’s decision was a “win for Idaho voters.” 
“Idaho voters deserve ballot language that tells them the truth, and I’m proud that we fought this battle,” Folwell wrote in an emailed statement to the Sun. “We look forward to Secretary McGrane and Attorney General Labrador complying with the Court’s direction and Idaho law.”
