name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Puerto Rico water crisis, youth marketing campaign: CT politics news
description: Plus: CT commemorates International Overdose Remembrance Day, new cancer treatment arrives, and officials highlight local Latino businesses.
text:
These news briefs are part of The Connecticut Mirror’s 2026 political coverage. For more Connecticut political news, sign up here for The Issue, the CT Mirror’s weekly politics newsletter.
CT officials pledge to support Puerto Rico during water crisis
Connecticut stands ready to offer any assistance it can to help Puerto Ricans as the island’s record drought continues, state officials announced Wednesday.
During a morning press conference, members of the CT-Puerto Rico Trade Commission joined Gov. Ned Lamont and other officials to discuss the water crisis. Connecticut is home to one of the largest Puerto Rican populations in the country, making the issue a personal one for many state residents.
Officials said that a formal request for aid has not been made yet, but the state is looking into ways to provide potable water and other infrastructure assistance. A group is expected to travel to the island in October to witness conditions on the ground.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
CT launches youth-oriented manufacturing marketing campaign
The Connecticut Office of Manufacturing has launched a new storytelling effort to boost awareness of manufacturing careers among young people.
The “I Can Make It” storytelling campaign highlights Connecticut’s modern manufacturing industry, focusing on aerospace, robotics, and shipbuilding. The state has promoted similar campaigns in recent years, including the “Make it Here” effort  started in 2023 and “I Got it Made” in 2024.
The latest campaign comes as the state makes significant investments in youth robotics and broader career pathways initiatives.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
Hartford Public Schools CFO resigns
The chief finance officer of Hartford Public Schools, Caitlin Richards, has resigned after nearly two years with the district. A spokesperson for Hartford schools confirmed Richards left after getting a job offer at Nashville Public Schools.
Hiring a CFO was the first of 64 recommendations the state made to HPS to help stabilize its finances. The district is now searching for a replacement.
Richards’ departure complicates an ongoing audit into the district’s 2024-25 finances. That audit began after questions arose in April about the accuracy of the district’s budget projections. 
HPS plans to release an exit interview with Richards pending the superintendent’s approval.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
A new cancer treatment comes to CT
Connecticut’s two biggest healthcare systems are teaming up to bring cutting edge cancer treatment to the state. This week Hartford HealthCare and Yale New Haven Health hosted a ribbon cutting for a new proton therapy center in Wallingford.
Proton therapy delivers more precise treatment than traditional radiation, helping to protect healthy cells and reduce side effects of treatment, physicians at the event said. It’s particularly useful in treating children, as well as adults with tumors located next to critical organs.
Previously, Connecticut residents looking to get proton therapy had to travel to Boston or New York.
— Katy Golvala, Health Reporter
CT’s paraeducator shortage grows significantly
The State Department of Education revealed Wednesday that the number of unfilled paraeducator positions in Connecticut has grown by over 400 since last year.
As of August, there were 1,264 unfilled special education paraeducator positions and 274 unfilled other paraeducator positions across the state.
Ajit Gopalakrishnan, chief performance officer for the department, hypothesized the recent $10 million grant to boost in-district special education services may be contributing to those numbers.
The state launched a new paraeducator academy in August with the goal of training 200 to 250 new paraeducators in the next year. The course is free and does not require a college degree.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
CT officials highlight local Latino businesses
More than 300 people attended the Hispanic Federation’s CRECER Latino Business Expo in Hartford on Tuesday, a chance for the local business community to engage with and support one another. The fairly new event was held in Connecticut for the first time this year.
Hartford Mayor Arunan Arulampalam and U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal addressed the audience during the event, with Blumenthal noting that the expo was a powerful reminder of the significance of Latino communities to Connecticut’s economy. According to the Hispanic Federation, Latinos owned 23% of the state’s small businesses in 2023.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
CT commemorates International Overdose Remembrance Day
Advocates were joined by elected officials on Monday in commemorating victims of drug overdose during ceremonies in Manchester.
The state has made strides in the past few years in its efforts to reduce the number of overdose deaths, with rates decreasing annually since the peak of around 1,400 in 2021. In 2025, an estimated 836 people died of an overdose.
At a ceremony at the Root Center, Sen. Saud Anwar, D-South Windsor, told those gathered that the biggest issues in the fight are philosophical, and that some officials “say not every life is worth saving.” 
— Laura Tillman, Human Services Reporter
Special education attorney to join education department
Connecticut State Department of Education has filled a new role for a special education attorney as it seeks to address a critical report released in January.
The report found issues in Connecticut special education — among them, a state complaint process lacking legal oversight and transparency. The new attorney, whose name has not been publicly disclosed, is meant to address those concerns.
State complaints are one way parents can take action if they feel their children aren’t receiving adequate special education services. Dissatisfaction with the process is widespread; advocates say the findings are often legally suspect and poorly enforced.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa labor experts speak on UnityPoint unionization efforts, worker challenges
description: As the United States honors the efforts of its labor movement and workers this Labor Day Weekend, Iowa labor experts say workers are “making the labor movement every day,” amidst weaker bargaining laws, attacks from corporations and other challenges everyone is facing, whether they hold a union card or not. Jesse Case, secretary-treasurer of Teamsters […]
text:
Teamsters Local 238 Secretary-Treasurer Jesse Case, left, and Jennifer Sherer, deputy director of Economic Policy Institute Economic Analysis and Research Network, speak on Iowa Press on Sept. 4, 2026. (Screenshot taken from Iowa Press video)As the United States honors the efforts of its labor movement and workers this Labor Day Weekend, Iowa labor experts say workers are “making the labor movement every day,” amidst weaker bargaining laws, attacks from corporations and other challenges everyone is facing, whether they hold a union card or not.
Jesse Case, secretary-treasurer of Teamsters Local 238, and Jennifer Sherer, deputy director of the Economic Policy Institute’s Economic Analysis and Research Network and director of the institute’s Worker Power Project, spoke on “Iowa Press” Sept. 4 about efforts of some Iowans to unionize and the issues impacting unionized workers in the state and across the country.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Sherer told “Iowa Press” moderator Kay Henderson and Gazette Des Moines Bureau Chief Erin Murphy that this is a difficult period for Iowa workers, and that in the 30 years she’s lived in Iowa, the state’s union representation density has fallen from above to below the national average.
In 2025, the U.S. union membership rate was 10%, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, and Henderson said currently just over 100,000 Iowans are union members, or around 6.8% of the population.
“But that’s not the end of this history,” Sherer said. “Workers are still rewriting it today, and this Labor Day and the next election cycle and everything that comes after will probably write the next chapter.”
UnityPoint nurses still in fight for unionization 
Nurses working in four Des Moines area UnityPoint Health locations are still waiting to hear a ruling from the National Labor Relations Board on their vote to unionize, as 251 of the 1,537 votes cast have been challenged. According to the National Labor Relations Board, 871 votes were cast to organize and 666 voted against the motion.
Case said he believes the workers won the election and that the challenges are a tactic by UnityPoint to stop them from organizing, something he said isn’t uncommon in healthcare. He called UnityPoint’s efforts to halt the union’s creation “one of the most expensive union busting campaigns in the history of labor.”
According to a May Economic Policy Institute report cited by Sherer in the discussion, UnityPoint Health spent more than $2.1 million on “union avoidance consultants” in 2025. The healthcare company came in second to Amazon, which spent more than $26.6 million, and the total spent on union avoidance topped $1.5 billion in the U.S.
“We think that the union and the workers are going to prevail with those labor board decisions, and then it’s going to, you know, take all hands on deck to get the employer to get to the table and negotiate a fair agreement because we expect them to stall on that too,” Case said. “And they really just need to step to the plate and do the right thing and negotiate in good faith with those workers who voted to organize under their federal rights.”
In response to a question from Murphy about UnityPoint’s claim that a union contract for its healthcare workers would be “too rigid” and reward seniority rather than performance, Case said all employers say that in these situations. Employers and workers need to have a partnership with negotiated terms and a voice for the workers, he said, as it makes the workforce more consistent, makes recruitment easier and can improve the work’s quality.
Union election filings in the healthcare industry have been increasing over the past few years, Sherer said, alongside general support nationwide for unions. However, even with more than 70% of U.S. citizens across age demographics and party lines supporting unions, she said federal and state labor laws “have gotten so weak” that the path to a union contract is murky, even without efforts from employers to quell calls to organize.
“I do absolutely think the UnityPoint example here in Iowa is a leading example of a trend we’re seeing everywhere,” Sherer said.
State, national challenges for workers
Despite U.S. employers adding 162,000 jobs to the labor market in August, according to the Associated Press, Sherer said the job market is “weak in certain important ways.” Beyond AI data center investment and a couple of other sectors, she said most industries are seeing either status-quo or declining numbers, and there is debate over whether the data center push will “turn out to be a temporary bubble.”
“Not a crisis, I don’t hear a lot of people yet predicting that we’re on the brink of a recession around the corner, but it’s not a healthy labor market, and particularly in states like Iowa, where we’re seeing pretty weak numbers,” Sherer said.
Artificial intelligence is becoming a threat to workers in many different fields, Case and Sherer said, from healthcare to white-collar industries. Case said he and others in unions are also worried about autonomous vehicles and investments from Silicon Valley in AI to “put driverless trucks on our roads.”
What may work in places like San Francisco and Austin, Texas, would not work in Iowa, Case said, and the idea of driverless vehicles brings up questions of accountability if there’s an accident and someone is hurt or killed.
An industry that historically could be found throughout Iowa, food processing plants, has been shrinking as well, Murphy said, leading to closures that impact hundreds of workers. Case said he sees the closures as “a product of consolidation of big (agriculture)” and monopolies created by Tyson’s, Cargill and JBS, and there are 11 packing plants across the country responsible for processing half of all of the beef here.
What makes it harder for Iowa workers when they are laid off due to consolidation, or other reasons, is the weakening of the state unemployment system, Sherer said. It’s harder now than it was a decade ago to predict household stability in the future with unemployment because benefits have been shortened in their length, Sherer said, making the market overall less healthy.
“If you pick an industry in this country, it’s generally run by four or five companies, and sometimes on a global scale. So there are monopolies that are controlling business in this country. It’s not good for our communities, it’s not good for workers,” Case said, “We need to really beef up the antitrust laws in this country and get some U.S. attorneys who are interested in fixing those monopolies, or at least holding them accountable.”
In response to a question about the impact of past comments by the Teamsters president about unions not being beholden to either the Republican or Democratic party, Case said “organized labor is not an extension of either political party, nor should we be.”
His local union has “represented” presidential campaigns in the past, Case said, including for former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris, but the union’s membership is split by thirds among Democrats, Republicans and independents.
Many independent voters are sick of both of the major parties, but what’s worse is a one-party system, which Case said has been the state in Iowa for years. With Republican control over state government, Case said collective bargaining rights were lost for 180,000 public sector employees, the state has the second-highest cancer rates and the worst water quality in the U.S. and “big money from New York and D.C.” has impacted policy-making to the “detriment of workers.”
“The reality is, we have to have a relationship with people on both sides of the aisle when we can and when they’re reasonable,” Case said. “Sometimes you can’t have a relationship with people because they’re just nut jobs, but where we can establish relationships, we have to have bipartisan relationships in some states and on the national level.”

title: University of Nebraska Medical Center breaks ground on Infectious Diseases Air Transport facility
description: OMAHA — A collection of officials representing the state and the University of Nebraska broke ground Friday on a new training facility at the southern edge of the University of Nebraska Medical Center campus. The groundbreaking ceremony launched the first phase of a $17.4 million project building an Infectious Diseases Air Transport training facility, set […[...]
text:
From left to right: Lee Williames, MD, director, Office for the Advancement of Military Medicine, UNMC; Christopher Kratochvil, MD, vice chancellor for external relations, UNMC; Gov. Jim Pillen; Mayor John W. Ewing, Jr.; H. Dele Davies, MD, chancellor of UNMC; Sen. Deb Fischer; Col. Elizabeth Schnaubelt, MD, director, Center for Sustainment of Trauma and Readiness Skills-Omaha, USAF; University of Nebraska President Jeffrey P. Gold, MD; Lt. Gen. John J. DeGoes, MD, surgeon general and commander, Medical Command, USAF; Lt. Col. Robert Schafer, JD, regent, University of Nebraska System; Congressman Don Bacon; Jennie Bartholomew, UNMC associate vice chancellor and Nebraska Medicine vice president, facilities management and planning.OMAHA — A collection of officials representing the state and the University of Nebraska broke ground Friday on a new training facility at the southern edge of the University of Nebraska Medical Center campus.
The groundbreaking ceremony launched the first phase of a $17.4 million project building an Infectious Diseases Air Transport training facility, set to open in early 2028. The facility will house biocontainment transport modules and an aircraft fuselage designed to provide advanced training for U.S. Air Force members with the Center for Sustainment of Trauma and Readiness Skills (C-STARS) stationed at UNMC.
A rendering of the Infectious Diseases Air Transport training facility to be built at the University of Nebraska Medical Center in Omaha. (Photo courtesy of UNMC)
U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said the project will cement Nebraska’s status as a leader in national defense, helping to care for the nation’s military and protect public health. Several speakers at Friday’s event said the facility will be the first of its kind in the United States.
“We are the home of global health security,” said Gov. Jim Pillen. “Nobody in the world does it better in any kind of challenge for health security.”
U.S. Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., said the University of Nebraska — and particularly UNMC — is the “gold standard” for fostering effective partnerships with the federal government and the military. Friday’s speakers highlighted UNMC’s quarantining American cruise ship passengers who were exposed to a deadly hantavirus earlier this year, as well as its role in Nebraska’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Bacon and other speakers also praised UNMC’s aid through multiple Ebola outbreaks. Lt. Gen. John J. DeGoes said UNMC helped train Air Force medical officials stationed in Kenya aiding with an ongoing outbreak in central Africa, while Bacon referenced UNMC treating three Ebola patients in 2014 during the largest and deadliest outbreak of the virus in recorded history.
At the time, Bacon said, he viewed moving Ebola patients to Nebraska as a “gutsy move,” but it paid off.
“You showed the world what you can do with a very hard task,” Bacon told attendees representing UNMC.
Col. Elizabeth Schnaubelt, director of C-STARS’ Omaha unit, said the facility will help the U.S. prepare for challenges that can’t be anticipated, like another pandemic. University of Nebraska President Jeffrey Gold said such a resource is invaluable, especially in a time of “geopolitical uncertainty.”
“If you think for one minute that today is not about protecting our freedom and protecting those who wear the cloth of our nation, think again,” Gold said.

title: New Mexico land commissioner announces uranium mining ban on state trust lands
description: New Mexico Commissioner of Public Lands Stephanie Garcia Richard on Friday signed an executive order that bans all new uranium mining projects on the more than 13 million acres of state trust lands she oversees.
text:
New Mexico Commissioner of Public Lands Stephanie Garcia Richard on Sept. 4, 2026, signed an executive order that bans all new uranium mining projects on state trust lands. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)New Mexico Commissioner of Public Lands Stephanie Garcia Richard on Friday signed an executive order that bans all new uranium mining projects on the more than 13 million acres of state trust lands she oversees.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Garcia Richard, a Democrat who has roughly four months left in her term and is running for lieutenant governor, said at a news conference Friday on the front steps of her office’s Santa Fe headquarters that the longlasting environmental and public health impacts of uranium contamination outweigh any potential revenues to state coffers uranium mining could provide.
She said the executive order is needed now, in particular, amid a recent uptick in uranium extraction proposals statewide, including in the Grants Mineral Belt, Canjilon and Pie Town areas. She attributed the renewed interest to President Donald Trump’s administration, which has sought to fast-track federal permits for uranium mining and identified two such proposals on Cibola National Forest land near Mount Taylor as “priority projects.” 
“New Mexicans have been overlooked by the uranium industry and the federal government for far too long, and now the Trump administration is once again completely ignoring these communities and pushing for aggressive uranium development nationwide, despite the fact that there still remain thousands of sites that are abandoned and need to be remediated,” she said. 
While there are no pending uranium proposals before the State Land Office, Garcia Richard noted that approximately 50 abandoned sites are on state trust lands, vestiges of the decades in the 20th century in which New Mexico produced most of the nation’s uranium ore. Those sites still risk contaminating nearby ground and surface water, she said.
Her executive order directs the State Land Office to prioritize cleaning up those legacy sites, in addition to “not making the problem worse through new project authorizations.”
The state Legislature this year approved the second round of $20 million in funding dedicated to remediating abandoned uranium mine sites, approximately 350 of which dot the New Mexico landscape. Previous funding has gone to clean up four abandoned mines on state trust land in McKinley County.
Garcia Richard acknowledged during the news conference that she is at the end of her second term as land commissioner and that her successor has discretion to overturn her executive order.
By the #s: NM gives $20M more to reclaim uranium sites, as search continues for those responsible

“We are putting this out there so that if a future land commissioner wants to mine uranium, they’re going to have to overturn this, and we will be asking them why they did not uphold this document,” she said.
Democrat Juan de Jesus Sanchez III is running against Republican Michael Jack Perry in the Nov. 3 general election to replace Garcia Richard as land commissioner. 
Sanchez stood in the small crowd gathered for the news conference Friday. He told Source NM after the news conference that he intends to keep the executive order in place if he’s elected. 
Perry did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment Friday on whether he, too, would uphold the ban.

title: Court says American Prairie bison can stay for now
description: A federal judge has ruled American Prairie can keep grazing bison on three federal grazing allotments as a federal lawsuit plays out. The decision by Judge Brian Morris blocks, for now, a Bureau of Land Management rule that would have removed 900 bison from three allotments where American Prairie, a nonprofit conservation organization, currently graze […]
text:
American Prairie bison being transferred. (American Prairie photo)A federal judge has ruled American Prairie can keep grazing bison on three federal grazing allotments as a federal lawsuit plays out.
The decision by Judge Brian Morris blocks, for now, a Bureau of Land Management rule that would have removed 900 bison from three allotments where American Prairie, a nonprofit conservation organization, currently graze the bison. 
The lawsuit, filed by American Prairie against the Bureau of Land Management and the Department of the Interior, seeks to stop a rule from being implemented that would drastically shift how bison can be grazed in the United States. That lawsuit is still pending.
In May, the BLM canceled six of American Prairie’s permits, which comprised more than 60,000 acres, using a new interpretation of the federal Taylor Grazing Act requiring livestock be “production-oriented” in order to use federal land.
Montana’s all-Republican federal delegation, and its statewide Republican officials, have heavily opposed bison grazing on federal grazing land. 
Gov. Greg Gianforte and the delegation had asked Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to take a look at the bison leases, saying the organization’s mission is at odds with the state’s economy, and said American Prairie’s bison removes the land from agricultural use.
Morris was not convinced that it was, pointing out about half of the bison American Prairie have produced have been bought. Those bison have been used to help start food sovereignty programs, increase herd size, and for hunting.
“No statutory language or judicial precedent exists that requires a livestock operation to focus exclusively on production and entirely ignore conservation, range improvement, preservation, or other values,” the court order reads.
The federal government and the state of Montana have also argued the bison were not true “livestock” and tried to redefine the legal meaning of the word. 
Using the definition of livestock in Black’s Law Dictionary, the order says, “Federal defendants make no argument that American Prairie’s bison herd fails to qualify as livestock under this definition,” and that such an argument would be “uncompelling.” 
The order declined to rule on three grazing allotments that American Prairie currently does not use for bison grazing, but had previously reached an agreement with BLM to use.
“Bison belong on this landscape, and today’s ruling gives them a chance to stay,” Alison Fox, CEO of American Prairie said in a press release. “For more than 20 years, our bison have grazed these lands under federal authorization and without grazing violations. The court recognized the concrete harm that removing them would cause, not just to our work, but to our Tribal partners and the broader effort to return bison to their native home.”
American Prairie also argued that if a previous Sept. 30 deadline for removal of the bison from the three allocations the bison currently graze on, there could also be significant concerns about long-term genetic diversity of their bison herd.
The Montana Attorney General’s Office declined to comment about the ruling when contacted on Friday.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Legislators move to support prison oversight
description: Legislators said increased oversight is likely coming to the Department of Corrections, potentially during the next session in 2027. Prison rights advocates have pushed hard for independent oversight of the agency, asking legislators to demand increased transparency and accountability.  On Tuesday, the Law and Justice Interim Committee voted 5-4 to support l[...]
text:
The state seal of Montana is pictured on Tuesday, Sept. 1, in the Montana Capitol in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)Legislators said increased oversight is likely coming to the Department of Corrections, potentially during the next session in 2027.
Prison rights advocates have pushed hard for independent oversight of the agency, asking legislators to demand increased transparency and accountability. 
On Tuesday, the Law and Justice Interim Committee voted 5-4 to support legislation that would create a program providing independent oversight of the Department of Corrections housed in the Governor’s Office. The bill will be introduced by either Rep. Zooey Zephyr, D-Missoula, or Rep. Katie Fire Thunder, D-Bozeman.
The oversight would come in the form of an ombudsperson position, of which Montana already has several, including the Department of Justice’s Office of the Child and Family Ombudsman. 
DOC Director Eric Strauss has previously said the department was “pretty agnostic” to the idea, but not inherently against the concept.
Montana Department of Corrections director Eric Strauss speaks during a Law and Justice Interim Committee meeting on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)
Fire Thunder introduced the legislation to the committee earlier this year. Catalyst Montana, an advocacy organization based in Missoula, has supported the idea, which was originally presented to legislators by Amanda McKnight, who began advocating for transparency after a severe water crisis at Montana State Prison a year ago.
People who have incarcerated family members, including McKnight, have been frustrated with what they say is poor communication from the agency, visits being canceled, slow medical care and inmate transfers to out-of-state facilities with little or no notice.
Some of those problems have been in part due to staffing and retention, a long-standing issue DOC has sought to address.
“This vote is a major victory for every family that has felt ignored, every correctional employee who has been afraid to speak out, and every Montana taxpayer demanding accountability from the system they fund,” McKnight said in a statement. “For too long, the Department of Corrections has largely been expected to police itself, and families have experienced the consequences when that oversight fails.”
She added that it “proves” grassroots voices can be heard by legislators and that she plans to keep fighting for the bill.
The legislation has not been a particularly partisan issue, and several of the “no” votes in the Law and Justice Committee were not because legislators thought it a bad idea, but because they said they didn’t think it went far enough. There were also slight concerns at the potential cost, which was estimated at $1 million to $1.5 million. This cost includes a similar model to a Child Protective Services ombudsperson, which includes an appointed investigator and an advisory council. 
Amanda McKnight, a prison rights advocate, testifies during a Law and Justice Interim Committee meeting on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026 at the Montana State Capitol in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)
“Having operated a correctional institution, I worry about constitutional issues,” said Rep. Steven Kelly, a Flathead Republican. “Medical care falls directly under the Eighth Amendment. If they go in and find that we are failing to provide medical care, that’s a big red flag, and that will land us in federal court. Whoever finds these things should have the ability to report it and expect somebody to do something. There’s nothing here that does that, and so while this looks good on paper, it’s a paper tiger.”
Medical issues in the system are indeed a concern, Strauss said Tuesday, as he reported to legislators on a recent visit he took to Tallahatchie County Correctional Facility in Mississippi, which has been the source of complaints.  The Montana DOC currently has 3,376 prisoners, with 587 of them — all men — held at the Mississippi prison. The state is contracting with that correctional facility due to overcrowding issues in Montana. The DOC moved all prisoners previously held in Arizona to the Mississippi facility earlier this year in an effort to have all of its out-of-state prisoners in one place. Both of those facilities are run by CoreCivic, a private company.
The Montana Department of Correction’s operational capacity is 3,450 prisoners, its data dashboard says. This includes men, women and juveniles.
Strauss said he found a deeply concerning problem involving inmates’ access to medical care, adding they’ve completed an audit and are in the process of finalizing a report about what happened.
“I heard repeatedly from many offenders down there that they had concerns about access to medications, access to appointments,” Strauss said.
Prisoners use tablets to communicate, and all Montana prisoners are issued one. It allows them to communicate, not only with their families, but within the prison itself, to address things like medical care. 
Strauss said a feature prisoners in Mississippi were using to communicate medical issues was not being received by prison staff. It’s a feature that’s disabled on tablets in other Montana facilities, but was turned on in the Tallahatchie facility.
Prison rights advocates have also pointed to an increase in prison deaths as 17 inmates have died in DOC custody this year. That’s the highest number since the COVID-19 pandemic, when 25 inmates died in 2020 and 20 died in 2021. Prison death statistics includes illnesses, natural causes and suicide.
Rep. Steven Kelly listens during a meeting of the Law and Justice Interim Committee on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026 in the Montana Capitol in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)
Four of those deaths have been at Tallahatchie County Correctional Facility in Mississippi. The other 13 have been in Montana. The Montana Department of Corrections has said their goal is to bring inmates back to the state, and Strauss again reiterated that on Tuesday.
“Our anticipated timeline, like I’ve communicated before, is aligned with the construction project at Montana State Prison,” Strauss said. “As soon as that’s done, sometime in early 2029, we would expect to return that full population back to Montana. So it is a short-term solution to short-term problem.”
Strauss said the facility is generally “quite nice” and air conditioned. He noted a lack of things for inmates at the prison to do, saying it was clear they were “bored.” As one example, inmates who had transferred from Arizona to Mississippi were not longer able to access music they’d purchased at the previous facility. 
Transferring music has been complex, but is something DOC is working on facilitating, he said. Inmates previously denied certain employment based on offense now have more job opportunities in Mississippi as well. This was due to a “inconsistent application of policy” from a service provider, Strauss said.
Tallahatchie County Correctional Facility also has a different policy for inmates receiving books from family. Strauss said they were able to change that policy for Montana prisoners to be in-line with how the process would go to send a book to an inmate in the state.
He spent six hours talking with Montana inmates housed at the Mississippi facility, he added. 
“There are many individual concerns that I encountered that we were able to resolve just by having a conversation,” Strauss said.
He added if state employees discover more systemic problems, they need to be noted and addressed with leadership of the Mississippi facility.

name: VTDigger
title: Tensions mount over teachers’ contract in Blue Mountain Union School District
description:
Negotiations in the three-town district in Orange County are reaching an unusual point that school board members blame on rising pressure to cut costs. The union sees it differently.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Tensions mount over teachers’ contract in Blue Mountain Union School District.
text:
A view of Wells River. Photo courtesy of Ascended Dreamer/Wikimedia Commons

Negotiations over teachers’ salaries in the Blue Mountain Union School District have reached a rare inflection point while teachers start the school year without a contract.
According to school board members, the lengthy negotiations are the result of Vermont’s sweeping new education reform law, which puts districts under intense pressure to cut costs and ratchets up penalties on taxpayers if they don’t. 
But union representatives don’t buy that explanation. They say board members twice rejected a tentative contract agreement because union members have complained to the board about the superintendent in the past. 
The conflict bubbled up this summer.  
After nearly a year of collective bargaining, representatives of the school board and the teachers union came to a tentative agreement in July, proposing a three-year contract that both sides supported at the bargaining table. But once the proposal went to the school board for approval, members voted it down twice this summer. 
Tensions reached new heights last week when the union that represents teachers in the district,  the Vermont-NEA, filed a complaint with the Vermont Labor Relations Board alleging that board members bargained in bad faith and retaliated against them. 
It’s rare for teacher contract disputes to escalate to a labor complaint, according to Darren Allen, communications director for the Vermont-NEA. He said it’s the first instance he’s seen during his 21 years in the job. 
Although the Blue Mountain Education Association’s latest contract expired in June, teachers are still getting paid. But Allen said they are likely making less money than they would under the tentative agreement the school board rejected. 
The Blue Mountain Union School District serves nearly 400 kids from the towns of Groton, Wells River and Ryegate in its single prekindergarten through 12th grade school. The district is part of the Orange East Supervisory Union. 
During a Wednesday night board meeting, members decided to go back to the union with a new draft of a proposed agreement, according to Orange East Superintendent Heather Lawler. 
For Blue Mountain teachers, morale is low, said local union representative Jessica Roy, who teaches third and fourth grade at the school. 
“We’re starting our year feeling uneasy about this whole situation and why it’s happening,” Roy said. 
Negotiations
The union’s complaint to the labor board, shared with VTDigger, includes its description of how the saga over teachers’ salaries began with bargaining a new three-year contract in September 2025. 
While negotiations dragged on, the teachers union spoke to its members in May to hear their concerns about working conditions. The union heard broad consensus that teachers lacked faith in Lawler, according to Roy, who declined to provide specifics about the complaints. 
Representatives from the union then presented those concerns to the school board on July 1. 
Soon after, representatives from the school district and the teachers union reached a tentative agreement at the bargaining table, according to the union’s labor filing.
And on July 13, union members met with Lawler to discuss their issues with her leadership. Some teachers accused Lawler of lying to them while others said she generally wasn’t trustworthy, according to Roy. 
After the union met with Lawler, the tentative contract agreement came up for vote at a July 30 school board meeting, and the majority voted it down — as they did a second time Aug. 5.
Lawler said in an interview that although “it’s been really hard” to hear criticism from the union, it didn’t influence the board’s decision to reject the proposed contract. 
The board voted the way it did because of financial concerns, Lawler said. She also said she feels like she’s been unjustly criticized for decisions that the board made as a whole. 
But the board’s rejection was out of the ordinary for contract talks, according to Allen, the union spokesperson. “Almost always, until now, a tentative agreement was a sure thing,” he said. 
The union alleges that school board members who helped reach the tentative agreement in bargaining then turned around and advocated against it to the full board, in violation of Vermont labor law. 
“They’re required to advocate for the deal they reached at the table,” Allen said. 
In an Aug. 6 statement, school board members said they deeply appreciated teachers and rejected the agreement for financial reasons. 
Tight funds
While bargaining is ongoing, both sides are restricted from revealing the specifics of the tentative agreement, according to Roy and Lawler. 
But, according to board member Dan LaCoss, the district estimates that the proposed teachers’ salaries for next year and the year after would put district costs above the state excess spending threshold. 
The excess spending threshold is a mechanism to impose increased taxes on districts that spend more than a certain percentage above the average statewide per-pupil cost. 
Legislation passed this year lowers that threshold year by year. For the next fiscal year, which starts in July, the excess spending threshold will be 115.5%, down from its previous 118%.
Any spending above the threshold results in extra taxation for local residents.
The school board wouldn’t approve a district budget that exceeded the state’s excess spending threshold, LaCoss said. At that point, it would instead look to cut staff positions or school programs, which it would prefer to avoid, he added. 
“Our concern is doing harm for our students,” he said. 
In the meantime, negotiations are expected to continue. Both sides are tentatively set to return to the bargaining table next week, according to Allen.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Tensions mount over teachers’ contract in Blue Mountain Union School District.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Jahana Hayes, angling for labor chair, suggests Dems failed unions
description: Hayes accused Democrats of slow-walking a labor agenda when the party enjoyed a power trifecta for two years when Joe Biden was president.
text:
A fiery U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-5th District, was introduced by the president of the Connecticut AFL-CIO at a Labor Day kickoff breakfast Friday as “the future chair of the labor and education committee.” The lawmaker did not object to the description.
Politico reported this week that Hayes, who is favored to be reelected to a fifth term in November, was weighing a bid to become chair of the House Education and Workforce Committee if Democrats regain the majority in the closely divided House of Representatives. 
To an audience of more than 200 union activists at a trade union hall in Hartford, Hayes accused congressional Democrats of slow-walking a labor agenda when the party enjoyed a trifecta of controlling the House, Senate and White House for the two years after Joe Biden was elected president in 2020.
“I’ve been thinking a lot about the promises that were made to labor, and a lot about how we should have done more when we had a majority trifecta, to not have to deal with the problems that we’re having right now today,” Hayes said. “That cannot happen again. If there is any lesson to be learned, that has to be it.”
The complaint of timidity could be read as a criticism of 79-year-old Congressman Bobby Scott of Virginia, the ranking Democrat on the Education and Workforce Committee and panel’s chair when the party was in the majority. Scott has stated he would seek the chair again.
Among those in the audience Friday was Luke Bronin, 47, the former Hartford mayor who defeated 78-year-old Congressman John B. Larson, D-1st District, in a primary last month. After making no endorsement before the primary, the AFL-CIO endorsed Bronin this week.
The House is the most favorable battleground for Democrats to end the trifecta enjoyed by Republicans with President Donald Trump back in the White House and narrow GOP majorities in the Congress.
“When we get back in the majority — when — we have to deliver on the promises that we’ve made, we have to make sure we’re fighting for everyone,” Hayes said.
Hayes, 53, was selected national teacher of the year in 2016 while a history teacher at John F. Kennedy High School in Waterbury. Encouraged to run by U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, she won the open 5th District seat two years later, becoming the first Black woman elected to Congress from Connecticut.
Hayes did not enumerate those unmet promises in her formal remarks, but in a brief interview, she mentioned the proposed Protecting the Right to Organize Act, better known in labor circles as the PRO Act. Among other things, it would protect workers from being fired for attempting to join a union.
Under Trump, the National Labor Relations Board has been neutered, Hayes said. The panel no longer has enough members for a quorum, leaving it unable to resolve complaints of illegal firings and disputes arising from union organizing efforts.
“A lot of the labor protections, there’s no enforcement there,” Hayes said.
Scott did introduce a version of the PRO Act in 2021, when Democrats held all levers of power. It passed the House but fell short in the Senate, where the Democratic majority was not large enough to avoid a Republican filibuster.
Unions are thriving in terms of public popularity, said Ed Hawthorne, the president of the Connecticut AFL-CIO.
“We are meeting at a moment when working people across the country are rightfully feeling angry about just about everything. We’re exhausted by the cost of living. We’re tired of the gridlock, and we’re frustrated with the political institutions that so often fail to show up,” Hawthorne said. “But right now, in the middle of all that cynicism, something extraordinary is happening. Trust in America’s labor unions is rising again.”
A Gallup survey released Tuesday showed unions with a 71% approval rating that extends a six-year period in which approval has stayed between 67% and 71%, rivaling the heyday of the labor movement’s popularity in the 1950s.
Nearly half of Americans want labor unions in the U.S. to have more influence than they do today, slightly more than double the 23% who want unions to have less influence, Gallup found. Another 26% want unions’ influence to remain the same.
The Labor Day breakfast is tied to unions ramping up campaigning on behalf of endorsed candidates. Hawthorne noted that a schedule of door-to-door canvassing had been distributed throughout the union hall.
“The trust in our labor movement is precisely why our union-to-union labor walks are so important,” Hawthorne said. “Starting next Saturday, we will do what we do best: talk to our members about the issues that matter most to working families and elect our champions, many of whom are in the room with us here.”

Gov. Ned Lamont and Ed Hawthorne, the president of the Connecticut AFL-CIO. Credit: mark pazniokas / ctmirror.org

With Hayes and Gov. Ned Lamont on stage with him, Hawthorne pointed to other polling showing that trust in unions exceed trust in the Democratic Party by a wide margin.
“Hey, you don’t have to rub it in that labor leaders are 20% more popular than Democratic politicians,” Lamont said. “But I’ll tell you why — because we live in a day and age where I think working families, the middle class, feel like they’re getting screwed. They want to make sure that people are standing up for them. And every day, your labor union is stepping up for you, fighting for you, fighting for wages, fighting for the benefits, fighting to make sure our society is just a little bit fair.”
While the labor approval rating is high, union membership is not. Only 5.9% of private sector workers are unionized in the U.S., versus 32.9% in the public sector.
At 16.1%, Connecticut is tied with Rhode Island at fifth for the states with the highest overall union membership. 
The state ranks first in union strength among state employees, according to a survey by the Commonwealth Foundation.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Republicans assert state agency improperly shifted cash among disability service programs
description: Several Republican members of the Kansas Legislature express irritation with a state agency's transfer of $24 million among state disability programs.
text:
Rep. Kyle Hoffman, a Coldwater Republican on the Kansas Legislature's joint budget committee, is among GOP lawmakers questioning the transfer of $24 million by the Kansas Department for Children and Families from among several disability service programs. This image is a 2022 photo of Hoffman at the Capitol. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Republicans on a legislative budget committee renewed discontent Friday with Gov. Laura Kelly’s administration, which reallocated millions of dollars that could have benefitted Kansans with intellectual or developmental disabilities.
Instead, GOP lawmakers said, approximately $24 million that should have been targeted at 5,300 people on the state’s I/DD waiting list was transferred internally by the Kansas Department for Aging and Disability Services. The cash was used to expand aid to Kansans with severe brain injuries, the frail elderly and people requiring technology assistance to grapple with a disability. A majority of the reallocation, approximately $19 million, was dedicated to needs of frail elderly Kansans.
“That’s the frustration,” said Rep. Kristey Williams, an Augusta Republican. “We have to trust our agencies to use the money as it was appropriated, and it was not.”
Rep. Kyle Hoffman, a Coldwater Republican, said the Legislature included in bill form an expectation that KDADS would shrink the I/DD waiting list to 4,800 in fiscal year 2024-2025 and to 4,000 in fiscal year 2025-2026. The waiting list has grown to 5,357, officials said. The state provides financial support to 9,800 people with developmental and intellectual disabilities.
Hoffman said KDADS Secretary Laura Howard shouldn’t have interpreted past conversations with House and Senate committees about reappropriating the $24 million as formal permission to do so. He said KDADS’ decisions conflicted with language in House Bill 2513, which was passed by the Legislature and signed by the governor.
“It kind of feels like that you’re saying. ‘Well, the law says I have to do this, but we don’t have the money so we’re not going to do that,'” Hoffman said. “There’s a big difference in having a discussion in a budget committee that this is what we’d like this money to go towards, than … what the actual bill said. To me, you’re misappropriating what (House Bill) 2513 says.”
Howard said movement of the one-time funding was endorsed by House and Senate lawmakers through a transparent oversight process tied to Medicaid spending. She said KDADS didn’t withdraw services from Kansans with intellectual or developmental disabilities. Nor, she said, did KDADS deny funding specifically appropriated by the Legislature to add slots within the I/DD system.
“Every slot that was authorized by the Legislature was filled,” Howard said. “Again, we requested the use of one-time funding from the Legislature and were approved. Everything we’ve done regarding this has been a very, very transparent process.”
Howard said the $24 million was drawn from unspent state appropriations tied to the I/DD and physical disability programs.
In the past, the Legislature adopted a budget proviso directing KDADS to shrink the waiting list to no more than 4,000. In some cases, Kansans continue to wait up to 10 years to receive I/DD services due to a persistent shortage of professionals willing to provide those services and access to direct state appropriations by the Legislature to reserve new slots in Medicare programs.
“The problem with the proviso is it doesn’t provide any funding to reduce the waitlist,” Howard said. “Where am I supposed to take that funding from my budget? Should I take it from mental health services?”
In August, House Speaker Dan Hawkins, R-Wichita, sounded an alarm about the KDADS’ maneuvering. He accused the agency of engaging in a “blatant bureaucratic shell game, and families waiting years for services deserve answers.”
Sen. Rick Billinger, a Goodland Republican who chairs the joint Legislative budget committee, said the service-delivery challenge with I/DD programs had historically been framed as a lack of providers rather than a shortfall in state funding.
“I think this is the first time I’ve heard that we’re lacking in funding,” Billinger said. “It’s always been the capacity, rather than the funding.”
Sen. Pat Pettey, D-Kansas City, said the Legislature should appreciate that addressing the I/DD wait list required direct financing from state government.
“Even though we all want to see an I/DD list that has no one on it, every person moving off the I/DD list always has a cost involved. That’s not a one-time cost. It’s unfortunate that this has become somewhat of a political football that’s being thrown around.”

title: Judge criticizes Trump pressure on prosecutors on reflecting pool vandalism charges
text:
WASHINGTON — A District of Columbia Superior Court judge Friday seemed inclined to bar any new felony charges against former Olympian David Hearn, after the Trump administration accused the Maryland man of damaging part of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman raised concerns about President Donald Trump’s public pressure campaign on the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, following a quiet earlier move by U.S. Attorney Jeanne Pirro  to dismiss the charges.Trump, who oversaw the multi-million-dollar renovation of the pool, has blamed vandals for the damage.“The president of the United States is pressuring your office… to recharge Mr. Hearn (on) what you have decided is meritless,” said Edelman, who was nominated by former President Barack Obama. Government lawyers could not answer whether the Trump administration might again try to charge Hearn, of Bethesda, with damaging the reflecting pool. Pirro’s motion for dismissal was without prejudice, which means the case could be filed again.“I don't know what the future will bring,”  Michael Spence of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia said. “Ten minutes from now that decision could change.” Hearn has pleaded not guilty to the charges. Reflecting pool dramaHearn’s case has preoccupied Trump, who faces public backlash and protest as he’s moved to reshape the historic landmarks and landscapes of the nation's capital. That has ranged from moving forward with a triumphal arch that dwarfs the tallest structure in the district, the Washington Monument, to removing iconic cherry blossom trees along the East Potomac Park.  Over the summer, the Trump administration charged Hearn, an Olympic canoeist, with more than $1,000 worth of damage to the reflecting pool on June 19. When Pirro asked the court to dismiss the charges, Trump was angered. Trump said that Pirro “choked” and “folded like an umbrella” and pushed for charges to be refiled.“Frankly, I think she choked because the judge was really vicious. Instead of going after the people that did it, the judge went after her and went after her department, and I guess she choked,” Trump told reporters. “I don’t know what the hell happened.”Pirro said her office wouldn’t have sought charges if the Interior Department, which manages the Lincoln Memorial, had initially shared more information about repair work on the reflecting pool.Supporters rallyAttorneys for Hearn, as well as dozens of supporters, gathered outside D.C. Superior Court before the hearing. They included Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, who slammed the Trump administration for initially bringing felony charges against Hearn. “Stop setting up our citizens for fraudulent purposes,” said Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee. 

 







Supporters of Olympian David Hearn of Bethesda, Maryland, who has pleaded not guilty to charges of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, gather outside District of Columbia Superior Court on Sept. 4, 2026. (Photo by Ariana Figueroa/States Newsroom)

After the hearing, Hearn gave a brief statement. “This is not about me, this is about defending democracy,” he said. One of his attorneys, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Fund, said if his client could be charged, then “every American is at risk.”Edelman said he would make a decision soon.

The five-year program awarded West Virginia nearly $199 million for the first year. It’s[...]
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Friday that $2.4 million of West Virginia's Rural Health Transformation Program funding will go toward three organizations to expand employer-based health services. (Screenshot courtesy  Morrisey's office)The state of West Virginia will award $2.4 million of its federal Rural Health Transformation Program funding to three organizations to expand worksite and employer-based health services. 
It’s the first announced allocation of the state’s funding from the federal money. The five-year program awarded West Virginia nearly $199 million for the first year. It’s meant to “transform the existing rural health care infrastructure and build sustainable health care systems that expand access, enhance quality of care, and improve outcomes for patients,” according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
Gov. Patrick Morrisey on Friday announced allocations of $1.17 million to the Spotted Owl Health Care Organization and its partner the Chesapeake Healthcare Center, $612,000 to Charleston Area Medical Center and $612,000 to the Cabell Huntington Foundation. The money will be used to help expand worksite clinics and employer-based healthcare services that residents access care where they work, according to a news release from the state.
“We are putting these historic resources to work to improve the health of West Virginians and strengthen our workforce,” Morrisey said in the release. “By bringing healthcare closer to where people work, we can identify health problems earlier, better manage chronic conditions, and help more West Virginians stay healthy and on the job. These first awards are another important step toward transforming healthcare delivery across our state.”
The Rural Health Transformation Program is funded by the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. It was part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which President Donald Trump signed into law last summer. The law made historic cuts to healthcare and food assistance spending in the United States.
Dale Witte, a spokesman for Vandalia Health, parent company of CAMC, said the hospital will use the money to establish a statewide network by integrating employer-based access points with Vandalia’s primary care locations, mobile clinical assets and telemedicine hubs.
The program, called Vandalia WorkWell Connect, aims to “identify chronic disease risk earlier, connect employees to timely primary and specialty care, support functional ability and work-status coordination, reduce avoidable health events, and generate standardized workforce and health outcome data for the State,” Witte said. 
The $2.4 million will come from West Virginia’s Health to Prosperity (HTP) initiative, one of seven key parts of Morrisey’s plan for the funding. Additional announcements of grants are coming, Morrisey said. Singh told lawmakers recently the program is on track to obligate its entire $199 million in Rural Health funds by Oct. 30 to meet a federal deadline.
“These first awards represent an important investment in the health of West Virginia’s workforce,” Singh said in the release Friday. “Expanding access to care through worksite clinics can help people address health concerns earlier, better manage chronic conditions, and stay connected to work and their communities. That’s good for workers, families, employers, and the State as a whole.”

name: WyoFile
title: Wind River church leader seeks stalking orders against protesters amid controversy
description:
The protesters deny making any threats and plan to challenge the request at an upcoming court hearing.
The post Wind River church leader seeks stalking orders against protesters amid controversy appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Darci Quiver pulled out her cellphone and pressed record as the law enforcement officer approached her vehicle. 
He pulled out a packet of papers. “Anybody can put in the paperwork. This is just to go to court,” he explained. The papers were a petition for a stalking order of protection filed against her, submitted by Foundations For Nations Pastor Sarah Lucas. 
The officer told Quiver she could defend herself against the requested order at a court appearance on Tuesday, Sept. 8, and in the meantime, she needed to stay away from the Lucas family — including their church property just outside Riverton on the Wind River Reservation. He advised her to take alternate roads to avoid the listed locations, “because if you’re in observation distance, spying distance, even with binoculars, that would be bad,” he said. 
“Thanks,” responded Quiver. 
“No problem. Good luck,” said the officer. 
“Consider me served,” Quiver replied. 
Quiver and fellow protestor Alice Thomas were both served with a petition for a stalking order of protection on Sept. 1. It’s the latest chapter in a mounting conflict between some tribal members and Foundations For Nations Church following a July 5 sermon that many Native community members found deeply offensive. In it, Pastor Sarah Lucas suggested Native people should turn away from their traditional ways, calling them a false “idol.”
Each Sunday since, protestors have lined up along Rendezvous Road outside the church, some carrying signs ranging from Bible verses to those that appear more threatening.  
While Sarah and her husband Jason Lucas, who serve as co-pastors and founders of the church, described recent protests as peaceful, they’ve also faced death threats online and significant disruption to their church programming and daily lives. 
For the past eight weeks, Sarah Lucas wrote in a statement as part of the order petition, protestors, including Thomas and Quiver, have shouted and displayed signs “that I consider threatening, degrading, or harassing. [Thomas’] repeated presence and conduct have caused me significant emotional distress and have also affected members of our church.” 
Alice Thomas, second from left, speaks with a Foundations For Nations parishioner who had come out to chat and hand out hand-written Bible verses during a Sunday protest in August. (Sarah Elmquist Squires/The Ranger)
In an interview, Thomas denied making threats of violence against the Lucas family. 
“I’ve never threatened her,” Thomas said. “I’ve never voiced that I was going to cause her bodily harm. I have never gone out of my way to seek [the Lucas family] out, other than to protest on the side of the road at the church.”
In an August interview, Sarah and Jason Lucas said that in the days after the controversial sermon, they hoped that the controversy would die down. Instead, they said they’ve faced persistent threats, and are ready to take legal action. “[There are] posts of them scalping me and burning down our church. And so you don’t know if that’s going to be true or not,” Sarah Lucas described, adding that the family had been in contact with the Riverton Police Department, Bureau of Indian Affairs, FBI and the Fremont County Sheriff’s Office. “We’re going to start moving forward with the law on harassment charges and things like that.” 
The spark of a sermon
The July 5 sermon came on the last day of the Northern Arapaho Tribe’s sacred Sundance ceremony. 
“I pray as the people coming out of Sundance today, their last day, they’re going back into community,” Sarah Lucas said during her sermon, which was recorded on video that went viral within days. “You have generations, generations, centuries of people doing this offering, going in and being, making vows to change, Father God. And we see no fruit.” 
The pastor encouraged members of her congregation, which includes Native parishioners, to give up traditional spiritual practices like Sundance that she said included idol worship. She focused on the Northern Arapaho Tribe’s traditional pipe, sometimes referred to as grandfather or old man, which is used at Sundance and is one of the tribe’s most sacred objects. 
“The pipe cannot hear your prayers. It’s just a piece of material, right? And this is a cycle that they’re caught up in, and this is all they’ve ever known,” Sarah Lucas said during the sermon. “And the Lord is saying ‘Tear down the idols, tear down the altars, the idol worship.” 
Two days after the sermon, more than 100 people gathered for the first of many protests outside the church. The video, memes, threats and criticism have circulated widely on social media. 
The Northern Arapaho Business Council told the Lucases to leave the reservation. But the Lucas family owns the reservation property and has vowed to continue to share their love of Christ through their church and programming. 
Continued conflict

Sarah and Jason Lucas are co-pastors and founders of Foundations For Nations Church on the Wind River Reservation. (Courtesy/The Ranger/WyoToday Media)

The Lucases also operate a food bank in Riverton, and shortly after the July 5 sermon, the Food Bank of Wyoming halted the contract that had supplied bulk food for distribution there. The Lucases said in an interview that Food Bank of Wyoming claimed to have received a complaint of discrimination. But they contend that they’ve never denied a needy person food at their nonprofit or discriminated against anyone, and that Sarah Lucas’ sermon is protected speech that has nothing to do with their food pantry operations. 
The Northern Arapaho Tribe crafted a policy in the weeks after the July 5 sermon, one requiring that outside organizations consult with the tribe to conduct recurring events and operations on the reservation. The Eastern Shoshone Tribe quickly followed suit with a policy of its own. 
When it announced the new policy, the Northern Arapaho Business Council said in a statement that after a thorough review of internal documents, it found no evidence of any formal agreements or correspondence with Foundations For Nations leaders regarding their operations on the reservation. The Lucases pushed back on that statement, sharing a thick packet of communication with tribal officials dating back to at least 2020 and showing evidence of repeated meetings and discussion about events and operations at their church property. 
“I’m writing in support of your kids’ summer program on behalf of the Northern Arapaho Tribe,” former Business Council Chairman Lee Spoonhunter wrote in a June 9, 2020, email to Sarah Lucas. “Please be safe and have fun!”
After weeks of relative silence following the July 5 sermon, Sarah and Jason Lucas sat down for an interview with The Ranger/WyoToday Media. They described navigating the persistent conflicts that have come as a result of the sermon, including partnering with a national law firm to file a formal discrimination claim with the USDA over their contract with Food Bank of Wyoming. Sarah Lucas reflected on the sermon, sharing an apology for how she delivered it that day. “However, the word of God remains the same. And I can’t apologize for something that I gave my life up for.”
Foundations For Nations church property sits just outside Riverton on the Wind River Reservation. (Sarah Elmquist Squires/The Ranger)
Day in court
On Thursday, Thomas shared photos of the protest signs she’s held week after week on Sundays outside the church. She acknowledged that others have posted threats against the Lucases online, but insists she’s never made threats or surveilled the Lucas family. 
“I can’t tell these people, ‘You can’t put that on there,’ because it’s their right to put whatever they want [on protest signs]. They have a freedom of speech; they have a right to protest,” she said. “I have not seen [Sarah Lucas] since July 5. I’ve never seen her in person other than sitting outside her church. I’ve never come face-to-face with her since.”
Thomas shared the papers she was served with for the order of protection petition, and denied many of the claims it contained. The court filing says that Thomas went to the Lucases’ home and photographed it, then posted the family’s address on social media. Thomas claims she simply took a screenshot of a Google maps image, and figured the location was common knowledge. She admitted that she’d taken a photo of the Lucas family’s rental property in an attempt to document that it was occupied. 
“The fear caused by Alice’s repeated conduct has significantly changed my daily life and behavior,” Sarah Lucas wrote in the petition. “I no longer feel comfortable walking to or from my vehicle by myself. My husband now escorts me to and from my car because I am afraid of being approached, confronted, followed, or harmed … Because Alice has repeatedly appeared at places where I live, worship, and regularly spend time, and because she photographed and publicly shared information about our property, seeing someone outside a window causes me to become fearful and concerned that Alice or someone acting because of her social media posts may be outside.”
Thomas said she intends to continue protesting, but she’ll move away from the church location and instead find a spot along Mission Road. “If I have to go post up at Mission Road with my protest signs, I will,” Thomas said. “And if that’s what she needs to feel safe, then that’s what she needs to feel safe. But I’m not going to stop protesting.” 
Thomas named a spot along Mission Road where the church isn’t within eyesight, but “it doesn’t matter which direction they come from, they will have to drive past us to get to her church, and they will have to see our signs every Sunday … I’ve been [protesting] since day one, and I’m going to continue to do this until she leaves. It’s too late for an apology now.” 
The Lucases said they’d prefer not to comment until their day in court on Tuesday. But in their interview last month, Lucas described frustration and fear as a result of the continued conflict, protests, and threats. “Our hearts toward the community remains the same … Our church needs to know that this is a safe place to come to … I had two non-Native Americans this Sunday saying, ‘I’m done with the harassment of the, taking pictures of us in my cars and putting it on social media. When can we get them for stalking, harassment?’ … Where’s the justice for what they’re doing?”
The parties are expected to appear in court on Tuesday afternoon for the petitioned orders of protection.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Fifth Circuit upholds dismissal of Jacksonians’ lawsuit against city over lead in water
description: The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals buildng in New Orleans.
text:
The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday affirmed the dismissal of a lawsuit against Jackson alleging the city knowingly allowed residents to drink contaminated water. A group of residents filed the lawsuit in 2022, before it was dismissed in U.S. District Court in 2024.
The plaintiffs — residents Priscilla Sterling, Raine Becker, Shawn Miller and John Bennett — alleged that the city’s actions and failures caused lead to enter Jackson’s drinking water and that city officials later misrepresented that the water was safe to drink. The lawsuit claims the contamination violated Jacksonians’ right to “bodily integrity.”
The allegations point to testing from the Mississippi State Department of Health from 2010 to 2013 that showed lead in the city’s water was “increasing at an alarming rate.”
“Rather than take the needed steps to stop lead from leaching further into the water, the City ignored warnings, even actively switching a section of the City’s water source from a safe groundwater system to the corrosive surface water system that was already causing lead to leach from its pipes into residents’ drinking water,” the plaintiffs wrote in their 2024 appeal.
The lawsuit named as defendants: the city, former mayors Chokwe A. Lumumba and Tony Yarber; former public works directors Kishia Powell, Robert Miller and Jerriot Smash; and Trilogy Engineering Services.  
In affirming the district court’s 2022 ruling, the court said that while the alleged deprivations of clean water and honest information are “grievous,” they “do not infringe upon any deeply rooted constitutional right.” The opinion added that the allegations aren’t comparable to bodily integrity cases the court has previously ruled on, such as those arguing assault or forced surgery.
“We are skeptical that the right to not be harmed by lead-contaminated water fits within the right to bodily integrity, and Plaintiffs point us to no historical tradition or Supreme Court precedent convincing us otherwise,” Judge Kurt Engelhardt wrote. 
Engelhardt added there is no “constitutional right to truthful information from officials during a public health crisis.” The plaintiffs, though, have other avenues to pursue justice in the matter, he said. 
“The Constitution does not provide a remedy for Plaintiffs’ injuries,” the opinion argued. “But that does not mean they are without a remedy. Plaintiffs may pursue tort claims against Defendants, elect officials who will better manage the water system and provide accurate information to the public, or petition their state and federal legislatures for other remedies.”
Jackson Mayor John Horhn said in a statement Friday, “We are pleased that the Fifth Circuit upheld the dismissal of these claims. The City remains committed to the health, safety, and well-being of every Jackson resident.”

title: DNR investigating fish kill, likely manure spill in Dry Branch Creek
description: The Iowa Department of Natural Resources is investigating the source of murky water and high ammonia levels in Dry Branch Creek that resulted in a fish kill.  According to a news release from the department, staff were notified Thursday of a possible fish kill and “a strong smell of manure” in the creek near Ossian.  […]
text:
Iowa Department of Natural Resources is investigating a fish kill in Dry Branch Creek, pictured here as it flows under 110th Street. (Photo via Google Earth) The Iowa Department of Natural Resources is investigating the source of murky water and high ammonia levels in Dry Branch Creek that resulted in a fish kill. 
According to a news release from the department, staff were notified Thursday of a possible fish kill and “a strong smell of manure” in the creek near Ossian. 
At the site, DNR staff observed dead fish and “cloudy” conditions in the creek. 
Water samples tested positive for ammonia, according to the news release. 
As staff examined the site, they found more dead fish three miles downstream as the creek exits Winneshiek County and flows into Fayette County. 
According to DNR water segment data, there have been three other fish kills in Dry Branch Creek, attributed to fertilizer, organic material or animal waste. 
DNR is still investigating the source of the incident, but advises downstream users to avoid using water from the creek.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Congressional debate up in the air in Nebraska’s 1st District
description: Debates for Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District are up in the air after public spats from the candidates.
text:
U.S. Rep. Mike Flood, R-Neb., left, and Democrat Chris Backemeyer will face off for Nebraska's 1st Congressional District in November 2026. (Candidate photos courtesy of respective campaigns | U.S. Capitol photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)LINCOLN — Debates for Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District are up in the air after public spats from the candidates. 
Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Flood and Democratic challenger Chris Backemeyer pointed fingers at each other after each declined particular dates to debate. Flood’s camp wanted to hold a debate before early voting ballots are mailed out later this month, while Backemeyer offered different dates in October due to scheduling conflicts. 
Flood’s campaign released a statement late Thursday afternoon, saying that Backemeyer had turned down multiple date suggestions for the Nebraska Public Media debate. 
“Nebraskans deserve an opportunity to hear from both candidates before voting begins. Chris Backemeyer told Nebraska media he wants to debate, but back-track Backemeyer turned down multiple dates when it came time to schedule it,” Brentin Ungar, Flood’s campaign manager, said in the statement. 
Hours later, Backemeyer released his own statement, saying Flood had declined the League of Women Voters’ invitation to its debate earlier this week, though the invitations had been sent out in July. The League of Women Voters, in an Aug. 31 newsletter, also said Flood had declined their debate. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Flood’s press release focused only on the debate hosted by Nebraska Public Media.
Backemeyer said if Flood “is so busy that he can’t talk to Nebraskans in the entire month of October, he should just come out and say it.” 
The former diplomat said the offer to debate on any day in October still stands. He added that Flood is running away from his record as he “doesn’t want to stand on a stage and defend a war with no strategy, a bill he admits he didn’t read, and tariffs crushing our farmers.” 
Nebraska Public Media spokesperson told the Omaha World-Herald the three outlets planning the debate “continue to talk with the candidates to identify a date that works for everyone.”
NPM, the World-Herald, and KRVN radio are involved in organizing the debate. 
The 1st District comprises 12 counties, including Lancaster County, which is home to heavily Democratic Lincoln, whose blue voters often are outvoted by the region’s more conservative smaller cities and rural areas.
Flood has won his past two U.S. House elections by 20 and 16 percentage points, respectively. Analysts, including the nonpartisan Center for Politics, the Cook Political Report and Inside Elections, consider the 1st District seat safely Republican — though national Democrats see the race as competitive.
In addition to Flood and Backemeyer, the America First Party has a candidate in the race, Dan Hartong. Libertarian Nik Sandman is also running. 
The general election is Nov. 3.
