name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC Senate’s pet projects give glimpse into budget with no direct nonprofit funding
description: Legislators made a gentlemen's agreement not to send money directly to nonprofits in the spirit of accountability.
text:
Legislators came to an agreement not to send money directly to nonprofits during the upcoming budget cycle, but that doesn't mean money won't still go to certain organizations. (Photo by Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA)COLUMBIA — When legislators passed a $350 million spending deal, they announced an agreement to change how the funding is doled out next year, including not sending money directly to nonprofits.
The Senate’s spending this year is an example of how that might look.
The Senate’s list of projects, which totals about $110 million, technically sends money only to local cities and counties, at the insistence of Finance Chairman Harvey Peeler.
But some spending will flow through local governments to nonprofits for work in the communities, including one conservation earmark by Peeler, according to backup budget documents provided by Gov. Henry McMaster’s office.
When announcing the changes on the floor last week, senators touted the idea as a way of increasing accountability in the process.
“My hope from that would be that local governments are going to try to monitor those nonprofits,” Senate Majority Leader Shane Massey said when legislators passed the spending bill. “That’s been one of my frustrations with nonprofits, is that you can’t monitor it.”
All told, more than $5 million in the Senate’s spending on local projects will go through a government agency to get to a nonprofit — a small fraction of the total.
The House, which did send money directly to nonprofits, is slated to follow next year, representatives said.
The agreement, which came as part of a deal to fund the hundreds of local projects left out of the full state spending plan, was not approved in the form of legislation or chamber rules. Instead, it’s a so-called gentlemen’s agreement between the chambers’ lead budget writers: Peeler and House Ways and Means Chairman Bruce Bannister.
The budget writers also agreed to keep spending more equal between the House and Senate and to pass a stopgap spending bill earlier in the year, preventing end-of-session gamesmanship between the chambers to avoid the possibility of a government shutdown.
Discussions about how to decide which projects get funded will continue, legislators said.
Critics of the process have pointed particularly to nonprofit earmarks. Past spending has gone to organizations with little background, religious affiliations or legislative ties. Some nonprofits have received money year after year, amounting to annual funding.
Churches, charities with little track record among nonprofits in line for $90M in SC budget

To create an added layer of government, senators this year included a “receiving entity” in their requests. The receiving local government can either use the money for a local project or disburse the dollars to a nonprofit.
For instance, Peeler sent $2 million to the city of York as one of his nine earmarks. The money will then go on to the Yorkville Agricultural and Education Society, a nonprofit, to preserve roughly 120 acres at the site of an abandoned orphanage.
The city of York didn’t ask for funding for the project, which is referred to as “Project Green Landing” in budget documents. But the city, which has backed the work, will become responsible for passing along the funds.
Peeler considered the project worth funding in a year of little nonprofit spending on the Senate side because of development from the Charlotte suburbs encroaching on York County, the Gaffney Republican said.
“Charlotte is spilling into York County, taking up agricultural land, any kind of vacant buildings, anything that doesn’t have something to save it,” Peeler said. “So, locals need to get behind it, and I felt like it was a worthy cause for an earmark.”
Direct funding
Legislators generally agree sending the funds through government agencies is a better method than giving the money to nonprofits directly.
“All of these projects on the Senate side are going to be subject to the oversight of state or county agencies,” said Sen. Chip Campsen. “We’re not just relying upon other entities other than that.”
“There’s more accountability and more experience,” the Isle of Palms Republican added.
Local governments are subject to regular audits, making it easier to track whether money is spent correctly. Adding a level of responsibility for local officials makes it more likely the money will get spent the way legislators intended, they said.
Since legislators control some of the funding local governments receive, they’re more likely than a nonprofit to ensure the money is spent appropriately, some said.
“I do think it’s a better way of doing it,” said Sen. Ed Sutton. “You’ve got another set of eyes looking at it.”
Sutton, a Charleston Democrat, requested funding for a resource center for homeless people run through the city of Charleston and nonprofit Star Gospel Mission. Charleston city officials asked for the money, and Sutton agreed the issue needed addressing, he said.
SC legislators approve $350M in earmarks, agree to changes next year

“I wouldn’t put my name on something I couldn’t defend myself,” Sutton said.
Local governments can have problems of their own, said Rep. Jordan Pace, who chairs the ultra-conservative Freedom Caucus.
Pace generally opposes earmarks as what he and his caucus view as examples of government overspending. Still, he agreed sending the money through local governments is a better idea than simply handing it to nonprofits.
Nonprofits aren’t subject to the same open records laws as governments, making spending more difficult to track. If legislators aren’t sure where money went, they have a harder time figuring that out if a nonprofit had it than a government entity, he said.
That doesn’t make local governments infallible, Pace said.
“It may have the veneer of accountability, but I don’t think it’s enough of a change to make the process palatable,” said the Goose Creek Republican.
If legislators are going to continue funding local projects, Pace would like to see a grant program put in place with solid caps on spending and a system of checks through government agencies. He proposed a bill that would do just that, though it had no chance. He introduced it when the Legislature returned last month for a one-day session to approve the $350 million in spending. He’d have to reintroduce it next year.
A place for nonprofits
Some legislators have floated the idea of removing nonprofits from the earmark process entirely. Others say nonprofits fill gaps government services don’t reach.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The state simply doesn’t do it all, and we have so many great nonprofits that provide necessary services,” said Sen. Deon Tedder.
That’s especially true in rural areas, said the North Charleston Democrat. Shelters for survivors of domestic violence, rehabilitation services and food banks are all often run by nonprofits, and without funding, those might simply cease to exist in certain parts of the state, he said.
Other organizations that aren’t providing life-saving resources can bring a major boon to the state, Tedder said.
That was why he requested money for the International African American Museum, which received $500,000 to boost its marketing. While the museum, which opened in 2023, receives donations, state support can help increase its reach and draw in more visitors, Tedder said.
More visitors could also fill fundraising gaps. In June, the museum announced furloughs for all employees through year’s end.
Tourists traveling to visit the museum will spend money throughout the entire area, Tedder said.
“It’s a great return on investment, and we need to continue to support it,” he said.
Campsen had the same line of thinking when asking for money to build a recreational area on Edisto Island, he said.
The rural sea island in Charleston County has a permanent population of about 1,600, excluding the beach town that’s actually in Colleton County. Such a small tax base can’t support major local projects, such as a public park, he said. The spending plan sends $1 million to nonprofit Edisto Island Youth Recreation to build a community recreation center.
“If it weren’t for this process, they would just be kind of left out,” Campsen said.
Even legislators who generally focus their attention on local governments sometimes find a nonprofit worth supporting. Sens. Ronnie Cromer and Danny Verdin both said they prefer to make requests for government-based projects but asked for money to help nonprofits this year.
Cromer’s ask sent $20,000 to St. Paul African Methodist Episcopal Church to fix up one of a dwindling number of Rosenwald schools, built during the 1920s to give Black children in the South access to education. The schools are an important piece of history and hold a special place in alumni’s hearts, said the Prosperity Republican.
SC had 500 Rosenwald schools for Black children. Nonprofits want to save the 44 that remain.

Verdin’s $500,000 will help restore the McCullough House in Honea Path to its early 19th century glory, he said. The oldest brick building in Greenville County, which dates back to 1812, is “a gem” for the state, and Verdin felt it important to make sure it keeps standing for years to come, he said.
“If you get the right equation, it’s very possible that nonprofits or not-for-profits can be incorporated into the process,” the Laurens Republican said.
Not every nonprofit is the same, said House Majority Leader Micah Caskey, R-West Columbia. Both nonprofits and local governments exist along a spectrum of capability, he said.
When deciding which nonprofits are deserving of funding, legislators said they look for a long track record of good work. Verdin is partial to “brick and mortar” projects that bring a visible change and keep a building standing. Cromer suggested funding projects that are already underway as opposed to those that are still theoretical, though he added that can be difficult.
“We’ve got a lot of nonprofits,” Cromer said. “It’s kind of hard to choose the ones that are the most worthy and to do that follow-up.”
A nonprofit should be able to show its impact in order to get state funding, Tedder said. He didn’t think nonprofits were so much of the problem as the process of deciding which projects get money.
As is, legislators send requests to the budget writers, who choose what to fund and how much money to spend. Legislators can submit supporting documentation about why they want funding for a certain project, but there’s very little scrutiny over where money goes, he said.
“We just need a better process of going through and vetting the requests,” Tedder said.
Legislators also agreed they need more accountability once the money is spent. During the debate over the spending plan, legislators in both chambers pointed fingers at each other and claimed their colleagues were less transparent about their spending.
Publicly available information on where taxpayer funds are going has improved significantly in recent years.
Gone are the days when legislators’ requests were hidden in vaguely worded lump sums to agencies, when only the budget writers knew where the money was going.
It’s been five years since a Senate rule began requiring a listing of all legislator-sponsored spending, which was supposed to allow public debate about the worthiness of individual projects. But the few words per project offered little-to-no actual information about the intended spending.
In 2023, legislators began providing McMaster paperwork to back up their requests so he wouldn’t veto them, which the governor’s office makes publicly available after the spending’s approved. Yet, some projects still don’t include documentation of where the money is going or why other than a brief statement written by the legislator asking for the funding.
And problems persist in making sure money gets where it’s supposed to go, legislators said. No follow-up exists on the back end, leaving legislators on their own to find out if the projects they funded ever got done.
How to address those concerns will be part of the ongoing conversations about how to move forward with earmark funding, Caskey said.
“We are leagues better than we were when I first got here in terms of transparency,” said Caskey, who was first elected in 2016. “But there’s more to be done.”

name: National
title: Federal appeals court to consider Louisiana’s arguments for banning telehealth abortion
description: Next week, the U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals will consider Louisiana’s arguments for tightening federal policy around a common abortion and miscarriage drug. The primary target of Louisiana v. Food and Drug Administration and similar lawsuits against mifepristone is to end a Biden-era policy allowing abortion pills to be prescribed without an in-person v[...]
text:
The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals will hear oral arguments for Louisiana v. U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Wednesday at the federal courthouse in New Orleans. Medication abortion has become the most common form of abortion since Roe v. Wade was overturned in 2022, and telehealth prescriptions have continued to rise. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)Next week, the U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals will consider Louisiana’s arguments for tightening federal policy around a common abortion and miscarriage drug. The primary target of Louisiana v. Food and Drug Administration and similar lawsuits against mifepristone is to end a Biden-era policy allowing abortion pills to be prescribed without an in-person visit with a provider. 
Medication abortion has become the most common form of abortion since Roe v. Wade was overturned in 2022, and telehealth prescriptions have continued to rise. The Biden administration loosened telehealth regulations in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. 
According to the Guttmacher Institute, a research think tank that supports abortion access, about 91,000 abortions were provided last year via telehealth prescription of abortion medication sent by mail to states with bans, including more than 9,300 in Louisiana.
Unpacking the fight over telehealth access to abortion medication

The FDA’s policy that mailing abortion pills is safe is unlikely to change in the next few months. The Trump administration has asked courts to delay the cases until it finishes a highly anticipated safety review about mifepristone. Numerous studies have concluded the medicine, which also is used to manage miscarriage treatment, is safe to prescribe through telehealth.
The case is one of three federal lawsuits — the others are being considered in Missouri and Texas — that could affect telehealth access to mifepristone nationwide.
“What this is doing is shutting down access to people in states that have committed to continuing to make abortion legal, and it will impact people in all 50 states,” said Melissa Grant, co-founder of carafem, which operates telehealth or physical health centers in 21 states where abortion remains legal.  
Earlier this year, the 5th Circuit ruled in favor of Louisiana’s motion to temporarily reinstate an old rule that patients could only receive mifepristone in person. The Supreme Court blocked that ruling, allowing telehealth abortion to continue as the case progresses. Whatever the appeals court rules this time, it will likely go back to the Supreme Court for a final ruling on Louisiana’s motion to reverse the policy until the case is decided on the merits.
Two years ago, the U.S. Supreme Court dismissed a lawsuit seeking to restrict mifepristone, brought by Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, ruling the doctor-plaintiffs did not have proper standing to sue.
But Gabriella McIntyre, legal counsel of Alliance Defending Freedom, which is helping to defend Louisiana and one of its residents, a co-plaintiff who says her then-boyfriend coerced her into taking abortion pills, believes her team can persuade the 5th Circuit on Wednesday that Louisiana has proper standing.



Quotation







If Louisiana wins this case, we’re going to see for the first time what it looks like under an actual Dobbs regime, where pro-life states get to enforce their laws protecting the unborn.


– Gabriella McIntyre, legal counsel of Alliance Defending Freedom


The state is arguing in part that the 2023 FDA rule violated the 2022 Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization decision by allowing for telehealth abortion and abortion by mail in states that banned abortion, like Louisiana. The FDA has so far argued Louisiana doesn’t have standing to sue and that it needs more time to review the drug’s safety. Two mifepristone drugmakers have intervened on the FDA’s side.
“If Louisiana wins this case, we’re going to see for the first time what it looks like under an actual Dobbs regime, where pro-life states get to enforce their laws protecting the unborn,” McIntyre said.
Abortion law expert Mary Ziegler said she expects the conservative 5th Circuit to side with Louisiana and that its justification will likely serve as a roadmap for the U.S. Supreme Court. 
“The 5th Circuit, they’re going to be writing almost like a proposed first draft for the U.S. Supreme Court,” Ziegler said. “Maybe the court has questions about standing again so, ‘We want to focus the hearing and the opinions on standing because we think that’s the hurdle that we have to overcome to get the five votes at the Supreme Court.’ Or do they talk about everything, and just sort of let the chips fall where they may?”
The Trump administration has reversed several Biden-era reproductive health policies, but not the 2023 rule, citing an ongoing review expected to be released after the November midterm elections. But recently confirmed Attorney General Todd Blanche recently promised faith leaders he will focus on restricting abortion pill access. 
Oral arguments will be livestreamed through the court system at 9 a.m. CDT on Wednesday.
Stateline reporter Sofia Resnick can be reached at sresnick@stateline.org.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: At the Minnesota State Fair, underdog candidates find an even playing field
description: Chip Tangen is sure to lose in November. He’s the Libertarian candidate for secretary of state. But there he is in the blazing heat at the Minnesota State Fair, waving to passersby and handing out campaign fliers with the enthusiasm of a candidate sailing to victory. The State Fair offers a unique opportunity to reach […]
text:
Chip Tangen, Libertarian candidate for Secretary of State, shows how few legislative districts have third-party candidates with his prize wheel at the Minnesota State Fair on Aug. 27, 2026. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer) Chip Tangen is sure to lose in November. He’s the Libertarian candidate for secretary of state.
But there he is in the blazing heat at the Minnesota State Fair, waving to passersby and handing out campaign fliers with the enthusiasm of a candidate sailing to victory.
The State Fair offers a unique opportunity to reach tens of thousands of voters for underdog candidates without well-funded campaigns or armies of volunteers — like minor party candidates, as well as Republicans running in indigo blue Minneapolis or Democrats in ruby red regions of greater Minnesota.
“It’s a good equalizer,” Tangen said at his post in front of the Libertarian Party stand. “Right next door is (GOP Attorney General candidate) Ron Schutz and then just beyond that is my opponent Tad Jude. We’re all talking on an equal basis with people.”
For Tangen, the state fairgrounds played a critical role in getting on the ballot to begin with. Minor party candidates for statewide office must collect 2,000 signatures, a threshold Tangen failed to clear in his campaign four years ago. Earlier this year, however, he and his wife attended an event at the fairgrounds and collected a few hundred in one fell swoop.
It may not close yawning gaps, but it does advance the goals many candidates pursue in longshot bids: promoting their ideas, injecting some more competition into our democracy and building support for others in the party.
Raising awareness about the plight of third-party candidates is the centerpiece of Tangen’s campaign. He thinks the state makes it too difficult to get on the ballot, which entrenches the two-party system and leaves voters with fewer choices.
“I do want to get the attention of one Minnesotan in particular, and his name is (Secretary of State) Steve Simon,” Tangen said. “I hope he stops by my booth, and we can have a conversation about ballot access laws.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Tangen used to be a Republican. He worked for U.S. Rep. Jim Ramstad, who represented Minnesota’s 3rd Congressional District for nearly two decades. Now he’s more of a swing voter longing for a viable alternative to the GOP and DFL.
Independent candidates can win, Tangen contends, citing former Gov. Jesse Ventura, though Ventura had the benefit of fame from his years on television performing piledrivers and power slams in the wrestling ring.
Tangen draws people to his party booth near the Department of Natural Resource’s native fish pond with the chance to win a prize by spinning a wheel with all 201 legislative races listed. If they land on the one with more than two candidates, they win a yellow bracelet. Everyone loves fair freebies.
Like a rigged ball toss game on the Mighty Midway, however, the odds are low: Just six legislative seats have a third-party candidate this year. There’s a better chance of landing on one of the 19 legislative races with only one candidate running.
All 19 candidates running unopposed are Democrats, who for the first time in history have fielded a candidate in all 201. It’s a remarkable feat that should help bolster their odds in statewide races by giving Democrats in red districts another reason to get to the polls.
“It’s because of our oppressive ballot access laws,” Tangen said.
‘The reverse door knock’
Doug Chapin estimates he shook about 1,000 hands each day he’s been at the fair in his bid to represent the 6th Congressional District, a seat held by powerful U.S. Rep. Tom Emmer since 2015.
“As a candidate, it’s kind of the ultimate hustle play,” Chapin said. “It’s like a reverse door knock.”
Doug Chapin, Democratic challenger to U.S. Rep. Tom Emmer, celebrates winning the animal calling contest with his cow moo at the Minnesota State Fair on Sept. 1, 2026. (Courtesy photo)
His greatest achievement from campaigning at the State Fair is likely to be his first-place prize in the animal calling contest at the Moo Booth  — not a seat in Congress. He received 10s across the board for his cow moo, beating out a slew of other local “celebrities” like a roller derby player and a Princess Kay of the Milky Way finalist.
Chapin isn’t offended by being called a longshot candidate. He knows Emmer, the 3rd ranking Republican in Congress, has won re-election five times with about 62% of the vote.
But Chapin also has the hallmark optimism of the underdog.
“As someone who’s studied election returns through the years, that’s a really soft 62%,” Chapin said. “I think it’s as much a function of the Democrats not actually running anybody trying to win.”
Chapin spent his career in elections policy and administration, overseeing the elections team at The Pew Charitable Trusts and founding a program in election administration at the University of Minnesota’s Humphrey School of Public Affairs.
He believes the district can be flipped, and his campaign is laying the groundwork, if not for this November then in 2028. He’s already committed to running again.
He points out that the district is rapidly growing and changing, and that Republicans face significant headwinds in the midterms with an unpopular president in the White House. He counted 33,000 people who voted for Sen. Amy Klobuchar in 2024 but not for a candidate in the 6th Congressional District race. If they voted for him, that could make him competitive.
“Folks out here are ready for something better,” Chapin said. “The goal is to win, but we’re looking to change the fortunes of Democrats across the district.”
Long odds, high hopes
John Nagel rejects the premise that he’s an underdog in his race against Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar in the 5th Congressional District, even though she’s won her last two general elections with 74% of the vote.
“People need change. They need a normal guy,” Nagel said. “They need someone who grew up here.” (Omar moved to Minnesota at age 14.)
John Nagel, Republican challenger to Rep. Ilhan Omar, talks to voters at the GOP booth at the Minnesota State Fair on Aug. 27, 2026. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)
Wearing a denim shirt with the state seal (the old one, of course) and a Lisa Demuth for governor pin, Nagel shook hands with voters perusing a table of free Minnesota state flags (the old ones, of course) and Alpha News hand fans at the Minnesota GOP booth.
He’s running on his Minnesota roots and experience as a state trooper of 30 years.
Nagel says he’s more of an independent than a Republican, despite having voted for President Trump three times. In Congress, he wouldn’t show favoritism to one party or the other, he said, likening his approach to the State Patrol, when he worked with Democrats and Republicans.
Case in point: Last time he was at the State Fair, he says he and another man rushed to help a person who collapsed in a seizure. The other man turned out to be the younger brother of Dean Phillips, the former Democratic congressman. The two got the person in an ambulance to receive medical care, proving to Nagel that bipartisanship is still possible.
“Troopers are different. We expect everybody to do their job, to do it well. And if you screw up, you’re going to be held accountable,” Nagel said.
But even with decades of law enforcement experience and his promise to tell it like it is, he had little to say about the conduct of the roughly 3,000 federal agents who descended on Minnesota during the immigration crackdown. He said some things could have been handled differently but couldn’t pass judgment.
“As a state patrol lieutenant, if somebody did something wrong … I will wait until the time the investigation is done,” he said
And the Trump administration blocking state law enforcement from participating in the investigations of the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti?
“I’m not going to second guess it,” Nagel said.
Nagel was approached by a young woman for a hug — the granddaughter of a former officer with whom Nagel walked the Minneapolis beat. She would vote for him, if she only lived in his district.

title: What’s open, closed on Labor Day 2026
description: Unlike some holidays, many stores will be open on Labor Day with only a few services unavailable across CT. Here's what to know.
text:
Labor Day weekend is considered the unofficial last weekend of summer by many, as the last days of the season often means the start of cooler weather.
Observed the first Monday of September, Labor Day celebrates the contributions of workers in the United States. 
This year the holiday falls a bit later than usual, on Sept. 7.
Unlike other federal holidays, most stores choose to keep their doors open on Labor Day with only a handful of services unavailable across Connecticut. That includes major mail or package delivery services, with only one major company planning to deliver on Monday.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: With Pretty Rocks bridge completed, full road use in Alaska’s Denali National Park set to resume
description: Visitors to Denali National Park will be able to motor over the full park road starting next year for the first time since a landslide made the route impassable in the late summer of 2021, the National Park Service said Thursday. Construction crews have completed a 475-foot-long bridge that allows vehicles to avoid an ongoing […]
text:
The completed Pretty Rocks bridge in Denali National Park is seen on Sept. 2, 2026. The bridge allows visitors to travel above an ongoing thaw-induced slide that made the park's sole road impassable at about the midpoint of its 92-mile distance. Vehicle traffic is set to resume next year now that the bridge is completed, the National Park Service said. (Photo provided by the National Park Service)Visitors to Denali National Park will be able to motor over the full park road starting next year for the first time since a landslide made the route impassable in the late summer of 2021, the National Park Service said Thursday.
Construction crews have completed a 475-foot-long bridge that allows vehicles to avoid an ongoing thaw-induced slide at a spot called Pretty Rocks, located about midway along the park’s 92-mile road.
“This is an exciting milestone for Denali and for everyone who has worked over the past five years to restore access to the west end of the park road,” Brooke Merrell, superintendent of Denali National Park and Preserve, said in a statement.
“Building a bridge across an active landslide in one of the most remote and challenging environments in the country required extraordinary collaboration, innovation and determination. We are grateful to the Federal Highway Administration, our project partners and the many people who made this possible, and we look forward to welcoming visitors back to the west end by bus in 2027,” she said.
Visitors on foot and bicycle are now allowed to cross the bridge to travel on the road beyond, the Park Service said. However, a bit more work must be completed to ensure that the road section on the west side of the bridge is ready for vehicle traffic next year.
The bridge project cost about $230 million, officials said. The money came from the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021, disaster-response funds and other sources.
The Pretty Rocks landslide is one of about 150 documented slides along the route, which is the sole road running through the park. But it is the slide that has caused the most trouble.
 

A temporary staircase at the East Fork turnaround area on the Denali National Park road, seen here in May of 2022, gave visitors access to the river plain below the roadbed and a route for exploring park territory beyond the Pretty Rocks closure area. (Photo provided by National Park Service)
 

	It is located at a high point along the road, near the scenic Polychrome Pass area. At the slide site, the rocky slope on one side of the road has been moving gradually for several years. More recently, the movement accelerated, creating maintenance and safety problems. In August of 2021, when large amounts of slope broke away, the Park Service closed the road to traffic.
The park road is generally closed to private traffic beyond the first 15 miles. Most road traffic is by shuttle buses that deliver visitors to hiking and camping sites. The landslide made the road impassable for those buses.
The chosen fix for the problem is the bridge, which passes above the still-moving landslide, along with some work within the road. One feature of the project is the installation of thermosyphons, devices that slow permafrost thaw by releasing heat from the ground.
Thaw of permafrost and melting within rock glaciers — geologic features that are combinations of rock and ice – have been identified as prime causes of the Pretty Rocks slide and other park landslides.
The steep terrain, presence of permafrost and other geologic characteristics made the project complex.
Previously, the Park Service aimed for completion in time to reopen the full road by 2025. Unexpected problems with clay pushed that target to 2026.
During the years of traffic closures at Pretty Rocks, park managers have directed visitors to alternatives. The area beyond Pretty Rocks remained accessible to those willing to hike a detour route down to the valley floor, using a temporary staircase. Customers of lodges just beyond the road’s edge, on private property at a site called Kantishna, were able to travel there by plane. And park managers have emphasized visitor and recreation opportunities in the park’s more accessible frontcountry.
Despite those accommodations, Denali visitation has been reduced during the Pretty Rocks construction years.
In 2019, the year before the COVID-19 pandemic, the park logged about 601,000 visitors. Visitation collapsed by about 90% in the pandemic year of 2020, according to the Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development. Over time, visitation began to recover. The total last year was 543,300, a Denali spokesperson said.
The landslide at Pretty Rocks, at about the halfway point of the Denali National Park road, is seen on May 5, 2023. The slide destroyed a section of road. The project to install a new bridge has been to allow the road to reopen has been challenging because of geologic and logistical complexities. Those include ice-rich permafrost, a band of difficult clay and overall remoteness, (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Recounts taking shape in two Democratic legislative primaries
authors: Sam Drysdale | State House News Service
description: Elections have come down to just a few votes in the high-profile showdown between 19-year legislator Sen. William Brownsberger and challenger Daniel Lander.
text:
THE WEEK’S ALMOST OVER, but two of Tuesday’s legislative races remain unsettled. 
Candidates in a pair of Democratic primaries are pursuing recounts in their races for state Senate and House seats. 
Elections have come down to just a few votes in the high-profile showdown between 19-year legislator Sen. William Brownsberger and challenger Daniel Lander to represent a district of northwestern Boston neighborhoods and surrounding suburbs, and the battle for an open seat in one of Massachusetts’s most purple districts on the South Coast. 
In a race with a reported difference of just three votes out of 24,261 by the AP’s latest unofficial numbers, Brownsberger and Lander have both pulled petitions with the Secretary of State’s office for district-wide recounts, according to the office’s spokesperson. Lander is leading with 12,132 votes to Brownsberger’s 12,129. 
A separate petition is needed for each ward or precinct where a recount is wanted, each with its own signature threshold — 10 for Watertown, Belmont, and Cambridge, and 50 for Boston precincts, all from registered Democrats.
One or both of the candidates would have to file the districtwide recount paperwork with local clerks by 3 p.m. Thursday, which would then head to the secretary’s office on Friday. 
To qualify for a district-wide recount, a race must be within a half a percentage of the total number of voters who cast ballots. It appears this race would qualify, though the AP’s unofficial count does not include provisional or hand-counted ballots.
If official results show by Saturday that it is within a half a percent, the secretary would order a district-wide recount to take place next week. Candidates can also collect petitions to recount on just a precinct or ward level if the election doesn’t qualify district-wide. 
“Thousands of voters braved everything from the rain to moving trucks to make their voices heard yesterday,” Lander’s campaign manager Will Woodring said in a statement on Wednesday, “and every single one of their ballots must be counted. We trust the process—and we look forward to a thorough, fair, and accurate count that reflects the will of the people.”
The race has been in the spotlight as Lander, a former senior policy adviser to Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, framed his challenge around generational change to the status quo and the divide between Brownsberger’s suburban Belmont base and Lander’s Boston home in Fenway. 
It has also been a proxy for tensions over property tax policies between Wu and Senate leadership.
Brownsberger is the highest-ranking member of the Legislature facing a challenger this year, the Senate’s third-in-command.
Lander entered the final stretch of the campaign with a coalition of support, backed by major labor organizations, the Massachusetts Working Families Party, Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Wu.
There is no Republican running for the Senate seat in November’s general election, so whoever comes out on top in the primary is likely heading for Beacon Hill in January. 
While close to 25,000 votes may be re-tallied in the Suffolk & Middlesex District, local election officials on the South Coast may also be recounting ballots next week. 
The 9th Bristol House district, covering Dartmouth and parts of New Bedford, was the only legislative election this cycle with contested primaries in both major parties for the seat that Democrat Rep. Christopher Markey is vacating. In an increasingly purple area, it’s one of the Republican’s best pickup opportunities.
Political newcomer Chester Tam won the Republican primary over New Bedford City Councilor Henry Bousquet, but Democrats are still locked head to head. 
Democrats Edward Pacheco and Stephen Medeiros are competing for their party’s nomination, with Pacheco 14 votes ahead of Medeiros at last count. 
Both campaigns confirmed to the News Service they are collecting signatures ahead of the deadline to return them to local clerks at 3 p.m. Thursday afternoon. 
The AP showed Pacheco with 2,469 (50.1 percent) votes to Medeiros’s 2,455 (49.9 percent). 
Pacheco said in an email, “Unfortunately,  I am only up by 14 votes, my opponent is refusing to concede and is seeking counsel to pursue a recount.”
“Every vote deserves to be counted,” Medeiros said. “And the voters deserve the true count when it is this close.” 
Pacheco is a bartender, transportation manager for a community nonprofit in Fall River and former Dartmouth High School security guard. He’s said he decided to run to “bring a working class person’s perspective to the State House.” His campaign has focused on housing, public safety and funding, and he’s listed priorities such as sealing eligible juvenile criminal records, establishing universal early childhood education, and adjusting local public safety funding formulas.
Medeiros is a real estate agent, and has focused his campaign on affordable housing for first-time home buyers and retirees, affordability more broadly, infrastructure improvements, and growing small businesses. He’s talked about creating tax-benefited savings accounts for first-time homebuyers and reforming affordable housing laws like Chapter 40B.
While both Democrats have positioned themselves as moderate, they’ve disagreed on certain issues such as rent control (Pacheco is open to the idea, Medeiros calling it a “Band aid” solution). 
The primary winner will face Tam, who has emphasized cost of living and the legislative audit during his campaign. 
Tam also unsuccessfully ran for the Dartmouth Board of Health last year, according to the New Bedford Light, and said he was interested in legislating on health issues after he was let go from his job at Mass General Brigham Hospital for refusing the COVID-19 vaccine. 
For now, both races remain unresolved. If the recounts move forward they could determine what comes next in both races: who takes the Senate seat, and who faces Tam in November.

text:
Daniel Young, a former federal prosecutor, has been appointed Virginia’s next state inspector general by Gov. Abigail Spanberger. His appointment is subject to General Assembly confirmation. (Photo courtesy of Virginia Governor's Office)Gov. Abigail Spanberger has appointed Daniel Young, a former federal prosecutor whose cases included an $80 million defense procurement fraud scheme, as Virginia’s next state inspector general. 
Young’s appointment is subject to confirmation by the General Assembly. The state inspector general serves a four-year term and oversees an office responsible for investigating alleged fraud, waste and abuse in Virginia government, conducting performance audits and reviewing state facilities and operations.
Most recently, Young served as an assistant general counsel at the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, which Congress created after the collapse of Enron to protect investors and oversee audits of public companies.
His career also includes work at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and more than five years as an assistant U.S. attorney in the Eastern District of Virginia, according to the governor’s office. 
In announcing the appointment Friday, Spanberger highlighted Young’s experience prosecuting fraud and overseeing accountability. 
“Mr. Young has a demonstrated record of prosecuting fraud, protecting taxpayers, and holding government accountable,” Spanberger said in a statement.
She also thanked former State Inspector General Mike Westfall, who was first appointed in 2018 by then-Gov. Terry McAuliffe, for his years of service and the office’s managers for sustaining the agency’s work during the search for a new permanent leader. 
“The commonwealth must always work with a focus on serving the public and protecting taxpayer dollars,” Spanberger said.
Young said combating fraud and corruption has been a focus throughout his public service career.
“As a proud Virginian, I am honored to have been entrusted by Governor Spanberger with the responsibility of serving as the next state inspector general,” he said in a statement. 
He also credited the inspector general’s staff for its work on government transparency and accountability. 
“The dedicated public servants who work in the Office of the State Inspector General are committed to making government more transparent and more accountable for all Virginians, and it is a privilege to support their efforts,” Young said. 
During his time as a federal prosecutor in Norfolk and Alexandria, Young focused on white-collar crime and appellate matters. Beyond the $80 million defense procurement fraud scheme, his major cases included a prosecution involving NASA contracting fraud. 
Both prosecutions received awards recognizing excellence from the Council of Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency. Young also handled appeals in major cases involving national security, a gang-related murder and crimes against children. 
At the SEC, Young defended enforcement actions involving fraud. He previously clerked for two federal judges after law school and worked as a litigator in private practice. 
That work included an active pro bono docket, according to the governor’s office. Young handled voting rights litigation and represented victims of loan-modification scams following the 2008 financial crisis. 
A Hampton Roads native and the son of a police officer, Young attended Princess Anne High School in Virginia Beach before graduating with honors from the University of Virginia, where he was a Jefferson Scholar. 
After college, he received a Jack Kent Cooke Graduate Fellowship and was selected as a fellow at Harvard’s Center for Public Leadership. He later earned his law degree from Yale Law School and a master’s degree in public policy from Harvard Kennedy School.
Young lives in Reston with his wife and their two sons.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT offers mental health resources for kids. Here’s what to know
description: CT officials are launching a campaign to raise awareness about urgent crisis centers, which provide emergency mental health services to youth.
text:
With the new school year now underway, state leaders are trying to improve awareness of services for children experiencing mental health crises.
Connecticut has urgent crisis centers in Hartford, New Haven, Waterbury and New London, as well as a mobile crisis intervention program available by calling United Way at 211. But Behavioral Health Advocate Howard Sovronsky said many residents and educators still don’t know about them. He and other members of the Transforming Children’s Behavioral Health Policy and Planning Committee are launching a marketing campaign to try to change that.
Lisa Paradis, whose daughter has severe behavioral health challenges, told reporters during a press conference this week that her experience with one of the urgent crisis centers had been “life-changing.”
“After our first visit there, we were able to, within a few hours, get her regulated. She was happy when we left,” Paradis said. “We were given services, we were given referrals for services … and true to their word, they followed up.”
Lisa Paradis speaks at a press conference to share her experience bringing her daughter to one of Connecticut’s urgent crisis centers. Sep. 2, 2026. Credit: Theo Peck-Suzuki / CT Mirror
Laine Taylor, chief medical officer at The Village, said big transitions like the start of a new school year can often be challenging for children. There’s a shift in expectations, stress from schoolwork and pressure to fit in with peers. All of that can have implications for a child’s mental health.
“When big life changes occur, it causes a lot of angst,” Taylor said.
Here’s what parents should know.
What to do if a child needs care
Urgent crisis centers operate as walk-in clinics, meaning there’s no need to make an appointment. The centers are equipped to help with a range of issues, including but not limited to suicide or self-harm, feelings of depression or anxiety, out-of-control behaviors and substance use. 
According to the Tow Youth Justice Institute, the centers exist to divert parents and children from going to the emergency room, which can be slow and often traumatizing. Each of the four centers has 72 daily slots.
United Way also offers mental health crisis support to anyone who calls 211 or 988, a suicide and crisis hotline. Callers may be referred to youth mobile crisis intervention where appropriate.
Early signs to look for
Taylor said even before problems become apparent, creating space to check in with one’s kids is important. “Just to take a beat and … be able to spend time with one another with no expectations, that alone actually opens the door to them being more likely to talk about these things that are hard,” Taylor said.
At the same time, Taylor said kids themselves often don’t realize something is wrong at first. “Until they really start to have explicit, scary thoughts, they may not even realize that there’s changes,” she said.
She said it’s important to “pay attention to your child’s sleeping patterns, how your child is eating. Are they still being [as] social as they were once before? Are they still motivated to … go to their sports activities?”
“Those kinds of basic changes in routine, those are your indicators that your kid might be going through something, and a reason to start to talk to them,” Taylor said.
What to do if you’re concerned
Taylor said parents with questions can always call an urgent crisis center, 211 or 988 to ask for advice.
“You could call mobile crisis [at 211] and be like, ‘Hey this what I’m noticing. Can you guys help me?’” Taylor said. “You don’t have to be at such a high acute space in order to utilize these resources.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Stadium’s blingy entrance will be new, but making the public pay for it is the same old
description: The movers and shakers and elbow-rubbers on the Las Vegas Stadium Authority this week perfunctorily rubber-stamped another $75 million of public funding to build a new entrance to the Las Vegas NFL stadium that will include, among other things, a station for Elon Musk’s preposterous tunnels (though perhaps surprisingly, not a ballroom). Discussion from autho[...]
text:
A rendering of the proposed portico at Allegiant Stadium shown as part of a presentation at the Las Vegas Stadium Authority meeting Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo: Dana Gentry/Nevada Current)The movers and shakers and elbow-rubbers on the Las Vegas Stadium Authority this week perfunctorily rubber-stamped another $75 million of public funding to build a new entrance to the Las Vegas NFL stadium that will include, among other things, a station for Elon Musk’s preposterous tunnels (though perhaps surprisingly, not a ballroom).
Discussion from authority members was confined to gushing about how glorious the stadium — and Southern Nevada’s spectacle-based economy in general — has been for one and all. (So pay no attention to the missing Canadians and the $5 gas, I guess.) 
The Las Vegas bread-and-circuses economic model does make a lot of money. The conventional narrative, happily chirped by the aforementioned mover-shakers and the nine out of ten Nevada politicians of both parties who’ve long been mainlining the Kool-Aid about publicly provided “incentives” for stadiums and companies and such, is that the money ripples throughout the community and lifts all boats.
And yet Nevada has sported the highest or nearly highest unemployment rate in the nation almost perpetually throughout the first quarter of the 21st century.
The Las Vegas metro area household median income (often the product of two or more earners), at just over $80,000 in 2024, is about $1,600 less than the national median. And in the city providing the spectacle economy’s its brand name, i.e., Las Vegas, the median household income falls more than $2,100 shy of the nation’s.
Neither the NFL nor Formula 1 nor data centers nor MrBeast, nor any of the other countless private sector entities the people of Nevada give cash and prizes to, need those government handouts. 
That’s especially true given Nevada is one of only five states without a personal or corporate income tax. How much more economic “incentive” do businesses need to bring their enterprises to Nevada?
But a cult-like dogma pervades the practice of “economic development” in Nevada (and most of the rest of the nation). According to the profession’s gospel, corporations, companies, and other for-profit entities (such as pro sports teams) won’t locate or relocate somewhere unless they get generous publicly funded support in the form of tax breaks, tax credits, and maybe some roadwork or other infrastructure tossed in if the entity is big and/or showy enough, like Tesla, F1, or the NFL. 
Most elected officials who enable the economic development giveaways seem to feel spending public money to help private business is more fun and exciting and splashy, and hence politically preferable, to focusing public spending on what those politicians evidently view as more mundane concerns such as public education, public transit, or public health. 
If the Raiders and the NFL’s stadium authority cheerleaders are hot for a new $158 million entrance to the football field, that’s fine. Making the public pay for half of it isn’t. Let the Raiders and Musk and Allegiant and the resort industry — and any other private entities who want to put their money where their team spirit is — pay for it. 
And if the authority’s got $75 million in tax revenue burning a hole in its pocket, spend it on, oh, affordable child care for the working families who make Las Vegas spectacle-based economy go. As an example.
Making the public pay for a stadium remodeling job is another in a long line of cases where very rich private interests play the Nevada public for a bunch of suckers and chumps, with the full and obsequious support of Nevada “leaders.” 
But this week’s exercise in groveling before special interests in the name of the Nevada public notwithstanding, there are signs of growing doubts in Nevada about the wisdom of government giveaways.
Last last year, Nevada’s Republican governor, Joe Lombardo, and the Democratic attorney general who is running against him, Aaron Ford, were both supporting a scheme to give billions of dollars of transferable, which means sellable, tax credits to California film corporations and one of the nation’s largest master planned community developers. But a sufficient number of state legislators stood up against what would have been the largest public subsidy in the state’s history, and the tax credit scheme failed.
In what might be another long-overdue indication Nevada elected officials are, if not wising up to the government giveaway racket, at least becoming more sensitive to public opinion against it, Lombardo and Ford are both scurrying to backpedal from their support for data center tax breaks.
Lombardo’s running an ad that says data center tax breaks “took money from our schools, and gave it to data centers.”
Ford’s running an ad that says tax breaks for data centers “have handed them over 200 million of your tax dollars.”
Such characterizations of Nevada economic development programs — took money from our schools, handed over your tax dollars — might have been leveled by the occasional critic over the years (raises hand). But hostile descriptions of the state’s principal economic development policies are nearly unprecedented among state politicians, and astounding to see from general election candidates for governor. (And all it took was the rise of a technology that makes a good deal of the human race wonder how or even if they will coexist with it.)
But no concern about the wisdom, fairness, and virtue of public giveaways to private interests was on display when the stadium authority blithely approved $75 million in tax revenue for stadium bling.
It’s hard to be disappointed in the authority itself. It was created to serve the Raiders and the stadium, not the public. It seems similarly pointless to blame the staff at the Governor’s Office of Economic Development, which routinely approves Nevada government giveaways. Rubber-stamping public goodies for the private sector is what they were hired to do.
A line of Nevada governors, legislators, county commissioners — and of course the industries and their executives those elected officials cater and answer to — are the ones who created and empowered all this government giveaway nonsense. The decisions of those purported leaders reflect a profound lack of, well, leadership, but an unseemly amount of comfort with narratives crafted over decades by corporate America.
We’re likely stuck with that caliber of leadership. There’s very little daylight between Lombardo and Ford on economic policy, and for each of them, data centers are a one-off in which they’re scrambling to catch up to strong bipartisan public opinion. As politicians often do, they’re following, not leading. Whichever one of them wins, don’t expect to hear them say Tesla, the NFL, or any other of the many non-data center recipients of Nevada tax breaks and subsidies are, to borrow the phrase in Lombardo’s ad, “taking money from our schools.” Even though they are.
Bits and pieces of this column were originally published in the Daily Current newsletter, which is free and which you can subscribe to here.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Let’s say a ballot question passes in November. What happens next?
description: Nine ballot questions are in the mix for November. Here’s what you need to know about what happens if they win approval from voters.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS VOTERS are on track to decide the most statewide ballot questions in a single cycle in 32 years. That will create a series of follow-up decisions for Beacon Hill. 
Nine measures are in the mix for the November ballot, tying the record last set in 1994. They range in topics from recreational cannabis to a state tax cap to unionization rights for public defenders to voter registration. 
So what happens if any or all of the proposals win at the polls? The answer is less straightforward than you might think. 
Most of the questions this cycle, once approved, would have the same status as any other law put on the books through more traditional channels. But that also means the Legislature and governor have the same power to change or repeal entirely a ballot law after it passes as they do any other law enacted five or 50 years ago. 
Legislative leaders have done just that in the past. 
The most likely outcome is that if voters approve a question, it takes effect with little or no legislative interference. But just because lawmakers are unlikely to tinker with the will of the populace does not mean they can’t or won’t. 
Are there limits on what Beacon Hill can do in response to a ballot question’s passage? 
If the question proposes a new law instead of a constitutional amendment, not really. 
Almost all of the measures in the mix this cycle are indeed proposed laws, so if they succeed, they would enter the codex known as the Massachusetts General Laws with the exact same legal standing as the myriad bills that move through the Legislature and are signed by the governor. 
Mechanically, there’s no real obstacle to the Legislature voting to alter the ballot law or spike it after it wins approval. The barrier is instead a political one: Do lawmakers want to take on the public-image risks of interfering with what voters say they want? 
What if a constitutional amendment were on the ballot instead? 
Those questions are different. Changing the state Constitution is a multi-year process requiring support from both lawmakers and voters, so once an amendment takes effect, like the surtax on wealthy households approved in 2022, Beacon Hill cannot alter it without going back to the ballot box. 
No constitutional amendments are on track to go before voters this year. 
The only question that is not a traditional “initiative petition” this time around is an attempt to repeal the state’s 2024 gun control law. That measure directly asks voters whether the language the House, Senate, and governor approved two years ago should stand or be gotten rid of. 
If a ballot question passes, how many different ways can it go from there? 
There are three main routes Beacon Hill can pursue after a ballot question passes. 
Option 1: Take no action, allowing the voter-approved measure to become law. This is the most common outcome. 
Option 2: Come in afterward and change what voters approved.  
Ballot questions are blunt instruments, and legislators often have thoughts on modifying what the proponents — or their lawyers — drafted.  
The shape of that action can vary. Sometimes, lawmakers pursue significant changes that don’t entirely alter the core idea. That’s what happened in 2017, when the House and Senate rewrote a ballot law approved the prior year that legalized recreational cannabis. The Legislature made significant alterations to tax rates and regulatory structures, and it drew heavy blowback from the question’s proponents, but at the end of the day, marijuana was still legal. 
Other times, policymakers are more heavy-handed. In 2000, nearly 60 percent of voters approved a proposal to lower the statewide income tax rate from 5.95 percent to 5 percent over a three-year period. 
But in 2002, two years into the transition and with the state in a financial pinch, Beacon Hill Democrats voted to freeze the tax rate at 5.3 percent and condition the remaining reduction on achieving a series of economic milestones. Massachusetts did not hit the last of those targets — meaning the income tax rate did not fall all the way to 5 percent — until 2019, nearly two decades after voters had their say. 
Option 3: Repeal, or just ignore, the new law. 
It’s the most politically risky, but because an approved ballot question simply becomes a law, there’s no explicit barrier preventing the Legislature from approving a follow-up measure undoing it. 
Just ask any veteran good-government reformer about the “clean elections” debacle. In 1998, two-thirds of voters supported a ballot question designed to make public funding available for electoral candidates if they agreed to significant limits on spending. Legislators recoiled at the idea, spent years refusing to fund the voter-approved system or fighting it in court, and then in 2003 tucked language into the annual state budget repealing the measure. 
For a more recent example of the broad reach of legislative power, look only as far back as 2024, when 72 percent of voters decided the state auditor’s office should have the explicit authority to examine the Legislature. Top Democrats in both branches argue that the measure violates constitutional separation of powers, refusing to comply with it and simultaneously declining to ask the state’s highest court to intervene. Heading into another election season, the matter is about as unresolved — and as toxic — as ever. 
Wouldn’t lawmakers face consequences if they didn’t follow what voters want? 
To a degree, probably. 
But it also depends on how significant their intervention is. Changing an effective date by a year or raising a particular threshold will land differently than, say, altogether undermining a law capping how much state government can collect in taxes.  
If lawmakers wanted to make changes, they might not sweat the electoral consequences given the dismal competition in Massachusetts. Most House and Senate races have only a single candidate on the ballot, so frustrated voters often don’t have any real ability to toss an incumbent. 
Does the margin of the vote on a ballot question change how lawmakers think about it? 
Not all that much. Rent control has been banned since a 1994 ballot question that passed with 51.3 percent support and 48.7 percent opposition. Despite that narrow margin, reviving the idea has been more or less dead on arrival among legislative leaders for three-plus decades, even after organizers launched an ill-fated ballot campaign to revive it this year. 
Contrast that with something like a tax deduction for charitable giving. Seventy-two percent of voters backed that idea in 2000, but that didn’t stop Beacon Hill from pausing the deduction in 2002 and keeping it on ice until 2023.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Derby High School yearbook faces backlash, but student press advocates defend free speech
description: DERBY — When the Derby High School yearbook from the 2025-2026 school year was distributed at the school’s back-to-school night at the beginning of August, students, parents and politicians were quick to react.  Many remarks had to do with content, specifically the pages with student’s hot takes. One student was quoted saying “Trump is the […]
text:
“There’s 2,000 students in the school, and we try to represent everyone in a way,” said Bree Stuhlsatz, former editor of the Derby High School yearbook, in response to a recent outcry. (Photo by Jacinda Hall for Kansas Reflector)DERBY — When the Derby High School yearbook from the 2025-2026 school year was distributed at the school’s back-to-school night at the beginning of August, students, parents and politicians were quick to react. 
Many remarks had to do with content, specifically the pages with student’s hot takes. One student was quoted saying “Trump is the worst president in US history.” Another student was shown in drag. One page was dedicated to the protests against ICE. A spread covered the division among the school that after the assassination of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk.
“There’s 2,000 students in the school, and we try to represent everyone in a way,” said Bree Stuhlsatz, former editor of the Derby High School yearbook. “A lot of people will say that we were anti-Charlie Kirk and all of that, but if you actually read the story, there’s nowhere where it says we’re anti-Charlie Kirk. We just write what’s going on.” 
The conservative account Libs of TikTok posted the pages on X and garnered national attention. South Carolina Rep. Nancy Mace commented under the post: “American tax dollars should not be funding this garbage in public schools.”
Republican state Rep. Blake Carpenter, R-Derby, called the pages “unacceptable” on his Facebook page.
“A yearbook should be something students can keep for the rest of their lives. It should preserve memories of their classmates, teachers, activities, athletics, accomplishments, and the moments that defined their time in high school,” Carpenter wrote in his post. “It should not become a vehicle for partisan political attacks.”
Carpenter went on to write that people have defended the yearbook by noting that the student newspaper has published articles on similar topics. He claimed that it was not the same. 
“A student newspaper exists to report news, publish opinions, debate issues, and cover current events. People read the article and move on,”  Carpenter wrote. “A yearbook is different. ” 
Kansas Reflector made multiple attempts to reach out to Carpenter for comment through email messages and phone calls, but he did not respond.
Stuhlsatz said that it was up to students on staff to write yearbook stories and not their adviser.
“I applaud all the younger students who want to write those tougher stories, because it’s a good thing,” Stuhlsatz said. “It’s good for the journalistic world, I would say. And as much as people say that politics shouldn’t really be in schools, it’s just the stuff that happened during our time, and a yearbook is meant to be a time capsule for all of us to look back on.”
Stuhlsatz said that she has different opinions about the yearbook than others in the newsroom, but she understood that this is what her fellow students wanted. 
“Because of that, with Hazelwood and Tinker v. Des Moines, it protects student journalists,” Stuhlsatz said. “So our administration legally can’t do anything to censor our yearbooks. … We’re meant as journalists to write what’s going on at the time, no matter if it’s a hard topic, or even if it’s an easy topic, we’re meant to just write about it. That’s what journalists of today do.” 
The Supreme Court cases Tinker v. Des Moines and Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier were landmark cases that protected students’ right to freedom of speech and expression.
Kansas Scholastic Press Association Executive Director Barbara Tholen explained that taking criticism is part of being a journalist.
“Sometimes people are going to be angry with what you write, and the First Amendment protects that,” Tholen said. “And to a certain extent, on those occasions when we would make somebody frustrated, I would think, ‘this is a learning opportunity for them.’” 
Tholen explained that sometimes the opportunities for authentic learning in schools involve making a tangible product and dealing with people being frustrated.
”That’s part of journalism,” Tholen said. “It was a matter of thinking like, ‘OK, what were the decisions that we made? Do we stand by those?’ Because sometimes you make a mistake and you regret it, and sometimes you’re like, ‘Yeah, 100%.” 
Tholen says that the public doesn’t always understand that process. 
“They get mad at something that’s random,” Tholen said. “They think, ‘Oh, it’s the adults, the adults let this happen,’ and I think, ‘Wait, in this case, like, in a lot of cases, we have students who have made decisions, and now they’re getting real feedback on those decisions and that’s OK.” 
Tholen says that if the first time students are allowed to make decisions and have someone disagree is after high school, it does them a disservice.
“I think that rather than people always see this as an institutional problem, I think we should see this as just big decisions and carry feedback. … Part of making decisions is living with the consequences,” Tholen said.
Tholen said there’s another side to the situation as well, the First Amendment side, that concerns her.
“I have concerns when people want to have government officials, in this case, the school board or whatever the state lawmaker wants to involve themselves in the free speech decisions that students are making,” she said. 
“One, educationally, I think it’s a bad idea, two, we do our students a disservice when we allow them to think that the First Amendment would allow government officials to interfere in the decisions they make.”
Tholen also pointed to the Kansas Student Publications Act, which protects student journalists from interference by school districts or administrators, as long as their work is not obscene or libelous. 
“Students need to understand how the First Amendment works,” Tholen said. “You can’t teach the First Amendment in a vacuum. … You want students to have that autonomy to make decisions, to learn from the feedback they get from the decisions that they make.” 
Susan Massy, Kansas state director for the Journalism Education Association, said that there have long been misunderstandings about student press rights. Massy was one of the teachers who fought for the Kansas Student Publications Act in 1992.
“ I feel like we are constantly having to define what student press rights are and what that means for school, particularly, school administration,” Massy said. “The content of a student publication is not determined by the adviser, it is not determined by the administrator, it is not determined by the school board. It is determined by the students who create that publication.”
Kansas State Sen. Mike Thompson, R-Shawnee, also wrote on his Facebook page that the yearbook showed that schools in Kansas are focusing on “unnecessary items.”
“School administrators across the state are constantly clamoring for more money, and blaming the legislature … even though the schools are fully funded as required by the Kansas Supreme Court,” he wrote in his post. “But the best evidence that schools are actively wasting money on things that do nothing to educate students was exposed in the Derby School District.”
Massy said that she found Thompson’s comments surprising.
“I feel like they’ve seen a very limited representation of what is in that book. I feel like they don’t truly understand what the bill says,” Massy said. “It clearly gives broad rights to students, not to advisers, not to administrators, it’s to students.”
Massy says that she wishes that lawmakers were more familiar with the Kansas Student Publications Act. 
“I think in Kansas, we have a very strong respect for the First Amendment,” she said. “But sometimes, I think that people in general have a strong respect for it, while still only wanting to protect it for those who agree with their opinions.” 
Despite attacks the law has seen in the past, Massy is reasonably confident that the act will weather this round of concerns and describes the law as a give and take. She also said that Kansas student journalists need to know is their rights.
”They need to always be aware that they may get feedback from what they publish. I don’t think the knowledge that the feedback is coming is reason not to publish, but I do think it’s important that they consider it,” Massy said.

title: BREAKING: Nebraska Supreme Court upholds validity of state medical cannabis laws
description: LINCOLN — The Nebraska Supreme Court on Friday unanimously upheld Nebraska’s two voter-approved medical cannabis laws following a legal challenge to the 2024 petition effort. Chief Justice Jeffrey Funke, in a 7-0, 49-page opinion, sided against the lawsuit from former state Sen. John Kuehn of Heartwell, a longtime opponent of medical marijuana, as well as […[...]
text:
Nebraska advocates for medical cannabis have worked for more than 12 years, and continue to wait, for a safe, regulated system in Nebraska, after winning voter approval in November. Pictured are many longtime advocates for the effort. (Photos courtesy of Nebraskans for Medical Marijuana)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Supreme Court on Friday unanimously upheld Nebraska’s two voter-approved medical cannabis laws following a legal challenge to the 2024 petition effort.
Chief Justice Jeffrey Funke, in a 7-0, 49-page opinion, sided against the lawsuit from former state Sen. John Kuehn of Heartwell, a longtime opponent of medical marijuana, as well as similar arguments from Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen and Attorney General Mike Hilgers. The duo had alleged widespread fraud and “notarial malfeasance” in the petition process.
Justices of the Nebraska Supreme Court (and when they were seated), front row from left: William Cassel (2012), Jeffrey Funke (2016, 2024 as chief justice) and Stephanie Stacy (2015). Back row, from left: Jason Bergevin (2025), Jonathan Papik (2018), John Freudenberg (2018) and Derek Vaughn (2026). (Courtesy of the Nebraska Judicial Branch)
Kuehn’s appeal sought to get around a Lancaster County District Court judge who affirmed that medical cannabis supporters had enough valid signatures to reach voters in 2024.
Kuehn initially sued Evnen. But in the end, the AG’s Office defending Evnen largely joined forces with Kuehn against the Nebraskans for Medical Marijuana campaign. Had the challenge succeeded, the campaign could have sought to rehabilitate challenged signatures in a second trial phase.
“Notaries are, in effect, walking stamps of approval,” Zach Pohlman, state deputy solicitor general, told the high court in December. “They are professional truth tellers. And so when they lie, that presumption of truth … gets pierced, and they become just like every other witness.”
In addition to the civil trial, Hilgers’ office secured misdemeanor convictions against a circulator from Grand Island and a notary public from York. The circulator pleaded guilty, and a jury convicted the notary. The notary is appealing his convictions.
Kuehn, Evnen and Hilgers named other circulators and notaries who they alleged committed wrongdoing. No other charges were filed related to the medical cannabis petitions.
Nebraska Supreme Court hears appeal in medical cannabis, election notary case

If the justices had reversed, the 2024 ballot sponsors would have needed to rehabilitate enough signatures to show at least 86,499 valid signatures on two petitions apiece for the voter-approved laws — to legalize and regulate the new medicine — to stand, or 172,998 total.
The campaign had 6,822 more signatures validated than needed when Evnen certified the measures in September 2024.
Lancaster County District Judge Susan Strong, who presided over the trial in Lancaster County just days before the 2024 election, ruled that about 1,500 signatures lost a “presumption of validity” across the two petitions, but she said those challenges still fell “well short” of affecting ballot access.
During oral arguments, Chief Justice Jeffrey Funke and Justice Jonathan Papik also appeared skeptical of the need for many petition signers to potentially recertify that they signed the petitions.
“So does that mean they’d call 86,000 signatories to testify that the petition was read to them, they understood what they were signing and they actually signed it?” Funke asked at the time.
“And do that quickly?” Papik added.
Justices Stephanie Stacy and William Cassel had also both hinted the case might be “moot” because of the result of the 2024 election or because signatures had already been verified.
District judge sides with Nebraska medical cannabis ballot sponsors in legal challenge

Papik pressed whether arguments from Kuehn and Hilgers’ office had ever been used. Papik was one of two justices who dissented from a 2020 Supreme Court decision that tossed the first petition effort from Nebraskans for Medical Marijuana from the ballot, arguing it was too broad. Supporters divided the legalization and regulation efforts in 2022 and, finally, in 2024.
The voter-created Medical Cannabis Commission has been rewriting its regulations to allow fees for new applications before granting any new licenses. That process is still in the early stages. The next commission meeting is scheduled for Sept. 14.
State lawmakers granted the commission the authority to collect fees during the 2026 legislative session, but the commission had already been working to finalize a previous set of regulations.
The decision comes amid an ongoing criminal investigation into significant allegations of fraud on at least eight different petitions in the 2026 election cycle. That consists of three proposed amendments to the Lincoln City Charter, four statewide ballot measures and one nonpartisan petition bid for Nebraska governor.
Centered in Lancaster County, six out-of-state circulators were arrested who assisted the Lincoln petition effort, and law enforcement is searching for a seventh as of Aug. 19.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, Evnen and election commissioners for Lancaster and Hall counties are also calling for changes to how signature gathering is operated in Nebraska.
Hilgers has called the 2026 situation a “sad period in Nebraska history,” and he’s repeated his assertion that the medical cannabis campaign was “top to bottom the most corrupt, the worst run, poorly executed, most disrespectful to voters in the State of Nebraska petition I’ve ever seen.”
Campaign supporters continue to stand by their campaign and push for implementation, including in the Legislature, where multiple cannabis-related bills have stalled since 2024, at least one after Hilgers’ intervention.
This is a developing story.
