title: Jones outraises Tuberville in August; Tuberville retains large funding edge
description: Democrats and Republicans running for Alabama statewide offices largely kept pace with each other in August, the last month before the kickoff of the fall campaign season. According to campaign finance reports filed this week, Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, lieutenant governor secretary of state and commissioner of agriculture and industr[...]
text:
Former U.S. Sen. Doug Jones (left), the Democratic nominee for Alabama governor, outraised Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville in the month of August, the last before the fall campaign takes off. (Photos by Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Democrats and Republicans running for Alabama statewide offices largely kept pace with each other in August, the last month before the kickoff of the fall campaign season.
According to campaign finance reports filed this week, Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, lieutenant governor secretary of state and commissioner of agriculture and industries are mostly evenly matched with the attorney general race being the only outlier.
Governor
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones outraised Republican nominee Sen. Tommy Tuberville in August, according to campaign finance reports. Jones raised $1.1 million while Tuberville raised $848,500 last month.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Jones also outraised Tuberville in July, receiving $622,000 in donations in July to Tuberville’s $290,000. However, Tuberville retains a substantial fundraising edge, finishing the month with $9.5 million on hand to Jones’ $2.5 million. Tuberville also spent more than Jones in August spending $573,200 while Jones spent $252,900.
Messages seeking comment were left with Tuberville and Jones Thursday.
Both candidates received major campaign contributions in August with Tuberville receiving a total of $315,000 and Jones receiving $20,000.
Tuberville did not receive any money from political action committees (PAC) last month but did receive $25,000 from Applied Digital Corporation, a Dallas-based data center development company, and a $100,000 donation from VGW Luckyland, a sweepstakes company from Colorado. Jones received $21,200 in PAC donations including $1,000 from the Blount County Democratic Club and $5,000 from the United Steel Workers.
Attorney General
Republican nominee Katherine Robertson has consistently outperformed her Democratic opponent Jeff McLaughlin in campaign donations, raising $180,300 last month.
A message seeking comment was left with Robertson Thursday. 
McLaughlin, who has been running a low-profile campaign, saw a significant increase in his campaign donations going from $100 raised in July to nearly $14,000 in August. A message seeking comment was left with McLaughlin Thursday.
Robertson received a $25,000 major campaign contribution in August and a total of $136,000 in PAC money including $10,000 from the Alabama Power Co. Employees State PAC; $50,000 from the Alabama Realtors PAC and $2,500 from the Boeing Company PAC. McLaughlin has not received any PAC contributions; he has traditionally refused to accept campaign contributions. 
McLaughlin did not spend any money last month. Robertson spent $15,800 last month leaving her with $197,000 on hand.
Lieutenant Governor
Republican nominee John Wahl raised $140,200 last month while Democratic nominee Phillip Ensler raised $41,500. Wahl also maintains the lead with cash on hand with $214,200 to Ensler’s $96,000.
Messages seeking comment were left with Wahl and Ensler Thursday.
In August, both candidates received PAC money. Wahl received $47,700 from PACs including $2,500 from the Alabama Federation of Republican Women PAC Account; $25,000 from Progress PAC and $10,000 from the ABC Merit PAC.
Ensler received less in PAC donations, including $1,000 from the Alabama AFL-CIO PAC; $1,000 from the Alabama CPA PAC and $2,750 from the Persistence PAC.
Last week, Ensler criticized Wahl’s campaign for receiving PAC donations saying his July fundraising “made some special interests nervous” in a fundraising email.
In July, Ensler raised $27,800 to Wahl’s $52,100, with $25,000 of Wahl’s money coming from a major campaign contribution.
Wahl also spent more than Ensler last month. Campaign finances show he spent $70,400 while Ensler spent $43,600.
Commissioner of Agriculture and Industries
Ron Sparks, the Democratic nominee for commissioner of Agriculture and Industries, out-raised his Republican opponent Corey Hill.
According to campaign finance records, Sparks, a former Democratic gubernatorial nominee who served as agriculture commissioner from 2003 to 2011, raised $29,500 to Hill’s $23,250 in August.
While Hill outpaced Sparks in fundraising in July raising $11,700 to Sparks’ $9,000, both candidates raised over $11,000 in June.
Sparks said in an interview Thursday evening the money he raised came from working hard to spread his campaign message.
“It just goes to show that the the people of Alabama have an interest in this race, and and I think they look at the job that we did, and we’re working hard and trying to raise as much as we can to get our message out,” Sparks said.
A message seeking comment was left with Hill Thursday.
Hill received $10,900 in PAC donations last month including $2,000 from the Alabama Beef PAC and $2,500 from the Alabama Federation of Republican Women PAC. Sparks received $15,000 in PAC contributions, including $10,000 from the Alabama AFL-CIO PAC and $5,000 from the IBEW PAC Voluntary Fund.
Hill spent significantly less money than Sparks did last month, with only $8,100 compared to Sparks’ $33,500.
Secretary of State
Democratic Secretary of State nominee Wayne Rogers also outraised his opponent Caroleen Dobson last month with $6,200 to Dobson’s $5,600. However, Dobson maintains a large cash on hand edge, with over $470,000 to Rogers’ $18,200. Dobson also spent more than Rogers spending $47,100 while Rogers spent $1,300. 
A message was left with Dobson Thursday afternoon. Rogers said in an interview Thursday that he was “pleased” with the money he raised.
“We have not done a whole lot of fundraisers or anything lately. Just have a lot of folks that are really good people that want to see us do well, and and I appreciate all the help that we got (last) month,” Rogers said.
Both candidates got donations from PACs.  Dobson received $3,500 in PAC contributions including $1,000 from the Alabama CPA PAC and $2,500 from the Alabama Credit Union Legislative Action Council while Rogers received $2,7500 from the Persistence PAC.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Republican Victor Marx faces fine over ‘unprecedented’ campaign finance violations
description: Victor Marx, the Republican nominee for Colorado governor, is starting to feel the heat from state elections officials over a litany of alleged violations of campaign finance laws. Regulators in the Elections Division of the Colorado secretary of state’s office are seeking a $51,427 fine against Marx’s campaign for accepting contributions over the legal limi[...]
text:
Victor Marx, the Republican nominee for Colorado governor, speaks at the 2026 summer conference of the Colorado Water Congress in Steamboat Springs on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Victor Marx, the Republican nominee for Colorado governor, is starting to feel the heat from state elections officials over a litany of alleged violations of campaign finance laws.
Regulators in the Elections Division of the Colorado secretary of state’s office are seeking a $51,427 fine against Marx’s campaign for accepting contributions over the legal limit. A hearing in the case is scheduled for Sept. 10 — and it’s only the first of several potential proceedings against the first-time candidate, which also include complaints alleging Marx is illegally collecting unlimited campaign contributions through his online merchandise store.
“Respondents’ noncompliance with applicable contribution limits was unprecedented,” the Elections Division’s wrote in an Aug. 31 filing in the case. “Respondents accepted and had the benefit of the prohibited contributions throughout Respondent Marx’s gubernatorial campaign and a competitive Republican primary election.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Colorado’s campaign finance laws limit individual donors to a maximum of $1,450 in contributions to a candidate for governor. The Elections Division investigated complaints filed against Marx in May and June by Darcy Schoening, a former state GOP official, who pointed to disclosure reports that showed contributions received in excess of the $1,450 limit.
The division’s filing lists a total of $83,560 in excess contributions from over 100 individual donors since Marx launched his campaign last year, with overages ranging from 27 cents to multiple thousands of dollars.
Marx had previously called the complaints a “nothingburger,” and said the “secretary of state has been great” in working with the campaign as it refunded excess contributions to cure the alleged violations. But regulators and the campaign are now at odds over whether all the issues have been resolved.
“Respondents have not, in fact, cured all their campaign finance violations,” wrote the division, which says only $61,029 in prohibited donations appear to have been refunded.
Marx’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
Part of the dispute stems from the Marx campaign’s claims that it has “reattributed” some excess contributions to spouses or other family members who are joint account holders with the contributors in question. In its own filing, the campaign says it contacted those individuals and “spoke with the joint account holders in order to determine whether any apparent overage could be reattributed to the other joint account holder.”
But elections officials say the campaign hasn’t properly reported those reattributions.
“Respondents have provided no credible evidence that the reattributed contributions were made from joint accounts and did not specify the contributors,” the division’s filing states. “Nor have Respondents provided credible evidence that they notified all joint account holders of the apportionment of the contribution.”
Additional complaints pending
Marx, who narrowly won the GOP nomination in June, is considered a heavy underdog in the race against the Democratic nominee for governor, Attorney General Phil Weiser. Colorado has elected only one Republican governor in the last 56 years, and Democrats are widely expected to gain ground in a favorable midterm election year.
Both of Marx’s GOP primary opponents said they would not support him in the general election, calling him a “grifter” and a “con man.” A ministry leader in Colorado Springs, he has struggled to answer questions about his sensational claims about his own life, including the practice of exorcisms and work overseas as a self-described “high-risk missionary.”
He faces additional campaign finance complaints, also filed by Schoening, in relation to his solicitation of unlimited donations through an online merchandise store, a scheme that one campaign finance attorney described as “patently illegal.” Those complaints underwent an initial review by the Elections Division and are still pending.
A third round of proceedings against Marx could follow Schoening’s latest complaint, filed on Aug. 27. Citing reporting last month by 9News, the new complaint concerns a new disclaimer linking Marx’s merchandise store to a Wyoming-registered business, “Not Shook LLC.” A campaign disclosure filed in July identified Marx as the company’s owner, which he subsequently called a “silly mistake.” An initial review of the latest complaint is due by Sept. 11.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Stockard on the Stump: Towns’ departure opens seat for Shelby Dems appointment
description: Thirty-two years after entering the Tennessee House, Rep. Joe Towns said farewell, resigning his District 84 post following his victory in the Criminal Court Clerk’s race in Memphis where, presumably, he won’t have to fiddle with the state Registry of Election Finance anymore. Towns, an old-school Democrat who does a decent Louis Armstrong impersonation, cap[...]
text:
After more than three decades in the legislature, Rep. Joe Towns of Memphis, photographed on May 7, 2026, has stepped down to serve as Shelby County Criminal Court Clerk. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Thirty-two years after entering the Tennessee House, Rep. Joe Towns said farewell, resigning his District 84 post following his victory in the Criminal Court Clerk’s race in Memphis where, presumably, he won’t have to fiddle with the state Registry of Election Finance anymore.
Towns, an old-school Democrat who does a decent Louis Armstrong impersonation, captured the election in August and was sworn into office last week, paving the way for someone else to represent much of south Shelby County. 
Towns’ top accomplishment in the General Assembly is likely passage of a constitutional amendment removing all traces of slavery from the Tennessee Constitution. He called it “psychotic” when Republican Reps. Susan Lynn and Chris Todd came up with backdoor opposition to his resolution in 2022 by saying state prisoners should be working. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
“How are you going to have a democratic society in a country that still has the vestiges of the most evil thing that befell this country over hundreds of years? And trying to, in any kind of weird, wacky way, justify tainting that, that’s a revelation of her character as it relates to that issue,” Towns said at the time.
Yet he wound up amending the measure to say it wouldn’t prohibit inmates from taking jobs. They have to pay for their condiments somehow.
Outside his legislative duties, Towns had a checkered relationship with the Tennessee Registry of Election Finance, which has been on his case for the better part of six years for failing to file campaign finance reports on time – or period. It just wasn’t his bailiwick.
In 2020, Towns infamously said he wouldn’t pay one more “copper cent” to the Registry. Yet he described himself as the “prodigal son” coming home when he made his case to the Registry board, and despite the proclamation paid a $22,000 settlement fee after the board reduced penalties totaling $66,000 when it voted via email to give him a break as the COVID pandemic struck.
Towns, who could not be reached this week for comment, still has matters pending before the Registry, one for failing to file a corrected campaign finance report and two for reports that were filed late. They’re set to be taken up Sept. 15, and his House account remains open, though his name is no longer on the House website for District 84.
No doubt, Towns had a way of speaking plainly in the House. For instance, he once reacted to a bit of idiocy from the other side of the aisle by saying something in the vein of, “They’ve done lost their damn mind.”
Whether someone can fill the void remains to be seen.
It is also unclear whether another member of the Shelby County legislative delegation will step in and sing “What a Wonderful World,” almost an annual rite for Towns when the House hit delays in the road toward sine die.
Where do we go next?
Towns couldn’t hold the House seat and the Criminal Court Clerk position simultaneously, so he resigned the legislative seat recently and turned in paperwork to retire. It could be one of his first timely filings.
The person he beat in the August Democratic primary, U.S. House advisor Kyler Gilkey, announced this week he is continuing his campaign for the District 84 seat after collecting 27% of the vote. Gilkey told the Lookout that the Shelby County Democratic Party is set to caucus at a special meeting in the next couple of weeks and vote to nominate him for the November ballot. No Republican candidate qualified for the race.
“Essentially, they would be picking the next representative for District 84,” Gilkey said.
On deck: Kyler Gilkey, who lost to Rep. Joe Towns in the August 2026 primary, expects to be selected by a caucus of the Shelby County Democratic Party to be the party’s nominee in the November general election. (Photo: submitted)
Gilkey acknowledged one other potential candidate has been making some phone calls to Democratic Party members, and there’s still some talk about a special election for the seat. So nothing’s etched in stone.
“This has been a combination of campaigning for a little bit over 11 months … and talking to folks in the community, gaining support or the endorsements of local community and elected officials, labor unions,” Gilkey said. He added that he’s been preparing to make his case to party executive committee members.
The Secretary of State’s Office confirmed that state law doesn’t prohibit a candidate who lost a primary election from being nominated by the same political party through a caucus process.
Democratic Party Chairman Willie Simon told the Lookout Thursday he received Towns’ official resignation paperwork and said party leaders from District 84 will convene to set the rules for replacement and ultimately pick a candidate. Two to three have put their names out, but others could enter the fray once the party posts the opening. 
New chief – at least for a bit
The Shelby County Legislative Democratic Caucus elected state Rep. Torrey Harris to serve as chairman for the next four to five months, replacing the late Rep. G.A. Hardaway, who died in April.
Asked if he would be able to lead the caucus in the same direction, Harris laughed and said, “I look forward to working with everybody. I think we are headed in the right direction. We have really great leaders. Rep. G.A. Hardaway led that caucus for many years, so I just look forward to being able to continue the service.”
Hardaway’s son, Rep. T.J. Hardaway, who was appointed to fill the seat in the wake of his father’s death, was elected as secretary. Hardaway and one other candidate filed to run a write-in campaign for the seat.
They will hold those Shelby caucus jobs until January when all the positions come up for re-election, according to Harris.
Between the write-in candidacy and the Towns replacement, Harris said he will have plenty of work over the next few months.
Rep. Torrey Harris, a Memphis Democrat, will serve as chair of the Shelby County Legislative Democratic Caucus, replacing the late G.A. Hardaway, who died in April. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
What investigation?
Harris handily defeated Arriell Gipson-Martin in the August primary 72% to 28%. The Tennessee Journal reported she was basing her campaign on ethics following a Nashville Banner story that Harris was under investigation by the FBI for running a fraudulent political action committee in support of presidential candidate Kamala Harris.
Rep. Harris declined to comment on the matter to the Lookout in April, but he said Thursday he’s heard nothing since the report surfaced.
“It was a bad joke,” Harris said.
Harris added he didn’t even know if an investigation took place because nobody has talked to him about it. 
Too close for comfort?
A former Tennessee Department of Transportation chief of staff, Steve Townsend, took a job with Spain-based Ferrovial about a year before it won the bid for the state’s first toll lane project along I-24 toward Murfreesboro, according to a report by The Tennessean.
The DriveTN group of six companies said it would construct the lanes at a cost of $9.2 billion and concede nearly $25 billion to the state, a figure that is raising eyebrows in the road construction industry. Considering two other bidders said they’d give up $7 billion and one asked for a subsidy from the state to take on the job, it was an eye-popper (can we find another eye reference?).
Democratic Rep. John Ray Clemmons of Nashville, no fan of the toll project, called for the state attorney general to look into the whole project. (Don’t hold your breath.)
Asked about Townsend’s possible connection to the project, TDOT sent this statement: “Consistent with TDOT procurement requirements, the DriveTN team implemented screening procedures and communication protocols that prohibited Steve Townsend’s engagement in, access to, or receipt of any information related to the I-24 Southeast Choice Lanes procurement.
“This disclosure was made to TDOT by DriveTN in accordance with the organizational conflict-of-interest provisions contained in the procurement documents. TDOT reviewed the disclosure and remains committed to ensuring the procurement is conducted in accordance with all applicable requirements, with appropriate safeguards in place to protect the integrity of the process.”
Bank downgrades Ferrovial stock over I-24 toll lane bid

Based on that response, Townsend didn’t tell the DriveTN folks to throw nearly $25 billion at the project to win the bid. 
Yet at least one international bank, UBS, downgraded Ferrovial’s stock to “neutral” based on uncertainty surrounding the I-24 project and a potential weak return on its investment and high upfront costs and capital expenses. 
DriveTN is to pay $1.5 billion initially and the rest of the “concession” money over roughly eight years of construction, according to the UBS report. 
Department of Transportation officials said at the bidding vote that the group’s payout had nothing to do with the fees it would charge motorists to use the lanes. Those will be based on the amount of traffic, time of day, etc.
Yet no revenue will come in until it finishes at least part of the toll lanes, potentially putting pressure on the consortium to pay off the debt. 
Of course, they could always make motorists on the LBJ Express in Texas pay the bills. It’s the least they could do since we sent Davy Crockett to fight — and die — at the Alamo, even though had a pretty good shooting eye. 
Seeking the end
A group of counties, including Metro Nashville, filed a motion in federal court this week asking a judge to declare victory for them in their lawsuit claiming the Trump administration withheld tens of millions of dollars for anti-terrorism efforts unless they adopted certain election-system policies to verify citizenship. (The official language is called seeking a summary judgment based on the facts, or some such.) Metro joined Harris County (Houston), Texas, El Paso County, Texas and Columbus, Ohio in challenging the feds.
Twenty percent of the federal funds would be withheld by the Federal Emergency Management Agency if the local government doesn’t comply with election specifications, and continued failure to go along with the game could lead to termination. 
Nashville could lose a pretty big chunk of change. 
Grants to Nashville in 2023 and 2024 totaled $1.7 million, $1.5 million in 2025, and the total for the Metro Nashville-Murfreesboro-Franklin region for fiscal 2026 is projected at $3.8 million. 
Lord knows the taxpayers can’t afford that. Just put it on my tab.
That’s Senator Kane to you. Former professional wrestler and immediate past mayor of Knoxville Glenn Jacobs is considered a serious contender to replace U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn should she become governor. (Photo on left: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout; photo on right: Getty Images)
Working ahead?
Former Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a frequent visitor to the Cordell Hull legislative building in Nashville, could be gearing up for a U.S. Senate run.
A potential replacement for U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn if she wins the Tennessee gubernatorial race this year, Jacobs would have to win an election in 2028 to fill the final two years of Blackburn’s six-year term. Remember, she said she would pick her replacement, and Gov. Bill Lee, when asked if she was stepping on his toes, said, “We’ll take governors one at a time.” (Thanks for taking a stand.)
Anyway, Jacobs updated his Facebook cover photo with a logo, “Glenn Jacobs for Tennessee.” Maybe he’s no longer going with “Kane,” his rasslin’ alter ego, or he just knows something.
“There’s flies in the kitchen / I can hear ’em there buzzin’”*

title: New restrooms, no spiral rampway: Here’s what’s new for Gamecock football fans this season
description: COLUMBIA — For those attending South Carolina’s opening football game Saturday against Kent State, it will be a new experience at Williams-Brice Stadium. They’ll be some confusion, a bit of frustration, maybe some dust as crews worked through this week to complete phase one of what the university calls a “reimagined” version of an arena […]
text:
"Welcome Home" will greet Gamecock fans walking into Williams-Brice Stadium, as seen on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Pete Iacobelli/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — For those attending South Carolina’s opening football game Saturday against Kent State, it will be a new experience at Williams-Brice Stadium.
They’ll be some confusion, a bit of frustration, maybe some dust as crews worked through this week to complete phase one of what the university calls a “reimagined” version of an arena that’s served as the school’s college football home since 1934.
There will be plenty of wow moments, too, at the new restroom facilities, the wider concourses, the multiple, gleaming, grab-and-go food and drink stations, and the premium Cockaboose Club near the venerable train cars lined up on the far side of the stadium.
USC gets final OK on $350M Williams-Brice Stadium renovations

When the $350 million project is completed — there are two more phases, mostly during the next two offseasons — it will be “one of the best” stadiums in the Southeastern Conference, according to South Carolina athletic director Jeremiah Donati.
The project was a long-planned endeavor to modernize a stadium that sometimes felt like it was still stuck in the last century, when fans didn’t worry so much about comfort and schools were not looking to improve profitability through premium space activities.
But college athletics, like many other areas, is in an era where those who pay, sometimes thousands of dollars, for tickets, parking, athletic department donations and concessions want amenities like comfortable seats, air-conditioned spaces to watch and reliable Wi-Fi to keep their smartphones and tablets updated.
Williams-Brice has more of that going forward.
One of the biggest complaints about the building Donati got after taking over as athletic director in January 2025 was about restrooms, specifically women’s restrooms.
The stadium had long lines for its woefully few bathrooms for women. This project has addressed most of those needs with 33, gleaming new restrooms for women — more than five times the fixtures it had before.
Throughout the entrances and walkways are fresh new signage with the school’s athletic tag lines, such as “Welcome Home” and “Forever To Thee.”
There are banners along the concourses of some of the South Carolina’s football greats and displays of game-day traditions like “Sandstorm” and “2001.”
Among the many new conveniences are the in-and-out, concession cafes where patrons can pick out hot food, cold sandwiches and beverages and pay through an electronic cashier that identifies what you purchased and quickly calculates your price.
There are several cold cases across the aisle with alcoholic drinks for those who wish a cold one while they watch the Gamecocks.

Lots of new concession stands, as seen on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026, are designed to enable football fans to get their drinks quickly without long lines. (Photo by Pete Iacobelli/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)

“The days of reaching into a tub of ice are gone,” Donati said.
A silver, metal Gamecock statue that was part of the one-time coaches’ offices in the demolished Floyd Building across from the Fairgrounds is set up in the redone East Entrance.
Nearby is a display featuring all the reigning state high school football champions in case any potential future Gamecocks from those schools are there on a future visit.
The area outside the student section, “The Cockpit,” has been expanded as a shady gathering area for them.
The visiting locker room has been moved across the field to the east side of the stadium, far away from Bluff Road. It’s spacious, clean and comfortable, serviceable for opponents. South Carolina planners did not take a page from other schools, like Iowa, in gamesmanship in choosing a color for the walls in the locker room.
“It’s not pink,” joked Wesley Malette, South Carolina deputy athletic director and chief marketing officer.
The switch was also done so visiting teams wouldn’t take the field from their traditional tunnel during South Carolina’s “2001” entrance.
Two of the most striking things fans will notice are the stairs on the Bluff Road side off the stadium and the absence of the nearby spiral rampway, a longtime defining feature of the building that was removed for the renovation.
USC celebrates record $358M in fundraising, other SC colleges also set records

There will be escalators installed for fan comfort in time for the 2027 season.
That phase will also include renovation of South Carolina’s home locker area along with a plush, modern recruiting room to entertain future generations of Gamecocks.
The university will expand its luxury areas and reseat the stadium, with capacity falling to about 73,459 from its current level of 77,500.
There will be some undone areas fans can’t help seeing this season. Crews will keep working throughout football season “to get a jump on what comes next,” said Greg Hughes, CEO of Contract Construction.
It’s an undertaking South Carolina had to do to keep pace with the rest of the country.
Donati, previously the athletic director at Texas Christian University in Fort Worth, Texas, had long heard about South Carolina’s unparalleled game-day experience. He wanted a stadium equal to that for fans.
“It will be one of the nicest stadiums in the SEC and the best game-day experience,” Donati said.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Plaintiffs say Tuberville is ‘constitutionally ineligible’ for governorship in reply brief
description: Plaintiffs challenging Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville’s candidacy told the Alabama Supreme Court Thursday that Tuberville was “constitutionally ineligible” to serve as governor.  In a 23-page brief filed in reply to Tuberville, Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall and the Alabama Republican Party (ALGOP), the plaintiffs’ attorneys accus[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. and Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville speaking at the Alabama Republican Party's Summer Dinner on July 31, 2026, at the Renaissance Hotel in Montgomery, Alabama. Plaintiffs who are challenging Tuberville's candidacy for governor said the senator is avoiding an "obvious and very inconvenient truth" in a reply brief Thursday. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Plaintiffs challenging Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville’s candidacy told the Alabama Supreme Court Thursday that Tuberville was “constitutionally ineligible” to serve as governor. 
In a 23-page brief filed in reply to Tuberville, Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall and the Alabama Republican Party (ALGOP), the plaintiffs’ attorneys accused them of avoiding an “obvious and very inconvenient truth.”
“Raising every conceivable procedural and legal roadblock they can muster, Tuberville and his political allies ask this Court to simply look the other way while he thumbs his nose at an Alabama constitutional requirement that has existed since this state was founded more than 200 years ago,” the brief said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Messages seeking comment from the Tuberville campaign, his attorneys, Marshall and the ALGOP were left Thursday afternoon. The plaintiffs are appealing a lower court ruling that it lacked jurisdiction to hear the plaintiffs’ challenge.
Tuberville, currently Alabama’s senior U.S. Senator, has faced questions about his residency for years. The plaintiffs’ complaint cites reporting including a 2023 Florida driver’s license, and homestead exemption in Auburn that Tuberville said he has been on since 2018 but was not added to until mid-2024.  
The lawsuit argues that Tuberville does not meet Alabama’s seven-year residency requirement for the governorship. 
Tuberville has maintained that he meets the requirement, but does not deny that he owns a home on the Florida coast. His lawyers argued last week that temporary absences do not strip a person’s resident status. 
The senator’s attorneys, Marshall and the ALGOP also argued last week that the judiciary does not have jurisdiction in the “election dispute” and that right belongs to the party.
Tuberville’s residency has been challenged multiple times within the party by Ken McFeeters, who ran against Tuberville in the gubernatorial primary. Each was dismissed, including one where Tuberville testified under oath. Plaintiffs said they could not challenge Tuberville’s residency within the party because they do not belong to the party.
The lawsuit is challenging the senator’s authority to be governor through a legal proceeding called “quo warranto,” not his May primary win. 
“Alabama has long held that it is up to the judiciary – undisputably a co-equal branch of our government – to uphold and enforce the provisions of the Constitution when threatened by unscrupulous politicians and others more concerned with their own power than the rights enshrined in our most sacred laws,” Thursday’s brief said. 
Because the case is not challenging the results of the primary, plaintiffs argued that a centuries-old law that Tuberville and Marshall referenced does not strip the judiciary of its power in this case.
“The statutory language is expressly limited to ‘any proceeding for ascertaining the legality, conduct, or results of any election’ or ‘any injunction, process, or order from any judge or court, whereby the results of any election are sought to be inquired into, questioned, or affected, or whereby any certificate of election is sought to be inquired into or questioned,’” the brief said. “Appellants challenge only Tuberville’s constitutional eligibility to now serve as the certified nominee—which presumes that the results of the primary are valid and correct.” 
The parties disagree over whether the quo warranto proceeding can be used in the first place. There is no precedent where the action has been used against a nominee. Under current legal precedent, quo warranto actions have only been successful against those who already hold public office. 
The plaintiffs argue that multiple Alabama Supreme Court cases have designated certified nominees as “quasi-officers” because they have access to resources the public does not.
“While declining to hold that quo warranto did not extend to certified nominees, the court has repeatedly held that quo warranto was the ‘exclusive remedy’ for challenging a person’s eligibility to hold office,” the brief said. 
Plaintiffs want the justices, all of whom are Republicans, to send the case back to Montgomery County Circuit Judge Brooke Reid, who dismissed the case in July due to a lack of jurisdiction after an hourslong hearing. Reid did not rule on the merits of the case. 
Alabama Supreme Court opinions are usually released on Friday mornings. Should they rule Tuberville is not eligible to be governor, there is not enough time for the ALGOP to replace him as a candidate and all votes cast for him would be void. Plaintiffs said that does not make the case moot.
“In any event, Alabama voters deserve to know whether Tuberville is constitutionally ineligible before they go to the polls in November,” the brief said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Restitution delivered for Virginia families in 6-year housing discrimination case
description: Damien and Angela Smith and their friends Amanda and Michael Mills said Wednesday they feel a sense of relief at the conclusion of their years-long housing discrimination case. Each couple has received nearly $420,000 in restitution, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones announced this week The families had retreated to a Smith Mountain Lake property in […]
text:
Smith Mountain Lake in Franklin County, Virginia. (Photo by Casey Johnson/Getty Images)Damien and Angela Smith and their friends Amanda and Michael Mills said Wednesday they feel a sense of relief at the conclusion of their years-long housing discrimination case. Each couple has received nearly $420,000 in restitution, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones announced this week
The families had retreated to a Smith Mountain Lake property in 2020, where they faced harassment and racially derogatory comments by owner Regina Smith. 
After a jury sided with the families in their case last year, Smith owed the families nearly $800,000. Smith’s 18-acre waterfront property has since been sold, facilitating the payments. 
The awards come after Turner failed to comply with multiple court orders and refused to pay damages following last year’s verdict. The Office of the Attorney General then initiated a special auction to sell her property and collect the court-ordered damages. Turner was also sentenced to 30 days in jail. 
Looking back on how the case began, Damien Smith, a Black man, said he’d been in the car when his white wife and their friends toured the site. Turner didn’t notice him.
“I told Angie ‘I’ll give it a try, but typically, you know, Black people in campgrounds in the South don’t mix,’” he explained. “I don’t think if (Turner) had seen me that night she would have let the sale go through.”
Amanda Mills said after the sale, Turner called her and expressed frustration at learning of Damien Smith’s race. She said wouldn’t have approved of the couples on her campground if she’d known, Mills recounted. 
Though Turner had initially seen the Smiths’ mixed-race son, she relayed to Amanda Mills that she’d assumed he was a “mistake from (Angie Smith’s) past.” 
“No child of any nationality, any race, is a mistake,” Amanda Mills said. “For someone to truly feel that way, so deep in their heart, it just shows how much room for improvement there is in this world.”
Hampton Roads tenants describe landlord’s abuse, retaliation after landmark fair housing settlement

The families said Turner pressured them to leave and refused to return their rental fees or allow them to sell their campers on site. 
“We ended up having to tear down decks and pull the camper out of there in order to get it sold for a much lesser value than what it was if it was on the water, and much less than what we paid for it,” Angela Smith explained. 
Turner’s comment about the Smith’s son disturbed the couples deeply and spurred the Smiths to file a complaint with the Virginia Fair Housing Board. 
Damien Smith was skeptical that it would yield justice but the case’s outcome represents the importance of “sticking to your guns,” he said. 
It’s arduous to pursue legal remedy for these types of wrongs, Helen Hardiman, a lawyer in the Office of the Attorney General, noted, adding that the rigorous process sometimes deters people from taking action. 
The Smiths and Mills had to make about a dozen court appearances over the years and continued to encounter Turner in that process. 
“(They) had to disrupt their lives and place themselves back in what I would imagine is pretty emotionally frustrating space to be in the same room with a woman who had discriminated against them all those years ago,” Hardiman said. 
The longrunning case, first undertaken by former Attorney General Mark Herring, continued by former Attorney General Jason Miyares, and now concluded through Jones, resulted in the state’s largest payout to individual complainants in the history of the state’s attorney general office and fair housing office. 
“Justice was slow here — delayed but not denied,” Hardiman said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: FOIA Friday: Special prosecutor clears Franklin County officials in open-meetings investigation
description: One of the less noticed features of the Virginia Way is the long-running tendency of the commonwealth’s leaders to conduct their decision-making behind closed doors. While the Virginia Freedom of Information Act presumes all government business is by default public and requires officials to justify why exceptions should be made, too many Virginia leaders in[...]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images)One of the less noticed features of the Virginia Way is the long-running tendency of the commonwealth’s leaders to conduct their decision-making behind closed doors. While the Virginia Freedom of Information Act presumes all government business is by default public and requires officials to justify why exceptions should be made, too many Virginia leaders in practice take the opposite stance, acting as if records are by default private and the public must prove they should be handled otherwise.
In this feature, we aim to highlight the frequency with which officials around Virginia are resisting public access to records on issues large and small — and note instances when the release of information under FOIA gave the public insight into how government bodies are operating.
 Lynchburg prosecutor finds no criminal conduct by Franklin County officials

A special prosecutor has concluded that several Franklin County officials committed no criminal conduct or violations of Virginia’s Freedom of Information Act following an investigation prompted by complaints from county residents, WDJB reported last week. 
Lynchburg Commonwealth’s Attorney Bethany Harrison was appointed to investigate the allegations to avoid a conflict of interest. The complaints involved Board of Supervisors Chair Lorie Smith, Vice Chair Nick Mitchell and County Administrator Steven Sandy.
After reviewing the allegations, exhibits, Virginia law, court decisions and publicly available county records, Harrison determined “the information presented did not provide sufficient evidence of criminal violations by Chair Smith, Vice Chair Mitchell or County Administrator Sandy.” 
She also found insufficient evidence to request a Virginia State Police criminal investigation.
The complaints cited emails obtained through FOIA requests showing Smith polling supervisors about how they intended to vote on several budget items, which complainants argued violated Virginia’s Open Meetings Act.
Other emails showed Sandy communicating with Smith and Mitchell about items to be placed on meeting agendas. The complaint alleged the officials sidelined other supervisors, including by suppressing a proposed solar development moratorium Supervisor Dan Quinn wanted brought to a vote.
Sandy criticized the allegations and their public release before the investigation was completed.
“I am grateful that this investigation has found no merit to the claims,” Sandy said.
Smith said Harrison’s findings represented “the beginning of the truth coming to light after more than a year of factual inaccuracies and baseless allegations.”
Mitchell also criticized the complaints, saying they had cost the county staff time and taxpayer dollars.
County Attorney Jim Guynn said residents have a right to question government decisions, criticize elected officials and seek public records, but said those rights do not justify “a sustained campaign of unsupported accusations, personal attacks, intimidation, or efforts to damage the reputation and personal well-being of public officials and employees.”
 Records show Purcellville stopped paying town manager in June

Purcellville Town Manager Kwasi Fraser has not been paid by the town since June 4, according to documents obtained by Loudoun Now through a Freedom of Information Act request.
Fraser’s employment status remained unclear, as the outlet’s reporting last month. He was placed on paid administrative leave in July 2025 following his arrest alongside Vice Mayor Carl Nett on charges of bid-rigging and conspiracy.
Town records show Purcellville paid Fraser just over $180,000 while he was on leave, a decision that drew criticism from residents.
The town has also paid Anthony Sabio $100,000 for serving as interim town manager for six months and allocated $130,000 to the Robert Bobb Group to provide interim town managers through the end of 2026. Assistant Town Manager Diana Hays received just under $2,500 for serving as acting town manager for three months.
Mayor Christopher Bertaut and Town Council members did not respond to requests for comment from Loudoun Now about why Fraser’s payments stopped or his employment status. The town declined to comment, citing personnel matters.
The timing of the halted payments coincides with a court-ordered suspension of Fraser and Nett.
Circuit Court Judge Randy Bellows approved a motion from Special Prosecutor Eric Olsen to suspend the two under legislation introduced by Sen. Russet Perry, D-Loudoun, and Del. John McAuliff, D-Fauquier, that took effect earlier this year.
Bellows ruled that Fraser and Nett qualified as town officials subject to the law and ordered their suspensions effective May 28.
Neither the legislation nor arguments before the court addressed whether officials would continue to be paid while suspended.
 


				The Mercury’s efforts to track FOIA and other transparency cases in Virginia are indebted to the work of the Virginia Coalition for Open Government, a nonprofit alliance dedicated to expanding access to government records, meetings and other state and local proceedings.			



 Virginia medical examiner’s departure raises questions over Tidewater cases

Questions have emerged about cases handled by a former assistant chief medical examiner in Virginia’s Tidewater district after officials learned she provided an inauthentic letter indicating she had passed a forensic pathology board exam, according to a Virginian-Pilot report from Aug. 19.
Officials with the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner learned in January that Dr. Fernanda da Silva Lameira had not passed the exam nearly two years earlier, despite the letter stating otherwise. She subsequently left the office.
In January emails to Virginia Department of Health administrators, Lameira denied knowing she had failed her first attempt at the exam. She wrote that she believed an ex-partner created the letter without her knowledge.
The Pilot recently obtained the emails and other documents that prosecutors have provided to several defense attorneys as part of their legal obligations.
Lameira disputed the concerns in an email, saying the story “is false and it doesn’t make any sense,” and maintained there was no issue with her court testimony.
She also said she signed a confidentiality agreement with the Virginia Department of Health stating that her firing was not public information and that she would not discuss it publicly.
As of August, it remained unclear how many autopsies Lameira conducted after joining the chief medical examiner’s office in July 2023.
 Turmoil in Mineral puts small town’s future in question

Mineral, a small Virginia town that once faced the possibility of being dissolved, could avoid that fate if its leaders can overcome months of political turmoil and dysfunction, the Daily Progress reported last week.
The Louisa County town of 555 residents has seen town council meetings marked by shouting, name-calling and cursing. There has also been an accusation of attempted blackmailing involving a failed honeypot scheme, while the town manager has been fired, rehired, fired and rehired again in less than a year. 
Checks intended for town vendors have gone missing, and until this month, two council members were engaged in back-channel negotiations with Louisa County over dissolving Mineral’s charter. 
Questions have also emerged over the town’s handling of public meeting records. 
Mayor Pamela Harlowe has acknowledged doctoring meeting minutes, making records of council proceedings difficult to track and understand. 
Before leaving the council, former member David Hempstead defended Harlowe’s approach during a Feb. 9 meeting, arguing that “not everything” needed to be recorded in open session and that “meetings don’t have to be public.” 
Under Virginia law, meetings of public bodies are generally required to be open to the public, except when they are lawfully convened in closed session.
Despite the turmoil, Mineral may still avoid dissolution. Whether it does could depend on the ability of town leaders to resolve their disputes and restore basic government operations. 
Have you experienced local or state officials denying or delaying your FOIA request? Tell us about it: info@virginiamercury.com

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana lawmakers mum on plan ‘to end property taxes on the home you live in’
description: A plan teased by some top Indiana legislators for eliminating homeowner property taxes is shrouded with silence.
text:
Sen. Ryan Mishler, R-Mishawaka, speaks during a State Budget Committee meeting on April 16, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)A plan teased by some top Indiana legislators for eliminating homeowner property taxes is shrouded in silence.
Those lawmakers have remained tight lipped about how they could pull off the multi-billion dollar move — and key Statehouse interest groups that closely follow property tax issues are anxiously waiting for details.
The plan “to end property taxes on the home you live in” was first touted with an Aug. 20 post to the campaign Facebook page of Republican Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Ryan Mishler.
The post promotes a “Property Tax Freedom” town hall and rally Sept. 29 in Warsaw, along with Rep. Craig Snow, R-Warsaw, and Sen. Chris Garten, who is poised to become the state Senate’s new Republican leader.
But they haven’t released any information about how they would eliminate the tax stream that provides much of the revenue for city and county governments and public school districts.
Even an apparent ally in efforts to dial back homeowner taxes — the group representing Indiana’s real estate agents — hasn’t been clued in on the plan.
“At least not to us at the state level,” Chris Watts, a vice president at the Indiana Association of Realtors, told the Capital Chronicle this week. “If they’ve consulted brokers locally, it’s not filtered up to us. So, yeah, we’re on pins and needles as well to kind of see what they’ve come up with.”
Neither Mishler nor Snow, who is vice chair of the tax code-writing House Ways and Means Committee, responded to multiple interview requests from the Capital Chronicle to their offices and their personal phone numbers.
Garten, R-Charlestown, declined an interview request via his office, which said he “is going to defer to Sen. Mishler.”
Questions abound about abolishment details
If such a major property tax proposal were to advance, it would undoubtedly become a leading topic of debate for the 2027 legislative session because of its wide-ranging impact.
Property taxes on owner-occupied homes amounted to nearly $4.1 billion, or 38%, of the $10.6 billion in statewide property taxes billed during 2025, according to a Legislative Services Agency report.
Screenshot of a post to Sen. Ryan Mishler’s campaign Facebook page.
That percentage is expected to decline in comparison with business, industrial, rental and agricultural properties in the coming years under an overhaul enacted in 2025 with Senate Enrolled Act 1.
Questions abound, however, about how a homeowner tax elimination would work and how local governments and schools could replace such a large revenue source.
“Of course, it creates a huge concern for local units of government on how that money would be backfilled,” said David Bottorff, executive director of the Association of Indiana Counties. “I don’t know if it’s a goal or objective, if it’s something you’re trying to phase in over four or five years, all those details matter on what that transition would look like.”
Mishler, R-Mishawaka, has floated ideas for sizable homestead property tax cuts before.
One proposal came in a 2024 bill he filed that would have created a potentially $1 billion fund for homestead tax cuts from money that the state now directs each year toward a pension fund for teachers first hired before 1996. Mishler, who has been the Senate’s top budget writer since 2018, has pushed through several special state appropriations to build up that pension fund so that the annual spending is no longer needed.
But that money might not be available for a few more years — and would still fall short of the homeowner property tax collections.
Options to raise other taxes or cut local funding
The leader of the lobbying group for Indiana’s cities and towns said he and Mishler talked generally this summer about homeowner property tax elimination and that discussion included allowing more increases in local income taxes.
Mishler was “very clear that the revenue would have to be replaced,” said Matt Greller, CEO of Accelerate Indiana Municipalities.
A major worry for local governments comes from possibly facing higher interest rates on money borrowed for construction and other projects. That’s because payments for such bonds have long been guaranteed from property tax revenue that is regarded as more stable than income or sales taxes.
Rep. Craig Snow, R-Warsaw, addresses a crowd on Dec. 18, 2024 in Indianapolis. (Whitney Downard/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
“Does it hurt us in the bonding market if we’re only using income tax to bond against?” Greller said. “Does the market look more or less favorably on that? What would that be in terms of increased interest costs?”
Legislators studied the prospects of abolishing property taxes in 2007. But they backed away after calculations showed a doubling or more of the state’s sales tax or income tax would be needed to raise a similar amount of money.
Those options of big hikes in other taxes — such as the 2.9% state income tax rate for 2026 —  or squeezing the budgets of local governments and schools haven’t changed over time, said Larry DeBoer, a longtime Purdue University economist who has studied Indiana tax policy since the 1980s.
“An income tax rate of 6 or 7 (percent) would probably do it, and that’s what has discouraged people in the past,” DeBoer said in an interview. “But we’re in an age of reform, I guess.”
“More questions, certainly, than answers”
Other property tax cut ideas are also being talked about, such as Gov. Mike Braun’s suggestion of ending home taxes for those older than 65 who’ve paid off their mortgages.
Another proposal from a Republican legislator would eliminate all property taxes and replace that revenue by extending the state’s 7% sales tax to include a vast array of currently untaxed services such as haircuts, construction labor costs and lawyer fees.
Indiana School Boards Association Executive Director Terry Spradlin said he has “more questions, certainly, than answers” about the homestead tax abolishment suggested by Mishler, Snow and Garten.
“It’s a very vague concept that only the flyer speaks to, without a plan to explain it,” Spradlin said. “So we’re all anxious to get more detail.”
The legislators are seizing upon a topic that has been a top campaign issue in recent years — and could push their proposal forward during the 2027 legislative session that starts in January.
“Those three are high-profile leaders of the House and Senate Republican caucuses,” Spradlin said. “So this has some merit, obviously, that we need to pay attention to.”

title: Cyber threats an immense and global challenge for New Hampshire’s water suppliers
description: A spate of cyberattacks on water systems in at least 12 states this July, which the U.S. government tentatively attributed to Iran, brought national attention to a growing concern for water operators in New Hampshire and across the country.  The New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services is not aware of any impacts to New Hampshire […]
text:
Electronic systems help run the city of Concord's water treatment facility, which sends millions of gallons of clean drinking water to residents each day. Cyberattacks on water systems in multiple states brought fresh attention to the importance of cybersecurity for critical infrastructure this summer. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)A spate of cyberattacks on water systems in at least 12 states this July, which the U.S. government tentatively attributed to Iran, brought national attention to a growing concern for water operators in New Hampshire and across the country. 
The New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services is not aware of any impacts to New Hampshire systems from that particular spree of attacks, spokesperson James Martin said in an email to the Bulletin. But, he added, “systems are always being probed.”
Would-be hackers, in other words, are constantly testing the cyber doors and windows of New Hampshire’s many public water systems. It’s a constant and evolving threat, operators told the Bulletin, and the advent and evolution of advanced artificial intelligence is rapidly making bad actors more capable. 
Like their counterparts across the country, New Hampshire operators and officials are locked in a scramble to stay ahead of this constantly shifting issue, said Joshua Corman, a cybersecurity professional based in Dover who runs a nonprofit intended to help local governments and utilities prepare for cyberattacks. 
The threat is big, Corman said, and especially hard for small water operators, like those in New Hampshire, to defend against. Operators said they were taking steps and looking for help to stay ready.
Widespread connection, widespread risk
Cybersecurity efforts have long centered on protecting information, like identities and sensitive documents, from unwanted eyes, Corman said. But there’s another realm where internet connectivity is important to modern life, and it’s one that has long received less attention: operational technology. This is physical infrastructure and operating systems that are computer-automated and, increasingly, connected to the web.
Internet connectivity allows staff to tweak and monitor equipment from afar, making operations more efficient, said John Boisvert, chief executive officer of Nashua’s Pennichuck Water and president of the New England Water Works Association. It might, for example, let technicians turn a valve from afar to adjust water pressure throughout the distribution system or tweak the amounts of sanitizing chemicals added to water.
Internet connectivity isn’t inherent to water treatment systems. At their core, these processes are a balance of physical engineering and chemistry, Boisvert said. But it’s increasingly common in practice.
In Concord, remote and automated operations allow the water treatment facility to run with less than half the staff it would require to operate offline, according to Jackson Keane, water treatment superintendent for the city. That saves on payroll. But Keane knows that increased connection also increases opportunities for hackers. 
Because remote operations have pervaded American water infrastructure — and that of other essential utilities — without concurrent investment in cybersecurity, the systems are left with security gaps, Corman said. Those have attracted the kind of unwanted attention exemplified in the July cyberattacks and others before them, including a 2023 attack on public utilities in Littleton, Mass. 
The attacks we know about are likely only part of the full picture.
“It’s likely that there have been more that we just don’t know about,” Boisvert said.
Hackers take many forms, from individuals operating domestically to coordinated efforts that are either sanctioned or led by foreign governments. The U.S. government has tentatively attributed the recent spate of cyberattacks on water systems to Iran. And, Corman said, weak spots in U.S. utilities’ firewalls are also an area of interest for the Chinese government.
Corman, whose resume includes time with the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, told the Bulletin he believes China may attempt to create widespread disruptions in American utility services to distract from an attempt to invade and seize Taiwan, a theory he shares with colleagues and has also spoken to in testimony before Congress.
In this way, vulnerabilities in water system cybersecurity can bring matters of geopolitics to the front doors — or, more accurately, kitchen sinks — of Americans.
For a small New Hampshire water supply, the scope of these threats can be daunting, Corman and Boisvert said.
The majority of New Hampshire public water systems serve small, rural communities, many with a small team that may struggle to keep up with evolving cyber threats. Pennichuck Water, by comparison, is large for New Hampshire, with multiple staff members dedicated to information technology and cybersecurity. But even for Pennichuck, keeping up with the threats requires constant attention, Boisvert said. 
“The threats to (smaller operators) are no different than they are to us,” he said. “That’s where the real difficulty comes.”
Drinking water sits in deep pools at the City of Concord’s water treatment facility. Before reaching these pools, where sediment filters out of the water, it has been subjected to a series of automated purification and pumping steps, some of which are controlled by remotely-operated machinery. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
The stakes
Talking about how cyberattacks could disrupt water service, and the consequences that would ensue, invariably gets “heavy,” Corman said. But it’s important, he believes, to consider worst-case scenarios in order to be best prepared.
The actual mechanics of an attack could see physical damage to the distribution system, whether from rapid pressure changes that could burst pipes or changes to pumps that make them quickly burn out, Corman said. Tampering with chemical additions or alarms that would ordinarily alert operators to system failures are other routes to harm.
A burst main or failed pump takes time to replace and can be extremely expensive, potentially creating a window where water could be restricted in the affected area.
To help frontline workers imagine what could follow a particularly catastrophic scenario, Corman runs crisis simulations as tabletop exercises, using a 20-sided die to introduce randomness. 
He ran one such exercise at Dartmouth College this spring, during a conference on cyber-resilient healthcare organized by the school’s Institute for Security, Technology, and Society. 
One participant, and an organizer of the event, was Institute Fellow Malcolm Schongalla, who is also employed as an emergency physician at Dartmouth Health-New London Hospital and teaches at the Dartmouth Geisel School of Medicine. (He spoke to the Bulletin about the event only in his capacity as a fellow with the institute, he said.)
The exercise simulated a loss of water to the Hanover and Lebanon area, asking participants — among them healthcare professionals, cybersecurity experts, emergency workers, and others — to problem-solve their step-by-step response. 
“What surprised me the most was how quickly decision-makers have to make consequential choices that have big impacts,” Schongalla said. “… It really forces you to confront stark choices. I was surprised at how quickly you have to make those decisions, and with how little information is available to you.”
A reliable water supply is crucial to the continued operations of a hospital, Schongalla said, for uses from the sterilization of instruments and patient rooms to food service, fire suppression, and even climate control. Without it, operations would rapidly become constrained.
At any hospital, and in any community, a sudden loss of water might lead to decisions like turning people away from the emergency department; postponing surgeries; and choosing how to prioritize services like dialysis centers, nursing homes, and the homes of local residents when there isn’t enough water available to go around.
“As an emergency physician, my patients and I would be on the front line of these attacks,” Schongalla said. 
Water pumps and electronic equipment at the Concord water treatment facility. (Photo by Molly Rains, New Hampshire Bulletin)
What can be done
Pennichuck Water relies on help from the state and federal government in order to stay up-to-date on their cyber defenses, Boisvert said. 
They have particularly valued consultation with the New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, he said. 
The Overwatch Foundation, a New Hampshire nonprofit, also works with municipalities to improve cybersecurity, including for water system operations infrastructure. 
But Boisvert would like to see more resources made available to water systems for readiness work, and he is concerned about the Trump administration’s cuts to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency staff and programming, including cuts that have reduced the amount of help available to critical infrastructure providers. 
Aid from that agency can be crucial to small operators, Boisvert said. 
“Those are the last places that we should be diverting funds away for other activities,” Boisvert said. 
Corman recommends engineering physical solutions, especially when moving goalposts make true cybersecurity preparedness feel out of reach. 
That could look like a pressure-moderating valve, which mechanically prevents the kind of rapid pressure changes that could disrupt a system, or a locally controlled time-delay device to keep hackers from rapidly turning implements on and off in an attempt to burn them out. 
Through his nonprofits, such as UnDisruptable 27, Corman works with public water systems to help implement these protections — which can also be less expensive than cybersecurity protection, he said. 
The principles behind Corman’s recommendations echo an idea raised by Keane: to be truly safe from cyberattacks, a water system may have to be fully disconnected from the internet. 
“Depending on how bad things get in the future, I wouldn’t be surprised if it did get that way. … But it is a huge cost,” Keane said, adding that voters would have to decide what path they want to take. 
But the solid foundations of water treatment are a major advantage that makes the worst-case scenarios less scary to Boisvert, he said. 
“The beauty of water treatment is it’s hydraulics and chemistry at its heart,” he said. “… There’s a really solid operational and engineering foundation we can fall back on, to be able to make sure that we can operate systems. … There’s storage in the system, there is reaction time, and there are things that we try to set ourselves up for, by building redundancy.”
Boisvert called for more regulation to make water system cybersecurity more robust across New Hampshire, in addition to added support and funding.
This matter also came up before the New Hampshire Legislature earlier this year. 
In March, legislators rejected a bill that sought to make water operators liable for damages if they did not have a certain level of cybersecurity protections in place for their operations. But they would later pass Senate Bill 589, from prime sponsor and Dover Democrat Sen. David Watters, which included some requirements for water and energy system cybersecurity. 
The bill calls for drinking water and wastewater system operators to implement cybersecurity protection programs, and allows the New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services to make rules about cybersecurity programs for the systems. That rulemaking process is beginning this month, according to a department spokesperson.
On the ground, stakeholders need more government support to fully understand the scope of the risks they may be facing, Schongalla said. 
Public preparedness is also part of the challenge — though increasing knowledge of the threat without inciting panic is also a delicate balance, Schongalla added. He called for individuals to think about their own emergency preparedness plans, including by imagining how their community losing access to water might complicate things.
“The resources and the systems that we’ve built up, you know, could be fragile under many circumstances, and it’s important to study ways to prepare,” he said. “… We’ve lived our whole lives expecting these services to be available. It’s hard for us to imagine what it’s like to not have them.”
Penacook Lake, in Concord, is the source of drinking water for the city, including Concord Hospital, residents, schools, and businesses. For this purpose, the water must be treated daily in a series of steps that are monitored by a combination of automated systems and human managers. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)

name: National
title: FEMA is off the chopping block. But disaster aid is still a guessing game.
description: State leaders are breathing a sigh of relief that the Trump administration’s threats to eliminate the Federal Emergency Management Agency have subsided.  But experts say there’s still confusion about President Donald Trump’s decisions to approve or deny disaster declarations, leaving states with uncertainty about whether they can expect federal recovery fund[...]
text:
Sisters watch as a skid-steer loader pulls a tree in Highmore, South Dakota, on June 29, 2026, after a severe storm that morning. The Federal Emergency Management Agency announced it will reimburse eight South Dakota counties and three tribes for storm-related infrastructure fixes. (Photo by Meghan O’Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)State leaders are breathing a sigh of relief that the Trump administration’s threats to eliminate the Federal Emergency Management Agency have subsided. 
But experts say there’s still confusion about President Donald Trump’s decisions to approve or deny disaster declarations, leaving states with uncertainty about whether they can expect federal recovery funds.
“The foundation (at FEMA) seems stronger than it did six months ago, but this is an unreliable administration when it comes to the fair and equitable distribution of disaster funds,” said Juliette Kayyem, faculty chair of the Homeland Security Project at Harvard University’s Kennedy School of Government and a former Obama administration official.
Trump has long called on states to take on a larger role in responding to disasters, and suggested early in his second term that FEMA might “go away” entirely. Kristi Noem, who served as Trump’s secretary of Homeland Security until she was fired in March, pledged at one point to “eliminate” FEMA, and slashed the agency’s spending and staffing during her tenure. 
Last month, the Senate confirmed Cameron Hamilton to serve as FEMA’s administrator, making him the first permanent agency leader during Trump’s second term. Hamilton, once a FEMA critic, had previously served as acting administrator, but was fired in May 2025 after saying he had become convinced the agency should not be eliminated. 
Experts say Hamilton’s return and Noem’s departure are signs of stability for FEMA. 
“It’s basically a return to regular order,” said Craig Fugate, who served as FEMA’s administrator under President Barack Obama. “They’re filling positions and reestablishing programs that got cut during the purge.”
State emergency managers say the leadership changes are welcome developments. 
“(Hamilton) he has the right attitude as far as supporting his employees and supporting the states,” said Lynn Budd, director of the Wyoming Office of Homeland Security. “I have a positive feel for that.”
Budd also serves as president of the National Emergency Management Association, a nonprofit comprising state and territorial emergency officials.



Quotation







The foundation (at FEMA) seems stronger than it did six months ago, but this is an unreliable administration when it comes to the fair and equitable distribution of disaster funds.


– Juliette Kayyem, faculty chair of the Homeland Security Project at Harvard University’s Kennedy School of Government 


While FEMA appears to be safe from the most drastic threats, states still face uncertainty over some agency programs they have long relied on. The agency has said that states must comply with Trump’s voting and immigration policies in order to qualify for Homeland Security Grant Program funding. A coalition of states and municipalities have sued, saying they stand to lose out on millions of dollars they need to prepare for terrorist and other security threats. 
The White House press office did not respond to a Stateline interview request. 
Trump decisions
Experts say the biggest challenge for emergency managers is the lack of clarity around Trump’s disaster approvals. While FEMA has clear thresholds that determine which disasters qualify for federal aid, the president has full discretion to approve or deny those requests for help.
Trump has been far more willing to grant disaster declarations for Republican-led states, at 89%, while Democratic-led states have seen only 23% of their requests approved, a Politico analysis found in March. 
Trump overruled the recommendations of his own agencies when he rejected federal aid for four Democratic-led states in July, Politico reported. 
Trump denies disaster aid, tells states to do more

“The bad news is you have a very unreliable administration and a very political president,” said Kayyem, of Harvard. “When it comes to states’ expectations, we can’t know what this White House will do.”
But some emergency management veterans said the denials aren’t a clear-cut case of political retribution. Fugate, the former FEMA administrator under Obama, noted that many of the disaster requests Trump rejected were snow-related. Trump’s administration has pushed to eliminate snow assistance from FEMA disaster aid, arguing that states should not receive federal reimbursement for plowing their own roads. Many of the northern states that have experienced snow disasters are represented by Democrats. 
For other disasters, Fugate said, Trump has a higher bar for granting federal recovery funds. 
“The administration’s been very clear they’re wanting to raise thresholds, even if they haven’t formally changed the numbers,” he said. “I’ve not seen them deny catastrophic disasters, major disasters. It’s the smaller marginal disasters that are really judgment calls.”
While saying he “ain’t a big fan” of the Trump administration, Fugate said shifting the financial burden for disaster relief from the feds back to the states has been a longtime discussion among both parties. 
Still, emergency managers said the White House should provide more clarity about what the new thresholds are and give states time to prepare for a bigger role. 
“There’s really never been feedback about why a disaster was denied,” said Budd, the Wyoming official. “That’s something I would hope to see in the future, creating more clarity in what exactly are we looking at when we go through the process of trying to request a major disaster declaration.”
State money
Some states have begun preparing for a drawback of FEMA support. Tennessee lawmakers established a statewide recovery fund intended to help communities hit by disasters that don’t qualify for federal aid. While Republican Gov. Bill Lee requested $100 million to create the fund, lawmakers ultimately approved $44.2 million earlier this year. Some legislators fear that won’t go very far. 
Trump wants states to handle disasters without FEMA. They say they can’t.

“Cutting it by more than half shows the State can’t afford for FEMA to cut back its support, much less to stop supporting states altogether,” state Sen. Jeff Yarbro, a Democrat, told the Tennessee Lookout in a statement. “Funded at its current level, this fund can only really fill a few gaps where FEMA is too slow or too rigid.”
Budd, the president of the emergency managers’ group, said other states are considering similar funds. 
“These are the types of programs that we as states need to look at, and something that I will have conversations about with our legislators in the future,” she said. 
But as states look at making those investments, Budd called on the White House to give them more time. 
“The very hard part about saying states need to do more is that it cannot happen overnight,” she said. “It will take time for states and lawmakers to build that.”
Stateline reporter Alex Brown can be reached at abrown@stateline.org.
