name: Mississippi Today
title: SEC sues LSU as athletes plead in court to regain eligibility with college sports season underway
description: FILE - Alabama offensive lineman Jaeden Roberts (77) blocks Missouri defensive tackle Sterling Webb (10) during the first half of an NCAA college football game, Saturday, Oct. 26, 2024, in Tuscaloosa, Ala. (AP Photo/Vasha Hunt, File)
text:
Athlete after athlete took the stand in a state courtroom near LSU on Thursday to explain why they should be allowed to return to play college sports after turning pro while the commissioner of the powerful Southeastern Conference argued against them and the league doubled down by filing a lawsuit against the school in federal court.
The extraordinary confrontation came just two days before the 11th-ranked Tigers open the football season at home against Clemson a few miles from the courthouse. East Baton Rouge Parish Judge William Jorden scheduled the hearing over his temporary injunction preventing the NCAA from barring former pros or fifth-year college athletes, a stance also taken by the SEC and other Power Four conferences with rules adopted last week.
Former New Orleans Saints defensive lineman Zxavian Harris and former Cleveland Browns tight end Dae’Quan Wright, two players who hope to suit up for LSU, sat next to each other in the gallery as the hearing began and both took the stand.
Wright testified that he would not have tried to turn pro had he known about the possibility of getting another year in college. He said he was paid a $25,000 signing bonus by Philadelphia and would gladly pay that back for the chance to play for LSU, adding that he made around $1 million during four years in college.
Two LSU soccer players, Jazmin Ferguson and Jocelyn Ollivierre, won court earlier court orders and have already played this season. Ferguson testified that she was paid $4,500 by a USL team, but ended her contract and paid the money back in hopes of clearing the way to play for the Tigers again.
FILE – Greg Sankey, commissioner of the Southeastern Conference, speaks during NCAA college basketball women’s SEC Media Day, Oct. 16, 2024, in Birmingham, Ala. (AP Photo/Mike Stewart, File) Credit: AP Photo/Mike Stewart
The athletes testified after SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey was on the stand for more than two hours, defending the league’s authority to enforce its week-old rules barring former pros from returning to play at its 16 member schools. He said school presidents and chancellors felt that they needed to establish a line between professional and college sports and that there needed to be ways to hold schools accountable.
“The line between professional sports and college sports needs to be maintained,” Sankey testified, adding that the league was concerned about incoming athletes being displaced from limited roster spots.
As he spoke, the SEC filed the federal lawsuit against LSU and its leadership in Alabama, alleging the school had “waged a deliberate and coordinated campaign to recruit professional athletes” in defiance of league rules. The court filing against one of the league’s founding members in 1933 seeks an injunction barring LSU from violating the SEC’s First Amendment rights by forcing it to “associate with conduct that is contrary to the conference’s purpose and mission.”
Legal experts said the filing was a backup in case the the SEC loses in state court. Outside the courthouse in Baton Rouge, plaintiffs’ attorney Tony Clayton said: “I got a problem with that. I mean, you go around, you can file this suit in any state. You’re suing LSU. Sue them in Louisiana. You go to our nemesis: Alabama. Really? So, so that lets you know what the commissioner is all about.”
Questioning of Sankey turns sharp
In questioning Sankey, attorneys for the athletes cited numerous examples of when SEC eligibility rules align with NCAA rules, suggesting the potential of collusion. They questioned why league members met last week to adopt stiff penalties for the very actions addressed in the Louisiana state court’s temporary injunction against the NCAA.
The attorneys also asked why the SEC singled out players who signed contracts with specific U.S.-based leagues — the NFL, NBA and WNBA — but not overseas pro leagues or women’s pro soccer leagues. When Sankey tried to qualify an answer about whether the SEC had previously punished a school for adding a player with previous pro experience, Clayton said, “I didn’t ask how to build a clock. I’m just asking what time it is.”
Sankey acknowledged that there had previously been no such punishment, but that it had been considered against Alabama last basketball season when the Crimson Tide briefly added a former G-League player.
There was no indication when Jorden might rule but the football season is already underway and most teams playing this weekend. The SEC requires its schools to submit final 2026 rosters for the season by Friday.
Players going to court has become common
The players in question also include former Denver Broncos defensive back Blake Cotton, who like Harris and Wright is hoping to join LSU and new coach Lane Kiffin.
Wright, who played for Kiffin last season at Mississippi, started practicing at LSU this week, too late to be eligible for Saturday’s home opener against Clemson under the NCAA’s required seven days of practice. Harris, who also played at Ole Miss last season, has committed to LSU, while Cotton, who played at Utah last fall, has been recruited by Kiffin.
All three are among a host of athletes who’ve argued in lawsuits around the country that they are unfairly being denied an opportunity to spend a fifth year in college under newly adopted NCAA rules allowing for five full years of competition. In all, the NCAA says there are approximately 450 athlete plaintiffs seeking additional eligibility through litigation, with some 300 of them winning the ability to play at least for now.
The athletes in the case who signed pro contracts have argued they did so only because current rules that would have allowed them another college season weren’t adopted until after their decisions to leave for the chance to make an NFL roster.
The SEC contends the question before the judge should be a narrow one regarding whether the conference “can enforce and require its member institutions to comply with SEC rules.” The SEC’s proposed punishments include significant fines, up to half-season suspensions for coaches and member universities’ loss of voting privileges on league business matters.
Sankey provided an affidavit stating that SEC university presidents had voted 15-0 in favor of the new rules, with LSU’s Wade Rousse abstaining.
The fight over eligibility between schools and their own conferences and the NCAA has simmered for months and spilled into politics.
Georgia Attorney General Chris Carr reportedly sent a letter of support to Sankey, encouraging him to take “all measures available” to punish LSU if it added former NFL players. Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill, who attended the hearing and chatted with plaintiffs’ attorneys before the proceeding, countered in a brief that the NCAA had subjected athletes in the case to a “classic bait-and-switch.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Pillen, Evnen, county election officials call for changes to Nebraska petition circulator laws
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, Secretary of State Bob Evnen and multiple county election officials are calling for changes to petitioning in the state amid multiple investigations of possibly fraudulent signatures statewide. Evnen said petitioners submitted about 767,000 signatures for review across 17 separate petitions this year. That includes 85,000[...]
text:
Lancaster County Election Commissioner Todd Wiltgen speaks at a news conference alongside Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen, Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen and Hall County Election Commissioner Tracy Overstreet, from left, at a news conference in the Nebraska State Capitol on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, Secretary of State Bob Evnen and multiple county election officials are calling for changes to petitioning in the state amid multiple investigations of possibly fraudulent signatures statewide.
Evnen said petitioners submitted about 767,000 signatures for review across 17 separate petitions this year. That includes 85,000 petition pages, each one of which can have no more than 20 signatures. The petitions included statewide ballot measures, Lincoln City Charter amendments and nonpartisan or partisan candidates for the Nov. 3 ballot.
Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen. Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Of the petitions, election officials in at least Lancaster County and Hall County caught and forwarded thousands of signatures suspected to be fraudulent to authorities. As of Aug. 19, six out-of-state circulators had been arrested, and law enforcement was searching for a seventh.
County law enforcement officers are actively reviewing signatures across at least eight 2026 petitions. 
Evnen couldn’t confirm whether more petitions or campaigns are under investigation because of the ongoing criminal investigation. He described attempted fraud as a “despicable act.”
“We caught the signature fraud. This is not an accident,” Evnen said. “This is the result of the hard work and dedication of our county election officials and the hard work and dedication of the people in the Elections Division of the Secretary of State’s Office.”
‘Open to suggestions’
Hall County Election Commissioner Tracy Overstreet hearkened back to 2024, when her office also flagged wrong dates of birth, wrong addresses, misspelled names and bad signatures on two medical cannabis petitions. Some purported signers, law enforcement said at the time, were deceased.
A Grand Island circulator pleaded guilty to having used an old phone book to add names. A jury this spring convicted a York notary for improper notarizations on the circulator’s petition pages. The notary is appealing his convictions.
Hall County Election Commissioner Tracy Overstreet. Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
This election cycle, Overstreet said, her office again flagged possibly fraudulent signatures.
“The bottom line here is that Nebraska’s system works,” Overstreet said. “It was, and it is, successful in identifying fraudulent signatures, which are then not counted toward the thresholds that need to be met to put measures on the ballot.”
Overstreet cautioned that while the process works, it comes at a cost to taxpayers, as county officials put in extra hours while petition supporters want a quick answer. 
Overstreet and Lancaster County Election Commissioner Todd Wiltgen are co-chairs of an Election Law Committee for a statewide association of all 93 county clerks, registers of deeds and election commissioners. Overstreet said the association is discussing possible improvements to signature gathering.
“Our association is pledging to work closely with the Governor’s Office, the Secretary of State’s Office, the Legislature’s Government, Military and Veterans Affairs Committee and the full Unicameral in making our gold standard election system even better,” Overstreet said.
Overstreet said whether to reform the notary process, to combat situations like that in 2024, has not come up in conversation, though a possible registry of petition circulators, similar to one for notary publics, has come up. Evnen said the role of sponsors in oversight will be part of discussions.
“We’re open to suggestions for all improvements,” Overstreet said.
‘Essential firewall’
Election officials in other states might verify a small sample of signatures, Evnen said, but in the Cornhusker State, signatures are reviewed line by line, by hand, until enough are verified according to state law.
The process includes verifying a signer’s name, date of birth and address with their information on file. If that information checks out, the voter’s signature is also cross-referenced.
Lancaster County Election Commissioner Todd Wiltgen. Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Wiltgen and his office flagged more than 13,300 signatures as possibly fraudulent on three petitions seeking to amend the Lincoln City Charter this year. The Good Government Lincoln campaign has said it supports Wiltgen’s work and his referral to law enforcement. The group restarted its efforts and submitted more signatures.
Wiltgen said all presumption is given toward a signature being valid, Wiltgen said, but there are multiple steps in checking, including for signature characteristics alone.
Pillen described the county process as an “essential firewall” achieved through a “robust, multilayered verification framework that we all need to be proud of.” At the “heart,” he said, are local officials.
Ending ‘bounty signatures’
Pillen and Evnen repeated their call Thursday to prohibit paying circulators per signature. Such a ban existed between July 2008 and August 2015. A bipartisan group of lawmakers approved that law, overriding a veto from former Gov. Dave Heineman, but seven years later, a different group of lawmakers reversed it, with no opposition, under then-Gov. Pete Ricketts.
Petition pages reviewed by local county election officials and returned to the Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office sit in the office for public inspection at the office’s Elections Division in downtown Lincoln on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Former state Sen. DiAnna Schimek of Lincoln, a longtime, powerful Democrat in the Legislature who also chaired the Legislature’s Government, Military and Veterans Affairs Committee, ushered in the 2008 ban. Pillen said she “got it right.”
“The process of bounty signature gathering is sabotaging legitimate petition initiative efforts. It’s as simple as that,” Pillen said. “It’s not the Nebraska way.”
Pillen joked that the “only place” Nebraskans should be hearing the word “bounties” is on the radio and TV Western drama “Gunsmoke.”
The first petition campaigns that could again pay per signature, and which later went to voters, were those seeking to opt Nebraska into Medicaid expansion statewide and locally amend the Lincoln City Charter to place term limits on the Lincoln mayor, each in 2018. Both passed.
Other suggested reforms
Evnen said he is also working on legislation that would restrict circulators to U.S. citizens and nonfelons and require that prospective circulators complete training detailing their job and responsibilities. Circulators would also need to affirmatively consent to the laws of Nebraska.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, at podium, and Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen, center left, join Election Commissioners Danielle Jensen (Douglas County), Todd Wiltgen (Lancaster County), Tracy Overstreet (Hall County) and David Jones (Sarpy County) for a news conference regarding thousands of signatures suspected to be fraudulent on 2026 petitions in the Nebraska State Capitol on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In addition to legislation, Pillen said there needs to be a cultural shift where petitioners “prioritize genuine voter engagement over raw volume” of signatures.
“I’m a believer that the people speak as the second house in Nebraska,” Pillen said. “I believe the people speak when we come together without being coerced by money.”
Evnen’s office has in the past also suggested moving up the petition deadline and expanding the time for officials to review signatures. But he said he hasn’t given further thought to that idea and expects technology will become more accurate and more cost effective in the future, too.
For now, Evnen said, “we’ll stick with what we have” with physical verification.
“Nebraskans once again owe a debt of gratitude to our counties because they do this heavy lifting, and they do it very, very well,” Evnen said. “They’re dedicated, responsible people who are highly competent in their work, and they’re the ones who give Nebraskans the elections that they can be proud of.”
‘Few bad apples’
Former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, who is challenging Pillen’s reelection under the America First Party ballot line, told the Nebraska Examiner that the reforms Evnen outlined “seem prudent.” His early nonpartisan bid for governor this summer went down in smoke, in part due to overlapping petition circulators who law enforcement say submitted fraudulent signatures.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, a Republican, bottom left, is running for reelection against former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, bottom right, Rick Beard of Omaha, the nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW party, top left, and former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, the nominee for the America First party, top right. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Lindstrom was one of the 42 of 49 lawmakers who reversed the pay-per-signature ban in 2015. He said he learned firsthand how that could backfire.
“The vast majority of people I don’t think are out there trying to scam,” Lindstrom said. “But a few bad apples ruin the bunch, and you had this ripe for fraud.”
Lindstrom reiterated that he will be pursuing legal action because of how his nonpartisan bid ended.
Former state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, Pillen’s Democratic challenger, said in a statement that the suspected fraud this year is a “historic attack” on Nebraskans’ right to govern themselves. She said that can’t go unanswered and is calling on Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers to appoint a special prosecutor.
“Governor Pillen has spent two years trying to block and override what Nebraska voters have already decided, and now he wants to use this fraud as cover to make the citizen ballot initiative process harder to use,” Walz said. “The people in Nebraska expect answers.”
‘False implications and phony innuendos’
While not giving specifics, Evnen used his time Thursday to push back on what he described as people “running around our state doing everything they can to make Nebraskans feel worried and unsure and uncertain about our elections.”
“They don’t have facts or evidence, so they’re peddling false implications and phony innuendos. It’s shameful what they’re doing,” Evnen said. “No state runs better elections than Nebraska. No state runs elections that are more secure and accurate than we do.”
A woman signs a Support Our Schools petition in Omaha. July 8, 2024. (Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)
Asked to clarify what he meant, Evnen said a “litany of things” regarding elections are being repeated statewide, including those he said his office has examined and found no validity. He did not give examples.
“We’re not vulnerable to these things, and yet they continue to get repeated,” Evnen said.
Evnen had been running for a third four-year term until May, when he lost the Republican primary to Scott Petersen of Omaha, who specifically criticized Evnen and has called for more significant changes to the administration of Nebraska elections.
Also running for Evnen’s seat are Democrat Sarah Slattery of Plattsmouth, Paul Rumbaugh of Omaha for the Nebraska Working People Party and former state Sen. Bob Krist of Omaha for the America First Party. Evnen has not endorsed anyone in the race.
Pillen repeated that election integrity is “about Nebraska” and that every Nebraskan should know that when they get out to vote, their voice will be heard with confidence in the outcome.
“We will continue to ensure that our ballots remain secure, transparent and driven strictly by Nebraskans,” Pillen said.
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: President Trump vows to campaign in Alaska for incumbent Republican US Sen. Dan Sullivan
description: President Donald Trump said Wednesday in Washington, D.C., that he will travel to Alaska to campaign on behalf of incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, who appears to be facing a close race against Democratic challenger Mary Peltola.  “I will go to Alaska to help Dan Sullivan get elected. … Dan Sullivan’s a great senator,” […]
text:
Former President Donald Trump prepares to speak in front of a crowd at the Alaska Airlines Center in Anchorage on Saturday, July 9, 2022. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)President Donald Trump said Wednesday in Washington, D.C., that he will travel to Alaska to campaign on behalf of incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, who appears to be facing a close race against Democratic challenger Mary Peltola. 
“I will go to Alaska to help Dan Sullivan get elected. … Dan Sullivan’s a great senator,” Trump said.
Because most U.S. Senate seats are in states controlled firmly by Republicans or Democrats, control of the U.S. Senate as a whole will be decided by a relative handful of races nationally, including the one this year in Alaska.     

U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, speaks to the Anchorage Chamber of Commerce on Nov. 24, 2025. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

A spokesperson for Sullivan’s campaign did not immediately return an email seeking comment on Thursday.
In the just-completed August primary election, Peltola had 49.5% of the vote; Sullivan had 41.4% of the vote. 
Despite that performance, a recent poll of voters likely to participate in November indicates a race that’s in a virtual dead heat. That poll is similar to others conducted earlier this year.
On Wednesday at the Oval Office, one reporter asked Trump why the race is so close.
“I don’t know. Well, it’s close for one reason that they have a phony Dan Sullivan,” Trump said. “This guy’s a phony and he was put up by the Democrats and they don’t admit it, but it’s been so proven.” 
The third person in Alaska’s four-way race for U.S. Senate is Dan J. Sullivan, a Republican from Petersburg who earned 2.5% of the vote in the August primary. 
Many of Dan J. Sullivan’s votes in the primary came from Democratic-leaning districts, and both he and people representing Peltola’s campaign have said that there has been no coordination between the two.
Despite that, the president, the incumbent and other Republicans have accused Dan Sullivan of nefarious actions without providing evidence.
On Wednesday, Dan J. Sullivan told Alaska Public Media that he was out picking mushrooms and hadn’t heard the president’s remarks.
When reached by the Alaska Beacon on Thursday, he declined comment. 
Trump incorrectly said Dan J. Sullivan had never voted. 
“He hasn’t voted for years. A totally pretty nonpolitical person, I guess, but never had any thought of running,” Trump said. 
State records show Dan J. Sullivan is a “supervoter” who has cast ballots in 17 state and local elections since 2017. 
“That guy got two and a half percent in the recent primary. And that’s — two and a half percent is a lot when it comes to winning elections. And it’s a disgrace,” Trump said.
Trump also criticized Alaska’s ranked choice general election system, saying it amounted to picking a name out of a hat. 
Under the Alaska system, voters are asked to rank the four candidates (and any write-ins) in order of preference. If one candidate receives more than half of the first-preference votes, they win.
If no one has more than half the votes, the lowest finisher is eliminated, and their votes go to voters’ second choices. The process repeats until only two candidates are left, and the person with the most votes wins.
It isn’t clear how much Trump’s influence would help the incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan. 
Alaska has voted for Trump each time he has run for president. In 2024, 54.5% of participating voters picked Trump for president, putting him 13 percentage points ahead of Democratic candidate Kamala Harris.
“It’s a long trip. I love Alaska. You know, I won Alaska by a landslide,” Trump told reporters attending a gathering of travel industry officials.
But since that election, Alaskans’ opinion of Trump appears to have soured. Public opinion polling conducted in August found that more than 56% of Alaskans have a negative view of Trump. 
In 2022, Trump visited the Alaska Airlines Center at the University of Alaska Anchorage to boost the campaigns of U.S. Sen. candidate Kelly Tshibaka, U.S. House candidate Sarah Palin and governor candidate Mike Dunleavy. 
Tshibaka and Palin lost their races that year; Dunleavy won his. 
As of Thursday, no one representing the president had booked the Alaska Airlines Center, a UAA official said.
Trump also visited Anchorage last year to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin. Though highly promoted as an opportunity to end the Russia-Ukraine war, the event resulted in little more than a photo opportunity.
Sullivan has been a mostly reliable vote in the Senate for Trump’s agenda since the president was re-elected in 2024. In 2025, Sullivan voted along with Trump on every major topic before Congress. This year, Sullivan has only occasionally voted against Trump’s goals, including once against the President’s plans to distribute $1.8 billion in public funds to supporters, including those convicted of participating in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol.
Trump said he is in regular contact with Sullivan.
“He would call me all the time because I think — no, I definitely know — nobody has helped Alaska like Donald Trump. We’ve invested billions and billions of dollars and created trillions of dollars in value,” Trump said, exaggerating trends on the ground in the state. 
According to Federal Reserve data, Alaska’s gross domestic product rose by about $3.5 billion between 2024 and 2025, continuing a trend that started in 2020. 
He also exaggerated the importance of Alaskan oil internationally.
“You have Japan, you have South Korea, you have all of these people now going to Alaska to load up with fuel, load up with oil, build pipelines, everything else,” Trump said.
Only about 5% of Alaska North Slope crude has been exported internationally this year. 
Trump said his trip to Alaska will be one of several that he intends to take before Election Day on Nov. 3. 
“I will be going to Alaska. I’m going to be going the last 30 days before the election. I’ll be making a lot of stops,” Trump said.
“I’m going to be campaigning for numerous people, both Congressmen — a few governors, I love the governors — but we’re interested in the Senate, and we’re interested in the House. So I’ll be campaigning for the House members and I’ll be campaigning for senators,” he said.

title: Federal judge’s order allowing an Idaho doctor to perform certain abortions is put on hold
description: A panel of judges has placed on hold a federal court order protecting an Idaho fetal medicine doctor from prosecution for abortions performed in specific circumstances.  The order means Idaho’s abortion laws are fully in effect, with only exemptions to protect the life of the mother, or in cases of rape and incest in the […]
text:
Idaho’s abortion ban applies to any stage of pregnancy, with affirmative defenses for cases of rape and incest with an accompanying police report and if an abortion is necessary to save a patient’s life. (Photo illustration by Getty Images)A panel of judges has placed on hold a federal court order protecting an Idaho fetal medicine doctor from prosecution for abortions performed in specific circumstances. 
The order means Idaho’s abortion laws are fully in effect, with only exemptions to protect the life of the mother, or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester if a police report has been filed. Doctors who perform abortions outside of those exemptions face felony penalties and revocation or suspension of their medical license. 
Idaho federal judge narrows abortion ruling to only protect Boise doctor who filed lawsuit

The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel on Thursday blocked a ruling that would’ve carved out new exemptions in Idaho’s strict abortion ban for the doctor challenging the law.
The order will be in place until Ninth Circuit judges are scheduled to hear arguments on Sept. 22. 
Previously, U.S. District of Idaho Court Judge B. Lynn Winmill wrote in an 81-page decision on Aug. 13 that abortions could be performed in cases where the mother faced serious health risks or risk of self-harm, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported.  
However, after Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador appealed the ruling, Winmill narrowed the decision to only protect the doctor who filed the lawsuit challenging Idaho’s abortion ban, Dr. Stacy Seyb. 
Seyb, represented by attorneys from the Lawyering Project and Legal Voice, challenged the constitutionality of Idaho abortion ban’s limited exceptions 
“The Constitution protects pregnant people’s access to life- and health-preserving abortion care,” Lawyering Project Executive Director Stephanie Toti said in an email to the Sun  “We are hopeful that the court of appeals will allow that care to resume after it hears oral argument later this month.”
 Idaho Family Policy Center attorneys file brief in support of law on half of Idaho lawmakers 

Attorneys with the Idaho Family Policy Center, a conservative Christian lobbying group, filed a brief in support of Idaho’s abortion ban on behalf of 54 Idaho state legislators. Idaho Family Policy Center Legal Director Caleb Pirc wrote that Winmill’s decision went beyond his authority. 
“The district court improperly made policy for the people of Idaho,” Pirc wrote. “It may have thought its  policy was better than the Legislature’s, but that was not its judgment to make.” 
The brief says that the authority to create abortion policy rests solely with the Legislature. 
The lawmakers represented by the brief include 37 House representatives and 17 senators, all Republicans, including leaders from both chambers.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri Supreme Court blocks gerrymandered congressional map, orders referendum vote
description: Missourians will vote in November on the gerrymandered congressional map muscled through the Legislature in 2025, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled unanimously on Thursday. The decision puts a congressional plan before voters for the first time since 1922 and affirms that the Missouri Constitution’s provision allowing voter-initiated referenda applies to redi[...]
text:
Missouri Supreme Court Chief Judge Ginger Gooch wrote the opinion that upheld the right of referendum on congressional redistricting plans (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Missourians will vote in November on the gerrymandered congressional map muscled through the Legislature in 2025, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled unanimously on Thursday.
The decision puts a congressional plan before voters for the first time since 1922 and affirms that the Missouri Constitution’s provision allowing voter-initiated referenda applies to redistricting plans as well as almost all other legislation.
“Because the plain language of… the Missouri Constitution authorizes a referendum as to ‘any act of the general assembly’ and no exception applies, the referendum petition was legal, sufficient, and timely,” Judge Ginger Gooch wrote in the unanimous opinion. “This court reverses the circuit court’s judgment.”
The court not only put the referendum on the ballot, it ordered Secretary of State Denny Hoskins to use the district lines drawn in 2022 for this year’s general election.
“The secretary and all of those acting in concert with him are restrained and enjoined from implementing, using, or mandating the use of the congressional redistricting (plan from 2025) for the November 2026 general election or at any other time thereafter unless and until (the act) is approved by the voters at the November 2026 general election and takes effect 30 days thereafter,” Gooch wrote.
The court’s decision reverses the ruling of Cole County Circuit Judge Daniel Green, who found that the U.S. Constitution’s provisions on elections delegate sole power over congressional redistricting plans to state legislatures. That tie to the U.S. Constitution will be the basis of an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, Attorney General Catherine Hanaway said in a news release Thursday.
“Never before in American history has a court overturned a congressional map after a primary and before a general election. This unprecedented decision clearly violates federal law and has thrust our state into a full‑fledged constitutional crisis,” Hanaway said. “Our office will move immediately to seek relief from SCOTUS. We are confident that the federal courts will not allow every Missouri voter to be disenfranchised—which is what today’s decision does.”
The political action committee People Not Politicians gathered more than 300,000 signatures to force the referendum.
“This is what democracy looks like, the people of Missouri demanded a voice, and the court just confirmed what we’ve been saying all along. People, not politicians, will have the final say,” said Richard von Glahn, executive director, in a news release. “This victory reaches beyond Missouri. In a year when map-drawing has become a national weapon, courts across the country are watching what happens here. A Missouri win for the referendum is a signal that the people still hold the power.”
That means the boundaries of Districts 1 through 6 will change, with the most dramatic difference in the 5th District drawn last year to help Republicans take a seventh seat in the state’s delegation.
The results of the Aug. 4 primary, held in the boundaries of the now-suspended map, were not altered by the decision. It will be up to the nominated candidates to determine what they will do in response to the altered lines.
The decision closes out most of the litigation surrounding the referendum. Several new precedents have been set that upheld the broad power of a governor to call lawmakers into session; upheld the power of lawmakers to revise congressional lines at any time; and, in the final ruling, showed the wide scope of the referendum power.
In all three of those instances, the court looked to the text of the constitution and the common meaning of the words used. And, in each case, what the absence of particular words meant.
For the governor and the Legislature, the court found nothing in the Constitution that would restrict their authority to engage in redistricting at any time. 
And the same held true for the referendum power. The Constitution doesn’t say a redistricting plan is exempt from a referendum so that means it is allowed, the court ruled.
“Because no such explicit exception for legislation drawing new congressional districts is found anywhere in the Missouri Constitution, the broad default language… subjecting ‘any act of the general assembly’ to referendum applies,” Gooch wrote.
This story will be updated.

name: VTDigger
title: The teenager left behind in Irene’s chaos
description:
Marble Arvidson, then 17, disappeared just as Tropical Storm Irene began devastating the region. Along with the anniversary of the storm is the anniversary of his absence.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  The teenager left behind in Irene’s chaos.
text:
A computer-generated rendering of what Marble Arvidson might look like at age 23. Police released this photo-illustration on the 10th anniversary of his disappearance.

This story by Virginia Ray was first published in The Commons on Sept. 1, 2026.
BRATTLEBORO — Marble Ace Arvidson was 17, a senior-to-be at Brattleboro Union High School, when he left a note on his bedroom door at his foster home at 503 Marlboro Road — the red house beside the Chelsea Royal Diner — on the afternoon of Aug. 27, 2011, the day before Tropical Storm Irene hit.
One roommate had seen him that afternoon. Another heard a knock, then heard Marble talking at the door with a man whose voice he didn’t recognize, in an exchange friendly enough that the two seemed to know each other.
Marble wrote his note, stuck it to his door and left with the man. Marble was 6 feet tall, 165 pounds, with shoulder-length strawberry-blond hair, and he was dressed the way he liked to be seen: black button-down shirt, black pants and the black hat from Guatemala he wore nearly everywhere.
“He always wanted to make a statement,” his aunt, Trish Kittredge, said years later.
The note said he was out with the “Gremlin Hoard” and would be back soon — his family remembers it as 20 minutes, or 30. He marked it 2:17 p.m. He had a date with his girlfriend at 4 p.m.
He never came back.
No one treated it as a disappearance until the next day. And by that time, the storm had the state’s full attention.
“By then, the river had breached at that point, and roads were being washed out, power lines were down, and the whole community was in crisis — not just this family,” Kittredge said.
Irene swallowed the case almost before it began.
Search crews, road crews and police were already stretched across a state of washed-out bridges and cut-off towns.
Volunteers who might have combed the woods off Route 9 were pulling debris out of the Whetstone Brook instead. Kittredge herself was a command sergeant major in the Massachusetts Army National Guard, called to active duty for the storm; when her nephew went missing, she was granted leave to go look for him.
She ran the search out of a tent in the Chelsea Royal’s parking lot, a few hundred feet from the door Marble walked out of. Kittredge had at the ready a banquet table, with grid maps, yellow sticky notes marking cleared ground, a box of orange vests and a station wagon full of posters.
Each searcher got a map, a whistle, a camera and a briefing before they went out. They walked riverbanks and logging trails; a canine team joined in, and riders took ATVs up the four-wheeler paths and through the back lots off Route 9. Strangers arrived to hand out hugs along with flyers.
“We’re doing cursory searches, so we are looking at the path of least resistance,” Kittredge said that September. “We don’t have any information about where he likely walked off to.”
The unfairness of the timing was not lost on anyone standing in that parking lot.
“Human life is worth more than mud, and I’ve got kids,” said Tina Fisher of Halifax, who came with two daughters to take posters. “If one of mine went missing, I’d want someone out there looking for them.”
Fifteen years later, Marble Arvidson, now 32 years old, has not been found.
The man who came to the door has never been identified.
Vermont State Police logged several unconfirmed sightings, the last of them in Brattleboro in April 2012; nothing since has held up.
When detectives took a fresh run at the case in 2021, Brattleboro Police Detective Lt. Jeremy Evans — now the police chief — said that what makes the case unusual is that there is nothing to pull on at all.
“Just boom, and he was gone,” Evans said.
The case remains open with Brattleboro police and the VSP. Marble Arvidson is listed with the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System, aka NamUs. A reward for information leading to his location stood at $10,000.
On Aug. 27, the anniversary of his disappearance, the VSP posted an appeal on Facebook for information that could help find him.
“Marble is an avid hiker and reportedly took his hiking boots with him,” the post read. “It may be possible that Marble became a victim of Tropical Storm Irene as this major storm hit on the same day Marble was last seen.”
His mother, Sigrid Arvidson, has said for years that the flood took the coverage her son’s disappearance should have had, and that assumptions about him — a foster kid, a boy, a young man with his own struggles — have never helped the investigation.
What she has asked of anyone who knew him is simple: Don’t decide in advance that what you remember is nothing.
“I’m his mom. I want to find my boy, and miss him. I love him,” she said. “He deserves to be found.”
Anyone with information is asked to contact the Brattleboro Police Department at 802-257-7950 or the Vermont State Police’s Westminster barracks at 802-722-4600.

title: US Supreme Court again urged to permit Trump vote-by-mail restrictions
text: The Trump administration asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday to overturn a lower court and allow it to enforce a U.S. Postal Service rule restricting mail-in voting.The trial judge, Indira Talwani of the U.S. District of Massachusetts, prejudged the rule before it was final when she issued a temporary restraining order last month and upheld it last week, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote. The rule only regulates standards of mail delivery and doesn’t interfere with election administration, Sauer argued.“Contrary to the claims of the district court and respondents that the Postal Service is trying to federalize the rules for mail-in voting, the Postal Service’s final rule imposes only modest envelope-design and addressee-information requirements for federal-election ballots sent via U.S. Mail,” Sauer said.Temporary restraining orders are not typically appealable, but Sauer argued that because of the impending midterm election, the court should hear the appeal. The rule carries out an executive order made earlier this year by President Donald Trump.Election Day is two months from Thursday. One state, North Carolina, is expected to begin mailing ballots Friday.Morning hearingThe government filed the application just hours after Talwani, whom former President Barack Obama appointed, heard oral arguments on whether to convert her two-week restraining order into a longer preliminary injunction to block the administration from applying the rule during the fast-approaching election.Over months of litigation, Talwani has communicated disapproval of the rule and the government’s legal arguments and appeared skeptical of USPS’s position Thursday, according to reporters in the courtroom.The rule would create new standards for the envelopes used to send ballots to people who vote by mail. It would also allow the federal government to verify voters receiving ballots are eligible. Democratic state officials and voting rights groups say that is an unconstitutional violation of states’ role in administering elections and goes beyond anything Congress has authorized the agency to pursue.In addition to constitutional concerns, the rule raises practical ones. Experts in election administration say mandating wholesale changes to mail-in voting this close to an election would cause chaos. All states made arrangements to design, print and send mail ballots months ago. Changing those plans at this late stage would send them scrambling to update ballot envelope designs, have them approved by the USPS, printed in bulk and sent to voters — along with several other challenges, states have argued in court documents.Multiple court decisionsThe Trump administration has fought in court for weeks to allow the rule to go into effect before the midterms. Administration officials appealed an earlier Talwani restraining order blocking enforcement of the rule. That appeal is currently before the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. The Supreme Court last month sided with the administration in a procedural ruling finding that the Democratic state officials and voting rights groups did not have the ability to challenge Trump’s executive order before USPS issued its final rule. The challengers quickly refiled suits to reflect that the rule had been published.The U.S. Justice Department and a handful of Republican-led states, including Missouri and Texas, defended the rule in the Thursday morning hearing, saying that it was a mail regulation within the agency’s purview, and did not seek to administer elections.Voting rights groups have argued the rule risks disenfranchising voters and solves no urgent problem. Several phases of mail voting under the rule would put legitimate ballots at risk of rejection, they said, while the administration has shown no evidence that mail voting is particularly susceptible to fraud, as Trump repeatedly has claimed.Portal problemsThe buildout of an online tool the Postal Service plans to use to enforce the rule’s requirements for ballot designs and voter eligibility has also encountered problems, according to an explosive whistleblower report this week.A USPS official provided a written declaration following Thursday’s hearing that the portal would be accessible to states that want to use it “sometime next week.”The whistleblower account published Tuesday detailed many problems with the tool, which the whistleblower said should have been a yearlong project but was rushed out in months.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico immigrant advocates launch platform for training, job opportunities amid federal threats
description: Somos Un Pueblo Unido, a New Mexico immigrant advocacy organization, on Thursday launched an online platform seeking to connect foreign-born residents with a variety of state workforce development programs aimed at connecting workers with industries that need them.
text:
Marcela Diaz, executive director of immigration advocacy group Somos Un Pueblo Unido, touted her organization’s launch Sept. 3, 2026, of Somos Futuro, an online platform aimed to connect New Mexico immigrant workers with job skills and education. (Source NM file photo)Somos Un Pueblo Unido, a New Mexico immigrant advocacy organization, on Thursday launched an online platform seeking to connect foreign-born residents with a variety of state workforce development programs aimed at connecting workers with industries that need them.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Marcela Diaz, the organization’s executive director, said the platform, Somos Futuro, represents the culmination of several years of advocacy, but also launches at a time when President Donald Trump’s administration is trying to exclude immigrants from the workforce. She referenced the Trump administration’s crackdown on non-English-speaking long-haul truck drivers and a recent lawsuit against states including New Mexico that allow some immigrants to receive tuition assistance.
According to the state Department of Workforce Solutions, 21% of the state’s agricultural workers and 24% of construction workers are immigrants. A 2024 study that Somos Un Pueblo Unido commissioned from the University of New Mexico also found Latinos make up 46% of workers in the state’s oil and gas industry, which the state increasingly relies on to fund education and other vital services.
Given the role immigrant workers play in buttressing the state’s economy, Diaz said she and other immigrant advocacy organizations have, over the last three years at the Roundhouse, convinced state lawmakers to provide roughly $40 million in funding through different pieces of legislation for English as a Second Language courses, job training and financial assistance to help immigrant families achieve career objectives or higher wages.
“It’s pretty terrible when you’re giving so much to the education system through your essential work and not have commensurate investments in your families and your communities,” she said. 
The platform, in English and Spanish, connects immigrant workers to as many of those new and existing programs as possible, including to adult education opportunities, English classes, high school equivalency programs, career training and professional certification courses. 
One such program, the Economic Transition Program, is geared at oil and gas workers who are seeking to find new careers. Somos’ 2024 UNM report found that roughly three-quarters of the 100 immigrant oilfield workers they surveyed wanted their children to work in another industry, citing the sometimes dangerous work environment and long hours. 
Many workers do not know about that program or others Somos Futuro seeks to highlight, Diaz said.  
“Even when the programs exist in Spanish or regardless of immigration status or with wraparound supports, a lot of our members and people in the community don’t have a one-stop shop for it. They don’t have information about it,” she said. “And so that’s why we decided to just share what we know.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Lawmakers consider how to protect voting access for people with disabilities, non-English speakers
description: Accessibility advocates are urging state leaders to prioritize access for voters with disabilities and those who require language assistance as lawmakers prepare to overhaul Georgia’s election equipment ahead of 2028. The 2026 midterms are heating up, but this election panel is focused on 2028 Thanks to a bill passed during the June special session, state […[...]
text:
A ballot-marking device displays accessibility options to allow voters with disabilities to independently select candidates of their choice. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderAccessibility advocates are urging state leaders to prioritize access for voters with disabilities and those who require language assistance as lawmakers prepare to overhaul Georgia’s election equipment ahead of 2028.
The 2026 midterms are heating up, but this election panel is focused on 2028

Thanks to a bill passed during the June special session, state leaders appear likely to select hand-marked paper ballots as the state’s primary voting method ahead of 2028. The shift away from the state’s current, machine-marked ballot system will likely come as a relief to some critics of the current voting equipment, who have repeatedly cited fears over machine tampering and called for ballots to be counted based on text that can be deciphered by humans.
But Georgia residents likely won’t see voting machines vanish completely. Under federal accessibility laws, every polling place is required to have at least one voting machine on hand for voters with disabilities, even in jurisdictions where most voters mark ballots by hand.
At a Thursday meeting of a special committee tasked with helping select Georgia’s next statewide election system, election officials and voting advocates gathered to map out what the next election system could look like — and what accessibility pitfalls state leaders should avoid.
Disability advocates call for preserved voter access
Headphones and hand-held tactile devices allow voters with disabilities to select candidates of their choice on ballot-marking devices. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
Jessica Mathis, a Savannah-based disability advocate with the nonpartisan organization REV UP Georgia, said her cerebral palsy makes it hard for her to fill out a hand-marked ballot. She urged lawmakers to ensure that the next voting equipment system maintains key accessibility features that she and other voters with disabilities say they rely on, such as options for audio and large-print formats of ballots, wheelchair access at polling places and priority access during peak hours.
“If I had to fill out a paper ballot by hand, my handwriting could be hard to read, and my ballot could be challenged or thrown out,” she said. “No one should lose that right because of how their hand moves a pen or whether they can get access to the voting equipment.”
Paul Lux, the Okaloosa County, Florida elections supervisor who was invited to present to the committee, added that voters should not be required to prove their disability when asking to use a ballot-marking device instead of a hand-marked ballot.
“The Americans with Disabilities Act does not allow you to look at a voter and determine their ability or disability,” Lux said. “So, if a voter asks to use the ADA equipment, we presume they are eligible to use it and we make it available to them.”
Groups like New Disabled South are also encouraging lawmakers to consider policies that allow curbside voting to give Georgians with disabilities more flexibility to cast their ballot, especially at polling locations that do not comply with federal accessibility requirements.
Immigrant voter advocates raise ballot translation issues
Georgia’s increasingly diverse electorate could also pose a new challenge for elected officials seeking to serve voters who lack proficiency in English.
Under Section 203 of the Voting Rights Act, local jurisdictions are required to offer ballot access in an additional language whenever there are either 10,000 residents or more than 5% of the population that speaks that additional language and has low English proficiency. 
Gwinnett County, where U.S. Census data shows more than 38% of residents speak a language other than English at home, has been required to distribute ballots in Spanish and English since 2016, and has voluntarily translated sample ballots into languages like Korean, Mandarin and Vietnamese. DeKalb and Athens-Clarke counties also voluntarily translate certain elections materials.
Still, the act of translating a ballot is not always smooth sailing.
“When we send out for translation services, oftentimes the context of the question may be misinterpreted,” said Kelvin Williams, the acting elections supervisor of Gwinnett County. One vendor, he added, once “translated ‘Georgia House of Representatives’ as a dwelling and not a legislative body.”
Gwinnett County is the only jurisdiction in Georgia that’s currently required to provide ballots in languages other than English, but federal determinations around which communities meet the criteria are reevaluated every five years.
Anar Parik, the policy manager at Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta, speaks to lawmakers about language accessibility on Sept. 3, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
Anar Parik, the policy manager at the nonprofit Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta, said that other parts of Georgia with large multilingual populations, such as Whitfield County, could soon be added to the list, and that translation capabilities should be seen as a key feature of any new election equipment the state considers.
Whitfield County has a large Hispanic population, and according to Census data, more than 31% of people there speak a language other than English at home.
“The new system should be capable of adding additional languages through a programming or software configuration without purchasing replacement voting equipment,” Parik said.
Sen. Max Burns, a Sylvania Republican who co-chairs the committee, added that the state will likely need to begin thinking about ways to standardize ballot translation and additional language requirements on a statewide level.
“Georgia is becoming more and more diverse,” he said. “As our population of non-English language speakers grows, we have to be in position to accommodate those needs.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Sometimes the best crop is grass
description: South Dakota farmers are sending Washington a message with their acres. It deserves attention.  This year, producers offered nearly 290,000 South Dakota acres for Conservation Reserve Program enrollment. About 54,000 acres were renewals and 237,000 acres were new land. The U.S. Department of Agriculture accepted about 209,000 acres. Those numbers suggest som[...]
text:
Grass sways in the breeze in a ditch outside of Union Center, South Dakota, on June 26, 2026. A field of sweet clover blooms in the distance. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota farmers are sending Washington a message with their acres. It deserves attention. 
This year, producers offered nearly 290,000 South Dakota acres for Conservation Reserve Program enrollment. About 54,000 acres were renewals and 237,000 acres were new land. The U.S. Department of Agriculture accepted about 209,000 acres.
Those numbers suggest something plain: Many South Dakota landowners are deciding some of their acres make more sense as grass than as another crop.
That comes at an interesting time in the farm bill debate. The Senate Agriculture Committee failed to advance its bill Aug. 6 amid disputes over food assistance and Republican absences. Chairman John Boozman says he will try again.
For farmers and ranchers who have waited years for a new farm bill, another delay is hardly welcome. But the conservation provisions are not necessarily finished.
South Dakota has some ideas already on the table.
Sen. John Thune has proposed changes to CRP that are included in the Senate bill. They would restore cost-share assistance for mid-contract management such as prescribed fire, help pay for fencing and water development, improve grazing and haying flexibility and raise the annual CRP payment limit.
Those changes may sound technical, but they matter. Grazing, prescribed fire and other management can improve forage and rejuvenate habitat for pheasants and other wildlife.

U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Sen. Mike Rounds, both Republicans from South Dakota, speak with an attendee of Dakotafest in Mitchell on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)

Sen. Mike Rounds has proposed something different. His bipartisan RANCH Act would give willing producers an option to take marginal cropland, restore it to perennial grass and, crucially, continue using it for livestock production.
The distinction is the point. The proposal is not about idling farmland.
The land could be grazed throughout the season. Producers would enter 10- to 15-year contracts, receive annual payments tied to county cropland rental rates and get help establishing grass. Highly erodible and poorly performing cropland would receive priority. The program could eventually cover as many as 20 million acres nationally, which is equivalent to 31,250 square miles.
South Dakota already has experience combining grass and agricultural production.
By 2024, about 1,800 South Dakota landowners had nearly 1.5 million acres enrolled in Grassland CRP. Those acres remain in grass while supporting sustainable livestock grazing.
Grassland CRP generally helps keep grasslands intact. Rounds is proposing the other side of the equation: helping willing producers turn some marginal cropland back into grass.
Researchers examining U.S. land-use changes from 2008 through 2016 found that 88% of newly expanded cropland came from grasslands — and nearly 70% of those acres produced below-average yields.  
South Dakota was among the places where grassland conversion was particularly significant.  Nationally, millions of acres went from grass to crops, much of it becoming below-average cropland.
That raises a practical question: If many acres converted from grass to crops proved to be relatively poor cropland, why should federal policy make continued cropping the most attractive option?
Crop insurance remains an essential part of the farm safety net. South Dakota producers know better than most what drought, excess moisture, hail and other weather risks can do to crops.
But risk protection and land-use flexibility do not have to be competing ideas.
Rounds’ proposal would give a producer another choice: establish perennial cover, graze cattle, reduce erosion and still earn an economic return from the property.
Wildlife would benefit as well. Perennial grass provides nesting cover for pheasants and waterfowl, holds soil in place, slows runoff and improves water infiltration.
Rounds announces bill to encourage converting cropland back to pasture

The coalition behind the RANCH Act is notable: cattle producers, wildlife groups and conservation organizations backing a proposal that restores grass while keeping land productive. That coalition challenges the usual assumption that agriculture and conservation belong in separate camps.
A productive cornfield should remain a productive cornfield. The same is true for good soybean ground.
But South Dakota also has wet spots, saline soils, eroded slopes and marginal fields where grass and cattle may make more economic sense than another crop.
The state’s congressional delegation is well positioned to explore that possibility.
Thune has already shaped the Senate’s CRP provisions. Rounds has proposed a new working-grasslands option. Rep. Dusty Johnson serves on the House Agriculture Committee, and the House has already passed its version of the farm bill.
As Congress takes another run at the bill, those ideas belong on the same table.
South Dakota farmers have already shown they will use conservation programs when those programs fit their operations and make economic sense.
Not every acre that can carry a planter necessarily should be planted. Better farm policy may be to give producers another economically sensible choice for those acres.
Sometimes the best crop is grass.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Trump administration approves Arkansas’ plan to consolidate functions of workforce boards
description: The federal government approved Arkansas’ plan to consolidate functions of its 10 independent workforce development boards, the state Department of Commerce announced Thursday. The approved plan also combines Arkansas’ required Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act and Carl Perkins Career and Technical Education Act state plans, a first for the state. The[...]
text:
Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders announced $10 million in grant funding for site development projects on Dec. 11, 2024. Clint O'Neal, executive director of the Arkansas Economic Development Commission and Commerce Secretary Hugh McDonald stand with Sanders. (Mary Hennigan/Arkansas Advocate)The federal government approved Arkansas’ plan to consolidate functions of its 10 independent workforce development boards, the state Department of Commerce announced Thursday.
The approved plan also combines Arkansas’ required Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act and Carl Perkins Career and Technical Education Act state plans, a first for the state. The Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act is a 2014 law meant to assist job seekers with gaining employment, as well as the education and training needed to do so.
It comes after the U.S. Department of Education and U.S. Department of Labor announced in May that 21 states submitted combined plans this year, compared to nine states in 2024. The plan details how the state will use its federal funds to achieve the goals of the two laws.
Presently, the local workforce boards set priorities for the area they cover, and partner with community colleges, training providers and employers for job training and other services.
Under the new plan, Arkansas Workforce Development Board will take over the functions of the local boards, helping create an “integrated approach” that “supports a comprehensive career pathway framework spanning K-12 education, post-secondary education, and employment,” according to the draft plan. Arkansas Workforce Connections, which is part of the Department of Commerce, will deliver the services.
Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders said in the press release that the results were what “conservative government looks like.”
“Arkansas taxpayers deserve a workforce system that spends its money on people, not paperwork,” the Republican said. “By consolidating ten boards into one statewide system, we are moving millions of dollars out of overhead and into training and serving hundreds more Arkansans every year.”
Central to the newly-approved plan is the reduction of administrative and operating costs “across the workforce system,” according to the draft plan. In a press release announcing the approval, the commerce department said the transition to a single statewide planning area will result in around $6 million being redirected from “duplicative” expenses to “direct services for Arkansans and employers.” 
The planned implementation date for the plan is July 1, 2027.
“The approval of our WIOA State Plan is a major turning point for Arkansas, enabling the state to modernize our workforce development efforts to better meet the needs of Arkansans and industry partners,” said Arkansas Secretary of Commerce Hugh McDonald.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: A dam owner drained this secluded pond. Connecticut state officials wants it restored
description: This article first appeared on CT Mirror and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License. Throughout most of her 40 years living on Old Killingly Pond, Susan Rosenstone Larrow had easy access to its placid waters, which she and her neighbors also touted as some of the clearest in the state. […]
text:
Justen Fisher shows the former water line, blue line, from before the dam drawdown in his backyard at Old Killingly Pond on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Sarah Gordon/CT Mirror)This article first appeared on CT Mirror and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.
Throughout most of her 40 years living on Old Killingly Pond, Susan Rosenstone Larrow had easy access to its placid waters, which she and her neighbors also touted as some of the clearest in the state.
From her upstairs studio, the former art teacher spent afternoons painting scenes of life on the pond: her husband, Gene, fishing with his two grandchildren from a dock in summer; amber leaves scattered along the shore in autumn; a bald eagle in search of fish, perched on a branch.
Then one morning last October, Rosenstone Larrow and her neighbors awoke to find water gushing out of the old stone dam that had held the pond in place for over a century. Spurred by concerns over the dam’s safety, state officials had authorized its owner, Wright Investors’ Service Holdings, to conduct an emergency drawdown of the pond.
In a matter of months, the pond shrank to a quarter of its former size, leaving behind acres of rocks and mud. Docks where generations of children had once learned to swim were left suspended over bare ground.
“I like painting rocks, I never thought I’d have this many to chose from,” Rosenstone Larrow said.
The decision to drain Old Killingly Pond — a man-made body of water on the border between Connecticut and Rhode Island — kicked off a campaign by local residents and town officials to restore the water levels in the pond and have the state take ownership of the dam, providing for its long-term maintenance.
On Tuesday, the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection announced it had taken the first step in an enforcement action against WISH, the dam’s owner, by sending the company a draft consent order to fix the dam and restore water in the pond to its pre-drawdown levels. Officials said the decision was made based on the agency’s determination that the continued drawdown of the pond would have an adverse impact on habitats for protected plants and animals, including several species of damselflies.
The agency didn’t comment on whether it was considering taking over the dam.

Water from Old Killingly Pond trickles through Killingly Pond Dam’s low-level outlet gate on Dam Road on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026.
Graham Stevens, the head of DEEP’s Bureau of Water Protection and Land Reuse, said Tuesday’s letter essentially invites WISH to enter into an agreement to make the necessary repairs to the dam. Should the company decline, he said, the agency has other enforcement tools at its disposal to get the dam repaired.
“Regardless of the negotiation outcome, this will be a long process, and this is just the first step,” Stevens said.
Stevens said WISH didn’t immediately reply to the letter Tuesday. He added that work to restore the dam and raise water levels would likely take several years and could cost “multiple millions of dollars.”
Old Killingly Pond is the first in a series of reservoirs created in the first half of the 19th Century by the construction of dams used to power local mills. Over time, the mills declined and they, along with the dams, passed through a series of owners before ending up in the hands of WISH, a holding company based in Mount Kisco, N.Y.
In an email on Tuesday, WISH’s acting chief financial officer, Harold Kahn, said the company has no business operations and no revenue. He declined to comment further on issues involving the dam.
Today, the pond is home to around a dozen year-round residents, along with several seasonal cottages that are occupied in the summer months. Before the drawdown, the pond was about 138 acres in size, split between Connecticut and Rhode Island.
Most of the land surrounding the pond is held in public trust by the two states, including portions of Killingly Pond State Park. The dam owned by WISH, along with most of the residences, are located within Connecticut.
In addition to the loss of waterfront property, residents and town officials said the drawdown has caused several wells feeding seasonal cottages to dry up and resulted in excess sediment flowing downstream to other reservoirs. Fire officials in East Killingly, a section of town that lacks access to hydrants, warned that the drawdown left them without a place to fill up tanker trucks needed to respond to fires.
Lower water levels also exposed a suspected Native American burial ground that had been flooded by the construction of the dam in the early 19th Century.
Residents along the pond say it’s unclear what work, if any, WISH performed to maintain the dam at Old Killingly Pond. Several said they were unaware the company owned the dam until it began draining the pond last year.

Seasonal resident Jamie Chaparro walks through exposed lake bottom at Old Killingly Pond on Tuesday, August 18, 2026. Before the dam drawdown, the area was covered in water.
Stevens, who oversees dam safety at DEEP, said the agency was notified by the owners last year that an inspection had found the dam was leaking water, raising concerns about its structural integrity. In response, he said, DEEP authorized an emergency drawdown.
“There was a fear that this dam might fail, and if it were to fail, it put at risk life and property — not to mention the environmental consequences of such a catastrophic event,” Stevens said.
Once the drawdown was complete and the risk of failure had abated for the time being, Stevens said, the owner was directed to come up with a long-term plan for safely operating the dam. In response, WISH proposed a plan to keep the pond drained in order to reduce pressure on the dam, Stevens said.
That proposal drew stong objections from local residents and elected officials in Killingly. Stevens said Tuesday’s letter effectively served as a rejection of WISH’s plan to keep the pond drained.
State Sen. Mae Flexer, D-Windham, announced the news of DEEP’s decision following a meeting Tuesday with the agency and town officials. Asked whether the idea of a state takeover was broached at the meeting, Flexer said the effort the get WISH to pay for repairs to the dam represented the “beginning of the process.”
“I think any takeover or ownership [change] is months away,” she said.
“Today’s action shows that DEEP has been methodically trying to find a solution to this issue,” Flexer added. “I’m grateful for them for taking action and holding these dam owners accountable.”
Residents, meanwhile, reacted to the news with a mixture of relief and trepidation over whether WISH would be responsive to the state’s efforts to broker a solution.

An acrylic painting of Old Killingly Pond by Susan Rosenstone Larrow
“Now we have to hope” that WISH agrees to fix the dam, Rosenstone Larrow said. “I’m not too convinced that WISH will do it.”
Justen Fisher, who lives with his wife and two daughters in a house the family had built on the pond, praised DEEP for being responsive to the pleas from the small community of residents on the pond.
“To feel the support and actually to feel being heard… it’s super relieving,” Fisher said. “Now we’ve got the state on our side, let’s take it to the finish line.”

name: VTDigger
title: Tar spot fungus likely won’t mute fall colors
description:
“The spores overwinter in the leaf litter, so they’re always around,” said Charlotte town tree warden Cliff Mix. But they come out in years when the living is easy — if you’re a plant pathogen.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Tar spot fungus likely won’t mute fall colors.
text:
A maple leaf with tar spot fungus. Photo by Noel Clark/VTDigger

This story by Scooter MacMillan was first published in The Charlotte News on Sept. 3, 2026.
You may have noticed browning trees with crinkled, dried-up leaves on Thompson’s Point Road in Charlotte.
You may also have noticed these trees were sugar maples, and you might have worried that the premature browning of what is traditionally one of our brightest performers in the annual polychromapalooza could indicate we’re in for a less than optimally colorful fall.
Birding aficionado and spice connoisseur Hank Kaestner said he has also seen isolated patches of similarly afflicted trees in Vergennes and Shelburne.
These prematurely browned and dried leaves are the result of tar spot fungus.
Charlotte town tree warden Cliff Mix said tar spot fungus, like most funguses and many pathogens, is spread by spores.
“The spores overwinter in the leaf litter, so they’re always around,” Mix said. But they come out in years when the living is easy — if you’re a plant pathogen.
We had a cool, wet spring and a moderate summer where, even when it got hot, it was generally wet. “It’s been perfect conditions to have this problem explode,” he said.
But it’s not much of a problem. Tar spot fungus does not hurt the trees, and next year things should be back to their normal chromatic brilliance — unless there has been another wet spring and summer. And if trees are afflicted with tar spot fungus for two or three years in a row, it could cause problems, Mix said.
Mix said he had also noticed that the isolated patches of browning trees seem more prevalent on Thompson’s Point Road than other places in town, but he doesn’t know why. Proximity to the lake could be part of the cause, but not the sole explanation since fungus-withered leaves don’t appear so prominently in other places in town near the lake.
There are other funguses and leaf diseases that can afflict trees, many of which are much harder on them than tar spot fungus, Mix said. Anthracnose is one of those. It is also a fungus that hits a lot of different trees but is particularly hard on sycamores, which we don’t have many of. But it can also be a problem for sugar maples.
Anthracnose is a group of common fungal diseases that cause dark, sunken lesions on the leaves, stems, flowers and fruits of many plants, but it also doesn’t usually kill trees, unless it recurs every year.
Last year, Mix said, people were learning a lot about the powdery mildew that was getting on lilacs. Like the others, it was given a leg up by a wet spring. It’s a problem particularly for lilacs growing in shaded areas. Lilacs in sunny places with good air flow often don’t have problems with powdery mildew.
“No matter which one of these pathogens it is, it’s just an annual thing,” Mix said. “The biggest problem would be if it happens consecutively year to year.”
If a pathogen recurs yearly, it can affect the roots, which can cause stress that will lead to decline, he said.
The occurrences of tar spot fungus-afflicted trees appear to be limited. Mix has 112 acres and hasn’t seen any evidence of the fungus anywhere on his property.
Mix doesn’t think the few, isolated patches of brown and withered leaves will affect our fall overall. He thinks conditions are ripe for a dazzling autumn with the mountains ablaze in color.
