name: Kansas Reflector
title: Federal government sues Kansas school district, accusing it of secretly transitioning children
description: TOPEKA — The federal government accused the Kansas City, Kansas, public school district of secretly transitioning children’s gender identity at school without their parents’ knowledge or consent in a lawsuit filed Tuesday.  The lawsuit says district policies keep information from parents, such as when a child chooses to go by another name or gender while […]
text:
U.S. attorney Ryan Kriegshauser, appearing here at an April news conference, says the Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools district shouldn't be surprised about a lawsuit that accuses the district of secretly transitioning children at school. The district and the U.S. Department of Education had been trying to reach agreement on school policies for months. (Photo by Grace Hills for Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The federal government accused the Kansas City, Kansas, public school district of secretly transitioning children’s gender identity at school without their parents’ knowledge or consent in a lawsuit filed Tuesday. 
The lawsuit says district policies keep information from parents, such as when a child chooses to go by another name or gender while at school. 
“The District maintains policies that direct staff to help students socially transition to a different gender at school and to withhold this information from parents as confidential,” the DOJ said in its court filing.
The court action, filed in Kansas District Court, said the Kansas City, Kansas, Public Schools district of violating two federal laws, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act and the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment.
Both laws are “designed to safeguard parental rights, including the rights to access and oversee information collected and maintained about their children in public schools,” a U.S. Department of Justice news release said. 
The release said the U.S. Department of Education made “extensive efforts” to reach a resolution with the school district so it would comply with federal law before filing the lawsuit.  
The school district said in a statement it is in compliance with the law. 
“Because this matter is now pending in federal court, the district will respond to the Complaint through the appropriate legal process and will not make any further comment at this time,” the statement added. 
The lawsuit provoked anger on social media from both sides of the issue. 
Erik Murray, a Kansas City businessman, recently ran and lost the Democratic nomination to run against U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall. Murray posted on Facebook, calling the lawsuit “a war on education.”
“This is a war on teachers and children. This is a war on poor people,” he wrote. “This is a war on the only majority minority County in this State. This is cruelty, and hatred, and bigotry on display.” 
Senate President Ty Masterson, Republican candidate for governor, said the lawsuit is what happens when “common sense gets thrown out the window.”
“Schools do not know children better than their parents,” Masterson posted. “They should not be keeping secrets from mom and dad, and they certainly shouldn’t be making deeply personal decisions behind their backs.”
The lawsuit shouldn’t be a surprise to the district, said Ryan Kriegshauser, U.S. attorney for the District of Kansas. 
“Public education functions effectively only when schools and parents engage in a genuine partnership,” he said in the news release. “When schools withhold information from parents, they undermine trust and disrupt the essential balance between families and public educators.”
In April, the DOJ said four Kansas school districts were in violation of federal civil rights protections — Olathe, Shawnee Mission, Topeka and Kansas City, Kansas. Reasons included allowing students to change their name or pronouns used at school without clear communication to parents and allowing transgender students to use restrooms, locker rooms and changing rooms that align with their gender identity.
Last week, the DOJ announced it would take enforcement action against Shawnee Mission and Olathe school districts. 
Topeka accepted resolution agreements with the Department of Education and the Olathe district signed a “voluntary resolution agreement” in May outlining the district’s commitment to giving students access to gender-specific facilities “strictly on the basis of sex.” The agreement was rejected by the Education Department. 
Shawnee Mission spokesman Jake Potter said the district’s last direct communication with the Department of Education was Aug. 11, when the department acknowledged receipt of a letter the district sent. 
In that letter, the district denied that its policies violated federal regulations and refused to accept a resolution proposed by the Department of Education.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: In the shadow of the federal fight over absentee ballots, NC is ready to start mailing them out
description: Despite the tangle of federal court rulings concerning U.S. Postal Service control of absentee ballot delivery, North Carolina Elections Director Sam Hayes said Thursday that counties are ready to start mailing ballots to people who request them on Friday as scheduled.  “All 100 county boards of elections are prepared to start that process, and North […]
text:
NC Board of Elections Executive Director Sam Hayes, at podium, said on Sept. 3, 2026 that counties are prepared to begin mailing absentee ballots to voters on Sept. 4 as scheduled. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline) Despite the tangle of federal court rulings concerning U.S. Postal Service control of absentee ballot delivery, North Carolina Elections Director Sam Hayes said Thursday that counties are ready to start mailing ballots to people who request them on Friday as scheduled. 
“All 100 county boards of elections are prepared to start that process, and North Carolina would be the first state in the country to send absentee ballots for the 2026 general election,” Hayes said at a news conference. 
The Postal Service is taking steps to comply with President Donald Trump’s executive order to control absentee ballot delivery. States would be required to submit names and addresses of people who have asked for mail ballots to a federal portal, along with barcodes on the envelopes. The Postal Service would refuse to deliver ballots to people not on the list. That plan is being challenged in federal court. 
“We’re closely monitoring legal developments,” Hayes said. North Carolina already complies with the barcode requirement. 
The Southern Coalition for Social Justice sent state election officials a letter Thursday saying that complying with the new Postal Service rule would violate state law. 
Hayes said North Carolina would comply with the Postal Service rule if courts allow implementation.
New NC voting rules delayed, but state elections board to consider workaround

State rule changes 
The State Board of Elections is also considering last-minute changes to the way counties handle absentee ballots. The board was to have discussed those directions to counties on Wednesday, but delayed consideration until Friday, the same day ballots go out. 
The specifics are a mystery. The changes under consideration have not been made public.  Hayes did not say specifically what the board will discuss, but said he did not anticipate the changes would have any impact on voters. 
Advice for mail-in voters
In an interview, Hilary Harris Klein, senior counsel for voting rights at the Southern Coalition for Social Justice, advised people who want to vote by mail to request their ballots as early as possible and get them back in the mail at least two weeks before the deadline for them to be received, which is 7:30 pm, Nov. 3. 
County boards of election may have more information about mail delivery timelines, she said. 
BallotTrax is available for voters who want to stay updated on the status of their absentee ballots. Voters worried that their mail-in ballots won’t arrive in time to be counted should have a back-up plan, Klein said. 
Requesting an absentee ballot does not require a person to vote by mail. People can change their minds and vote in person.
Parker Holland, state director of elections administration, said at the news conference that if mail-in voters monitoring BallotTrax see that their ballots have not been counted by election eve, they can vote in person on Election Day and call their county board of elections to tell them to “spoil,” or disregard, their absentee ballot. Safeguards at the county level will flag any voter who attempts to vote twice.
Instructions and barcodes
Marian Lewin, 1st vice president of the League of Women Voters of North Carolina, said in an interview that the most common mistake she’s seen voters make with absentee ballots are people failing to put their ballots in the correct envelopes. 
Ballots and envelopes have matching barcodes. Voters within a household sometimes swap envelopes, so the barcodes don’t match. Most people don’t understand how the ballot and the envelope are linked, she said. 
Lewin has been an elections worker or observer in Wake County for decades. She has spent hours watching Wake elections officials count absentee ballots. 
The absentee ballot package comes with two envelopes. Completed ballots are supposed to be sealed in the inner envelopes, with copies of photo ID in a clear sleeve on the outside of that envelope. That sealed ballot envelope goes into the outer return mailing envelope. 
Common problems include voters failing to seal their ballots in the proper envelope, or having copies of their IDs sealed in the inner envelopes with their ballots, Lewin said.
“Put the ballot in the envelope and seal it,” she said. “Don’t let it be loose in your mailing envelope.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Billings area legislative race draws two write-in candidates
description: The path back to Helena appeared smooth for State Sen. Daniel Zolnikov, up until about three weeks ago.   Zolnikov has been a lawmaker since 2013 and filed to run for re-election to Senate District 22, representing part of Billings, this year. He ran unopposed in the Republican primary in June, and the Democratic candidate was […]
text:
Sen. Daniel Zolnikov, R-Billings, sits prior to a Montana Senate floor session on Wednesday, April 30, 2025. (Jordan Hansen/Daily Montanan)The path back to Helena appeared smooth for State Sen. Daniel Zolnikov, up until about three weeks ago.  
Zolnikov has been a lawmaker since 2013 and filed to run for re-election to Senate District 22, representing part of Billings, this year. He ran unopposed in the Republican primary in June, and the Democratic candidate was not certified after paperwork errors, leaving Zolnikov unopposed again. 
But when the Secretary of State’s Office finalized candidates for November’s ballot in recent weeks, two individuals filed as write-in options, challenging Zolnikov. 
“It makes the odds twice as hard for two people to be trying to get on a ballot line,” Zolnikov told the Daily Montanan. “If you really wanted to take me out, you would support one write-in candidate.”
The two candidates working to convince voters to take the extra steps of remembering, and then writing their names on a ballot are Elijah Tidswell, a Republican, and Cari Olson, a Democrat — though write-in candidates are officially “nonpartisan.”  
“Write-ins are rarely successful, and I think more often than not they’re just a protest vote,” said Elijah Tidswell, one of the write-ins. “But I don’t think of this as a protest. We’re getting signs, we’re knocking doors, we’re doing the work.”

Write-in candidates rarely win elections, though in Montana, some municipal and county precinct committee races — low-turnout elections — have seen some candidates prevail. 
The blank line often included at the end of the list of qualified candidates is often used by voters wanting to have a little fun and avoid making a choice between candidates. 
Maryland Matters, a States Newsroom affiliate, reported that in 2016 more than 45,000 people wrote in candidates for president, and each state governs the write-in process differently. 
Last year, the Montana Legislature altered the state’s rules around write-in candidates in two ways: Candidates who lose a primary are no longer allowed to run a write-in campaign for the general election; and candidates must officially declare as write-in candidates 90 days before the general election. 
The Secretary of State’s office exercised its discretion overseeing state elections to remove the write-in line from ballots that don’t have declared write-in candidates, which election officials say is efficient, as undeclared candidates aren’t officially tallied anyways. 
That move is one of many issues Olson has with Montana politics, and if she were elected it’s a legislative change she would seek. 
“There was not one bill that did this,” Olson told the Daily Montanan. “(Secretary of State) Christi Jacobsen on her own took that right away from us Montanans.”
Olson said that she supports more political power stemming from everyday Montanans. She would like to make it easier to vote for any candidate, and also easier to recall elected officials. 
“If I win, I’m going to make it so easy to recall myself, I’m going to be hated by every other politician,” said Olson, who has worked in Democratic politics for years. 

Tidswell, a real estate agent, has also been involved in his party’s political sphere for years, having previously run for the state Senate in 2022, losing by 12 points in the general election. 
He was the chairman of the Montana Young Republicans until this year, and survived a vote of no confidence that sought to remove him from that role in 2025. He was re-elected to his position last fall, but resigned this spring after butting heads with the state GOP. 
Tidswell said the issues he ran into are “emblematic of the larger Montana civil war,” which has seen more conservative Republicans who hold leadership positions clash with more moderate members in recent years. 
“I’m definitely seen as more of an ‘old-school Republican,’ or I guess they’d label me a moderate, or a RINO,” Tidswell told the Daily Montanan.
His primary motivation for getting into the race at such a late stage was in response to the public pushback to a data center project planned just north of Billings. 
“I know there’s a lot of people calling for full bans right now, I don’t know if that’s possible to get passed,” he said. “But there has to be at least some responses from our government and elected officials towards these concerns.”
Both Tidswell and Olson are making data center concerns a key part of their campaigns, in opposition to Zolnikov, whom Olson has nicknamed on her social media pages as “Data Center Danny.” 
Zolnikov chairs the Energy and Technology Interim Committee and has passed numerous bills focused addressing privacy rights and technology regulation, including a “right to compute” bill last session which includes a framework for companies to build critical infrastructure, which can include data centers. 
“I’m running because of data centers, data centers, data centers,” said Olson, who supports a full ban of data centers in the state. “At some point we need to wake up and understand that our politicians are putting corporations over us.”
 Zolnikov told the Daily Montanan that data centers like the one Quantica is proposing near Billings will bring in millions of dollars of investment into the state, provide for much-needed infrastructure upgrades and allow Montana to export a new product — data. 
“With these companies we’re not just selling megawatts of Montana power, we’re selling a product,” Zolnikov said. “In a capitalistic world, that’s a good thing.
Zolnikov told the Daily Montanan that there are no financial benefits for him, personally, if Quantica’s data center is built. He previously worked for Broad Reach Power — which formerly was a holding company for assets that became Quantica — but on other energy development projects. 
He acknowledged many of the concerns people have about these large projects, including water and energy use, but said there are ways to address those through policy. 
“We have some of the strongest water rights in Montana — an interim committee is working on that right now,” he said. 
The interim committee he leads, meanwhile, is working to address energy concerns. 
“We’ll ensure there will be a new rate class for large loads, and ensure they can’t shift that burden onto retail and residential customers,” he said. “If they build their own energy generation, that surplus goes into the grid to help customers and overall tax burdens in communities could decrease. 
“I see a lot of benefits.”
Zolnikov says that drawing two opponents in the last month on the back of rising debates over data centers shows that the issue really “grew legs” since spring. 
“I think it’s good that it’s become a big issue, it draws attention to the consumer protection bills we will have in the Legislature,” he said. “That’s a big benefit, as long I stay in office to pass them.”
Tidswell said that despite the odds, he’s fully invested in his campaign.
“At the end of the day, I’m running this campaign like I’m on the ballot but a little bit harder,” he said.
The race for state Senate District 9 has also drawn a write-in candidate, Nate White, who described himself as a philosopher to the Choteau Acantha.  
That election includes Democrat Noy Holland of Choteau against longtime lawmaker Rep. Llew Jones, who won a tight primary and battled legal challenges to his candidacy for the senate seat.

name: Michigan Advance
title: US Supreme Court declines to hear application on Michigan citizens-only voting ballot measure
description: U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh declined an application from Americans for Citizen Voting-Michigan seeking to appeal a deadlocked decision by the Michigan Board of State Canvassers that left a citizens-only voting proposal off the November general election ballot due to a lack of valid petition signatures. The decision was posted without a filing[...]
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court, on April 9, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh declined an application from Americans for Citizen Voting-Michigan seeking to appeal a deadlocked decision by the Michigan Board of State Canvassers that left a citizens-only voting proposal off the November general election ballot due to a lack of valid petition signatures. The decision was posted without a filing or opinion on the court’s docket Thursday, the day before the November ballot must be finalized.
Sponsors of the ballot measure filed the application Monday, requesting an emergency injunction from the nation’s highest court. They argued that the due process rights of Michiganders who signed the petition were violated when the Board of State Canvassers determined that affidavits validating nine rejected signatures were submitted too late and as such could not be used to validate those signatures, which would have put the petition over the required threshold. 
However, in the state’s response to the application, filed on Wednesday, lawyers argued that the relief requested by the sponsors — an injunction that would force the state to place the referendum on the November general election ballot — would be granting the applicants “all the relief they could ever recover for their claims.” The state argued that the application does “little to justify such an unusual request, other than to repeat the number of signatures they gathered—without acknowledging or contending with the high number of signatures that were found to be invalid.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Mark Brewer, a lawyer for the opposition to the proposal, wrote in a message to the Michigan Advance that his clients are “pleased with the decision by Justice Kavanaugh.” 
Lawyers for the applicants did not immediately respond to requests for comment. This story will be updated when a response is received.
Americans for Citizen Voting also filed a petition with the Michigan Supreme Court — the more standard avenue for recourse against the Board of State Canvassers’ decision — four days before filing its application with the U.S. Supreme Court. The response from the state notes that, as there has been no hearing or opinion issued by the state court, the application is highly unusual for asking the nation’s highest court to be the first court to review their claims.
As of Thursday evening, the only order issued by the state Supreme Court was to accept a number of amicus briefs, but no order had been made on the actual application from the ballot petition sponsors. 
The measure, if passed, would have established strict voter ID rules — which opponents argued would have disenfranchised many legal voters. 
The Board of State Canvassers will meet on Friday morning to finalize the ballot — including voting on ballot language for the citizens-only voting measure, though it is still not expected to be on the ballot.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: ‘The knives are out’ as candidates make final sprint to the primary
description: A quiet summer overall in the Democratic primary races for attorney general and lieutenant governor has turned increasingly combative in the closing days of the campaigns. Lieutenant governor candidate Xay Khamsyvoravong on Thursday accused incumbent Sabina Matos of relying on a dark-money super PAC to keep her reelection bid afloat. Matos’ campaign has deni[...]
text:
An Instagram ad by Keith Hoffmann, a Democrat running for Rhode Island attorney general, criticizes rival Kim Ahern’s tenure leading the state Cannabis Control Commission (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)A quiet summer overall in the Democratic primary races for attorney general and lieutenant governor has turned increasingly combative in the closing days of the campaigns.
Lieutenant governor candidate Xay Khamsyvoravong on Thursday accused incumbent Sabina Matos of relying on a dark-money super PAC to keep her reelection bid afloat. Matos’ campaign has denied the allegation.
Attorney General hopeful Keith Hoffmann on Wednesday had to correct his campaign’s closing ad after Barrington Rep. Jason Knight claimed it misled voters by including the endorsement of a gun safety group that actually backed Knight’s campaign. Hoffmann was also accused on Friday by Kim Ahern’s campaign of failing to disclose stock holdings in companies he prosecuted while part of the AG’s office. 
“The knives are out,” observed Matt Ulricksen, an associate professor of political science at the Community College of Rhode Island.
Multiple polls show a large swatch of voters remain undecided in both races just days before the Sept. 9 primary. A survey released Aug. 27 by the University of New Hampshire found 46% of likely voters surveyed on the AG’s race were undecided. More than a third of voters were undecided in a WPRI-Emerson College survey published two days prior.
In the five-way race for lieutenant governor, the WPRI-Emerson poll also found that more than 4 in 10 voters were still undecided in the primary, which also includes former state Sen. Cindy Coyne of Barrington, Providence City Councilor Sue AnderBois and Ponaganset High School science teacher Ross McCurdy.
“Negativism moves votes,” Ulricksen said. “As much as we decry negative campaigning, the research is solid.”
So many ads, so little time left
The AG campaigns have spent heavily trying to break through to voters over the summer, primarily through television commercials highlighting their credentials to be Rhode Island’s top lawyer.
Hoffmann was the first out with an ad, landing a spot in July as part of a $1 million media campaign. A review of order forms filed with the Federal Communications Commission show Hoffmann’s campaign has spent $784,441 on more than 5,900 ad spots across Rhode Island’s broadcast and cable TV networks.
FCC filings show Ahern’s campaign has spent over $418,000 on television with 1,694 commercial spots since joining the airwaves the week after Hoffmann. Knight’s campaign has spent over $319,000 on 1,948 ad spots across Rhode Island’s broadcast and cable networks. Warwick Rep. Joe Solomon has expended nearly $280,000 on 800 broadcast TV spots.
“When you look at those airwaves, it is constantly Keith,” Ulricksen said.
Hoffmann’s campaign has also called Ahern a “sloppy prosecutor” on social media, referencing a high-profile murder trial in 2017 in which a Superior Court judge declared a mistrial, faulting Ahern and another prosecutor over failures to disclose evidence to the defense. 
Ahern defended her conduct during a WPRI debate on Aug. 12 stating “no personal or professional violations were found on the state.”
Another post promoted by Hoffmann criticized Ahern’s tenure leading the state’s Cannabis Control Commission, which has yet to license any new retail stores nearly four years after recreational sales were legalized by the General Assembly. Josh Block, a spokesperson for Aherns’ campaign called the attacks “a desperate effort by Keith Hoffmann to spread lies.”
Hoffmann said in an interview with Rhode Island Current he only went negative against Ahern because she attacked him first, including in the WPRI debate where she criticized his heavy self-funding and lack of prosecutorial experience.
“We responded. Period,” Hoffmann told Rhode Island Current.



Quotation







Negativism moves votes. As much as we decry negative campaigning, the research is solid.


– Matt Ulricksen, an associate professor of political science at the Community College of Rhode Island


Hoffmann has loaned himself $760,000 since he launched his campaign last year. That includes $210,000 infusion made Aug. 28, according to disclosure forms filed Wednesday with the Rhode Island Board of Elections. 
Knight has loaned himself $138,000 this election cycle, and Solomon loaned his campaign $100,000.
Ahern in a past statement boasted about being fueled entirely by donations and that the “attorney general is not a job to be bought by the highest bidder.” But Ahern’s latest disclosure forms show she loaned her campaign $295,000 between Aug. 25 and 31. 
Block said the money was needed to respond to Hoffmann’s paid attacks.
“It was important to put in what they can in order to create a more level playing field for voters,” he wrote in an email to Rhode Island Current.
Ahern sought to level the playing field Aug. 28 by accusing Hoffmann and his wife of holding stock in companies involved in cases he handled at the attorney general’s office, including Daimler Truck and pharmaceutical companies.
“For a senior leader in the Attorney General’s Office to fail to disclose a personal financial stake in the outcome of their own case is a major red flag, and for that same person to now be seeking the Attorney General’s Office for himself should be concerning to all Rhode Islanders,” Ahern said in a statement.
Hoffmann maintains he did nothing wrong.
“I’ve filed and disclosed everything as required and have always followed all office policies,” he said.
State law requires all state-appointed officials and employees “who hold a major decision-making position in a state agency” to file financial disclosure forms with the Rhode Island Ethics Commission.
Jason Gramitt, the Ethics Commission’s executive director, said the state’s annual financial disclosure requirement generally applies to agency heads and other top-level officials. He said a director of policy at the AG’s office would generally not be required to file.
“Most state employees don’t file and are not required to file financial disclosure statements,” Gramitt said in a recent interview.
Lieutenant governor candidate Xay Khamsyvoravong, right, accused incumbent Sabina Matos on Sept. 3 of relying on a dark-money super PAC to support her reelection bid. Matos’ campaign denied the allegation. (Photos by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current).
The lieutenant governor’s race has been a much quieter affair financially.
FCC filings show Khamsyvoravong’s campaign spent nearly $122,000 for 381 ad spots across broadcast and cable between the start of early voting and the Sept. 9 primary. Coyne committed more than $96,000 for 349 commercial spots across Rhode Island’s broadcast networks. AnderBois spent a little over $63,000 on 502 ad spots.
Matos and McCurdy have remained off television.
But Matos has not escaped scrutiny over campaign spending, with Khamsyvoravong now making one of the organizations supporting her a central issue in the final days of the primary.
Khamsyvoravong cited donations to the Democratic Lieutenant Governors Association from “pharmaceutical companies, a private-prison company involved in President Donald Trump’s ICE detention infrastructure and Big Tech.” Forms show the association then transferred $100,000 to the DLP PAC, which has used the money for radio ads and mailers supporting Matos.
“Rhode Islanders should never have to wonder whether their elected officials are willing to mislead voters to advance their own political careers,” Khamsyvoravong said in a statement.
Christa Thompson, Matos’ campaign manager, said in an emailed statement to Rhode Island Current that the lieutenant governor has not accepted corporate PAC donations in her own fundraising.
“Sabina Matos’s anti-corporate and bona fides are clear,” Thompson said in an emailed statement. “When she’s reelected as Lieutenant Governor, she’ll keep leading that fight to lower grocery costs, and that’s where her focus is in the next four days.”
Early voting remains underway through 4 p.m. on Tuesday, Sept. 8. The winner of the next day’s Democratic lieutenant governor primary will face Republican John Loughlin in November. The victor of the four-way AG’s race will face Alan Gordon in the general election.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Top New Mexico Senate Republican calls on Rep. Romero to resign from Epstein commission, House seat
description: New Mexico Senate Minority Leader Bill Sharer (R-Farmington) on Thursday called on the state lawmaker leading the state’s commission dedicated to investigating Jeffrey Epstein’s activities in New Mexico to resign. He added that he has asked the State Ethics Commission to investigate.
text:
New Mexico Senate Minority Leader Bill Sharer (R-Farmington), pictured on Jan. 20, 2026, called for Rep. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe) to step down from the Epstein “truth commission” and the state Legislature amid allegations that she violated state law by working for a local prosecutor’s office. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)New Mexico Senate Minority Leader Bill Sharer (R-Farmington) on Thursday called on the state lawmaker leading the state’s commission dedicated to investigating Jeffrey Epstein’s activities in New Mexico to resign.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rep. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe), a licensed attorney, has come under increasing scrutiny after Republicans in the state Legislature called for an ethics investigation into whether she was breaking state law by holding a part-time job with the First Judicial District Attorney’s Office. While Romero had previously said that she obtained permission to take the job, Attorney General Raúl Torrez earlier this week said that she relied on a 2024 opinion from his office that was “read more broadly than intended.”
The 2024 opinion concerned whether state Rep. Andrea Reeb (R-Clovis) could work as a special prosecutor in the state’s case against actor Alec Baldwin. While it found she was allowed to do so, she left the job after Baldwin’s attorneys argued it was unconstitutional for a sitting lawmaker to work as a special prosecutor. Reeb currently also serves on the Legislature’s special Epstein investigatory subcommittee.
Romero resigned from her job with the local prosecutor’s office earlier this week. In a statement issued via a New York-based public relations firm that holds a contract with the Epstein “truth commission,” Romero defended her employment there and accused Torrez of seeking to disrupt the commission’s work.
Sharer, on Thursday, criticized Romero for issuing that statement to the press via the Epstein commission’s contracted communications firm. According to the Legislature’s website, that contract with New York-based Dini von Mueffling Communications began on Aug. 11, via the Legislative Council Service, and has a cap of $60,000.
“The evidence suggests she used taxpayer dollars appropriated for a truth commission investigating one of the most notorious predators in modern history to instead pay a contractor to clean up her own political mess,” Sharer said. “That is not what that money was for, and it is exactly the kind of self-dealing New Mexico’s Governmental Conduct Act was written to stop.”
Sharer added that he has asked the State Ethics Commission to investigate.
Neither Romero nor Dini von Mueffling Communications responded to requests for comment. The other three members of the Epstein commission also did not respond to requests for comment.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Elon Musk wades into Maine’s Senate race
description: A Republican consulting firm working to reelect Susan Collins received the second largest share of spending from Elon Musk’s super PAC last month.  America PAC has spent just over $170,000 in Maine’s U.S. Senate race, which Democrats view as a key pickup opportunity to gain control of the upper chamber. Overall, a Federal Election Commission […]
text:
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine tours the Maine Energy Marketers Association Technical Education Center in Brunswick on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)A Republican consulting firm working to reelect Susan Collins received the second largest share of spending from Elon Musk’s super PAC last month. 
America PAC has spent just over $170,000 in Maine’s U.S. Senate race, which Democrats view as a key pickup opportunity to gain control of the upper chamber. Overall, a Federal Election Commission disclosure released Wednesday showed the super PAC spent over $800,000 last month on races with Republican incumbents and candidates in competitive districts. 
“First of all, I wasn’t aware of that donation,” Collins told reporters in Brunswick on Thursday. “I knew he was going to get involved in political campaigns, but I had not heard that there was a specific donation.” 
The August disclosures reveal what are expected to be the first in a series of donations from Musk, the world’s richest person, who has reportedly authorized his super PAC to spend $100 million to $120 million to help elect Republicans in November, two unnamed sources told the New York Times this summer. 
Red Maverick Media LLC, the primary direct mail vendor for Collins based in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, received four separate donations dedicated to Maine’s Senate race from America PAC in late August. 
Texas’ Senate race between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico received the most money from Musk’s PAC, around $248,000, followed by Ohio ($105,675), New Hampshire ($91,458.50), Iowa ($54,600), Michigan ($25,605) and Alaska ($17,235).
Speaking of Musk’s time leading the Department of Government Efficiency at the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, Collins said on Thursday, “I don’t agree with him on everything, but I do agree with him that we need to eliminate waste and be much more efficient in government.”
On that note, Collins called the reports of fraud in Maine’s Medicaid system “absolutely unacceptable.” Vice President JD Vance and Mehmet Oz, administrator of the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, on separate visits to Maine have expressed similar concerns.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services has disputed claims that the agency is not cracking down on fraud, announcing earlier this month that it suspended payments to five providers and terminated two providers’ contracts for subjecting residents to serious health risks and unsafe conditions.

name: VTDigger
title: For some patients seeking drugs like Ozempic, the best path is to just get sicker
description:
Now a federal pilot program is broadening access to the weight loss medication for some Medicare patients.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  For some patients seeking drugs like Ozempic, the best path is to just get sicker.
text:
Boxes for the medications Wegovy and Zepbound. File photo by JoNel Aleccia/AP

For many, drugs like Wegovy and Ozempic seem a miracle. But for those without the extra $300 to $1,200 it can cost to buy the drugs out-of-pocket, getting insurance coverage for the diabetes drugs, which are known to alleviate a slew of other weight-related health conditions, can prove a nightmare.
The story is all too familiar to Dr. Michelle Dorwart, the president of the Vermont Academy of Family Physicians and a family doctor at a community health center in Burlington.
“It’s really tough. You are thinking, ‘Wow, this could really be helpful for this person,’” she said, describing her work with patients who may benefit from the drugs, “but it’s really hard to get covered.” 
Now, a new Medicare pilot program is offering a glimmer of hope for some Vermonters who have struggled to access the weight loss and diabetes medications. 
The drugs, called GLP-1s, work by mimicking a natural hormone that regulates the amount of sugar in blood, which in turn slows down digestion and makes the brain feel more satiated. They originally were approved for managing diabetes but have increasingly been found to work for weight loss, too. 
Up until July 1, a Medicare patient could not get insurance coverage for a GLP-1 for weight loss specifically, according to Natalie Powers, a pharmacist and the director of clinical programs at Kinney Drugs.
The nationwide Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program allows Medicare beneficiaries with drug coverage to access one of three different weight loss GLP-1 drugs if the beneficiaries meet a set of broadened criteria. Medicare is the federal healthcare program for those 65 and above or those with certain chronic illnesses. Under the new pilot, the drugs cost patients $50 a month. 
The program began July 1 and is set to run as a pilot through the end of 2027. 
Given how new the pilot is, it’s hard to know exactly how many Vermonters have taken advantage of it — of the more than 170,000 Medicare eligible Vermonters, about 140,000 could qualify for the pilot with their drug coverage. But clinicians are optimistic that they will now be able to write prescriptions for patients who previously could not get the weight loss drugs covered by insurance. 
Dorwart shared the story of one patient with fatty liver disease who couldn’t get insurance coverage for GLP-1 drugs — the drugs only have FDA approval to treat “moderate-to-advanced” manifestations of the disease. 
She made multiple calls trying to help the patient get coverage; she did an ultrasound that showed some build up of dangerous scar tissue, but not enough that it was severe enough for coverage — “Which is just crazy, right?” Dorwart said. 
The best thing to do was to send the patient home and “wait until her liver disease gets worse,” Dorwart said. 
It’s a situation that’s often familiar for those who are prediabetic, have sleep apnea or other weight-related health conditions that the drugs aren’t yet approved to treat.
“There are people who are kind of almost hoping that they’ll have diabetes,” Dorwart said. “It is a hard place to be because they want to be healthier and prevent complications from their diseases and they can’t. They can’t use this tool to do that.”
Now, any Medicare patient with a body mass index of 35 and above is eligible for the drugs — a BMI of 30 or above is considered obese. Those with lower BMIs who have heart failure, uncontrolled hypertension or chronic kidney disease are also eligible. So are those who are prediabetic, have had a stroke or a heart attack or have artery disease in their limbs. 
About 30% of Vermonters 65 and older have a BMI of 30 or above, making Vermont one of the least obese states in the nation, according to a 2024 ranking by United Health Foundation.
“We’re really excited that this is expanding care for these patients who really are going to find benefit from them,” Powers said. 
She hopes that the 18-month pilot will yield enough evidence for the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services and other insurers to see if increasing access to weight loss medication results in lower overall healthcare costs and better health outcomes. 
“If you can decrease hospitalizations and long-term effects of having a heart attack, having a stroke, having uncontrolled hypertension that leads to chronic kidney disease, it’s going to save millions and millions of dollars in the healthcare system,” Powers said. 
To Dorwart, the logic is obvious, too: “Ultimately, if you’re avoiding complications, you’re saving money,” she said. 
But she added that the “greater benefit is to the individual, who’s having better health.”
She warned against treating GLP-1s as a cure-all. Their use for weight loss and associated conditions is still so new that clinicians need to wait to see the long-term impacts, she said. 
And in her practice, Dorwart sees more Medicaid than Medicare patients. That population — as well as those with private insurance — is still not included in the pilot program. 
“Any effort to lower costs is great, and if it actually ends up helping people, then that was awesome,” she said. “I’m hopeful — cautiously optimistic.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Kratom bills clear first votes in North Dakota Legislature
description: Two bills with different approaches to restricting kratom in North Dakota cleared their first hurdles Thursday in the Legislature, but they appear to conflict and might complicate the special session as lawmakers look to leave Friday. House Bill 1628, which would allow but strictly regulate pure-leaf kratom for people 21 and older, passed the House […]
text:
Sen. Michelle Axtman, R-Bismarck, speaks on the Senate floor during a special session of the Legislature on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Two bills with different approaches to restricting kratom in North Dakota cleared their first hurdles Thursday in the Legislature, but they appear to conflict and might complicate the special session as lawmakers look to leave Friday.
House Bill 1628, which would allow but strictly regulate pure-leaf kratom for people 21 and older, passed the House in an 86-6 vote. Senate Bill 2408, which would permanently ban natural and synthetic forms of kratom, passed the Senate in a 46-1 vote. 

More special session coverage

The chambers now swap the bills for their second votes on Friday. It’s unclear how much support exists in the House for a total kratom ban, a key vote that could either resolve the special session’s main issue or complicate the matter as lawmakers are eyeing the exits before the Labor Day weekend.
The House bill includes licensing and labeling requirements, criminal penalties for violations and enforcement authority by the attorney general. In the House debate, state reps discussed the bill’s costs, its $10,000 licensing fee for retailers and whether cities or counties could ban kratom on their own.
Some lawmakers pointed out the bill keeps natural kratom available to people who use the substance for pain relief, with more time in the months ahead for the 2027 Legislature to further address kratom.
Kratom bills advance, including a permanent full ban in North Dakota

“It’s unregulated. We need to regulate it. This isn’t a perfect bill, the one exact bill I’d like, but on the other hand, it’s a major step in a direction to protect all of our constituents that use this every day,” said Rep. Eric Murphy, R-Grand Forks, who teaches biomedical sciences at the University of North Dakota School of Medicine and Health Sciences. 
Under the bill, the attorney general’s office would have to write and adopt rules – a lengthy process – before licenses could be issued to kratom processors and retailers. Likely “very little action” would be taken from the bill in the AG’s office before the 2027 Legislature convenes in January, said Rep. Don Vigesaa, R-Cooperstown.
The Senate bill, brought by Sen. Michelle Axtman, R-Bismarck, would classify kratom alkaloids and synthetic derivatives controlled substances on the same level as LSD and heroin.
Criminal penalties for ingestion and possession would rise in severity with repeated offenses, starting at an infraction – punishable by up to a $1,000 fine – and going all the way up to a class C felony for three or more possession offenses, punishable by up to five years in prison and a $10,000 fine.
The Senate’s debate focused on how some people use kratom for pain and how addictive medical professionals have said the substance is. The discussion also touched upon withdrawals, treatment resources and law enforcement.
“I’d like to make sure that we’re a leader in this space and that we don’t stand in the way of this ban and then become a state that is the dealer to many of this addictive drug,” Axtman said.
Public, lawmakers debate kratom regulation versus full ban in North Dakota

Sen. Jeff Magrum, R-Hazelton, who has used natural-leaf kratom capsules for back pain, pointed out that lawmakers chose not to study kratom issues last year. More than a year later “we went (from) not even interested in studying this issue to a total ban, which doesn’t make any sense to me,” Magrum said. He called it “a reasonable and logical plan” to solely ban synthetic products and pass regulations on natural kratom.
Sen. Kristin Roers, R-Fargo, a registered nurse, said the “much smarter move” is to advance the ban and continue monitoring kratom issues, “and if at some day we decide that we can find some sort of thoughtful and deliberate regulatory structure we can do that when we feel that that is prudent.” 
Several House Republicans in a caucus meeting said they wanted to have the option of regulating natural leaf kratom while also banning synthetic substances. 
“I thought we had two options: one to deal with synthetic and one to deal with natural, and that we would make our choice on each one,” Rep. Ben Koppelman, R-West Fargo, told the caucus.
House Majority Leader Mike Lefor, R-Dickinson, noted the public testimony and overwhelming committee support for a full ban, which he urged the more than 80 House Republicans to support.
Kratom products are displayed on a Bismarck store wall on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Other House Republicans say they oppose a total ban for essentially pulling the rug out from under people who use natural kratom for pain relief. Some said synthetic products are already temporarily prohibited federally by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, a move Gov. Kelly Armstrong has said precipitated his temporary ban of all kratom in August.
For about a month, all natural and synthetic kratom products have been banned in North Dakota by the governor’s executive order, and a synthetic derivative called 7-OH is outlawed by an emergency pharmaceutical rule. 
Friday is the third day of the special session the governor called for the Legislature to address kratom. Some House Republicans wondered about potential scenarios involving the kratom bills that might push the special session beyond Friday. 
Senate Majority Leader David Hogue, R-Minot, said, “Both houses support a ban on all synthetics and derivatives, and we’ll find a way to do that, and that’s all I’d like to say about that.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Mellor posts his military service records online in response to GOP rival’s attack
description: Republican congressional candidate Vic Mellor released a small cache of military documents online Thursday to substantiate his service record — a day after his Republican primary rival for Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District seat accused him of embellishing his rank. On Wednesday, Dr. Stephen Skoly’s campaign sent an email blast to followers with quest[...]
text:
Republican congressional candidate Vic Mellor poses with a military working dog in an undated photo taken during his service in the U.S. Marine Corps. Mellor released the photo on Thursday after his primary opponent Stephen Skoly attacked him about his military record. (Photo courtesy of the Vic Mellor campaign)Republican congressional candidate Vic Mellor released a small cache of military documents online Thursday to substantiate his service record — a day after his Republican primary rival for Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District seat accused him of embellishing his rank.
On Wednesday, Dr. Stephen Skoly’s campaign sent an email blast to followers with questions about Mellor’s military record. Skoly had no doubts that Mellor served in the Marine Corps, but said his campaign had received a set of documents from the National Archives and Records Administration in response to a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request. One document identified Mellor’s final rank as corporal. Mellor has previously said he was a sergeant, a more senior rank. 
Skoly, 70, an oral surgeon, challenged Mellor to release his service records and other documentation. Mellor’s campaign followed up Wednesday afternoon with a press release accompanied by his military discharge record which lists his final rank as sergeant. 
“This baseless attack on my military record demonstrates a disturbing lack of judgment by Dr. Skoly,” Mellor, 56, said in a statement. “It’s very odd behavior, to say the least.”
Records list Mellor’s specialties as military police and military police dog handler. He served in the Marine Corps from Dec. 8, 1987, to Dec. 7, 1995, including active duty from Aug. 18, 1988, to Aug. 17, 1992, according to the federal records shared by Skoly’s team.
On Thursday afternoon, Mellor took to X to post a quartet of documents which appear to further substantiate his service record. 
Among the records Mellor dropped Thursday is a Marine Corps appointment certificate naming him “Sergeant (Meritoriously).” The certificate became effective Nov. 2, 1991, which predates Mellor’s August 1992 departure from active duty.
Dr. Stephen Skoly, a Republican candidate for Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District, walks through a campaign event at Marasco’s in Cranston on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Corroborating this is the DD-214 — a document summarizing a service member’s career upon release or discharge from active duty — that Mellor’s campaign released Wednesday, shortly after Skoly’s email attack. That document lists Mellor’s rank as sergeant and his pay grade as E-5, which is a sergeant. 
Mellor also released documents Thursday intended to verify his work supporting presidential security. Skoly had written in his Wednesday email that the records his campaign had received did not appear to substantiate Mellor’s claims about his time on Marine Helicopter Squadron One, or HMX-1, in service of the president. 
Mellor’s Thursday records drop, however, included a letter dated Sept. 3, 1991, from an assistant security officer with Marine Helicopter Squadron One, or HMX-1, which lauds then-corporal Mellor for his help with the unit’s “presidential support mission” in Paris and Athens in July that year.
Mellor’s canine companion during the presidential outing had also been scrutinized by his opponent’s campaign, which pointed to a video of Mellor saying during a campaign event, “My dog was so good at it [bomb sniffing] that we became assigned to the President of the United States.” 
The records obtained by Skoly’s campaign indicated Mellor had performed “military-working-dog service at the Norfolk complex” in Virginia, but not his presidential support work for HMX-1. 
Republican CD2 candidates will debate after all; Mellor, Skoly accept invite from NBC10

“Base K9 service is honorable service,” said Skoly’s Wednesday email. “It is not, by itself, an assignment to the President.”
According to the letter Mellor released Thursday, however, the Marine and his four-legged partner conducted bomb searches, with the latter “a vital part of the security mission” that took place in July 1991. 
Mellor replied to his post Thursday with two photos of him in uniform — one of him standing amid a group of fellow servicemembers, and a solo portrait in camo fatigues, leash in hand and dog by his side.
Mellor also posted online an April 1990 set of Marine Corps orders directing him to temporary additional duty involving the Fleet Antiterrorism Security Team, or FAST, for a Navy security exercise in Charleston, South Carolina. Skoly had noted Wednesday that FAST was also missing from the assignment history supplied in materials his campaign received from the National Archives.
Neither Skoly nor his campaign could be reached Thursday for additional comment on the new documents released by Mellor.
Mellor campaign manager Patricia Morgan, a former state representative as well congressional candidate herself in 2024, said Thursday she did not know why the National Archives response differed from the records released by Mellor. She floated the idea that the Skoly campaign did not release everything it may have received from the federal government.
“Perhaps the Skoly team just released the ones that was convenient for them,” Morgan said. “They were looking to dig up dirt.”
“It’s really pretty clear he was a sergeant,” Morgan added of Mellor’s service.
Republican Vic Mellor is shown at a State House event in support of Second Amendment rights in May 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
Final rank is FOIA eligible
Neither Skoly nor Mellor’s documents have been independently verified. Rhode Island Current has asked the National Personnel Records Center, which is the branch of the National Archives that maintains military service records, for comment and to help explain the discrepancy. As of Thursday afternoon, the agency had said it was working on a response.
A veteran’s “final rank” is listed on the National Archives website as FOIA-eligible information, something which can generally be publicly released as part of an Official Military Personnel File. 
A DD-214, meanwhile, is formally known as a “Certificate of Release or Discharge from Active Duty” and, per the National Archives, “contains information normally needed to verify military service for benefits, retirement, employment, and membership in veterans’ organizations.”
The Archives website additionally states that an Official Military Personnel File may include a variety of service forms, including DD-214s, as well as “Service Status/Changes/Revisions.” 
The Republican rivals’ dueling documents could form a point of contention during a televised debate scheduled to be taped at WJAR NBC 10’s Cranston station on Friday afternoon. The half-hour debate will air Saturday, Sept. 5, at 5:30 a.m., and Sunday, Sept. 6, at noon.
The winner of the Republican primary will face Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner in November for the CD2 seat.

name: Mississippi Today
title: At DELTA FEST, HBCU leaders discuss how to prepare students for the evolving Southern economy
description: Yolanda W. Page, president of Stillman College, speaks about HBCUs and the future of the workforce as moderator Melissa Faith Payne and Corey Wiggins, president of Tougaloo College, listen during Delta Fest at the Westin Jackson, Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026.
text:
Leaders of historically Black colleges and universities want their institutions to prepare students for the rapidly changing workforce and careers in industries such as infrastructure, manufacturing, healthcare and education. 
They also said they want to ensure companies benefiting from the talent HBCUs produce also reinvest in those colleges and communities.
The leaders discussed those issues in two panels Wednesday during the first day of DELTA FEST, a three-day event that brought dozens of nonprofit executives, business leaders, entrepreneurs, politicians and community leaders to downtown Jackson. The event focused in part on how communities across Mississippi, Alabama, Arkansas, Tennessee, Louisiana and Georgia can benefit from more than $200 billion in capital investment in the region from industries such as manufacturing, healthcare and education.
Bobbie Knight, president of Miles College in Fairfield, Alabama, said HBCUs shouldn’t just produce talent that companies can recruit away. Instead, Knight said, leaders should create partnerships with corporations and companies to generate investments and opportunities for students that can also benefit the colleges and their surrounding communities.
Members of the audience listen as Bobbie Knight, president of Miles College and Kellei Bishop Samuels, chief of staff and vice president for institutional effectiveness, research, assessment and planning at Tuskegee University, have a discussion during Delta Fest at the Westin Jackson, Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
One example is the Bessemer Built, a college scholarship initiative in Alabama. QTS Data Centers, a Virginia-based company and developers of a $14.5-billion data center campus called “Project Marvel,” committed $8 million to the program, which will pay Bessemer City High School graduates through the class of 2030 at least $10,000 each to attend specified Alabama schools including Miles College. The program is part of the company’s long-term investment in the city of Bessemer. 
Elsewhere in Alabama, Tuskegee University has tried to align its academic programs with workforce needs, said Kellei Bishop Samuels, chief of staff at the university.
As demands for pilots and aviation workers grew, the university expanded its aviation science  program after receiving $5.29 million more in federal funds in February.
“We are supplying the talent pipeline for the state to ensure that needs of the state are being met,” Samuels said. 
Building corporate, nonprofit, governmental and private partnerships also requires stable university leadership, Knight said. Frequent leadership turnover can make it more difficult for HBCUs to develop the long-term corporate and philanthropic relationships needed to attract investment.  
Bobbie Knight, president of Miles College, left, and Kellei Bishop Samuels, chief of staff and vice president for institutional effectiveness, research, assessment and planning at Tuskegee University, have a discussion during Delta Fest at the Westin Jackson, Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“As president of a college, your main job is to bring resources into the institution,” Knight said. “If you’re going to have major donors and partnerships, they want to make sure you’re there, or the leadership is going to be there for the long term, whether it’s board or presidency.” 
In general, university presidents are serving an average of 5.9 years, according to the American Council on Education. The average tenure is even shorter for HBCU presidents: 4.22 years, according to a January report from the United Negro College Fund. Presidents of private HBCUs are serving an average tenure of 4.42 years, according to the report. 
The evolving use of artificial intelligence could provide an early test of how HBCUs navigate corporate partnerships. AI is one of the biggest changes institutions have confronted in recent years, said Yolanda Page, president of Stillman College in Tuscaloosa, Alabama. College faculty should embrace and update curriculum to mold students skills for the future workforce, she said. 
Tougaloo College has become central to discussions around AI and data center development, President Corey Wiggins said. Plans to build a data center near the Tougaloo campus have sparked community conversations about how local resources such as water, energy and land will be affected. 
Tougaloo leadership aims to build relationships with corporate and governmental partners to drive economic change at the college and in Jackson and Hinds County, Wiggins said. Part of that relationship-building will center on a justice framework, which is part of the legacy of the private historically Black college. 
Corey Wiggins, president of Tougaloo College, speaks about HBCUs and the future of the workforce as moderator Melissa Faith Payne and Yolanda W. Page, president of Stillman College, listen during Delta Fest at the Westin Jackson, Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Tougaloo leadership will hold institutions and people accountable for how they treat the community, Wiggins said.
“Our students deserve more, right? How do we strengthen the institution so we can deliver for our young people on campus and deliver for the community around us?” 
Ultimately, Page said, the goal of any HBCU leader is to ensure their graduates stay in their communities after graduation. 
It is also important for leaders to find employment for local residents, not just the students they serve, she said.
“We have to think outside of our box and beyond our respective gates,” Page said. “That’s how we can have community impact and see more communities thrive.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida’s universities are off-limits for anyone in the US ‘unlawfully’
description: Students must be lawfully in the United States to attend Florida’s universities, the board that oversees the university system voted Thursday. The measure received no debate or discussion, except from members of the public during public comment. The Board of Governors approved the measure, on the consent agenda, after receiving preliminary approval during a[...]
text:
View from the FIU campus. (Photo via FIU)Students must be lawfully in the United States to attend Florida’s universities, the board that oversees the university system voted Thursday.
The measure received no debate or discussion, except from members of the public during public comment. The Board of Governors approved the measure, on the consent agenda, after receiving preliminary approval during a meeting in June.
Undocumented students could be banned from state university enrollment under looming rule change

Roberto Garcia, an instructor at Florida Gulf Coast University, which hosted the Board of Governors meeting Thursday, was among those who spoke in opposition to the policy.
“At its core, this regulation asks our universities to look at an academically qualified student, someone who has done the work, earned the grades, met the standards, and demonstrated that they are capable of succeeding here and tell them that none of that matters because of their immigration status. I cannot reconcile that with the purpose of public higher education,” Garcia said during his allotted two minutes to address the board. 
The policy kicks in for the 2027-2028 school year.
It doesn’t outright bar someone “unlawfully” in the country, but instead deems them ineligible to enroll at an institution “which, for the two most recent academic years, did not admit all academically qualified applicants.”


The University of Florida received nearly 96,000 applications for the current academic year and accepted 19,012 of them.
During the previous school year, Florida State University received nearly 86,000 applications and accepted nearly 21,000. Ultimately, 6,603 enrolled.


No Florida Board of Education members debated or questioned a similar policy that panel approved in June for the 28 Florida College System institutions, including adult education courses, often designed to help students earn high school diploma equivalencies or learn English.
Earlier this summer, Gov. Ron DeSantis said he is “fully supportive of it.”
“I think what they are doing is the right thing to do, and I think it’s putting the students in Florida that are growing up here, going to our schools, Florida residents. … It’s putting them first,” DeSantis said. 
In 2014, Gov. Rick Scott signed a law allowing undocumented college students who attended Florida high schools to pay in-state tuition. The bill was championed by then-state Sen. Jeanette Nuñez, later lieutenant governor under DeSantis. Nuñez is now president of Florida International University.
Last year, the Legislature repealed that policy.
According to Higher Ed Immigration Portal, about 8,000 undocumented students graduate from high school in Florida every year.
Students who are not in the country legally may have graduated from a Florida high school and perhaps came to the country as an infant, knowing only a life in the United States.

name: VTDigger
title: Save New England’s wildest forests before it’s too late
description:
The roadless rule protects 260,000 acres of the White and Green Mountain national forests. The Trump administration wants to rescind it.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Save New England’s wildest forests before it’s too late.
text:
This commentary is by Zack Porter, the executive director of Standing Trees, which works to protect and restore forests on New England’s public lands.
This summer, did you stand on top of the Presidential Range, Mount Moosilauke or Franconia Ridge? Did you follow the Long Trail through the Green Mountain National Forest or the Appalachian Trail through the White Mountain National Forest?
Did you take a scenic drive along Vermont’s Route 100, through one of New Hampshire’s or Maine’s spectacular notches or over the Kancamagus Highway?
There’s a good chance you enjoyed one of these experiences, because these are among the most scenic and popular landscapes in eastern North America, visited by millions of locals and tourists each year, and they are core to our identity as New Englanders. Unknown to most people, one conservation tool — the U.S. Forest Service’s 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, known as the “roadless rule” — is the glue that holds all of these iconic places together across Vermont, New Hampshire and Maine, and it’s currently on the chopping block with the Trump administration. The public has until Sept. 21 to weigh in with their comments.
The roadless rule guards against most road building and logging in the most sensitive areas of our national forest system. In New England, it protects 260,000 acres, including more than one-quarter of the White Mountain National Forest. Nationwide, the roadless rule safeguards 58.5 million acres, or about a third of all national forest lands, from Alaska’s coastal rainforests to the deep hollows of the Southern Appalachians, and countless landscapes in between.
The roadless rule is arguably the most important conservation measure ever established by any federal agency, but it isn’t as well-known as it should be. Unlike national parks, national monuments or wilderness areas, you won’t find “inventoried roadless areas” depicted on any hiking maps, and you won’t come across a sign on the trail. But don’t be fooled: They serve many of the same purposes as those better-known designations, ensuring that America’s healthiest and most intact forests continue on a wild path for generations to come.
AllTrails, a widely used app for finding outdoor adventures, recently highlighted that 15 of the 50 most popular hikes in inventoried roadless areas around the U.S. are in just one national forest: the White Mountain. You read that correctly; a national forest with well under 1% of all national forest acreage contains 30% of the most popular hikes in inventoried roadless areas in the U.S. As New Englanders, that’s something to be proud of, and it’s something worth fighting to protect.
Of course, stunning scenery is just one part of what makes these places so special. Inventoried roadless areas store vast amounts of carbon, protect against floods and droughts, and support our region’s native biodiversity, including imperiled species like the northern long-eared bat, brook trout, Canada lynx, Bicknell’s thrush and American marten, among many others. They also produce the clean, cold water coming out of your tap. A recent study found that in New England, the roadless rule helps to protect drinking water for at least 8.8% of Vermont residents and 7.3% of New Hampshire residents. The Merrimack River, which originates in the roadless areas of the White Mountains, also provides drinking water to 7% of Massachusetts residents.
But maybe these are the kinds of facts and figures that the Trump administration doesn’t understand, so let’s use a language that’s more familiar to our president: money. Put simply, the roadless rule is a cash register for the American public, providing taxpayers billions of dollars in ecosystem services and generating billions more in tourism revenue each year. The Forest Service has a $10 billion road maintenance backlog. Instead of building more roads that fragment habitat and pollute streams, scarring mountains with clearcuts that increase flooding risks to our communities and cutting timber that is better sourced from private lands, protecting our national forest roadless areas is a low-cost, high-reward solution for the economy and environment.
For 25 years, the roadless rule has worked harder than any other conservation tool in the Forest Service’s toolbox. Submit your comment before the deadline of Sept. 21 to protect the roadless rule for future generations, and tell your members of Congress to support the Roadless Area Conservation Act.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Save New England’s wildest forests before it’s too late.
