name: Alaska Beacon
title: Final Journey: Carlisle begins its ninth repatriation of students who never made it home
description: This story was originally published by ICT. WARNING: This story contains disturbing details about boarding schools. If you are feeling triggered, here is a resource list from the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition. CARLISLE, Pennsylvania — The Carlisle Barracks Post Cemetery is once again solemnly shrouded with black privacy fencing a[...]
text:
Black privacy fencing shrouds the Carlisle Barracks Post Cemetery on Monday, Aug. 31, 2026, as officials prepare for the disinterment and repatriation of the remains of 12 students who died while attending the notorious Carlisle Indian Industrial School more than 100 years ago. The repatriations are scheduled to run from Sept. 1 to Oct. 12, 2026. (Photo by Charles Fox/Special to ICT)This story was originally published by ICT.
WARNING: This story contains disturbing details about boarding schools. If you are feeling triggered, here is a resource list from the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition.
CARLISLE, Pennsylvania — The Carlisle Barracks Post Cemetery is once again solemnly shrouded with black privacy fencing as families and tribal leaders gather to reunite with ancestors who died while attending the Carlisle Indian Industrial School.
Disinterments are set to begin Tuesday, Sept. 1, of the first of 12 students who will be returned to their homelands over the next six weeks as part of the Office of Army Cemetery’s annual repatriation of remains of children who died at the school.
Among the first to go home will be three students from the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes, who arrived at Carlisle together on April 15, 1890. They all died of tuberculosis over the the next few years.
Descendents and tribal leaders gathered at Carlisle on Monday, Aug. 31, to help them begin their journey home. A celebration is planned for their arrival in Montana.
“The community becomes the family,” Dyan Youpee, the tribe’s cultural preservation director, told the Fort Peck Journal, referring to a phrase that is at the heart of the planned celebration welcoming the children home.     
Christine Redstone was one of three students from the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribe who died while attending the notorious Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania. The remains of Redstone and two other students, Peter Howe and Richard Morgan, were set to be disinterred beginning on Sept. 1, 2026, and repatriated to their homelands in eastern Montana. (Photo by Charles Fox/Special to ICT)
 
Youpee told ICT the event is designed to “shed positive, healing light on the repatriation efforts, journey and reburial.”
The repatriation experience can be a wrenching emotional journey for descendants and tribal leaders, as they retrace the footsteps of ancestors who never have made it back to their families, paired with the triumph of finally bringing them home.
For the Office of Army Cemeteries, which oversees the Carlisle cemetery along with other Army facilities, this will be the ninth round of disinterments, with forensic archaeological and anthropological experts from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.
Since the repatriations began in 2017, the remains of 58 students have been returned home, leaving numerous gaps among the headstones in the cemetery. Of the 138 graves that remain, the burial sites of 22 children are designated as unknown, with the identities lost to human error when the cemetery moved in 1927.
“The Office of Army Cemeteries team is inspired by the strength and courage from the Native American and Alaska Native Tribes as they make this journey to bring their children home,” Renea Yates, director of the Office of Army Cemeteries, stated in a press release.
“Navigating the disinterment and return process requires the highest level of professional care and compassion and we are committed to providing the expert assistance needed to return their loved ones to their families and communities,” Yates said.
The Army reimburses families for their travel to participate in the disinterment process, the transfer ceremony that follows, and the cost of transport and reburial of the children. After the transfer of custody, families and tribes are free to rebury these children to a location of their choice.
 Government assimilation
The students, who ranged in age from 11 to 18, also include four Alaskan Native students, and a student each from the Comanche Nation, Absentee Shawnee Tribe, Shoshone Paiute Tribes, Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians and the Keweenaw Bay Indian Community.
Most of them died from tuberculosis, although the cause of death was not listed for several of the students in school records.
The barracks housed the Carlisle school from 1879-1918, where nearly 8,000 students from more than 140 tribes attended as part of a government assimilation program that separated them from their families, language and culture. It was the first federally funded, off-reservation Indian boarding school in the U.S., and it served as a model for boarding schools across the U.S. and Canada.
Alaskan Native students Lucy Spaulding (shown as Spalding on the gravestone) and Mabel Stack (shown as Stock) died while attending the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania more than 100 years ago. Their remains are set to be repatriated back to southeastern Alaska in September 2026. ( Photo by Charles Fox/Special to ICT)
The research of the Alaska Native Heritage Center, known as ANHC, has been instrumental in bringing home the four Alaskan Native students scheduled for disinterment.
“When we do research aimed at bringing home our children, we hope to bring healing to our communities affected by the era of assimilation and its continuing effects,” Benjamin Jacuk, director of Indigenous Research and Healing at ANHC, recently told ICT. “Our work is to bring home the children above all else… Because at the end of the day these children are worth that hard work and that trust.”

The Carlisle Barracks Post Cemetery has been closed to visitors since Aug. 14, and access to the cemetery, enclosed in privacy fencing, will be restricted to federal staff along with tribal members and their families until the completion of the scheduled disinterments, tentatively set for Oct. 12.
 Homecoming preparations
At Fort Peck in eastern Montana, organizers are optimistic the event will bring out a large welcoming crowd.
On July 31, Youpee and others did a non-stop 89-mile Awareness Walk from one end of the reservation to the other to make sure everyone was aware of the upcoming event. Organizers have encouraged people to arrive wearing orange shirts to acknowledge boarding school survivors or traditional regalia, and to create an escort of horseback riders and a caravan of cars to welcome the children home as they reach the reservation border.
More than 135 years after the children left their homelands, the homecoming is an attempt to show love and recognition to the three students.
Organizers want to ensure they are not forgotten or reduced to names on school records, in hopes the community comes together to make sure that no child comes home alone.
 COMING HOME
The remains of 12 students who died at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School are set to be disinterred starting Sept. 1 through Oct. 12. The students include four Alaskan Natives, three from the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes, and students from five other tribes across the U.S.
Alaskan Natives
*Mabel Stack arrived on Oct. 24, 1903, at age 11, and died Aug. 14, 1904, of tuberculosis. Her last name is listed as Stock on the gravestone and Stack in the Carlisle records, but Booth is believed to be her correct last name.
*Edward Angalook, who is listed as Angelook on his gravestone, arrived Nov. 23, 1903, at age 18, and died Sept. 24, 1905 of tuberculosis.
*Lucy Spaulding arrived Oct. 24, 1903, at age 14, and died March 25, 1905, of tuberculosis. She is listed as Spalding on her gravestone, although her correct last name is believed to be Guthrie.
*Tummassak arrived on Nov. 14, 1897, at age 12, and died on April 8, 1900, of tuberculosis. She is listed as Tomicock on her gravestone and also as Tomiclock in Carlisle archives.
Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribe
*Peter Howe arrived at the school on April 15, 1890, at age 16, and died six years later on June 5, 1896, of tuberculosis.
*Richard Morgan arrived  April 15, 1890, at age 17, and died March 25, 1891, of tuberculosis.
*Christine Redstone arrived April 15, 1890, at age 15, and died July 19, 1899, of tuberculosis.
Comanche Nation
*Frances Bones arrived on Nov. 8, 1894, at age 14, and died on May 7, 1895. Her cause of death was not listed in Carlisle records.
Absentee Shawnee Tribe
*Fannie Gibson arrived on Dec. 24, 1899, at age 17, and died on Dec. 6, 1900, of tuberculosis.
Shoshone Paiute Tribes
*Della Atkins arrived on Dec. 13, 1900, at age 17, and died 12 days later on Dec. 25, 1900. Her death was attributed to a brain tumor.
Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians
*Susie King arrived at the school on Oct. 25, 1890, at age 16, and died Oct. 21, 1891. Her cause of death was not listed.
Keweenaw Bay Indian Community
*Margaret Davis arrived at the school on Sept. 15, 1889, at age 14, and died Dec. 21, 1892, of tuberculosis.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: SJC sides with Nahant’s choice to eminent domain Northeastern land
description: “In short, the town's stated purpose for the taking is a proper public purpose” that aligned with past actions by the town indicating interest in preserving the area, and not a bad faith ploy, wrote Justice Elizabeth Dewar for a unanimous court.
text:
THE TOWN OF Nahant had the right to seize property owned by Northeastern University, blocking a planned university science center expansion, to preserve the parcel for open space, the Supreme Judicial Court ruled on Thursday.  
The ruling settled eight years of debate and litigation over a 28.7-acre parcel known as East Point at the edge of the tiny peninsula community. 
Town Meeting voters in 2021 decided to use eminent domain powers to claim about 12 of 21 acres and access rights to land owned by Northeastern University since the 1960s to preserve it for conservation.  
University officials argued successfully before a lower court that this was simply a pretext to stand in the way of a planned 55,000-square-foot development, and that it was effectively letting the town sidestep limits on local zoning powers. 
But the state’s highest court disagreed. 
“In short, the town’s stated purpose for the taking is a proper public purpose” that aligned with past actions by the town indicating interest in preserving the area, and not a bad faith ploy, wrote Justice Elizabeth Dewar for a unanimous court. The court, she wrote in a 43-page opinion, was also “unpersuaded” by the university’s other arguments against the taking. 
The court reversed the Superior Court’s summary judgment in favor of Northeastern and sent the case back for an order establishing the town’s right to take the property. 
The town is “pleased” by the SJC’s reversal of the Superior Court ruling, Town Administrator Alison Nieto said in a statement, and “looks forward to moving forward with this process.” 
Northeastern did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
Both Northeastern and the tiny North Shore community own part of East Point, which includes the university’s Marine Science Center and a coastal open area overlooking the Atlantic Ocean, with beaches, a meadow, woodlands, cliffs, and other shoreline. 
Northeastern’s land has long housed a 31,083-square-foot research facility, repurposed from three former military bunkers, as well as other smaller structures and parking lots. The rest of the land to the east was largely kept as open space, with uplands, wetlands, and a beach. Alongside that land, the town’s 8 acres on East Point operate as a public park. 
That open space and Northeastern’s land were designated as a “Natural Resource Zoning District” in 1991. In the years since, the SJC noted, public planning and public surveys demonstrated an interest from Nahant and its residents in protecting East Point’s open space, conserve natural areas, and provide access to the coastline. 
In 2018, the university announced plans to expand its presence with a new Coastal Sustainability Institute, anchored by a 55,000-square-foot building. All three members of Nahant’s Board of Selectmen announced their opposition to the project, the high court noted. 
Years of public back-and-forth followed, with locals decrying possible infrastructure strains, disruption to the habitat, and the impact on the beauty of East Point. 
A supermajority of Nahant Town Meeting voters in 2021 authorized the Board of Selectmen to create easements on Northeastern land “for open space, recreation, conservation and/or historic preservation purposes.” The move would block development on a portion of the site and allow public access. 
The town filed a petition in the Superior Court requesting authorization to take the property and create the easements. Northeastern opposed the petition, arguing that despite Nahant’s claims that the taking was to preserve open space and for related purposes, the action was actually for the sole purpose of stopping Northeastern’s project.  
The SJC took up the case, with justices seemingly troubled about whether they should parse the motivations of the town’s voters. 
“To be sure,” Dewar wrote, “it is undisputed that the town pursued the taking in response to Northeastern’s announcement of the project, that there was vehement opposition to the project on the part of town officials and residents, and that the taking would in effect block the project.” 
But that is the nature of reserving land for conservation, she noted. 
“It is axiomatic that taking a conservation easement will have the effect of preventing development; preventing development is the very purpose of imposing such an easement on land valued as an open space resource,” she wrote. 
Justices dislike second-guessing the intentions of a Town Meeting or other local legislative body. The court’s posture in cases like this is to presume that the reasons given for using town powers are valid, unless the property owner can prove otherwise. 
The long history of the town acting to try to use East Point for conversation and recreation cuts against Northeastern’s claim that the motive was “solely” to block the project, the court concluded. 
As to the public policy implications, Northeastern argued that Nahant was pulling a fast one to get around the state Dover Amendment, which bars municipalities from imposing zoning ordinances or bylaws that regulate or restrict the use of land or structures for educational purposes on land owned or leased by a nonprofit educational corporation. 
“The Town is using the threat of eminent domain as a cudgel to force Northeastern to submit to regulation that the Town is powerless to effect through its zoning powers,” the university wrote in its brief. 
But the high court rejected the claim. As the Legislature has limited the way cities and towns can use their zoning powers on educational parcels, Dewar wrote, it could have done so with eminent domain powers if it wanted. So as long as the taking was for a constitutional public purpose, like conservation, this was a perfectly legitimate use of eminent domain powers.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma wildlife officials release severance agreement after two-year legal fight
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – After  more than two years of litigation and tens of thousands in legal fees, a state agency Thursday released the severance agreement for its former executive director. The agreement between the Oklahoma Wildlife Conservation Commission and J.D. Strong showed nothing revealing, but only was released after Oklahoma Voice obtained a judgment r[...]
text:
The headquarters of the Department of Wildlife Conservation pictured in December 2023. (Photo by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – After  more than two years of litigation and tens of thousands in legal fees, a state agency Thursday released the severance agreement for its former executive director.
The agreement between the Oklahoma Wildlife Conservation Commission and J.D. Strong showed nothing revealing, but only was released after Oklahoma Voice obtained a judgment requiring it be made public. 
It outlines the terms of Strong’s $169,341 severance payment and indicates that he was “being separated from the Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation” under a state law permitting reduction in force.
Strong, who officials have said resigned, agreed his employment would end at the close of business on Dec. 6, 2023, the agreement said. That was the same day that the wildlife governing board approved the severance agreement. 
The document contained a confidentiality clause that Strong’s “personnel records” would be kept private unless a court order compelled the agency, governing board or an individual commissioner to release them or they were otherwise required to do so by law. 
Oklahoma Voice immediately requested a copy of the severance agreement under the Open Records Act but was denied. Editor Janelle Stecklein sued on behalf of Oklahoma Voice in May 2024 seeking the document’s release.
On July 16, Oklahoma County District Judge Don Andrews ordered its release, finding that the severance agreement was not exempt from the Oklahoma Open Records Act, regardless of the confidentiality clause.  
“We hope this case reminds public bodies to act with careful consideration when choosing secrecy over transparency because the public has an inherent right to know about the workings of their government and taxpayers have to foot the bill when the government erroneously withholds records under the act,” said Leslie Briggs, Oklahoma local legal initiative attorney for the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, which represented Oklahoma Voice.
The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press has filed a motion to be reimbursed $60,657 in attorneys fees and $317.68 in other costs stemming from the multi-year litigation. A hearing is set on that in 2027.
Micah Holmes, a spokesperson for the wildlife department, said Thursday that their counsel at the Attorney General’s Office included a confidentiality provision in the severance agreement. 
“By not releasing this document we were simply complying with the provisions agreed upon by all parties in the agreement,” he said.
Strong, who had served as the agency head since 2016, did not respond to a request seeking comment.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Gov. Sherrill, White House spar over denial of disaster relief
description: The Trump administration won’t provide federal aid to help New Jersey with costs associated with a blizzard in February. Gov. Sherrill said the move is political.
text:
Exterior view of Norwood Public School on Summit Street as snow falls on February 23, 2026. Gov. Mikie Sherrill is criticizing President Trump for denying federal aid to help the state recover costs associated with the storm. (Photo by Kena Betancur/Getty Images)Federal officials have denied New Jersey’s appeal for a major disaster declaration tied to a February winter storm, leaving the state without $84 million in anticipated federal aid.
Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat who took office weeks before the storm, blasted the decision as the latest example of President Donald Trump weaponizing disaster funds against Democratic-led states.
“Once again, Donald Trump is using the federal government to punish those he sees as his political enemies, and everyday New Jerseyans are paying the price,” she said in a statement Thursday. “Natural disasters don’t care about political parties.”
She said that the Federal Emergency Management Agency agreed that disaster relief was warranted, but Trump “overruled the experts — and common sense — leaving New Jersey taxpayers holding the $84 million bag.”



Quotation







New Jersey communities were buried under record snowfall. But apparently if you live in a state Trump doesn’t like, you’re on your own.


– Rep. Frank Pallone


Asked to respond, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said there is “no politicization in the President’s decision on disaster relief unlike the Biden Administration.”
“New Jersey has the fiscal and operational means to respond to this snowstorm, yet Governor Sherill wants taxpayers across America to pick up the bill,” Bis said in a statement. “President Trump provides a more thorough review of disaster declaration requests than any Administration has before him and ensures American tax dollars are used appropriately and efficiently by the states to supplement—not substitute, their obligation to respond to and recover from disasters.”
The storm hit New Jersey Feb 22 and 23, dropping nearly two feet of snow across the state and knocking out power to more than 100,000 residents, just weeks after another blizzard hit the state in January. The storm caused 15 deaths, hundreds of car crashes, and nearly $100 million in statewide damages.
New Jersey filed its initial request for a major disaster declaration on April 7. The Federal Emergency Management Agency denied it in July, one of several rejections that month for Democratic-led states, including Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and New York.
The Sherrill administration appealed the decision on July 20.
Sens. Cory Booker and Andy Kim, both Democrats, echoed Sherrill’s criticism in a joint statement, arguing the state clearly met the federal bar for assistance. The two said the severe storms New Jerseyans saw in the winter are “exactly the kind of catastrophe that this support is designed to respond to.”
“Without good explanation or justification, Trump’s government is again politicizing disaster relief and denying New Jersey the support needed. This is a completely unacceptable decision – we will continue working with Governor Sherrill and communities across our state to find solutions so that New Jersey is prepared for future winter storms,” they said.
In August, Rep. Frank Pallone (D-06) called on Republicans to investigate Trump’s denial of the state’s disaster declaration. He said Wednesday that the GOP chairs of committees with jurisdiction over the Federal Emergency Management Agency have not responded.
“New Jersey communities were buried under record snowfall. But apparently if you live in a state Trump doesn’t like, you’re on your own,” said Pallone.
According to a memo compiled by House Democrats in July 2026, Trump has approved disaster aid requests from Democratic governors at a rate of 23%, compared to 89% for Republican-led states.

title: Form allows hundreds with felony convictions to find their voter eligibility
description: In the first statewide election since Florida created a process to allow those with felony convictions to learn whether they are eligible to vote, an advocacy group says it helped more than 400 people submit an inquiry with the state’s Division of Elections. The development comes nearly eight years after Floridians approved Amendment 4, designed […]
text:
Screenshot of top of form that individuals with felony convictions in Florida can complete and send to the state's Division of Elections to verify voting eligibility.In the first statewide election since Florida created a process to allow those with felony convictions to learn whether they are eligible to vote, an advocacy group says it helped more than 400 people submit an inquiry with the state’s Division of Elections.
The development comes nearly eight years after Floridians approved Amendment 4, designed to restore voting rights to nearly 1.5 million people with felony convictions. But the process became onerous in 2019, when Republican lawmakers passed an implementing bill that required payment of all outstanding fines, fees, and restitution before those voting rights could be restored.
Meanwhile, the state failed to provide a centralized database for citizens to research the debts they owed. The Florida Rights Restoration Coalition, the group behind Amendment 4, filed a lawsuit against the state in 2023 “for its unwillingness to fix Florida’s broken election system.”
The two sides ultimately came to a negotiated settlement. The result was that the state agreed to provide Floridians with felony convictions who were uncertain about their legal financial obligations to fill out an advisory opinion request form with the state.
“In the past year, I’d say we filed over 400 advisory opinions on behalf of returning citizens or helped them file their own advisory opinions so that the state is giving them clarity on their eligibility to vote,” said Raven Lightsey, executive director for the FRRC.
Raven Lightsey is the executive director with the Florida Rights Restoration Coalition (from their website).
The rule giving the Division of Elections responsibility for advisory opinions was issued in November 2024. It says the division must respond within 90 days of receiving the form to indicate whether an individual is eligible or ineligible to register and to vote.
“Sometimes, in some cases, that 90-days mark sometimes gets passed, in some cases due to discrepancies in the applications,” Lightsey said.
The Phoenix reached out to the Department of State earlier this week to ask how many advisory opinions it’s fielded since the request form went live, as well as how often it’s been able to provide an opinion within 90 days. The department had not provided that information by time this story was published.
Different policies and procedures?
Once provided with the information about their voting eligibility, individuals need to work through their local clerk of the court to fulfill their financial responsibilities. Lightsey said sometimes there is a lack of consistently between what the state provides and what the clerks say about what the former felon owes.
“We know that the clerks of the court are independently elected for their counties,” she said. “Sometimes they have different policies and procedures in terms of how they process collection costs versus fees that were assessed at the time of sentencing, so one of the things that we’re trying to work on is some alignment between the state’s advisory opinion process and the clerk of court’s understanding on how to use that information to apply payments to people’s fines and fees accounts.”
A spokesperson for the Florida Court Clerks & Comptrollers couldn’t provide much clarity on that issue.
“Questions regarding how a particular individual’s financial obligations are reflected in local court records would need to be directed to the clerk of the court in the county where the case originated,” said Kasey Hyde, external communications manager for the Florida Clerks.
The Florida Restoration Rights Coalition went to court in 2023 following what it and other voting-rights advocates described as a dark a moment in the movement to restore voting rights to what they refer to as “returning citizens.”
That would be Aug. 18, 2022, five days before the primary election in Florida, when DeSantis announced that 20 individuals had been arrested by officers with the FDLE and the Florida Election Crimes Security unit for breaking election law (later amended to 19). Subsequent reporting found that many of those charged had been told by a government official that they could vote, while others received voting information cards in the mail.
FRRC doesn’t support centralized database
During the most recent legislative session, Broward County Democratic state Sen. Tina Polsky filed legislation (SB 132) that would have required the Florida Commission on Offender Review to develop and maintain a database with information to assist a person about whether they qualified to have their voting rights restored. The measure went further than similar legislative efforts, winning unanimous approval in two committees.
However, the House companion never received a hearing.
The FRRC doesn’t support that legislation, worried it “exposes” people who are already sensitive to the criminal legal system, Lightsey said.
“Having a centralized repository like that is not the safest thing for returning citizens. I think that the state can do a little bit better than just having a centralized repository of everybody having a felony conviction, for example,” she said.
“I think what we need are systems that talk to each other so that the system that the state is using to determine  a person’s voter eligibility through that advisory opinion process, they’re using the four-corners rule — which means I’m looking at what was accessed at the time of sentencing, while clerks are looking at, ‘Well, here’s all the collection costs. Plus your fines and fees which you owe us.’
“Those collection costs are not a barrier to voting. And so what we need is clarity on that statute first, and then having systems built around that who speak to each other across the state, so that I’m not hearing one thing from the state and another thing from my local clerk.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s forgotten Abenaki war captain
description:
An Abenaki captain and his soldiers fought alongside Vermont's militia against the British in the Revolutionary War, some giving their lives for a nation not yet their own.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s forgotten Abenaki war captain.
text:
Dear Editor,   
Kyle Neece’s recent story in VTDigger about “three Vermonters whose histories are lesser known” was very interesting. However, the writer could have chosen a Native American who was even less well known than “Indian Joe” and far more important. 
When the American Revolution began, an Abenaki leader in Vermont and New Hampshire raised a company of Abenaki soldiers who fought alongside the Yankee militia commanded by Gen. Jacob Bayley. The Yankees knew the Abenaki leader as Captain John Vincent or, more commonly, as Captain John. 

READ MORE

Bayley’s war records reveal he had 50 Abenaki soldiers on his payroll. In 1777, when Bayley led his Yankee militia column out of Newbury to battle the British army at Saratoga, Captain John and his Abenaki soldiers marched with them. Some of those Abenaki soldiers gave their lives for Vermont, New Hampshire and the United States. 
Charles Calley Newbury, Vt.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s forgotten Abenaki war captain.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi issues Lafayette burn ban after senator puts heat on agency amid drought
description: Severe drought conditions have impacted farmers across the state, like this cotton grown by Walter West, Jr. of Hazelhurst, Friday, Sept., 22, 2023.
text:
The Mississippi Forestry Commission confirmed Thursday a burn ban is in place for Lafayette County after a lawmaker who represents the area publicly criticized the agency’s process.
Sen. Nicole Boyd, a Republican from Oxford, sent a letter Wednesday to the commission questioning why it hadn’t issued a temporary burn ban for the county. In addition to little rainfall over the last month, Boyd said the county has had to handle 16 different fires since the beginning of August.
“I understand the stated reason is that Lafayette County has not experienced enough fire activity,” the state senator wrote to State Forester Russell Bozeman in a letter she posted to Facebook. “That rationale is backwards. A burn ban is a prevention tool, not a reward for waiting until enough fires have already occurred.”
Lafayette County Board President Brent Larson said the county initially requested the ban Wednesday morning, but was verbally denied by one of the state’s regional foresters.
“The normal course of action is, we approve it, I sign off on it, send it to (MFC), they sign off of it,” Larson told Mississippi Today. “They have never given us a problem, never.”
Larson claimed MFC denied the ban because the area hadn’t seen enough wildfires. 
“We hadn’t had rain at all in a month, hardly, and you’ve got people out here we’re trying to protect,” he said. “I was mad, I mean I was disgusted and dumbfounded.”
MFC on Thursday told Mississippi Today that a ban had been put in place that morning after the agency received the necessary information from Lafayette County. 
“Our goal is to work closely with local officials and make timely decisions based on the best information available to protect the public and our firefighters,” Bozeman said in an emailed statement, asking “all Mississippians” to use extra caution with outdoor burning. 
“(MFC) shares Senator Boyd’s concerns about wildfire risk and public safety. The Commission’s initial determination was based on the information available to our wildfire professionals at the time. There is no predetermined number of fires required to approve a burn ban; rather, we evaluate the totality of available conditions, including drought, rainfall, fuel conditions, weather, fire activity, and other relevant factors.”
Sen. Nicole Boyd, R-Oxford, speaks during the Mississippi Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council meeting at the Carroll Gartin Justice Building in Jackson, Monday, Nov. 3, 2025.
In addition to Lafayette, the commission on Thursday approved burn bans for eight other counties: Copiah, Rankin, Jefferson, Covington, Grenada, Lawrence, Franklin and Jefferson Davis. A county can request a ban, and then MFC approves the request, the agency’s website says.
A burn ban status prevents “anything with an open flame that produces an ember,” the agency defines, including campfires, bonfires, fire pits, fire rings, burn barrels, debris burning and field burning. Propane, gas and charcoal grills are allowed, as well as propane and gas heaters. Violators can receive fines from $100 to $500.
The Delta is seeing the worst of the ongoing drought, according to data from the U.S. Drought Monitor. Parts of Bolivar and Washington counties are seeing “exceptional drought” — the highest level on the monitor’s intensity scale — while parts of Sunflower, Leflore and Humphreys counties are having “extreme drought.” There are no active burn bans from the state in those counties.
It’s unclear when Lafayette County requested the burn ban or what initial response it received from MFC. The county’s Board of Supervisors President Brent Larson did not respond to calls for a clarification, and Fire Department Chief Wes Anderson declined to comment, citing “political things going on.”
The city of Oxford on Tuesday asked residents to conserve water during a “historically high summer demand” during the ongoing drought. The notice highlighted the strain caused by outdoor irrigation, which makes up over 50% of the city’s peak water consumption.
“We are relying on our community’s proactive cooperation to protect the City of Oxford water system,” the notice read, asking residents to cut back on watering times by 50%. 
Below average rainfall for August, more drought expected
Most of Mississippi was under a heat advisory as of Thursday, according to the National Weather Service, which means the heat index for the area has surpassed 105°F. The past month has seen lower rainfall throughout the state when compared to an average August. Greenville, for instance, recorded just 0.44 inches of rain for the month, compared to the nearly 3 inches it usually sees that time of year.
“Earlier in the summer, we had a lot of low-level moisture, and a combination of that higher humidity and hot temperatures, that’s what’s pushing our heat indices well into the advisory and warning categories,” NWS Memphis meteorologist Corey Chaskelson said.  
Chaskelson said the forecast for his office’s area, which covers north Mississippi, shows little chance of rain over the next week. The ongoing El Niño event, part of a global weather pattern, is resulting in drier and warmer conditions, although those are common for the region this time of year, he explained. 
The Mississippi State Department of Health cautions residents to stay hydrated during extreme heat and to avoid alcoholic and caffeinated beverages. For other tips, including signs of heat stroke, visit the MSDH or CDC website.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Watchdog’s illegal campaign contribution complaint dismissed by State Board of Elections
description: The State Board of Elections has closed an investigation into complaints that a member of the Cumberland County Board of Elections made an illegal campaign contribution in 2022 and another member failed to report it. The complaint was filed in March by longtime North Carolina campaign finance watchdog Bob Hall, who on Thursday shared the […]
text:
Voting at the Portland Expo in Maine’s June 9, 2026 primary election. (Photo by Jim Neuger/Maine Morning Star)The State Board of Elections has closed an investigation into complaints that a member of the Cumberland County Board of Elections made an illegal campaign contribution in 2022 and another member failed to report it.
Bob Hall (File photo)
The complaint was filed in March by longtime North Carolina campaign finance watchdog Bob Hall, who on Thursday shared the state board’s letter dismissing the complaint due to “insufficient evidence.”
“This letter is to inform you that the campaign finance investigation into a donation made by Bree Eldridge stemming from your March 27, 2026 complaint is complete,” the letter said. “The complaint has been closed. The investigation revealed insufficient evidence of a violation.” 
As NC Newsline previously reported, Hall accused Brenda “Bree” Eldridge, the board’s current secretary and a former chairwoman of the Cumberland County Republican Party, of making an illegal $25,000 campaign contribution. He also accused current board chairwoman Linda Devore of not reporting the alleged infraction to the state board. Devore was a member of the county election board at the time. 
Brenda Eldridge (Photo: Cumberland County Board of Elections)
Eldridge said Thursday that she’s glad the matter is behind her.
State board investigators “proved exactly what I had said; that the accusations were false and I’m just ready to move on,” Eldridge said.
Devore said the outcome was not unexpected. She said Eldridge provided investigators with all of the banking records they requested, which proved there was no wrongdoing.
Linda Devore (Photo: Cumberland County Board of Elections)
“I know it takes a while for things to be thoroughly investigated,” Devore said. “I think they did a very thorough job, and everybody appreciates their work, and I’m happy to be moving on.”
In the complaint, Hall alleged that Eldridge “intentionally collected contributions from anonymous sources and used the funds to help make, or reimburse herself for, a $25,000 contribution in her name to the Cumberland County Republican Party.” 
He told NC Newsline in March that it’s a violation of state law to make a campaign contribution with someone else’s money or in the name of another donor. Unlawful contributions of more than $10,000 are a felony. Felonies have no statute of limitations in North Carolina.
Hall said his complaint was based on internal GOP documents, affidavits and recorded interviews indicating multiple donors gave money. The complaint included statements from Eldridge, Devore and former party treasurer Richard Button substantiating the charges, but all three now “disclaim those statements,” he said. 
NC campaign finance watchdog files complaints against two Cumberland County elections officials

Eldridge allegedly made the contribution to pay Gen. Michael Flynn’s fee as the featured speaker at a county party fundraising event that year. Flynn was national security adviser for 22 days during the first Trump administration. He resigned in February 2017 in the wake of reports that he lied about discussing U.S. sanctions against Russia with that country’s ambassador before Trump took office.
“I think the board needed to hear from somebody who gave Eldridge money that she didn’t report,” Hall said. “There was speculation that members of the military, who are barred by DOD [Department of Defense] regulations from partisan fundraising, donated money through Eldridge to help pay Gen. Flynn’s fee, but nobody came forward so that made the investigation difficult.”
Hall had asked the state board to remove Devore from the county board, citing state law that gives it the authority to remove a county board member for “incompetency, neglect or failure to perform duties, fraud, or for any other satisfactory cause.”
Hall also complained that Devore has a history of alleged bias and authoritarian leadership. During the recent 2026 primary, he claims Devore “inappropriately and negligently insisted” that a tent promoting certain candidates remain inside the 50-foot buffer zone at an early voting site, he said. 
State law bans political activity within 50 feet of the entrance of voting sites. 
Devore said the voting site complaint was a “misstatement of the facts” of what happened and was dismissed by the state board in April.
“What I did visiting that site was exactly what is expected of a board member,” Devore said.

name: National
title: Women on parole face higher rates of mental health, housing challenges
description: Women on parole report higher rates of housing instability, poor health and serious mental health and substance use disorders than men on parole and than women who weren’t on parole, according to a new analysis from the nonpartisan think tank Council on Criminal Justice. For people leaving prison, parole is a period of transition that […]
text:
Computers line the walls of a reentry center inside the Women’s Eastern Reception, Diagnostic and Correctional Center in Vandalia, Mo. Incarcerated women preparing for release can use the computers to search for employment and other resources while on parole. (Photo by Amanda Watford/Stateline)Women on parole report higher rates of housing instability, poor health and serious mental health and substance use disorders than men on parole and than women who weren’t on parole, according to a new analysis from the nonpartisan think tank Council on Criminal Justice.
For people leaving prison, parole is a period of transition that can involve finding housing and work, reconnecting with family and accessing health care while also meeting the conditions of supervision. How well those pieces come together can shape whether someone successfully settles back into the community — a key part, some argue, of reducing future involvement with the criminal justice system and promoting public safety.
The council’s latest report examined nationally representative 2021-2023 data from the National Survey on Drug Use and Health, comparing women who reported being on parole both with women who were not on parole and with men who were on parole.
About 13% of women on parole reported moving three or more times in the previous year, compared with 2% of women who were not on parole and 6% of men on parole, according to the analysis.
Women’s prison population, correctional costs projected to grow through 2035

Women on parole also were more likely to report poor health. About 29% rated their overall health as fair or poor, compared with 16% of women not on parole and 17% of men on parole.
About 24% of women on parole met the criteria for a severe mental health disorder, compared with 7% of women not on parole and 10% of men on parole, according to the council’s report. About 25% of women on parole also reported experiencing a major depressive episode during the previous year, compared with 10% of women not on parole and 12% of men on parole.
The analysis found that substance use disorders were common among people on parole, but severe disorders were more prevalent among women. About 32% of women on parole met the criteria for a severe substance use disorder, compared with 24% of men on parole and 3% of women not on parole.
The disparity was especially large for opioid use. About 18% of women on parole met the criteria for a severe opioid use disorder, compared with 5% of men on parole and 0.4% of women not on parole.
Health and housing can make the demands of reentry harder to manage, including maintaining employment, attending treatment and supervision appointments, and managing family responsibilities, according to the report.
Women on parole also were more likely than men on parole to report living in a household with minor children. About 29% of women on parole lived in a household with at least one child under 18, compared with 19% of men on parole and 30% of women who were not on parole.
The survey, however, did not indicate whether respondents were parents, caregivers or financially responsible for the children, according to the report.
Health insurance coverage also differed among the groups. About 11% of women on parole reported being uninsured, compared with 7% of women not on parole and 20% of men on parole, according to the analysis.
The report’s authors wrote that the findings point to the need for reentry planning that goes beyond supervision requirements to address housing, health care, mental health and substance use treatment and family responsibilities. The authors could not determine whether the conditions preceded or resulted from criminal justice involvement, but the findings strongly suggest women on parole face distinct reentry challenges.
Stateline reporter Amanda Watford can be reached at awatford@stateline.org.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Warrants for Flock searches? Kentucky lawmakers may add more rules for public cameras
description: FRANKFORT — Kentucky lawmakers may consider legislation to require law enforcement officers to get a warrant before searching Flock cameras in the future.  Lawmakers on the Judiciary Committee heard from supporters on Thursday about how Flock cameras can help police officers quickly find suspects, but also heard from opponents about how bad actors can misuse[...]
text:
Kevin Kane, the director of governmental affairs for Flock Safety, speaks at a microphone during a Judiciary Committee meeting on Sept. 3, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)FRANKFORT — Kentucky lawmakers may consider legislation to require law enforcement officers to get a warrant before searching Flock cameras in the future. 
Lawmakers on the Judiciary Committee heard from supporters on Thursday about how Flock cameras can help police officers quickly find suspects, but also heard from opponents about how bad actors can misuse the devices. 
Flock cameras are a type of automatic license plate readers that have gained controversy in recent months. In Louisville, a detective was disciplined after allowing a federal agent to use the city police department’s Flock system for unauthorized immigration-related searches earlier this year, and is again under investigation for searching for a vehicle assigned to another employee. In southern Indiana, a sheriff deputy was charged with official misconduct after making more than 2,000 searches on Flock cameras for his ex-girlfriend’s car. 
Several Northern Kentucky communities have ended Flock camera programs. Kentucky Republican U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie has filed legislation to prevent federal funds from being used to install and maintain Flock-style automated license plate readers, called the “Flock-Off Act.” 
Kevin Kane, the director of governmental affairs for Flock Safety, told the committee on Tuesday Flock cameras are used by more than 6,000 law enforcement agencies in the country and that an average of 27 missing persons a day are found by police departments using Flock. 
Elizabethtown Police Chief Jeremy Thompson said the technology has been a boon for his department, having aided in a search for a kidnapped child and finding cars originally stolen in another county. However, social media has “been toxic on this particular topic,” Thompson said. 
“I understand the concerns, but I’m telling you, in nearly 30 years of law enforcement, this is the best piece of technology to assist law enforcement in real-time information to help solve crime, to make our citizens safer,” the chief said. 
However, representatives from the progressive American Civil Liberties Union of Kentucky and the libertarian Cato Institute  highlighted the reported cases of misuse of Flock cameras. They suggested lawmakers revisit and expand regulations in a recently passed law regarding the use of automatic license plate readers
Kate Miller, the advocacy director of the ACLU-KY, said the bill had “important guardrails,” but the organization suggests more changes, like pausing contracts for Flock cameras, reducing data retention further to 48 hours and having independent agencies annually audit use of the cameras. 
Laura Bondank-Harmon, the manager of legal programs for Cato, pointed to a June U.S. Supreme Court decision that when police officers used a “geofence warrant” to get cell phone data of users near a specific place and time, it was a search under the 4th Amendment. She, too, praised the Kentucky law, but called it a “good start.” 
Some policy changes she proposed included requiring officers to get a judicial warrant before searching a camera database with exceptions for situations like stolen cars and active Amber Alerts, establishing a cause of action for victims of illegal surveillance searches, giving members of the public a way to review audits for their license plates, shortening the data retention period and having Kentucky agencies review out-of-agency requests for database searches. 
Rep. TJ Roberts, R-Burlington, told reporters after the meeting he would have more to say in the future on specific legislation, but he has concerns such as the “overextended retention of data” from cameras like Flock’s and the data being accessed without a warrant. The General Assembly returns to Frankfort for its next session in January. 
“Most Kentuckians are law-abiding, peaceful citizens who are just looking to go to work, raise their family, and live a good life,” he said. “That said, we cannot render everyone a suspect because if you say that those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear, that’s like saying you shouldn’t care about free speech because you have nothing to say.”
Flock Safety license plate readers are typically mounted on tall poles, with a camera and solar panel on top. The company says its technology is used in more than 6,000 communities across 49 states in partnership with thousands of law enforcement agencies nationwide. (Photo courtesy of Flock Safety)
Republican House Whip Jason Nemes, of Louisville, said GOP lawmakers have not discussed the issue as a caucus yet, but he would be supportive of the idea of requiring a warrant for searches except in some emergency situations. 
While Nemes praised Louisville Police Chief Paul Humphrey and his department’s policies regarding Flock, Nemes said “nobody can know what individual officers are doing all the time” pointing to the Indiana deputy situation. 
“We just need more protections in place, and while at the same time, I know a lot of people want to get rid of Flock cameras, I don’t think that’s responsible either,” Nemes said.
During the meeting, some lawmakers expressed skepticism about the technology and said they’ve heard a myriad of concerns in their districts. Rep. Jennifer Decker, R-Waddy, said as the cameras advance, people are worried about living in a “surveillance state that George Orwell warned about in his dystopian novel, ‘1984.’” 
“The question isn’t whether we trust the people now in charge,” Decker said. “That is one question many have, but the bigger question is that our constitutional system limits government power precisely because we don’t know who will possess the power tomorrow.” 
Rep. Nima Kulkarni, D-Louisville, said that private companies like Flock Safety should not be responsible for regulating themselves because, but it is up to lawmakers to do so. 
“We will need to make sure we, as a legislative body, work with you to make sure that those safeguards are put into place, balancing public safety with the privacy interests of our constituents,” she told Kane.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Justice says he’s considering challenging Morrisey for governor of West Virginia
description: WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — While Sen. Jim Justice considers challenging Gov. Patrick Morrisey in the 2028 gubernatorial primary, the pair took the stage Thursday at The Greenbrier to deliver economic-focused talks with a flavor of stump speeches.
text:
U.S. Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., and Gov. Patrick Morrisey speak at the West Virginia Chamber of Commerce’s annual meeting and business summit at The Greenbrier resort in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia, on Sept. 3, 2026. (The West Virginia Chamber of Commerce photo)WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — While Sen. Jim Justice considers challenging Gov. Patrick Morrisey in the 2028 gubernatorial primary, the pair took the stage Thursday at The Greenbrier to deliver economic-focused talks with a flavor of stump speeches.
They’re both highly competitive, and the next Republican primary for governor could shape up to be an expensive, dramatic show down. 
National outlet Politico published a story Thursday morning saying Justice was “seriously considering launching a campaign to return to the governor’s mansion.” Justice, 75, said on MetroNews Talkline a few hours later that he’s considering a run.
Morrisey declined to comment about Justice when asked for a response.
“It’s literally, what, 20 months into my first term. That’s the last thing I want to focus on. I want to deliver,” Morrisey said. “I want to keep delivering on big wins for West Virginia, like we announced today. Helping our families, not playing politics. I want to make sure that we’re doing those really incredible things to help families who are struggling, that’s what my focus is.”
The governor and Justice recently traded jabs on social media — or, as MetroNews reporter Brad McElhinny called it, a “slap fight” — about the historic Greenbrier Hotel. The luxury resort is now partially owned by the Justice family after a recent $500 million financial deal resolved outstanding debt for the Justices linked to The Greenbrier. 
The U.S. Senator and governor spoke at the West Virginia Chamber of Commerce’s 90th annual meeting and business summit at the resort. The event brings together the state’s business heavy hitters and politicians — and potential campaign funders with deep pockets. 
Justice was up first to speak, delivering the kind of speech he’s known for: touting a deep love for West Virginia, a dislike of D.C. politics and some folksy flair with references to “Toby and Edith,” his hypothetical average West Virginia couple he often refers to when speaking.
There was also an obvious unhappiness with the state of economic development in West Virginia — a criticism some lawmakers have lobbed at Morrisey’s office while the state has a big need for jobs. 
“What did we do — we went out and got the business, we went out and competed with others,” Justice said. “That’s what you have to do, for crying out loud, it’s not going to come to you.”
“It’s energy, energy, energy, energy. West Virginia is right dead in the bullseye,” he added. 
Morrisey was more focused on what he has accomplished in the last 19 months. He said that his administration has focused on economic development “every single day.”
“We’re announcing $81 billion in investments in West Virginia, and $96 billion total since October of 2025. That includes more than 19,000 projected jobs,” Morrisey said. “Think about that. We’re going to tap into the coal, gas and nuclear energy that America desperately needs to compete successfully with China.”
The governor also focused on his investments in healthcare with $199 million in federal Rural Health Transformation funds and grants, along with $145 million in federal, state and other resources to address West Virginia’s poor water quality and wastewater infrastructure over the next year. 
Steve Roberts, president of the West Virginia Chamber of Commerce, said West Virginia is unique in how it’s able to bring a U.S. Senator and governor in the same room and on the same day. 
“This is an advantage shared by so few states and is a true leg up for our state,” Roberts said.
Morrisey announces new data center project 
Justice as governor led a very proactive Economic Development Authority team, opting to use tax incentives to lure business. He touts Nucor and Berkshire Hathaway as hallmark economic wins during his time as governor.
“Go after it right now. Don’t be afraid to invest in yourself. Invest in West Virginia,” Justice said, pushing the crowd to focus on diversifying its energy portfolio. “You got to be hungry like a pit bull and go get it. Think about it. Go get it. Compete. Compete with other states … You see the things we did.”
In contrast, Morrisey likes to highlight when zero state dollars are invested in new businesses. He announced at The Greenbrier that Randox, a North Ireland-based health and toxicology company, will invest $13 million into the state to create 100 jobs without any state dollars contributed. 
“It’s important that taxpayers know where their money goes,” Morrisey told reporters after his speech. “I’m not here to be critical of anything that happened in the past, but we’ve always viewed success from an economic development perspective as having stronger fundamentals. That’s why we talk about water and sewer a lot. That’s why we talk about roads and infrastructure, broadband.  … It’s more important to get infrastructure that everyone can benefit from as opposed to just one or two people.”
Morrisey announced at The Greenbrier that Starwood Digital Ventures plans to bring a data center for Mason County. The company plans to invest $12 billion in the state and fund the infrastructure costs.
“We had very direct conversations with them because we want to make sure that power bills do not go up. Period. … This is not going to get passed on to the ratepayers, consistent with my ratepayer pledge as well, and with the law that’s in place, and also having a closed circuit water loop to minimize the water,” Morrisey said. 
Environmental groups and concerned residents in West Virginia have pushed back on data center developments, particularly in rural Tucker County, due to potential harm to public and environmental health and more. 
Justice also discussed data centers during his remarks, asking the crowd, “Do we really want to be left out?”
“There’s a way to have your cake and eat it too. There’s a way to absolutely preserve and eliminate the scare,” he said. “If you’re going to come to West Virginia and you’re going to do something in West Virginia, you need to be taking care of everybody — the environment, water, … the electricity bills, the noise, you’ve got to take care of everybody, and there’s a way to do it. And I don’t know all the details, but there’s an absolute way to do it.”
Roberts said that he’d like to see a governor with a focus on education. West Virginia continues to see a very low workforce participation rate.
“The role of education is still of paramount importance. As our previous speakers have said, the relationship between teacher and student is so important. Let’s always remind ourselves that success starts and is rooted in education,” Roberts said.
Justice was an ultra-popular two-term governor from 2016 to 2024. Elected as a Democrat, he switched to the Republican Party in 2017 at a rally for President Donald Trump. 
During the 2024 gubernatorial race, Justice did not back Morrisey and instead endorsed Moore Capito. Morrisey, 58, won a four-way primary against Capito, Mac Warner and Chris Miller with 33% of the vote, then easily beat Democratic challenger Steve Williams in the November election for governor. 
Earlier this year, Justice and Morrisey differed in their endorsements of legislators in heated Republican primary races.

title: Montana court filing system part of nationwide ‘data breach’
description: The Montana Supreme Court announced on Wednesday that the court’s backup data files were part of a nationwide breach earlier this year.  Chief Justice Cory Swanson said in a press release that the Montana Office of Court Administrator was alerted by the company Thomson Reuters of unauthorized access to the files in the company’s C-Track […]
text:
The Joseph P. Mazurek Justice Building, home to the Montana Supreme Court and the state Department of Justice. (Jenna Martin for the Daily Montanan)The Montana Supreme Court announced on Wednesday that the court’s backup data files were part of a nationwide breach earlier this year. 
Chief Justice Cory Swanson said in a press release that the Montana Office of Court Administrator was alerted by the company Thomson Reuters of unauthorized access to the files in the company’s C-Track case management system and electronic filing system used by the state’s court system. 
The state’s E-filing system is used by the Supreme Court, District courts, and some other lower courts.
“Because of the data that may have been included in the unauthorized access, many people who have been involved in any case in any Montana court may be affected,” Bowen Greenwood, Clerk of the Montana Supreme Court, told the Daily Montanan in an email..
According to the notice from Thomson Reuters, the breach occurred in March 2026 and ended in June. 
A company notice about C-Track said the unauthorized activity was discovered on June 30, and data had been accessed in March from courts in Kentucky, Alabama, Pennsylvania, Montana, Nevada, North Dakota, South Carolina, Tennessee, New Hampshire, Ohio, Wyoming and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
Court administrator Dave McAlpin was informed of the issue on July 23, and Swanson said the team has been working to resolve the problem since then. 
“Since learning of the data breach, the Montana court team has worked tirelessly to identify whether any Montanan has been harmed by it,” Swanson said in a statement. “We appreciate the rapid support of other state Supreme Courts and the National Center for State Courts. We will continue to work with the TR and C-Track teams to ensure our courts operate without fear of compromise of personal privacy.”
All data was stored entirely on the Thomson Reuters system, and the breach “was not the fault of Montana or any other state court system,” according to the press release. 
A website dedicated to the C-Track data breach indicates the company’s investigation showed that the court records affected could potentially contain individuals’ names and possibly one or more of the following: Social Security number, driver’s license number, medical information, date of birth, and health insurance information. Certain confidential, redacted or sealed information may have been impacted.
“Once we learned the extent of the incident, we coordinated with ThomsonReuters and the other impacted states to issue simultaneous public announcements of this large-scale event,” the press release said. 
In Montana, court administration staff received a copy of state data that had been accessed and is still reviewing the data with the Thomson Reuters security team to determine if private or confidential information was accessed. 
The Office of Court Administration said that most of the accessed data appears to be publicly available information, but some personally identifiable information including driver’s license numbers and dates of birth was also found in the accessed files. 
Montanans who are concerned their personal identifying information may have been included in the security breach should go to www.ctracknotification.com or call 1-833-918-5294 toll free Monday through Friday between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. Central Time (excluding major U.S. holidays). If you have a speech or hearing impairment and use a TTY, please call 711. Be prepared to
provide engagement number B 17184 7.
Thomson Reuters will provide 12 months of free credit monitoring and identity theft protection to anyone affected.

name: Delaware
title: Dover airman case highlights online grooming as Delaware prepares trafficking summit
description: Federal complaint does not charge human trafficking, but advocates say the allegations illustrate grooming tactics and vulnerabilities that can precede exploitation. By George D. Rotsch, Editor of Delaware LIVE DOVER, Del. — Federal charges against a Dover Air Force Base airman accused of using Snapchat to communicate with a 15-year-old girl before transport[...]
text:
Federal complaint does not charge human trafficking, but advocates say the allegations illustrate grooming tactics and vulnerabilities that can precede exploitation.
By George D. Rotsch, Editor of Delaware LIVE
DOVER, Del. — Federal charges against a Dover Air Force Base airman accused of using Snapchat to communicate with a 15-year-old girl before transporting her from Pennsylvania to Delaware are drawing renewed attention to online grooming, child exploitation and the warning signs of human trafficking.
Dylan Williams, 27, is charged with coercion and enticement, transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity, and travel with intent to engage in illicit sexual conduct, according to a federal criminal complaint filed Aug. 28 in U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware.
Investigators allege Williams began communicating with the teenager through Snapchat in June, knew she was 15 and later drove from Delaware to Pennsylvania to pick her up. Authorities found the girl at Williams’ Camden-area residence Aug. 20 after her parents reported her missing, according to the complaint.
The FBI alleges Williams admitted picking up the girl and bringing her to Delaware. Court records also describe alleged sexual encounters in Pennsylvania and Delaware.
Williams is an active-duty airman stationed at Dover Air Force Base, according to the complaint. The Dover Police Department, FBI, Air Force Office of Special Investigations, U.S. Marshals Service and Pennsylvania authorities participated in the investigation.
The charges are accusations. Williams is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.
Grooming can begin online
While the Williams complaint does not allege a commercial exchange, advocates say cases involving online enticement can help parents and the public understand tactics that also appear in trafficking cases.
Those tactics can include gradually gaining a young person’s trust, introducing sexual conversations, encouraging secrecy, isolating the child from family members and convincing the child to leave a safe environment.
Trafficking does not always involve kidnapping, physical restraint or an organized criminal network. Exploiters may present themselves as romantic partners, protectors, employers or friends before using emotional dependency, threats, housing instability, substance use or financial pressure to gain control.
Young people experiencing family conflict, homelessness, prior abuse, social isolation or a lack of stable adult support can be particularly vulnerable. Social media, gaming platforms and messaging applications can give offenders direct and private access to young people.
A child may not recognize the relationship as abusive and may believe he or she willingly participated. Advocates say that makes it important for adults to look beyond whether a young person describes the relationship as consensual.
Delaware cases remain underreported
The full extent of trafficking in Delaware is difficult to measure because victims may fear retaliation, distrust authorities, depend on their trafficker or not recognize that they are being exploited.
The National Human Trafficking Hotline identified 32 trafficking cases involving 61 victims in Delaware during 2024. The organization identified 31 cases in 2023, 28 in 2022, 30 in 2021 and 26 in 2020.
Those figures represent situations reported to and identified by the hotline. They are not a count of arrests or prosecutions and should not be treated as a complete measure of trafficking in Delaware, according to the National Human Trafficking Hotline.
Delaware’s location between Philadelphia, Baltimore and Washington, combined with its major highways, tourism industry and seasonal workforce, creates opportunities for both sex and labor exploitation. However, advocates caution against assuming trafficking is primarily caused by interstate highways or strangers moving victims from place to place.
Many cases originate within families, relationships, workplaces or online communications involving people the victim knows.
Summit aims to improve recognition
The Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors will bring survivors, national experts, law enforcement officials, medical providers, mental health professionals and community leaders together for Delaware’s inaugural Human Trafficking Awareness, Prevention and Action Summit.
The public summit will be held Friday, Oct. 2, at Hyatt Place Dewey Beach. Registration remains open through Sept. 18.
The program is intended to explain what trafficking looks like in Delaware, challenge common misconceptions and help professionals and residents recognize potential exploitation without putting a victim in greater danger.
Sessions will focus on survivor experiences, law enforcement, mental health, direct services and medical care. Topics are expected to include familial trafficking, trauma affecting children and adults, substance use, multidisciplinary response teams and vulnerabilities affecting boys and members of the LGBTQ community.
Kevin McNeil, a retired police officer and survivor of trafficking and sexual abuse, will deliver the opening keynote address. Survivor, therapist, author and comedian Marty MacGibbon will discuss the intersection of trafficking and substance abuse and close the conference with a presentation on mental wellness, self-care and trauma-informed practices.
The summit is open not only to professionals but also to parents, educators, business owners, hospitality employees, faith leaders, volunteers and other residents who want to understand the warning signs.
An invitation-only executive roundtable will be held Thursday, Oct. 1, bringing together Delaware leaders to examine policy, training and service needs.
The Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors was established in 2014 as Meet Me at the Well Delaware. The organization provides individualized support to survivors seeking to leave sex trafficking and rebuild their lives, including mentoring, advocacy and connections to housing, employment and treatment.

Who may attend: Professionals, organizational leaders, service providers and members of the public

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado challenges Trump rule blocking Medicaid funding for gender-affirming care
description: Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser sued the Trump administration Wednesday over its attempt to prohibit states from using federal Medicaid funds for gender-affirming healthcare.  The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts alongside other Democratic-led states, says the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services cannot categorically b[...]
text:
Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser, a Democrat, announced a $1 million settlement with a Colorado property manager for unlawful charges to tenants Tuesday, Jan. 9, 2024 at the Colorado Bar Association office in Denver. (Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser sued the Trump administration Wednesday over its attempt to prohibit states from using federal Medicaid funds for gender-affirming healthcare. 
The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts alongside other Democratic-led states, says the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services cannot categorically ban states from covering medical care it disfavors without congressional authorization. A rule the department proposed in December 2025 would prohibit reimbursement for gender-affirming care for Medicaid recipients under 18 and Children’s Health Insurance Program recipients under 19.
“The Trump administration is once again singling out transgender youth, this time by trying to deny them access to medically necessary care simply because they rely on Medicaid,” Weiser, a Democrat running for governor, said in a statement. “Parents, in consultation with trusted medical providers, know what is best for their children, not federal political appointees in Washington. This rule is unlawful, it interferes with Colorado’s authority to provide healthcare to our residents, and we are challenging it in court.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Congress granted states the authority to determine which healthcare services its public insurance programs cover when it established the programs in the 1960s, the lawsuit says. The Trump administration does not have the statutory authority to override state agency decisions and individual treatment decisions healthcare providers make. 
Weiser’s office said more than 90% of the 30,000 public comments on the proposed rule opposed it. Last year, Weiser and a group of other attorneys general opposed an executive order from President Donald Trump that threatened federal funding of any hospital or healthcare facility that offered gender-affirming care to patients 19 or younger.
Federal courts have repeatedly blocked the Trump administration’s efforts to restrict access to gender-affirming care for transgender youth, including the 2025 executive order, a subsequent declaration from Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and another rule to restrict Affordable Care Act coverage for gender-affirming care.
A measure on the Colorado ballot in November would ban healthcare professionals from performing gender-affirming surgeries on minors. The measure would also prohibit state and federal funding, including Medicaid, from being used to pay for gender-affirming procedures.
The two major hospitals that provide gender-affirming care to minors in Colorado do not offer surgeries to minors, and gender-affirming surgeries on minors are rare. Several families of transgender children sued Children’s Hospital Colorado for its cessation of gender-affirming care for minors.
