title: Trump's newest order on birthright citizenship blocked in federal court
text: A federal judge in Maryland Wednesday blocked President Donald Trump’s second attempt to redefine birthright citizenship. In a preliminary injunction, U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman barred the Trump administration from carrying out the president's executive order that would deny citizenship to babies born in the United States to parents deemed part of a designated terrorist organization or to parents who purposefully came to the U.S. to gain citizenship in what critics call “birth tourism.” The executive order also aimed to deny citizenship to children born to foreign diplomatic staff and children born in U.S. territories where Congress has not passed a law granting citizenship, which is only American Samoa.In her order, Boardman said this summer's Supreme Court ruling affirmed the country’s long understanding that babies born on U.S. soil were guaranteed American citizenship. “The 2026 Executive Order is almost certainly unconstitutional as applied to the certified class for the simple reason that the Supreme Court in Barbara already decided that the children in the class are citizens at birth,” she wrote, referring to the earlier case. “This Court must, once again, preliminarily enjoin enforcement of the President’s most recent attempt to strip the right to citizenship from them.”The White House did not immediately respond to States Newsroom's request for comment.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: FEMA to reimburse eight South Dakota counties, three tribes for storm-related infrastructure fixes
description: The federal government will reimburse up to 75% of public infrastructure repair costs from storms that hit eight South Dakota counties and two Native American reservations in late June and early July, the Federal Emergency Management Agency announced Wednesday. The Oglala Sioux Tribe, meanwhile, is in line for the same level of reimbursements for repairs […]
text:
Matilyn Kerr, left, and sister Brittany Kerr watch as a skid-steer loader pulls a tree from Brittany Kerr's yard in Highmore, South Dakota, on June 29, 2026, after a severe storm that morning. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)The federal government will reimburse up to 75% of public infrastructure repair costs from storms that hit eight South Dakota counties and two Native American reservations in late June and early July, the Federal Emergency Management Agency announced Wednesday.
The Oglala Sioux Tribe, meanwhile, is in line for the same level of reimbursements for repairs to public infrastructure caused by storms in early June, and individual tribal members will be eligible for financial aid to cover some property losses from that incident.
Gov. Larry Rhoden requested a presidential disaster declaration from the Trump administration in late July, in a letter laying out $4.5 million in public property damage from a storm system that moved through the state between June 28 and July 3. 
Governor of South Dakota seeks federal help for damages from summer storms

Rhoden said, first in a Tuesday evening social media post and again in a press release on Wednesday, that President Donald Trump called him directly to tell him about approving the state’s request for a disaster declaration. 
On X, Rhoden shared a post from Trump in which the president wrote “South Dakota is a special place, which I won by Historic margins, three times, and I will always deliver BIG for them.”
The disaster declaration for the state as a whole will reimburse public property repair costs in Beadle, Bennett, Buffalo, Day, Hand, Hughes, Hyde and Stanley Counties, along with the Crow Creek and Lower Brule reservations. Roads, power systems, parks, recreation areas and public facilities were damaged in the storm, with the heaviest impacts in Hyde and Beadle counties.
Lower Brule Sioux Tribe President Boyd Gorneau told South Dakota Searchlight on Wednesday that the tribe lost some center-pivot irrigation systems on its agricultural land in the storm. 
FEMA sent a press release on disaster declarations for South Dakota on Wednesday, but the release did not include dollar figures. 
A FEMA spokesperson told Searchlight the reimbursement isn’t limited to the $4.5 million in damage cited in Rhoden’s request to President Trump, whose post said he’d “approved” $3.4 million — a figure that would cover 75% of the cost to repair that damage.
The actual amount paid in reimbursement will be based on the cost to repair infrastructure, the spokesman said, provided local governments and state officials adhere to FEMA guidelines and protocols.
The same will be true for the Oglala Sioux Tribe’s public infrastructure. The tribe, which requested a disaster declaration separately, was hit with flash flooding June 2-4 after a heavy rain and hail storm.
During the first round of storms, according to the National Weather Service, “6 to 7 inches of rain fell in a short period, causing streets and ditches to fill extremely quickly,” in addition to strong winds and hail. A tornado touched down near Ideal in Tripp County the following day, damaging mostly agricultural land.
The individual assistance program, part of the FEMA announcement for the tribe, will allow residents to work with FEMA to obtain “grants for temporary housing and home repairs, low-cost loans to cover uninsured property losses and other programs to help individuals and families recover from the effects of the disaster,” the spokesperson wrote in an email.
A separate press release from FEMA on the tribal disaster declaration said that tribal members who experienced losses in the storms “should document their damage, keep any receipts for repairs, and file a claim with their insurance provider.”
“Information on how individuals may apply for federal disaster assistance will be announced when it is available,” the press release said.
The FEMA spokesperson said the tribe has not requested a disaster declaration for a more recent hailstorm, which dropped baseball-sized hail on some areas of tribal land, damaging school buses and homes and forcing a delayed start to the school year.
The tribe’s public information officer did not immediately return calls and emails seeking comment on Wednesday.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Yellowstone’s ‘thumping’ hot springs
description: Yellowstone National Park is rightly famous for spectacular geysers. It also has hot springs that create thumps you can hear and feel. Black Sand Pool, in Yellowstone National Park’s Upper Geyser Basin (near Old Faithful), is a hidden gem.  Although it is not far from a road and is very accessible via an easy trail, few […]
text:
Black Sand Pool, in Yellowstone National Park's Upper Geyser Basin. The hot spring is known for it's thumping behavior, which occurs every few minutes due to collapse of bubbles within the spring.  The thumping is strong enough to be heard and felt by anyone nearby. (USGS photo by Mike Poland)Yellowstone National Park is rightly famous for spectacular geysers. It also has hot springs that create thumps you can hear and feel.
Black Sand Pool, in Yellowstone National Park’s Upper Geyser Basin (near Old Faithful), is a hidden gem.  Although it is not far from a road and is very accessible via an easy trail, few people visit the hot spring.  Those that make the short walk and stay a few minutes are rewarded with a special treat—every several minutes the pool starts to thump, and it is strong enough to feel and hear. It’s as if a giant in an underground cavern is striking the cavern’s ceiling with a hammer.
Another famous “thumper” is Doublet Pool on Geyser Hill, also in Upper Geyser Basin.  The thumping at Doublet Pool varies over time, lasting up to a few minutes with intervening quiet times that have varied between 13 and 35 minutes in recent years.  The thumping is so strong that you can see the water in the spring “jump.”
Doublet Pool, fringed by geyserite, in the Upper Geyser Basin of Yellowstone National Park. (National Park Service photograph by Jacob Frank)
One of best places in Yellowstone National Park to see this process in action is Firehole Spring, which is along Firehole Lake Drive in Lower Geyser Basin.  This small one-way side road off the main highway is often closed due to bear management and also poor road conditions (the road lies on very hot ground and so the asphalt tends to melt), but when it is open, Firehole Spring is along the north side of the road just before Great Fountain Geyser.  The spring’s water is very clear, providing a view of bubbles that rise from the vent at the bottom of the pool.  The bubbles often collapse as they rise, creating an audible “thump” as they implode.
Many other hot springs in Yellowstone also thump—for example, pools in Norris Geyser Basin.  But what causes this activity?
The collapse of the bubbles is due to the variable temperature and pressure conditions within the hot springs. As bubbles rise within a thermal pool, their volumes increase and internal pressures decrease.  At the same time, the cooler temperatures near the tops of the pools cause the steam in the bubbles to condense back into liquid water, and this, combined with the decreasing internal pressure, causes the bubbles to implode. If the bubbles are large enough, the thump can be felt.  The components for thumping are not that common, which explains why only a few hot springs in Yellowstone demonstrate that behavior.
Scientists investigated the thumping at Doublet Pool by deploying seismometers around the area to record how the thumping changes with time. They found a number of interesting correlations.  For example, when strong winds blew, the time between thumping was longer than on calm days. This is because the wind cooled the pool by removing heat from the surface.  There were also changes that corresponded to activity at nearby features.  In September 2018, Ear Spring, a short distance from Double Pool, erupted for the first time in decades. At that time, the interval between thumping periods at Doublet Pool was only about 13 minutes—a very short time period that may have been due to an overall increase in thermal input to Geyser Hill.
Firehole Spring, located along Firehole Lake Drive in Yellowstone National Park’s Lower Geyser Basin. The spring is characterized by a thumping behavior that is caused by the implosion of bubbles rising from the base of the pool due to changing temperature and pressure conditions within the pool. The bubbles can be seen in this picture as the whitish mass in the center of the pool. (USGS photo by Mike Poland)
That the rate of thumping seems to change due to heat input indicates that monitoring the thumping interval could be a useful way to track hydrothermal activity in a region. For instance, if interval between thumping at Doublet Pool suddenly starts to decrease, it might be a sign of deeper variations in heat input that could impact other thermal features in the region, perhaps even leading to the formation of new thermal features as occurred in 2023.
If you have a chance to visit Yellowstone National Park, be sure to check out one of the thumping springs—Doublet Pool, Black Sand Pool, and Firehole Spring are easily accessible. You can literally hear and feel the changes that are happening in one of the most spectacular hydrothermal systems on Earth.
Yellowstone Caldera Chronicles is a weekly column written by scientists and collaborators of the Yellowstone Volcano Observatory. This week’s contribution is from Michael Poland, geophysicist with the U.S. Geological Survey and Scientist-in-Charge of the Yellowstone Volcano Observatory.

name: WyoFile
title: Pitching 940-acre data center, Prometheus Hyperscale asks Natrona County to bypass state review
description:
Data center developers pitch local control to a packed room during discussion with county commissioners regarding proposed $500 million campus near Casper. 
The post Pitching 940-acre data center, Prometheus Hyperscale asks Natrona County to bypass state review appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
CASPER—Natrona County commissioners took no action Tuesday after developers of the proposed Prometheus Hyperscale data center asked them to consider an industrial park zoning designation, which would speed up build time by exempting the $500 million project from state industrial siting review.
At the Natrona County Courthouse, Prometheus founder Trenton Thornock and Build Wyoming Director Eric Schlidt presented the request during the workshop portion of the board’s meeting — during which no decisions are made — in front of a packed house of supporting and skeptical residents alike. Per the presentation, Prometheus intends to apply for a planned unit development to zone 940 acres south of Interstate 25 on the Falls Ranch property situated between Casper and Glenrock.
Eric Schlidt with Prometheus Hyperscale’s Build Wyoming, left, and Prometheus founder Trenton Thornock sit among the Natrona County Board of Commissioners audience just prior to their workshop discussion about plans to build a 1.5-gigawatt data center campus to the southeast of Casper. (Greg Hirst/Oil City News)
Thornock told commissioners that an industrial park designation allows developers to seek an exemption from the Wyoming Industrial Siting Council while keeping county-level oversight. He described industrial siting processes as “cumbersome and time-consuming,” adding the exemption would not remove “any applicable environmental or regulatory requirements.”
State agencies like the Department of Environmental Quality and the Wyoming Department of Transportation would still regulate air, water and roads, Thornock said, adding that the DEQ’s Industrial Siting Division has three employees and the seven-person siting council meets quarterly, which slows project reviews.
“Local control in my opinion is much better than state siting oversight,” he said. “You, the county commissioners and local officials, know your community and their needs better than a state siting council.”
Thornock added that county-level permitting allows local officials to negotiate directly with developers for road maintenance and infrastructure funding rather than waiting on state formulas from Cheyenne.
Project background and design
Prometheus announced plans in late 2025 to build a 1.5-gigawatt data center campus on Falls Ranch property — owned by Texas billionaire Russell Gordy — north of Interstate 25. Plans at the time would have placed the data center portion in Converse County and the power generators in Natrona County. 
County officials said after pushback from neighbors regarding noise, heat and traffic, developers shifted the site to other Falls Ranch property south of the interstate, bringing the $500 million campus entirely within Natrona County. 
Converse County commissioners previously adopted a policy to streamline industrial park designations for the project in April, but rescinded it a month later after the Wyoming attorney general found the county lacked the statutory authority to create independent exemption procedures outside standard zoning rules. 
Thornock previously said the proposed data center relies on a closed-loop cooling design using a blend of water and food-grade propylene glycol. The blend is used for five to six years before being hauled off by a supplier for recycling, requiring no ongoing water draw or wastewater discharge for cooling.
On Friday, Prometheus announced a partnership with Evansville-based Mesa Power Solutions to supply natural gas generators. Previously, the company had said it would deploy Jenbacher generators to power the first phases of development. Either arrangement would allow the center to produce its own power on-site without drawing electricity from the public utility grid. 
Friday’s announcement added to the announced partnerships with Spiritus, which says it develops carbon-negative power infrastructure, and Casper Carbon Capture, which agreed to provide land and access to permitted underground carbon storage wells. 
Schlidt estimated the data center portion of the project would support roughly 3,000 temporary construction jobs at peak build-out and 150 permanent positions, and generate between $80 million and $115 million in recurring annual property taxes.
It seems that the county loses a part of its leverage in those negotiations if things have been fully permitted.Commissioner Peter Nicolaysen
Thornock said the campus footprint requires 300 acres for on-site power generation and 640 acres for data center halls west of Big Muddy Creek. He told the board that prospective tenants need a clear path toward local permits, warning that delays could push the company to move resources to alternative project sites in Texas. 
During the meeting, there were no other details provided regarding a site plan, project timeline or potential customers.
Uinta County advances project
Prometheus pointed to its work in southwest Wyoming as a model for how it plans to work with Natrona County.  
In June, the Uinta County Board of County Commissioners approved a zone change from agricultural to industrial use for the Atlas Industrial Park Subdivision. That decision cleared the way for Prometheus to plan a 640-acre campus on Thornock’s family ranch outside Evanston.
Thornock told commissioners that Uinta County placed rules directly onto the company’s conditional use permits. The county handled the project through two separate permits, dividing rules between power generation and the data halls.  
“These are the kind of good-neighbor things that have very specific conditions around how we have to operate our facility both during the construction phase and later on,” Thornock said. 
Before making decisions on those permits, Uinta County planning staff traveled to the Nova data center in Jordan, Utah, Thornock said. The visit allowed staff to see closed-loop liquid cooling systems in person. 
He offered to arrange a similar tour for Natrona County officials.  
Thornock said the company also met with Evanston and Uinta County fire agencies to establish safety rules for on-site backup batteries.  
Natrona County commissioners listen to a presentation by Prometheus Hyperscale founder Trenton Thornock and Build Wyoming Director Eric Schlidt on Tuesday during their workshop meeting at the Natrona County Courthouse. (Greg Hirst/Oil City News)
Natrona County commissioners question developers
Commissioner Peter Nicolaysen questioned the timing of potential community agreements. Thornock said Prometheus prefers negotiating community benefit agreements after county permits are finalized. The company faced accusations of bribery in Uinta County when talks ran during the permitting process, he said.
“It seems that the county loses a part of its leverage in those negotiations if things have been fully permitted,” Nicolaysen said, “and so I would prefer that those things work in tandem, go through the permitting process, but also be moving forward and making progress on the community benefit agreement.”
Nicolaysen also pressed the developers on road access, utility impacts and cooling fluids. Thornock said primary access for construction and operations would come from a newly constructed Interstate 25 interchange, with Hat Six Road reserved as a secondary emergency route.
Commissioner Dallas Laird asked audience members to raise their hands to show whether they supported or opposed the development, then addressed the developers.
“Opinions are different than facts,” Laird said. “And agreements, in my opinion, if they aren’t in writing, they don’t mean anything. So, we’re going to take a really hard look at this.”
Natrona County Board of Commissioner meeting attendees who are against the proposed Prometheus Hyperscale data center project near Casper raise their hands Tuesday at the request of Commissioner Dallas Laird. (Greg Hirst/Oil City News)
Public comment split over landscape, local control
The commissioners took more than an hour of public comment from the dozens of residents packing the courtroom.
Katherine Dvorak of Casper questioned how initial water use would affect area wells and raised concerns about heat output from generators during hot summers. Sherry Johnson, a lifelong Casper resident, urged commissioners and audience members to drive out to Hat Six Road before supporting rezoning efforts.
”Please go take a look at that land because you people need to understand once you allow that behemoth, our landscape will never look the same,” she said. “We’re talking what, 150 jobs? It’s not worth our landscape. We can’t get it back. Once it’s gone, it’s gone.”
Erika Cook said she lives downstream and downwind from the site. The natural gas power plant was her primary concern.
“Gas generators on this scale would turn our rural prairie into a polluted industrial nightmare,” she said. “We would hear and feel the noise from this power facility 24–7, 365 days a year in our home. This is not what we bargained for when we invested our life savings in our peaceful family home.”
Casper resident Sherry Johnson speaks to the crowd about her concerns regarding the proposed Prometheus Hyperscale data center during the public comment portion of the Natrona County Board of Commissioners meeting on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026, at the Natrona County Courthouse. (Greg Hirst/Oil City News)
Brad Isner, a neighbor of the project’s initial site, said company officials have not provided answers to questions about construction camps, traffic and emergency services.
Meanwhile, supporters urged the board to keep project reviews under local control rather than handing oversight to state boards in Cheyenne.
“What we need to ask is if we have the potential as a community to welcome business development, handle it locally, or do we want to let Cheyenne determine our fate and the impacts and be in charge of the money that comes back to this community?” Casper resident Tassma Powers said. “Because that’s what industrial siting does.”
Keegan Fox of Casper told commissioners that public officials should base decisions on verified facts rather than fear or unverified promises.
“A responsible ‘yes’ doesn’t ignore legitimate concerns and it doesn’t allow speculation to become a substitute for evidence,” he said. 
Colton Dillion, who lives off Hat Six Road, said the development would sit near his home, but he welcomed the opportunity to attract advanced technology jobs to Wyoming.
“Data centers are very efficient businesses in terms of space, in terms of noise, in terms of negative externalities of pollution,” he said. “I would really invite you to think about what is the alternative and what are these other opportunities that we could give to our children.”
The first thing that has to happen is if we pass an industrial zoning matter so that it can be handled by us.Commissioner Dallas Laird
Fred Fichtner, chief operations officer for Mesa Power Solutions, said large infrastructure projects help local suppliers and trade workers compete for work, while geologist JoAnn True said that Natrona County has experience with big projects as it manages oil fields, pipelines and refineries. She urged commissioners to vet the project while creating jobs that give younger residents reasons to stay in the state. 
Commissioners balance property rights, community impacts
In their closing comments, Nicolaysen and Chair Jim Milne said the board must balance community concerns with the rights of private landowners. Laird framed the current technology infrastructure race as an issue of national defense. He said that domestic computing facilities keep American technology out of foreign hands.
“[President Donald] Trump has said it too,” the commissioner said. “He says we have a war going on with China and Russia over who’s going to take over with this AI business. And that’s what this data center is all about. … Do you want China running your AI or Russia running your AI or do you want Natrona County commissioners and the state of Wyoming and America running AI?”
Commissioner Casey Coates, who in June said he had no interest in industrial parks, cautioned against reacting with panic instead of focusing on tangible facts. 
“When we ask for the protection of the government, we really ought to be careful because government at times can be overreaching and those protections that we ask for can be overly applied to ourselves,” Coates said. “Do we not like something because of what it is, or do we have real impacts? If we have real impacts, let’s address those.”
Commissioner Dave North said that state environmental regulators handle water rights and industrial pollution under state statutes.
“The state engineer is the one that takes care of the water,” he said. “That is not our responsibility. That’s not our job. That is up to the state. The DEQ takes care of a lot of stuff. That’s their job. That is not our job.”
Potential county timeline
Commissioners told residents that any formal vote on the Prometheus project remains months away.
Laird said the county can’t set a firm schedule because the developer hasn’t submitted an application. Once filed, any proposal must go through multiple public steps before the commission can act.
“The first thing that has to happen is if we pass an industrial zoning matter so that it can be handled by us,” he said. “This has to go through our zoning board first and they have to decide whether it’s something we should be doing, and then we have to have another meeting where you all come down and we hear from people again, and then we make a vote.”
Laird added that even if the board approves a zone change, Prometheus would still have to apply for separate conditional use permits and meet state rules.
“This isn’t something you’re even going to see a building for for a couple years, I wouldn’t think,” Laird said.
North said the county will demand answers before taking any action.
“That’s a totally different process that takes a lot of time, and there’s a lot of hard questions that we’ve been asking and we will continue asking,” North said. “And before it comes before the commission, those questions are going to have to be answered. That’s the way that works.”

title: Coal increased its share of Iowa electricity generation in 2025, report shows
description: Iowa Environmental Council’s annual “condition of the state” report on Iowa’s electric generation shows that while wind continues to dominate Iowa’s electricity generation sources, there has been a “reversal” in the state’s progress to meet energy demand with renewable sources.  For the first time in several years, according to the report, the share of energ[...]
text:
Wind energy continues to dominate Iowa's electricity generation. Pictured are wind turbines near U.S. 80. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Iowa Environmental Council’s annual “condition of the state” report on Iowa’s electric generation shows that while wind continues to dominate Iowa’s electricity generation sources, there has been a “reversal” in the state’s progress to meet energy demand with renewable sources. 
For the first time in several years, according to the report, the share of energy generated by coal increased in 2025. 
The environmental council holds that for other sectors to reach climate goals of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, the electricity sector needs to be “carbon-free” by 2035. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While the report says this goal is “achievable and necessary” a statement from MidAmerican Energy Company, one of Iowa’s top utilities and a subject of the report, said the request “oversimplifies an extraordinarily complex challenge.”
“It ignores the costs, reliability considerations, and operational realities that utilities must manage on behalf of customers every day,” the company said in a statement. 
The utility also said the report lacks “any meaningful acknowledgment” that utilities are responsible for “keeping the lights on,” maintaining affordability and reliability – not just emissions reductions. 
“Iowa’s energy future has never been a choice between reliability and environmental progress,” MidAmerican said. “The real challenge is achieving both in a way that customers can afford and the electric system can support.” 
More coal in 2025
According to the report, the share of electricity generated from coal in 2025 was 3% more than the share in 2024. 
Steve Guyer, Iowa Environmental Council’s senior energy policy counsel and an author on the report, said in a webinar Wednesday the change is “troubling.”
When comparing the council’s latest report with figures from its 2025 report, both Alliant Energy Corporation and MidAmerican, Iowa’s largest utilities, had a greater share of generation from coal in 2025 than they did in 2024. The IEC reports look at figures from the year prior to when the report is released.
In 2024, 21% of MidAmerican’s generation mix came from coal and 64% came from wind energy. In 2025, 27% of the mix was coal and 59% was wind energy generation. Alliant’s energy generation mix, according to the report which pulled figures from Federal Energy Regulatory Commission filings, included 12% coal and 50% natural gas in 2024. In 2025, 20% of the company’s resource mix came from coal, and 42% came from natural gas. Wind decreased from 37% to 32% from 2024 to 2025 in Alliant’s resource mix, however solar increased from 1% in 2024 to 6% in 2025. 
A graph from Iowa Environmental Council’s 2026 report shows an uptick in coal generation in Iowa. (Graphic courtesy of Iowa Environmental Council)
While MidAmerican and Alliant represent the majority ownership of utility coal generation in the state, the report notes that smaller interests, like power cooperatives and municipal utilities, play a role “in keeping coal generation online cannot be discounted.” 
The report said that despite the recent reversal toward coal, the overall trend in Iowa over the past 26 years shows that “wind and solar power is affordable and reliable, and we should be transitioning away from coal” ahead of 2040 and 2049, which are the goals set by Alliant Energy and MidAmerican, respectively, to end coal generation. 
“Although wind and solar continue to meet more of the energy demand, there has not been a corresponding reduction in fossil plant operation,” the report said. 
A spokesperson for Alliant said the company remains “focused on our commitment to balancing reliability, affordability and sustainability for customers, while making progress toward our goal of net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.” 
An array of solar panels in Dubuque, Iowa. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
MidAmerican said it has done “exactly what advocates of a renewable energy future have asked utilities to do” over the past 20 years by investing “billions” in wind generation, “dramatically” reducing reliance on fossil fuels and cutting emissions by “significant amounts.” 
“Since 2004, we have added 7,631 megawatts of wind generation and 141 megawatts of solar generation,” the statement said. “We also have approval to add 800 megawatts of solar, the largest solar approval in Iowa history.” 
These accomplishments, MidAmerican said, have also resulted in reductions in emissions, and below-average electricity costs for customers, “even as total generation has increased.”
Impact on public health and finances 
According to the report, greenhouse gas emissions from power plants has continued to decline over the past 20 years. In 2024, emissions from power plants accounted for 16% of Iowa’s overall greenhouse gas emissions. Agriculture and residential/commercial/industrial uses continue to account for the greatest share of greenhouse gas emissions, at 29% and 28% respectively. 
The report notes, however, that certain sectors, such as the residential, commercial and industrial sector and the transportation sector, cannot achieve net zero emissions without a “carbon-free electricity sector” to power their operations. 
Despite power plant emissions making up a smaller chunk of overall emissions, the report holds that electricity generation from coal plants accounts for the greatest share of air pollution. The report cites an Iowa Department of Natural Resources report which tags electricity generation as the point source industry with the greatest contributions to various air pollutants. 
The environmental council’s report emphasizes the industry’s connection to particulate matter 2.5 pollution, PM2.5, or “fine inhalable particles” that have a diameter about 30 times smaller than that of a single human hair, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
These fine particles can contribute to asthma, premature death in people with heart or lung conditions, heart attacks and decreased lung function. The report noted some research that links PM2.5 and other air pollutants as contributing factors to certain types of cancers. 
“While many factors may contribute to cancer risk, we have to keep in mind that exposures to air pollution are increasingly being recognized as important contributors,” Guyer said. 
The link between coal plants and PM2.5 pollution was also part of a recent Iowa Environmental Council report examining the Sioux City community. However, a spokesperson with MidAmerican said the report’s conclusions that a nearby coal plant was contributing to the region’s air quality conditions were “based primarily on correlations.” 
The environmental council’s 2026 electric generation report also said the air pollutants and greenhouse gas emissions from coal plants pose a financial risk in the state through increased healthcare costs, impacts to agriculture and overall contribution to climate change, which is costing Iowans more in home insurance premiums. 
“Climate change, this is happening,” Guyer said. “We can’t ignore it. We can’t pretend it doesn’t exist. More and more evidence is pointing to the need to actually do something.” 
The report holds that Iowa’s utilities are “uniquely positioned” to achieve a generation mix of 100% renewable energy by 2035, if they “aggressively act” to take advantage of tax incentives for renewable energy projects. 
And, it says, utilities need to “aggressively” add solar, wind and energy storage options to meet projected 31% to 93% load growths in the next 20 years. 
“The best way to meet projected increased customer demand is the addition of solar, storage, and wind,” the report said. “The pursuit of 100% renewable energy starts with an honest accounting of the costs of coal, an acknowledgement that we can transition to 100% renewable energy, the complete elimination of coal generation by 2030, and the addition of more solar, storage and wind.” 
MidAmerican said it plans to add new solar generation in the next three years, and to “continue investing in renewable energy resources where they make sense for customers and the system.” 
“We will continue investing in Iowa’s energy future, but we will do so responsibly, balancing environmental goals with our obligation to keep electricity reliable and affordable for the customers who depend on us every day,” the statement said.

name: VTDigger
title: ‘Everyone’s friend’: Family describes slain Derby woman as her killer gets 30 years in prison
description:
The man guilty of murder apologized to the victim’s family, telling them,“I know I could have walked away. I should have walked away.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘Everyone’s friend’: Family describes slain Derby woman as her killer gets 30 years in prison.
text:
Jakiy Keith appears during his sentencing hearing in Orleans Superior criminal court in Newport on Wednesday, September 2, 2026. Keith pleaded guilty in the 2024 shooting death of Kayla Wright. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
A former Connecticut man has been sentenced to 30 years to life in prison on a murder charge for fatally shooting a Derby woman inside a Northeast Kingdom home where he helped run an illegal drug operation.
Judge Rory Thibault handed down the sentence to 26-year-old Jakiy Tramaine Corey Keith on Wednesday in Orleans Superior criminal court in Newport after a hearing that stretched over two days. 
Keith had earlier pleaded guilty to second-degree murder for shooting and killing 29-year-old Kayla Wright of Derby inside a home in Troy. He also pleaded guilty to a charge of unauthorized removal of a body as part of a plea deal with state prosecutors. 
Thibault spoke for a little more than 45 minutes about the circumstances surrounding the case before imposing the sentence, calling the killing a crime of domestic violence.
“What is particularly aggravating is that the Troy drug house was effectively back open for business as soon as the remains of Ms. Wright were disposed and the kitchen cleaned up,” Thibault said. 
“The defendant continued to use the residence as a base of operation to continue his drug activity uninterrupted and unabated,” the judge added. 
Police said Keith shot Wright several times early in the morning on Feb. 2, 2024. 
According to court records, Keith and Wright were arguing in the moments leading up to the shooting, and Keith feared that Wright was going to tell authorities about the drug operation.
Wright and several other people traveled to and stayed at the home over time for illegal drug activities, with dozens of people coming and going daily, according to court records and testimony during the sentencing hearing. Several people have also been arrested on other charges as part of the investigation.

Captain Karl Gardner of the Vermont State Police testifies during a sentencing hearing for Jakiy Keith in Orleans Superior criminal court in Newport on Wednesday, September 2, 2026. Keith pleaded guilty in the 2024 shooting death of Kayla Wright. A police interview of Keith is seen behind Gardner. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Vermont State Police Capt. Karl Gardner testified Wednesday that authorities were conducting an investigation into illegal drug activities at the Troy residence in the weeks leading up to Wright’s fatal shooting. 
Gardner also testified that police had obtained an “active” search warrant for the residence as part of that investigation but had not yet carried out the search before Wright’s death.
Wright’s body was found days after the shooting inside a large toolbox container in the Missisquoi River in Troy, court records stated. 
Keith had initially been charged with first-degree murder, a charge that was reduced as part of the plea agreement. That agreement allowed Keith’s attorney, David Sleigh, and Orleans County State’s Attorney Farzana Leyva to argue for any sentence allowed by law. 
A charge of second-degree murder carries a sentence of 20 years to life in prison. 
Leyva asked the judge Wednesday to sentence Keith to 50 years to life in prison. The prosecutor said Keith had exploited people, including Wright, who were addicted to illegal drugs for his own benefit. 
“Kayla was trying to break the very dependency that gave the defendant power over her,” Leyva said. 
“After the killing, there was time to summon help, contact law enforcement, and tell Kayla’s family the truth,” Leyva wrote in a sentencing document filed ahead of the hearing. “Instead, Kayla’s body was placed inside a toolbox while her blood was cleaned from the residence and evidence was destroyed.”
Sleigh, Keith’s attorney, had asked the judge to impose a sentence of 20 years to life. 
He told the judge there was no guarantee that Keith would be released on parole after serving his minimum prison term. Sleigh said Keith would need to earn his parole through his actions while incarcerated.
Sleigh, in his sentencing document, wrote that his client suffered from a troubled and volatile upbringing in Hartford, Connecticut, and became involved with the drug trade fueled by the allure of the money he was making from it.
“Jakiy now sees his younger self as a different person,” the defense attorney added. “Jakiy has reoccurring dreams in which he is talking to his younger self with the wisdom he has now. In those dreams, Jakiy tells himself to find another path.”
Three of Wright’s family members also provided victim impact statements before Thibault imposed the sentence. 
They called Wright a kind, honest and compassionate person with a love for animals. They added that although she was small in stature she had a big personality, telling the judge that she was “everyone’s friend.” 

Byron Wright, father of murder victim Kayla Wright, weeps as he listens to testimony during a sentencing hearing for Jakiy Keith in Orleans Superior criminal court in Newport on Wednesday, September 2, 2026. Keith pleaded guilty in the 2024 shooting death of Kayla Wright. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Samantha Perkins, Wright’s twin sister, had strong words for Keith, repeatedly calling him a “loser.” 
“Lock him up and destroy the keys,” Perkins said in asking the judge to impose the harshest sentence possible.
Perkins said that at the time of her sister’s death, Wright was working to address her addiction to drugs and had been admitted to a long-term treatment program in California. Wright, said Perkins, had a plane ticket but was killed before that trip was set to take place.
“Kayla’s opportunity to get clean was taken,” Perkins added.
Keith then addressed the judge. He told Wright’s family members he was sorry and accepted responsibility. 
“I know I could have walked away. I should have walked away,” Keith said, adding of Wright, “She is not here because of me. I am truly sorry.”
The plea deal in the case allowed a separate sentence in a federal case against Keith to run at the same time as his sentence on the state charges.
Keith was sentenced in June to a little more than 13 years in prison after pleading guilty to federal charges of conspiracy to distribute cocaine and fentanyl as well as a separate count of carrying and using a firearm in a drug-related crime. 
Among the witnesses testifying during the sentencing hearing Wednesday in the murder case was Terron Pendleton, who said he saw the fatal shooting. He said Keith shot Wright three times in the home’s kitchen and that Keith then ordered him to help clean up the scene and put her body in the toolbox.
Later that day, Pendleton said, Keith addressed other people in the house about the shooting. “He said he had an ‘Oh, shit’ moment,” Pendleton recalled.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri GOP calls for Joplin legislative candidate to withdraw after arrest
description: Thomas Ross, the Republican nominee for Missouri’s 161st House District, is being held without bond in the Joplin City Jail after being arrested Wednesday on an “unspecified warrant,” according to the city’s public safety portal. Missouri Republican Party Chairman Peter Kinder called on Ross to “immediately withdraw his candidacy” in a social media statement[...]
text:
The Missouri Capitol in Jefferson City on May 12. (Jason Hancock/Missouri Independent).Thomas Ross, the Republican nominee for Missouri’s 161st House District, is being held without bond in the Joplin City Jail after being arrested Wednesday on an “unspecified warrant,” according to the city’s public safety portal.
Missouri Republican Party Chairman Peter Kinder called on Ross to “immediately withdraw his candidacy” in a social media statement Wednesday. Kinder cited the “serious and deeply troubling” circumstances of his arrest and said the people of the district, which covers most of Joplin, “deserve a nominee who can devote his full attention to earning their trust and representing their interests.”
The Jasper County Republican Central Committee joined Kinder in calling for Ross’ withdrawal, indicating in a social media statement that “the circumstances are serious and raise significant concerns” for voters.
Under state law, Ross has until Sept. 8 — the eighth Tuesday before the election — to withdraw. The law says a court order necessary to remove a candidate’s name from the ballot “shall be freely given upon application by the candidate.”
Staff with the Joplin Police Department and the City of Joplin said they were unable to share additional information about the charges Ross faces.
Candice Jamoles, a public affairs specialist for U.S. Attorney R. Matthew Price of the Western District of Missouri, told The Independent Wednesday morning that while she knew of the arrest, she could neither confirm nor deny the existence of a federal investigation. 
Jasper County Prosecuting Attorney Theresa Kenney is out of the office this week, according to a staff member reached by The Independent Wednesday afternoon.
Ross defeated his opponent in the Aug. 4 Republican primary, Louise Secker, by only 32 votes. He had unsuccessfully challenged Republican state Rep. Lane Roberts for the seat in 2022 and 2024.
Roberts, who is term-limited, endorsed Secker as his successor, describing her in a July 9 social media post as “an honorable person who tells the whole truth, not half the truth, or a version of the truth.” 
Secker also substantially outraised Ross. Campaign finance filings show she had received $96,974 in contributions as of July 27, while Ross’ committee reported $34,784 in receipts. Ross had loaned his campaign $14,000.
Neither Secker nor Roberts responded to requests for comment from The Independent.
Democratic nominee Aaron Metzger told The Independent his “thoughts are with (Ross’) family during this devastating time.”
“This doesn’t change my belief that the people of Joplin deserve real representation, and I will continue my campaign delivering that message,” Metzger said.
Ben Peters, director of communications for the Missouri House, told The Independent in an emailed statement that “it would be inappropriate to comment on any pending legal matter involving a candidate for office.”
“The House trusts the legal process,” Peters wrote, “and will continue to monitor the situation while law enforcement and the courts handle the matter accordingly.”
Ross is not the first Republican legislative candidate in recent years to face calls to withdraw amid serious allegations. 
In 2020, Rick Roeber of Lee’s Summit refused bipartisan calls to end his campaign after his adult children accused him of physical and sexual abuse. The allegations became public weeks before the November election, and Roeber denied them and went on to win by about 300 votes. 
After he took office, a House Ethics Committee investigation found the allegations credible and recommended his expulsion. The House voted 153-0 in April 2021 to remove him from office.
Another southwest Missouri Republican, Tricia Derges of Nixa, resisted calls to resign after she was indicted on 20 federal felony counts in February 2021, shortly after taking office. House Republican leaders stripped Derges of her committee assignments, expelled her from the GOP caucus and called on her to step down, but she remained in office while the case proceeded. 
She resigned in July 2022 after a federal jury convicted her of 22 counts, including wire fraud, illegally distributing controlled substances and making false statements to investigators. She was sentenced in 2023 to six years and three months in federal prison and was moved to a halfway house in August.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Lawsuit over doctors supervising nurse practitioners adds new twist to long NC debate
description: A nurse practitioner is suing over state rules that require oversight from a doctor for her to run her practice.   Jamie Gallagher says in a lawsuit filed in Wake County Superior Court that the requirement for her to have a contract with a doctor in order to practice violates her rights and is an unnecessary […]
text:
The nurse practitioner who founded the menopause center Peri & Pause is suing to be able to operate without contracting with a supervising doctor. (Courtesy photo)A nurse practitioner is suing over state rules that require oversight from a doctor for her to run her practice.  
Jamie Gallagher says in a lawsuit filed in Wake County Superior Court that the requirement for her to have a contract with a doctor in order to practice violates her rights and is an unnecessary expense. 
Gallagher founded Peri & Pause, a menopause and perimenopause care clinic with offices in Wake County. The lawsuit says she is required by state law to have a supervision contract with a doctor — which, in her case, costs $16,500 a year — who does not oversee her day-to-day work. 
Lawyers with the Pacific Legal Foundation are representing her in the lawsuit that names N.C. Medical Board President Dr. Anuradha Rao-Patel and Racquel Ingram, chair of the N.C. Board of Nursing, as defendants in their official capacities. Jean Fisher Brinkley, communications director for the N.C. Medical Board, declined to comment on pending litigation. N.C. Board of Nursing representatives did not return calls Wednesday. 
The lawsuit says that the state medical board and nursing board are in charge of enforcing rules that violate Gallagher’s rights. 
Experienced nurses with advanced degrees have pushed for years to have the legislature change that law so they can work independently without doctors’ supervision. Some advanced practice nurses, which include nurse practitioners, have said they have to pay for supervision that amounts to little more than paperwork and a few conversations a year.  
Bills ending the supervision requirement have had bipartisan support in recent years, but doctors’ groups oppose dropping it, and the bills have not become law. 
Hampered by opposition from doctors’ groups, nurse practitioners want to change state law to give them more freedom to treat patients

The contracts, known as collaborative practice agreements, do not require face-to-face meetings, chart reviews, or direct supervision, the lawsuit says. 
“North Carolina thus gives a private physician continuing control over whether Dr. Gallagher may practice a profession the State itself has determined she is qualified to practice. The mandatory collaborative practice scheme violates Dr. Gallagher’s fundamental rights: the fruits of her labor, due process, and equal protection guaranteed by the North Carolina Constitution,” the lawsuit says. 
In an interview, Gallagher said she loves the doctor with whom she has a collaborative agreement. They meet twice a year over lunch to talk and sign paperwork. But requiring these contracts is bad for the state because it limits expansion of healthcare to underserved areas, she said. 
“Limiting access that nurse practitioners can provide is harming health in North Carolina,” she said. And the contract requirement puts unnecessary restrictions on how she can use her license and experience, Gallagher said.  
Gallagher started Peri & Pause in May 2024 with virtual patient visits. She now has two brick-and-mortar locations in Wake County and has a goal of opening a third.
But the doctor with whom she contracts said he cannot take responsibility for more of her nurse practitioners, the lawsuit says. So expansion would require her to find another doctor willing to sign another contract, which means an additional expense.
If nurse practitioners lose their supervising physicians, their practices are at risk, the lawsuit says. 
Arbitrary laws are delegating to private citizens — doctors — something that is a state responsibility, Gallagher said. 
“They get to give nurse practitioners the ability to work or not,” she said.

title: Rep. Jeff Crank leads resolution against Democratic Socialists of America
description: One day after U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank led a successful resolution in the U.S. House of Representatives to condemn socialism, local leaders of the Democratic Socialists of America called the move a “waste of time” as the political ideology gains momentum in American politics. The non-binding resolution, which passed the House on a 220-192 vote […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank sponsored a resolution that condemns socialism "in all its forms." (Courtesy of Jeff Crank campaign)One day after U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank led a successful resolution in the U.S. House of Representatives to condemn socialism, local leaders of the Democratic Socialists of America called the move a “waste of time” as the political ideology gains momentum in American politics.
The non-binding resolution, which passed the House on a 220-192 vote Tuesday, “condemns and denounces socialism in all its forms, including the Democratic Socialists of America, and opposes the implementation of socialist policies in the United States.” It contends that socialist ideology historically leads to communist regimes.
It is Crank’s first successful piece of legislation after nearly two years in office. The Republican is running for reelection in the Colorado Springs-based 5th Congressional District.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Colorado’s four Republican representatives voted for the resolution, while its four congressional Democrats voted against it. The Democrats who voted for the resolution are all from competitive districts in other states.
How democratic socialist Melat Kiros stunned Colorado politics with congressional primary win

“Instead of fighting for working families, Rep. Crank continues to live up to his name and waste time on the House floor complaining about DSA and calling to strip voting rights from minorities,” Denver DSA co-chairs Susie Ramsey and Katie Blake said in a statement about the resolution. “With politicians like him bleeding Americans dry while cheering on endless war and imperialism, it’s no wonder that socialism is more popular than ever. It’s the only tool we have to defeat fascism at home and its impacts globally.”
In another statement, Colorado Springs DSA co-chair Justine Cortez also criticized the vote.
“(Crank) has wasted his time on a symbolic resolution condemning the Democratic Socialists of America because he knows that we, as a worker led and worker funded organization, actually fight for the people of El Paso County in a way he only half-heartedly pretends to,” she said.
The congressional resolution comes as DSA-backed candidates across the country find electoral success. That includes New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, New York congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and Melat Kiros, who defeated longtime incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette in the Democratic primary for Colorado’s 1st Congressional District. DSA announced on social media in July that its membership doubled over the last year with over 120,000 total members.
“The condemnation is yet another attempt from conservatives, and neoliberals alike, to preserve their status quo in the face of rising popularity for socialism, because both parties continue to serve the interest of capital and imperialism at the expense of the working class” Andrew Thompson, a Denver DSA member on the organization’s National Political Committee, told Newsline.



Quotation







(Crank) has wasted his time on a symbolic resolution condemning the Democratic Socialists of America because he knows that we, as a worker led and worker funded organization, actually fight for the people of El Paso County in a way he only half-heartedly pretends to.


– Justine Cortez, Colorado Springs DSA co-chair


DSA is a political and activist organization, not a political party, that supports single-payer healthcare reform, labor union protections, decreases in police and prison funding and strong environmental regulations under the Green New Deal framework. President Donald Trump has repeatedly denounced DSA and its endorsed candidates as extremists and communists, and Republicans have linked mainstream Democrats with DSA during the midterm election cycle.
“It is imperative as Members of Congress that we recommit ourselves to the Constitution and stand firm against this insidious push for socialism,” Crank said in a statement. “The vast majority of Democrats voted against my resolution to condemn socialism in all its forms. Ten to 15 years ago, a resolution like this would’ve passed the House unanimously. The DSA is a threat to the American values that make our nation great.”
Kiros said in a statement the resolution ignores the issues Americans worry about.
“Jeff Crank has time to write a resolution condemning universal access to healthcare and fighting for working people, but not one word about the gas and grocery prices crushing his constituents right now,” she said. “He rubber-stamped Trump’s war with Iran, and now the people he represents are paying for it every time they fill up their tank or buy groceries.”
The resolution also included a call to enact the SAVE America Act, which would require proof of citizenship and in-person photo identification in order to vote, a bill that Democrats opposed, fearing it will disenfranchise many otherwise eligible voters. That bill has passed in the House but is languishing in the Senate. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York cited the bill’s inclusion in Crank’s resolution as his reason for voting against it.
The resolution is mainly symbolic and will likely serve as a messaging vote for Republicans in the midterms.

name: VTDigger
title: Holland Food Shelf announces closure after months of financial uncertainty
description:
The service had lately been providing sustenance to roughly 700 people per month in the northern border community, most of whom were regulars, according to leadership.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Holland Food Shelf announces closure after months of financial uncertainty.
text:
Tomatoes are displayed at the Holland Food Shelf as a visitor looks at vegetables. Photo courtesy of Don Stevens/Abenaki Helping Abenaki

Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
The Holland Food Shelf announced Wednesday that the organization would close, following months of financial uncertainty.
According to Don Stevens, executive director of Abenaki Helping Abenaki, the food shelf’s nonprofit operator, the service has become financially unfeasible. The food pantry has served residents of Holland, Derby and the surrounding community on Vermont’s border with Canada in Orleans County since 2021.
“It’s not an easy decision,” Stevens said in an interview Wednesday. The service had lately been providing sustenance to roughly 700 people per month, he said, most of whom were regulars.
The pantry announced in August 2025 that it would close imminently, due in part to the loss of grant funds from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. But in the weeks that followed, an anonymous donor stepped in to keep the organization afloat through the winter, offering up to roughly $44,000 in contributions.
A year later, funds have run down once again, Stevens said. Grant funding and support from a variety of local and federal sources has declined or is no longer available, he said, and the costs of renting and running the facility became too high. 
Food distribution from the building the pantry has been renting from the town stopped July 31, with staff “looking into options moving forward,” a statement from Stevens said earlier this summer. But after a potential alternative space nearby fell through due to uncertainty around infrastructure and utility costs, among other overhead expenses, he said, the closure became indefinite.
Michele Capron, who lives roughly 10 minutes from the pantry, said she began receiving food “off and on” from the organization after losing her job during the Covid-19 pandemic.
“I needed some extra help,” she said.
The community stands to lose an important service, Capron said, particularly given how many of those in need are elderly.
Heather Boren, a resident of nearby Coventry who works for the North Country Supervisory Union, agreed, saying she had seen the food shelf provide fresh food to the area for years.
“There’s a lot of people in the community that need that, you know, to sustain them,” she said.
The extra 15 miles to reach the nearest food pantries in Newport or Island Pond might be a real barrier for some residents in the area, she and Capron added.
Carrie Stahler, the Vermont Foodbank’s government and public affairs officer, echoed residents’ concerns. Areas like Orleans County tend to have high need for food access but scant resources to put toward the problem, she said. Census data indicates that Orleans County’s poverty rate is roughly 12%, about a third higher than the 9% rate statewide. 
Without commenting on the Holland Food Shelf’s particular situation, Stahler said the state’s food assistance network has undergone “some belt-tightening” as Covid-era funds ran out. Food pantries like Holland’s, she said, often “struggle to be self-sustaining because they don’t have a population who can continue to support them with donations.” 
The Holland Food Shelf’s challenges, though disappointing, are far from unique, Stahler said.
Stevens said the ripple effects of the pantry’s closure will extend beyond direct recipients. The organization’s two part-time staff have been laid off, he said, and local farmers from whom he sourced meat and other products will lose a customer.
Abenaki Helping Abenaki was also recently given a space in Cabot, he added, at the former Covenant Hills Christian Camp. Food distribution and other services will continue there for “our citizens,” he said, referring in part to the state-recognized Nulhegan band of the Coosuk Abenaki Nation, of which Stevens is chief. 
In the future, Stevens hopes the food assistance service could eventually serve the general public from the location in Cabot. He’d consider any option for making such a pantry viable again, Stevens said.
Meanwhile, in Holland, residents say the food shelf will be sorely missed.
“We have to be creative. We have to figure out new ways to help people,” said Boren. “If someone’s suffering, we have an obligation as a human being to help them.”

title: More states are putting panic alarms in schools
description: Three states this year have enacted laws that require or allow schools to use mobile, wearable, wireless or silent panic alarms to quickly summon emergency responders. The new laws in Illinois, Virginia and West Virginia bring the number of states with such laws to 13, with 10 of them acting since 2023. Another dozen states […]
text:
Three states this year have enacted laws that require or allow schools to use panic alarms to quickly summon emergency responders. Ten other states have such laws and a dozen more are considering them. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)Three states this year have enacted laws that require or allow schools to use mobile, wearable, wireless or silent panic alarms to quickly summon emergency responders.
The new laws in Illinois, Virginia and West Virginia bring the number of states with such laws to 13, with 10 of them acting since 2023. Another dozen states have legislation pending.
Known as Alyssa’s Law, the measures are named for 14-year-old Alyssa Alhadeff, one of 17 people killed during the 2018 shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida. Make Our Schools Safe, a nonprofit founded by Alhadeff’s mother, has advocated for the legislation.
Although all the laws are grouped under the Alyssa’s Law name, they involve different technologies. While some of the laws require schools to use a particular device, others just allow schools to consider implementing some sort of emergency alert system.
Texas, for example, requires silent panic alert technology in classrooms, while Utah mandates that certain members of the school staff wear mobile alert devices. Virginia allows school boards to equip employees with wearable silent panic alarms, but doesn’t require it. The laws also differ in how the devices connect with police or other emergency responders. Funding mechanisms also differ from state to state.
The cost of such systems varies. But several years ago, the school board in Gwinnett County, Georgia, the largest in the state, approved $7 million to purchase the CrisisAlert system from CENTEGIX, an Atlanta-based technology company that provides emergency response systems to schools and hospitals. The CrisisAlert system provides school staff members with a wearable button that can be used to call for help.
A report released earlier this year by CENTEGIX found that 88% of the more than 346,000 alerts generated by its wearable panic-button systems during the 2025-2026 school year involved everyday issues such as fights and students leaving campus without permission.
Ten percent of the alerts were medical emergencies and 2% were for suspicious behavior or a campuswide emergency.
“Wearable incident response badges help reduce delays by enabling staff to discreetly initiate alerts from anywhere on campus,” the report states. “Their value comes not only from speed, but from their ability to deliver clear, reliable communication.”
But Kenneth Trump, president of National School Safety and Security Services, a consulting firm, said the fact that relatively few of the alerts were for emergencies suggests that schools should not be mandated to use panic buttons or similar technologies.
Stateline reporter Robbie Sequeira can be reached at rsequeira@stateline.org.

title: Wyoming lawmakers change course on property tax reform amid signs of waning support
description:
Legislative panel votes down a bill that it supported a year ago to repeal residential property taxes. 
The post Wyoming lawmakers change course on property tax reform amid signs of waning support appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Two months before Wyoming voters will decide whether to further reduce the state’s residential property taxes, the Legislature’s Joint Revenue Committee rejected a plan this week to repeal the tax altogether, marking a shift in a years-long effort to revamp the state’s tax system. 
The legislation would have given voters the opportunity to amend the Wyoming Constitution to eliminate property taxes altogether, while a companion bill would have raised sales taxes to backfill the resulting revenue loss. The committee backed the same measure last year, but the legislation died after the House ran out of time to consider it. 
The panel’s decision Tuesday to rebuff additional cuts came amid the release of new data showing that the majority of Wyoming homeowners did not take advantage of a major tax cut that was recently implemented by lawmakers.
Residential property taxes have been a focal point for lawmakers for the last four years amid a jump in home values and subsequent rise in property tax bills. Since 2022, the Legislature has expanded the state’s tax refund program, capped annual increases and amended the constitution — with the support of voters — to put residential property into a separate tax class. Lawmakers also added several exemptions to statute statute, creating a complicated web in the process. 
While homeowners once packed committee meetings demanding lawmakers take action and ease residential property taxes, that’s since changed. Last year, about two dozen Natrona County homeowners urged the Revenue Committee to skip further cuts, citing impacts to public services. In Wyoming, property taxes do not fund state government but instead support local services like education, law enforcement, libraries, water and sewer. Following the tax cuts, municipalities around Wyoming reported making cuts to various services.
At the committee’s meeting Tuesday in Casper, no homeowners testified one way or the other, prompting Rep. Liz Storer, D-Jackson, to ask the committee, “What is the purpose of these bills?”
Rep. Liz Storer, D-Jackson, during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature’s budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
“And why would we take the time to continue to move them forward, also given that I do not think they will be met with success in the next Legislature?” Storer said. “So help me understand your reasoning.”
The incoming Legislature will indeed look very different from the one represented on the committee after voters largely rejected candidates aligned with the Wyoming Freedom Caucus, which led much of the charge to cut property taxes. That included Republican Sen. Bob Ide, who first brought the idea to eliminate property taxes to the committee in 2025. Ide lost his reelection bid to Casper’s Senate District 29. 
“I think it’s a fair question from Representative Storer,” he said at Tuesday’s meeting, before pointing to property tax reform in Florida and Tennessee. 
“The motivation here is property ownership is not really true right now,” Ide said. “You pay your house off and you still rent from the government.”
“Biblically,” Ide added, “I think you were always supposed to — you never taxed the land. They had a jubilee — tax the fruits of the land.” 
Sen. Cale Case, a long-time Lander Republican who won his primary election, pushed back. 
“I don’t really buy the argument that you don’t really own your house because the government taxes your property,” he said. “We have had property taxes the entire history of America.”
Property taxes are fundamental to communities, Case added. 
“That’s why they fund local services,” he said. “And it’s very important to have people that live in those communities fund those communities.” 
Sen. Bob Ide, R-Casper, during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile)
The committee voted 7-6 with one excused not to sponsor the bill. Five of the six “aye” votes were lawmakers who lost their reelection bids, including: Ide and Reps. Gary Brown, R-Cheyenne; Jayme Lien, R-Casper; Robert Wharff, R-Evanston; and Tony Locke, R-Casper. All five lawmakers are either members or allies of the Freedom Caucus.
Meanwhile, the committee also rejected legislation that would largely prohibit mill levies from being assessed on residential property, and voted to table three other property-tax related bills until lawmakers meet in November. 
One of the tabled bills relates to the citizen-initiated ballot measure that voters will settle in the general election. On Nov. 3, voters will have the final say over whether to create a 50% residential property tax exemption for qualified homeowners. 
A 25% exemption is already on the books after lawmakers passed such legislation in 2025. The exemption was applied automatically in its first year, but homeowners had to apply for the reduction in 2026. Only about 44% of eligible homeowners applied, the Department of Revenue told the committee Monday. 
The single residential property tax bill the committee voted to sponsor this week would advance a decision by voters from two years ago. 
In 2024, voters approved a constitutional amendment to segregate residential real estate from other forms of property for taxation purposes. Previously, the Wyoming Constitution grouped residential with commercial and agricultural property, which made it difficult for lawmakers to respond to surging home values with changes that only addressed how homes are taxed. 
The success of the amendment, however, cleared the constraint for lawmakers, though they haven’t taken advantage of it yet. That could soon change after the committee voted to sponsor legislation that would separate residential property in state law and lower its assessment rate from 9.5% to 8.3%. 
The committee’s next meeting will be Nov. 19 and 20 in Cheyenne.
